headline: Dow bullish on PE pricing into 2027 - Resource Recycling
summary_text: Polyethylene heavyweight Dow expects “momentum” to extend through the end of the year and into 2027, helping to support higher PE pricing. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call Oct. 22, executives cited elevated feedstock costs, declining inventories and constrained production resulting from the US war in Iran as support for a cumulative 12 cents in nominated price increases for October and November PE contracts. September contracts rose by 5 cents/lb, CEO Karen Carter said. Although overall Q3 sales volumes fell by 1% on the year, Carter pointed to war-related production disruptions in the Middle East. Excluding those constraints, quarterly sales volumes in Packaging and Specialty Plastics grew by 2% on the year, she said, “and we’re getting more growth in the fourth quarter as well.” Carter cited September data from the American Chemistry Council (ACC) as evidence of tightening supply, with inventory down by 5 days of supply and 400 million pounds. This represents the largest draw on PE stocks in more than a year, she said. PE spot prices also rose ahead of the earnings call – increasing by 6 cents/lb on the week. “So we should go into 2027 with that momentum, and we expect from an oil-to-gas ratio that it will remain constructive,” she said. “And of course, we’re going to continue to double down on our advantaged feedstock capacity here in North America.” ... Over the past decade, North American ethylene and polyethylene production capacity has grown significantly, as Dow, ExxonMobil, Shell and others built massive new plants to take advantage of cheap, plentiful feedstock unlocked during the shale gas boom. Natural gas liquids (NGLs) – primarily ethane – can be fed into steam crackers to produce ethylene more efficiently and cheaper than naphtha sourced from crude oil. US ethane prices are “a bit on the rise as well,” Carter said, outpacing benchmark natural gas price movements. She added that every 3 cents/gal of higher pricing for ethane requires about 1 cent/lb of PE to cover that cost, and Dow’s Q4 guidance assumes ethane prices in the mid-high 20s cents/gal, “marginally lower than where we sit today.” Carter attributed the ethane price increases to growing exports, as steam crackers in other global regions are favoring ethane in their feedstock mix, amid elevated crude oil prices. In addition, Golden Triangle – a joint venture between Chevron Phillips Chemical and QatarEnergy –.plans to start production at its new Texas ethylene/PE complex in early 2027, increasing demand for ethane. ... Carter estimated that global ethylene operating rates are in the low 80s%, though Dow believes plant utilization could return to mid-cycle level by the end of the decade, around the time the company’s net-zero cracker in Alberta is expected to start up. Original industry estimates put necessary capacity rationalization at 10% globally to return to those rates, she said, and about half of the required amount has already been announced, with an additional 8% being speculated. “You’re seeing the rationalizations and of course we know that there’s capacity that’s coming online,” Carter said, but PE demand continues to grow faster than GDP. Dow has repeatedly referred to this measure as justification for continued long-term investment in vast new ethylene/PE capacity despite a multi-year slump in demand and global overcapacity. ... Dow also provided an update on its steam crackers in the Middle East and Asia. - Equate JV in Kuwait: one cracker running at full rate, and several derivative units idled due to storage limitations - JV in Thailand: one cracker restarted, second one has planned maintenance - Sadara JV with Saudi Aramco, partially restarted with a cracker and PE trains online, but liquids units remain down due to persistent logistics constraints

headline: Dow, Orbis talk EPR, demand at Pack Expo - Resource Recycling
summary_text: As plastic recyclers struggle to navigate a persistent downcycle, war-related tailwinds are helping reframe the narrative surrounding PCR adoption, stakeholders said during Pack Expo this week in Chicago. Particularly for polyolefins, abundant cheap virgin resin has presented a major roadblock for recyclers, whose PCR resin is typically priced at a premium to virgin material. Amid uncertainty surrounding extended producer responsibility (EPR) laws for packaging and PCR content mandates, as well as a patchwork of state regulations and shifting goalposts for brand commitments, recyclers have struggled to compete. Rapid price spikes for virgin PE and PP during the onset of the US war in Iran gave recycled commodity values a lift in early summer. But the longer-term takeaway is that end users are seeing the value of having reliable domestic feedstock at the ready, executives from Dow and Orbis said during interviews at the show. Michigan-headquartered Dow is the world’s largest producer of polyethylene. Wisconsin-headquartered Orbis produces reusable packaging products, such as pallets, racks and containers, made of HDPE and PP. Holly Kennedy, senior business sustainability manager at Dow, said brands that were already working on qualifying PCR realized the added value, beyond compliance with laws set to take effect starting in 2027. Some customers have said the supply constraints and related pricing volatility have changed how they think about procurement, she added. And while sustainability is important for procurement teams, their top priority is supply security, she said. “So they’re like, ‘Wait, this is another lever that I can pull to make sure that we have material available and we have product on the shelf for our customers.'” ... Orbis’ Lynn Hediger, vice president of manufacturing and product engineering, said geopolitical developments were encouraging interest in localizing supply and production. Record-high diesel fuel prices have made transportation prohibitively expensive, while tariffs as high as 50% have sent some prices soaring, particularly for metal products. “It’s extremely difficult to bring plastic-based products or steel-based fabricated products like racks into the United States” because of the tariffs, he said. So customers are looking inward for economic reasons, “but I think they’re also realizing the length of the supply chain is a little bit easier if it’s not spread out all over the world.” ... While the EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) seems a world away, companies operating in Europe are forcing what Hediger called a “global acceptance” of the sweeping program. Orbis is seeing demand for consistent packaging systems between North American and European operations, particularly with CPG, beverage and other consumer-facing companies. “They want to be able to tell that story globally, and so they’re just forcing those decisions here,” Hediger said. In the US, California and six other states are implementing packaging EPR laws, and several states, including California, New Jersey and Washington, have PCR content mandates. In some ways, Hediger said, states are “paying attention to the regulations that are coming out in Europe and adopting a lot of the same features – maybe not called exactly the same, but the spirit of it is very similar. So you do see that that influence is coming.” And similar to the PPWR effect, when an economy as large as California or New Jersey adopts legislation, it can drive overall demand in the interest of simplicity and efficiency, he said. ... For Dow, the three most important aspects of effective EPR are providing financing for managing complex waste streams like packaging, mandating recycled content and addressing non-mechanical recycling processes, said Adwoa Coleman, senior sustainability manager of ecosystems and EPR for Dow North America. While EPR policy focuses primarily on increasing collection and processing of used packaging, providing feedstock supply, “we need the other side of the equation to work as well,” Coleman said. “So demand that would be ensured by mandates that actually require producers to use PCR is a big deal,” as with the New Jersey PCR requirement. Dow would “broadly like to see more PCR mandates, more geographies, more application spaces, and just more use where practical, of course, from a technical perspective,” she said. Dow also believes that to hit the recycling rates set by EPR laws, policy should be technology-agnostic. “It’s very clear that mechanical recycling alone can’t get us to those numbers, and that we need complementary technologies,” Coleman said, such as chemical recycling. The company also wants mass balance accounting methods to accommodate non-mechanical recycling. Dow bought US mechanical plastic film recycler Circulus in 2024 and previously announced investments and offtake agreements in chemical recycling in Europe and North America. But in August 2025 the company canceled a planned chemical recycling project in Böhlen, Germany.

headline: ResinSmart Says Buyers Must Look Beyond October Resin Price Increases
summary_text: September polyethylene increase takes hold despite soft demand and healthy supply. FORT WORTH, Texas, Oct. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire-PRWeb/ -- Resin buyers face another round of pricing pressure in October after a 5-cent-per-pound September polyethylene (PE) increase took hold despite soft domestic demand and growing inventories. "September showed that an increase can go through even when supply and demand fundamentals don't necessarily support it," said Michael Workman, executive director of commercial at ResinSmart. "That doesn't mean buyers should automatically accept the next one. They need to understand what's changed in the market and whether the increase is supported by actual costs or tighter supply." "Buyers should be asking suppliers to show how much of an increase is tied to real cost changes, and challenging anything beyond that." — Michael Workman, Executive Director of Commercial, ResinSmart Dow and NOVA have since announced additional 7-cent-per-pound increases for October, even as PE availability remains healthy and spot ethylene holds steady at 23 cents per pound. With little change in market fundamentals since September, buyers have reason to challenge the full increase. ResinSmart says October pricing conditions are mixed. Some resin categories face legitimate feedstock pressure, while others still offer room to negotiate. Polypropylene (PP) remains favorable for buyers, with September contracts settling 2 cents per pound lower and no October increases proposed. However, an extended outage at LyondellBasell's Lake Charles facility and additional downtime expected in November could affect supply later in the quarter. Meanwhile, higher benzene contract prices give producers a stronger cost argument for polystyrene (PS) and nylon increases. The October benzene contract settled at $5.27 per gallon, up 70 cents from September, though spot benzene has eased from its highs. ResinSmart is tracking potential PS increases of 9 to 10 cents per pound and proposed nylon increases of 14 to 15 cents per pound. ... The developments reinforce the importance of evaluating each resin independently. September's PE increase shows that an increase can succeed without significant supply constraints, but buyers still have room to negotiate based on feedstock costs, material availability and demand. "The key is knowing where the pressure is real and where buyers still have leverage," Workman said. "Procurement teams that understand the market fundamentals behind each increase will be in a stronger position when negotiating."

headline: Material Market Update - October 20, 2026 | Matium
summary_text: Good morning folks, The market has picked up. End-users in the packaging sector are reporting record months, and spot prices for PP, PE, and PET are all higher than they were a month ago. Playing back the tape, Q2 was overbought, Q3 was oversold, and Q4 is rebounding. That's good for everyone selling right now, but I'd be careful about reading too much into it. The oversupply that pushed prices down in Q3 is still there, and the broader economy outside of AI is slowing. If you're a trader, this is not the time to take on big inventory at elevated prices. PE Spot PE is trading in the 40s and 50s, up from the 30s. Demand is relatively stronger, but the supply side hasn't changed. PE is still the most oversupplied resin we have, construction and Ag are still weak, and Golden Triangle is adding capacity. Regrind and repro are in the 30s, so the spreads off resin have improved. In a balanced market, this would signal regrind and repro pricing to go up. Since PE is oversupplied, it is more likely resin prices drop toward secondary options. ... Behind the veil of AI, the market has been tightening for a tough road ahead. The Fed is raising rates, inflation is 3.4% and consumer sentiment is at a four month low. Manufacturing is still growing with PMI at 54.5, but it's slowing. Mortgage ... ### 1. US Lawmakers Urge Protection of Domestic RPET - US lawmakers are urging the US Trade Representative to address the impact of foreign government-supported overcapacity—particularly from Asian countries—on domestic recycled PET (RPET) markets, citing resulting low prices and recent US plant closures. - The group recommends targeted, data-driven trade actions against PET imports, improved traceability for recycled content, and enhanced enforcement to prevent market-distorting practices and protect US recycling operations. - Recent data highlights the severity of domestic challenges: more than a quarter of US PET recycling capacity was lost in the past year, and feedstock prices hit an all-time low, increasing the urgency for federal intervention. - Industry stakeholders, including the Association of Plastic Recyclers, back these efforts, emphasizing the need for better trade data differentiation between virgin and recycled PET to inform policymaking and enforcement. ... ### 2. Canada's Tariffs on US Plastics Take Effect Source: Plastic Today - Canada enacted retaliatory tariffs targeting US plastics products after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $27.6 billion in Canadian imports, escalating cross-border trade tensions. - The US plastics trade balance with Canada has fluctuated, but tariffs on molds particularly disadvantage US manufacturers, potentially reducing their market share in Canada. - Estimating the exact value of US plastics exports exposed to Canadian tariffs is complex, but approximately $945.98 million, or 12.1% of total US plastics exports to Canada in 2025, now faces double-digit tariffs. - The disruption threatens highly integrated North American supply chains, with industry experts stressing the importance of maintaining stable trade frameworks under USMCA to preserve manufacturing competitiveness. ... ### 3. ADS Flexes New Recycling Capacity against Resin Spikes - Advanced Drainage Systems (ADS) faced a drop in recycled resin usage to 38% of total purchases in fiscal 2026, its lowest in five years, driven by more favorable virgin resin market conditions and war-driven price spikes in virgin polyolefins. - The company responded with agile supply chain tactics, ramping up recycled material procurement and leveraging a $30 million Georgia recycling plant expansion to offset rising virgin resin costs, aiming for improved recycled material consumption in 2027. - ADS, which is responsible for roughly 30% of US color HDPE bale purchases, influenced short-term market pricing as it accelerated buying and capacity expansion; recycled color HDPE prices saw significant turbulence, nearly doubling in May 2026 before dropping by 42% in August. - Despite growth in overall sales, revenue from remanufactured (recycled plastic) products has declined due to increased sales of products that cannot, by regulation, incorporate recycled content, highlighting regulatory impacts on recycled material utilization. ... ### 4. Recycled Plastics Markets Navigate Pricing Pressures, Policy Delays - Recycled plastics markets are dealing with fragmented feedstock and resin pricing, squeezed converter margins, and significant uncertainty driven by shifts in trade policy, freight costs, and reliance on imports, particularly for rPET. - US rPET remains vulnerable to import logistics, freight, and tariffs, with regional pricing disparities influenced by programs like California's PMDP, while stable pellet pricing and softer demand continue to pressure converter margins across recycled resins. - Recycled HDPE bale pricing stabilized in September after a period of sharp declines, while rPP markets confronted diminishing appetite for lower-grade materials due to abundant, competitively priced virgin resins. - Recent policy delays, such as New Jersey's extension of food packaging exemptions, may postpone incremental demand for food-grade post-consumer recycled materials and raise industry concerns about similar regulatory stalling in other states. ... ### 1. BASF Confirms Talks to Acquire Evonik Industries - BASF and RAG-Stiftung are in exploratory talks about a potential takeover of Evonik Industries, a move that could combine their operations into an $84 billion European chemicals giant. - The proposed merger aims to achieve greater scale, streamline operations, and shift business focus toward higher-margin markets, continuing BASF's recent portfolio adjustments, such as divesting its automotive coatings unit. - Evonik is undergoing a major restructuring program—cutting 3,200 jobs and reorganizing business units—to strengthen its growth and competitiveness, especially in response to challenging market conditions. - Both companies are implementing aggressive cost-cutting measures to weather structural and economic crises in the chemicals sector, aiming to bolster their positions in lucrative and future-oriented markets. ... ### 4. MacroCycle, Meta Partner to Scale rPET Manufacturing - MacroCycle Technologies has partnered with Meta to supply environmental attribute certifications (EACs) linked to recycled PET (rPET) produced at MacroCycle's upcoming commercial plant in the Southeastern U.S. - The deal supports MacroCycle's scale-up of its novel solvent-based SolvoGenesis recycling technology, which converts mixed and contaminated PET waste into virgin-quality rPET at a lower energy cost compared to traditional methods. - Meta's multiyear EAC purchase offers long-term demand, providing the financial backing MacroCycle needs to construct the plant, expected to produce 5,000 tons of rPET annually, addressing domestic shortfalls amid rising imports and shrinking U.S. rPET capacity. - This agreement aims to reduce supply chain emissions for major corporations like Meta while stimulating adoption of lower-carbon plastics, potentially speeding the growth of sustainable material markets in the U.S. ... ### 3. FDA Releases New Guidance on Drug, Biologic Container Closure Systems - The FDA's updated draft guidance for container closure systems (CCSs) in drug and biologic packaging sets stricter requirements for extractables and leachables testing, directly impacting plastics suppliers and pharmaceutical packaging manufacturers. - Plastics manufacturers must now provide more thorough chemical characterization data and implement rigorous controls over additives, stabilizers, and processing aids, working closely with pharmaceutical companies during material selection and qualification. - The guidance adopts a risk-based quality management approach and increases expectations for manufacturing, distribution conditions, and container closure integrity testing, emphasizing the entire packaging system's lifecycle and potential vulnerabilities during shipping or storage. ... ### 1. New 3D Printing Technologies Accelerate Injection Molding Operations - Advanced metal additive manufacturing techniques, including both paste and powder-based 3D printing, are enabling plastics injection molders to incorporate conformal cooling channels that significantly reduce cycle times—up to 70% in some cases. - Technologies from companies like Mantle and 3D Systems allow for the creation of complex cooling channels and high-precision inserts that deliver more consistent cooling, enhanced part quality, and reduced scrap rates across multiple manufacturing sectors. - Real-world applications have demonstrated substantial operational benefits: companies report faster design and production cycles, lower temperatures across molds, reduced production work hours, and improved profit margins from these innovations.

headline: Golden Triangle Polymers Cracker Set to Start Up | Argus Media
summary_text: At a glance - The first new US Gulf Coast ethane cracker in more than four years is preparing for startup, marking a major milestone for the North American petrochemical industry. - Despite pandemic disruptions, inflation, trade uncertainty, and global oversupply concerns, the $8.5 billion Golden Triangle Polymers project pushed ahead when others paused. - Backed by Chevron Phillips Chemical and QatarEnergy, the world-scale facility will add 2.08 million tonnes/year of ethylene capacity and 2 million tonnes/year of polyethylene production. - The project reflects continued confidence in the long-term competitiveness of US ethane-based production and export markets. - As global petrochemical markets adapt to shifting trade flows and geopolitical volatility, Golden Triangle's startup could help shape the industry's next chapter. ... The US Gulf coast is set to see its first ethane cracker startup in over four years. Back in the late 2010s, Gulf coast cracker startups seemed almost like an everyday occurrence. But since 2020, a pandemic, a Chinese buildout that surpassed the US in capacity, trade wars and even hot wars have all added enough to the mix of uncertainty to bring the US’s buildout to a halt. So why, at the end of this year, will the US be adding a cracker and new polyethylene for export? The US Gulf coast’s first cracker startup in four years is itself a story of navigating all the market volatility that has characterized the 2020s and taking a risk, despite it all. ... But literally the next day, Chevron Phillips Chemical (CP Chem) took a final investment decision on a new 2.08mn t/yr cracker in Orange, Texas, with two derivative 1mn t/yr high density polyethylene units set to export pellets to the world. The announcement of the Golden Triangle Polymers came in the form of a joint venture with QatarEnergy, much like ExxonMobil’s JV cracker with Sabic. It would be another pairing of and American major with a Middle Eastern state oil company for a world scale cracker with integrated derivative units. Four years later, that cracker is now on the verge of starting up. On September 22, the Golden Triangle Polymers announced it was undertaking activities to prepare the $8.5bn facility for completion. By the last week of September, thermal cameras were showing heat for the cracker, with test runs already starting, market participants told Argus. From all indications, the cracker is set to start up by late December or early January, with market sources close to the unit indicating the unit could even be slightly ahead of its current schedule. ... Back in 2022, much like now in 2026, US ethane’s structural cost advantage in the production of ethylene and polyethylene became even more pronounced, given the run-up in global crude oil and naphtha prices in the wake of a major war involving an oil-exporting nation that began in late February. In this rising crude oil environment, US global ethane advantages stood firm, even as ethane’s cash costs domestically themselves had surged in the first half of 2022 on rising natural gas, eroding US ethane-HDPE margins at the time of Golden Triangle’s FID. But crackers and polyethylene plants have 3–5-year schedules from FID to startup and are themselves multidecade investments. Startups are ideally timed with the ending of the margins trough, even though no one can time this perfectly. ... One risk in the early 2020s was surging inflation and interest rates. Chemical companies were less likely to build new crackers in the US given the increase in the cost of materials, capital, and labor. But CP Chem partnered with QatarEnergy, who comprises 49pc of the Golden Triangle Polymers JV. A state-owned Middle Eastern enterprise provided the deep pockets to see the project to completion, in case of any unexpected cost overruns or delays. An even greater risk was China’s massive buildout of crackers and polyethylene units in the 2020s. This began to take its toll on global polyethylene margins. In Europe and Asia ex-China, shutdowns and rationalization have increased. While it may seem like a different era, just at the start of 2026, LyondellBasell was lamenting the collapse of even its otherwise cost-advantaged North American integrated-PE margins, which averaged $580/t in 2025, $250/t below the historical average of $830/t. Into this environment, the Golden Triangle Project seemed to be entering at the start of the year. ... But as the uncertain 2020s rolled on, the year 2026 threw one curve ball that the US petrochemical industry was able to hit out of the park. The US-Iran war and its subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz that cut off roughly 20pc of the world’s polyethylene, sent integrated US margins surging in the second quarter. CP Chem likely would have wished to have started up its crackers and PE units in March. Instead, a six-month delay pushed back timing from its mid-2026 date to early 2027. This surge in margins has since fallen back since peaking in mid-April, but globally it advantages the US, not only in terms of its feedstock, but also with regards to its unimpeded exports, meeting a tightened global market. No where is this clearer than looking at CP Chem and Qatar Energy’s sister project in Ras Laffan, in Qatar. Iran launched a missile at Ras Laffan Industrial City in March, and that site’s success remains largely dependent on events in the Mideast Gulf and strait of Hormuz. The global petrochemical industry has yet to emerge from its trough and may just be in a new normal and not fully realize it. And for the Golden Triangle Polymers, underlying capital recovery questions will linger for some time, but the project will be starting up in a more advantaged global environment than it did a year ago.

headline: US/Canada September PE contracts settle up 5¢/lb | World Ports Organization
summary_text: Houston, 9 October (Argus) — September contracts in the US/Canada polyethylene (PE) market largely settled higher by 5¢/lb during the week, as rising export prices helped to support higher domestic prices. There were some reports that certain producers had invoiced only a 3¢/lb increase for the month, but the majority of producers pushed through the full 5¢/lb increase to the wider market. Some buyers are now pressing for producers to grant non-market adjustments that will take those 5¢/lb increases down to 3¢/lb, but so far, any non-market activity is believed to be not widespread. The increases came as crude oil prices moved above $/bl in mid-September on supply concerns out of the Middle East due to the US-Iran war. The increases in global energy prices raised feedstock prices for global PE, which allowed producers to push US export prices higher. Even as crude prices have eased from those earlier highs, US export prices have been able to maintain their increases, which helped to sustain the increase in domestic contracts. Export prices are continuing to rise this week. Between 2-9 September, US export prices rose by 4-8¢/lb on an fas Houston basis, depending upon grade. High density polyethylene (HDPE) high molecular weight film has seen the highest increase of 8¢/lb over the period due to tightness for that particular grade, while linear low density polyethylene (LLDPE) butene has seen a lesser increase of 4¢/lb over the period due to more plentiful supply. ... For October, US and Canadian producers have announced increases of 7¢/lb for contracts. Buyers say they see little to support additional increases after the September increase, but other market participants said it will depend on what happens with export prices over the course of the month.

headline: Dow Circular Plastics at Colombiaplast 2026: PCR and More
summary_text: At Colombiaplast 2026, Dow laid out its circular plastics roadmap for the press: by 2035, everything it sells into packaging must be reusable or recyclable; by 2030, it aims to commercialize 500,000 metric tons a year of circular and renewable solutions; and by 2050, it intends to be carbon neutral. In Latin America, that strategy is already on the market as resins containing up to 100% post-consumer recycled plastic. ... According to the figures the company brought to Colombiaplast 2026, Dow, headquartered in Midland, Michigan, has net sales of around USD 40 billion, roughly 35,000 employees and 98 manufacturing sites in 31 countries. Its largest operations are in the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, the United Kingdom, China and Thailand. ... ## Latin America’s Polyethylene Market Is Growing Faster Citing Dow Business Intelligence data, the company put the Latin American polyethylene (PE) market at about 9.2 million metric tons, with a compound annual growth rate of 2.6% between 2023 and 2028. The US and Canadian market is larger, at around 14.9 million metric tons, but is expanding more slowly: 2.4% a year over the same period. The region, in other words, is still adding volume. And a large share of that polyethylene ends up in flexible and rigid packaging, the segment where recyclability and recycled-content requirements bite hardest. ... Dow frames its ambition around three commitments: - Close the loop (2035). 100% of Dow products sold into packaging applications will be reusable or recyclable. - Transform the waste (2030). Turn plastic waste and other alternative feedstocks into 500,000 metric tons a year of commercialized circular and renewable solutions. - Protect the climate (2030 and 2050). Cut net annual carbon emissions by 5 million metric tons by 2030, a 15% reduction from its 2020 baseline and 30% from 2005. By 2050, Dow intends to be carbon neutral across Scopes 1, 2 and 3, including product benefits. ... ## Three Routes to Circular Resins Dow is working along three pathways to bring circular content into its resins. Each suits different applications, and each has limits the company itself spelled out. ### Mechanical Recycling and REVOLOOP™ Resins This is the most widespread route: post-consumer plastic (PCR) is collected, washed and re-pelletized. It helps brands meet recycled-content goals or mandates and can lower the carbon footprint. It does come with two constraints: PCR may affect the properties of the final product, and food-contact options are limited. Dow’s answer to the first is the REVOLOOP™ line: formulated, single-pellet resins that already contain certified PCR, so converters get consistent quality without having to do the blending themselves. Target applications include trash bags, stretch and shrink films, caps and closures, wire and cable, and roofing membranes. Each grade comes out of a four-link collaboration. Recyclers supply the material; Dow’s materials science handles compatibilization, property enhancement and PCR analytics; Pack Studios develops the application; and the value chain (converters, equipment manufacturers, brand owners and retailers) takes it to market. The stated goal is recycled material that performs on par with virgin resin. In Latin America, the REVOLOOP™ portfolio already has grades by country: | Country | Grades | PCR content | Certification | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Mexico | 4 translucent LDPE and LLDPE grades | 70–80% | Green Circle; RecyClass in process | | Colombia | REVOLOOP 9237C (colored) and PCR LDPE XB 81810.44 (white) | 98% and 70% | Green Circle (9237C) | | Brazil | White and colored HDPE; translucent LDPE and LLDPE | 95% (HDPE) and 70% | RecyClass | | Argentina | LDPE, HDPE and several LLDPE grades | 70–100% | RecyClass / INTI on several grades | Source: Dow, press presentation at Colombiaplast 2026. These grades are already on store shelves. Dow showed commercial packaging with REVOLOOP™ content in all four countries: shrink films with 30% PCR in Mexico and Brazil; home care packaging with 20% and 30% PCR in Brazil; hygiene packaging with 30% and home care packaging with 20% in Colombia; and liners with 30% PCR in Argentina. ... ### Advanced Recycling: From Plastic Waste to r-Naphtha The second route targets plastic that mechanical recycling cannot handle. Waste is collected and sent to a sorting and pre-treatment facility; an advanced recycling process then converts it into pyrolysis oil. That oil is cleaned up into r-naphtha, which is fed into the cracker and comes out as polymer again. Compared with mechanical recycling, the output performs like virgin resin and is food-contact compliant. It also reduces the use of fossil-based virgin plastic, allows material to be recycled repeatedly and opens an outlet for plastics that were not previously recycled. Other players are also working on food-grade recycled content, as Envapack reported on Interzero’s food-safe recyclates from household packaging. ... ### Bio-Circular Polyethylene The third route replaces part of the fossil feedstock with bio-based waste such as corn stover or used cooking oil. Dow stresses that these sources do not compete with food production and that the resulting resin matches fossil-based quality, with a potentially lower carbon footprint. The presentation illustrated this route with footwear and medical products, and with ENGAGE™ REN, its renewable polyolefin elastomers line. The company also used the occasion to clear up a loosely used term. “Bioplastic” is an umbrella word: it can mean bio-based, biodegradable or both. Dow’s focus is bio-circular PE, a bio-based but non-biodegradable polyethylene that is recycled just like conventional PE. It belongs to a different family from PLA, PHA or PBAT. ... ### How Circular Content Is Certified: ISCC PLUS Mass Balance Advanced recycling and bio-circular feedstocks are accounted for through mass balance. Circular or bio-based feedstocks enter production alongside conventional ones; what comes out is a mix, but a proportion equal to the circular input can be sold as such. That share is certified by an independent third party under the ISCC PLUS (International Sustainability and Carbon Certification) scheme. Because most Dow resin grades are available with this certification, the company says the bio-circular option fits almost any application: food packaging, industrial films, infrastructure and wire and cable, rigid packaging, transportation, pipe, hygiene and consumer goods. ... Dow’s technical team also presented concrete flexible and rigid packaging cases: - Frozen food. Using INNATE™, ELITE™ and DOWLEX™ GM resins, a frozen vegetable bag gained impact resistance. According to Dow, the result was fewer breaks and punctures, and a package that keeps its integrity throughout the supply chain, exports included. - All-PE stand-up pouch designed for recycling. A mono-material MDO/PE structure with ELITE™, ELITE™ AT, INNATE™ and AFFINITY™ replaces multilayer laminates containing PET or PP and opens the door to downgauging. Dow reports that it was validated across the value chain and performs well enough for commercial use. - Pet food. A mono-material PE bag using MDO technology meets what this segment demands: puncture, tear and drop resistance, grease barrier, low dimpling, strong shelf appeal and hermetic seals. Dow says it performs on par with traditional structures and, unlike them, is recyclable. - Lighter rigid packaging. With CONTINUUM™ bimodal HDPE and the Health+™ line, a bottle and its caps shed weight without losing strength during filling, transport and use. Less material per unit means lower cost and less CO₂ equivalent.

headline: October 2026: A Mostly Flat-to-Down Price Trajectory for Volume Resins | Plastics Technology
summary_text: #### August 2026: Commodity Resin Prices Drop Prices for nearly all volume resins were trending flat-to-down with the exception of polystyrene (PS) and nylons 6 and 66, with these increases attributed to spikes in feedstock costs and industry consolidation and despite lackluster demand and well-supplied markets. Still looming heading into fourth quarter is the uncertainty of the U.S.-Iran conflict and potential weather disruptions as the peak of hurricane season is entered. In addition, there’s uncertainty around the impact of tariffs and counter tariffs, particularly with Canada. Below are the views of purchasing consultants from Resin Technology Inc. (RTi); David Barry associate director of polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP) and PS for Dow Jones Energy (formerly OPIS’s PetroChemWire); Michael Greenberg CEO of Resintel, the market intelligence service of The Plastics Exchange (TPE); Scott Newell, executive VP polyolefins at distributor/compounder Spartan Polymers; and Mike Burns of Plastic Resin Market Advisors. ... Entering September, Greenberg addressed the overall state of the domestic polyolefins market. “Domestic buyers were more reserved,” Greenberg explaisn. “Processors continued to buy what they needed, but there was little urgency to build inventory ahead of month-end.” He also noted that industry data shows both PE and PP inventories in comfortable positions. Barry acknowledged the U.S. tariffs on Canada and subsequent counter tariffs. “Raw resin trading remains unimpacted for now,” Barry says. “However, tariffs on finished plastic goods are creating friction, with some converters already facing immediate, large-scale order cancellations. ... ## PE Prices Flat August PE prices appeared to rollover, despite suppliers’ previously nominated hikes of 5-10¢/lb for the month. Spot prices were flat-to-lower, according to Barry, Greenberg, Burns, and Kevin Mekaru, RTi’s procurement director for commodity resins. This after dropping a total of 25¢/lb in the June-July time frame. Meanwhile, Dow and NOVA issued price hikes of 5-7¢/lb for September. “Producer price initiatives remain in place, though support is thin,” Greenberg noted. “So far, no other producers have broadly followed with September initiatives, and the current spot market provides limited evidence that August increases will gain wide traction. The market is simply not tight enough, and buyers know it.” Barry says the market is in a pretty steady equilibrium in terms of supply-demand, partially due to an earlier uptick of exports to China, which now appear to have pulled back as prices there dropped recently. He saw a bit lower pricing for both spot resin and exports. Both he and Mekaru see a flat-to-down trajectory in the September-October time frame, with potential for a slight decrease as a build-up of supplier inventories was largely expected. “Pricing is unlikely to adjust lower until October/November and any events could potentially increase prices significantly,” Burns says. “Strong domestic demand could be a leading factor in the event of a disruption. Domestic pricing should track lower with global prices.” He says record production and below-average exports will favor processors ahead of 2027 contract negotiations. ... Prices of PS were once again on an upwards trajectory, as August prices were expected to settle between 5-11¢/lb higher, following a drop of 6¢/lb in July and increases of 33-34¢/lb between March and June, according to Barry and Brian Balboa, RTi’s senior business unit leader for PS and polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Balboa thinks there will be another much smaller increase in September with October prices flat. The sharp July-August trajectory is solely linked to the August benzene contract price which settled at $4.58/gal from July’s $3.64/gal — a 94¢/gal increase that translates to the 9-10¢/lb sought by PS suppliers. That’s based off the fact that a 10¢/gal benzene price change typically equates to a 1¢/lb change in PS resin formulation. Balboa notes that part of the higher benzene price is due to a somewhat tighter supply resulting from lower imports from South Korea and Japan. Barry maintains that benzene is well supplied going into October, when PS demand typically drops. These sources feel PS prices could settle up closer to 7¢/lb, based on flat demand. Barry reports the implied styrene price was 2.7¢/lb lower going into September than the 50.3¢/lb four weeks prior.

headline: Bi-Weekly Plastics Report - September 23, 2026
summary_text: ## Current Conditions - Polyethylene (PE): U.S. PE markets remain relatively stable and have resisted drops in prices. Suppliers have attempted to push offers higher, but most buyers have been able to negotiate pricing back toward prevailing levels as product availability remains adequate. The market feels supportive but demand destruction, destocking, and affordability concerns are preventing a more sustained price rally. - Polypropylene (PP): U.S. PP markets continue to trend lower despite elevated crude oil and international feedstock prices. Planned outages at LyondellBasell's Lake Charles facility and Braskem's Neal, West Virginia plant should prevent the market from becoming significantly oversupplied in the near term, but those outages also reduce propylene consumption and therefore do little to tighten the upstream monomer market. ... ## Trade Polyethylene (PE) exports remain one of the strongest outlets for North American producers. Export volumes have remained strong through September as buyers continue to favor North America because of reliable resin availability, competitive pricing, and ongoing uncertainty surrounding Middle Eastern and Asian supply. North American PE export spot prices increased during the latest week, with LDPE and LLDPE up 1 cpp, HDPE blow molding up 1 cpp, and HDPE HMW film up 2 cpp. Global logistics remain supportive of U.S. exports: Middle Eastern supply into the Americas is still severely restricted, while congestion and operational disruptions continue affecting Asian shipments. Freight from Asia into South America also remains elevated, improving the relative competitiveness of U.S. resin. However, there are early signs that the export boom could moderate into October. Asian demand has begun to soften as higher resin prices squeeze converter margins and finished-product manufacturers reduce operating rates. New PE capacity is also scheduled to enter service across China during Q4, particularly in HDPE and LLDPE, while another wave of imports is expected to arrive in September and October. These developments could reduce Asian import requirements and eventually increase competitive pressure in other export markets. ... ## Outlook The near-term PE outlook is relatively stable in North America, but the market increasingly appears to be transitioning from a supply-disruption story toward a demand and affordability story. Middle Eastern and Russian production losses remain significant and global logistics have yet to normalize, which should continue supporting U.S. export opportunities and keep global resin prices above where they would otherwise trade. As long as the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea continue to have disruptions, there will be less suppliers of PE globally and help support U.S. PE pricing. At the same time, the underlying global PE balance is shifting back toward length. Fundamentals in the U.S. are still relatively long, but the pick up in demand has led to the days of inventory in the U.S. dropping - even with builds in inventories. Rates of PE are extremely elevated but we could see Asian demand ease in October. However a risk to the upside remains as higher crude oil, feedstock, insurance, and freight costs are therefore providing the price floor rather than outright resin scarcity. ... PE and PP prices remain supported by elevated crude, feedstock, freight, and geopolitical risk premiums, but neither market appears fundamentally short. Demand destruction has become increasingly visible in Asia, buyers remain resistant to high resin prices, and restocking is unlikely to accelerate until prices become more attractive. North America should remain relatively advantaged because of its lower production costs and export position, but the return of Middle Eastern supply and continued capacity additions in Asia could inject some downward pressure in 2027.

headline: US Polyethylene Makes Inroads into Asian Market - Latest News | Plas.com
summary_text: In mid-September, US polyethylene (PE) spot export prices rose notably, with concentrated buying from Asian buyers opening a cross-regional arbitrage window. Platts assessments show US HDPE blow molding grade in Houston was assessed at $1,135/ton on September 14, up $110 from September 1; LLDPE and LDPE rose $66 and $33, respectively. The core driver was not domestic US supply-demand changes, but a shift in global trade flows. After supply disruptions in Asia and the Middle East, buyers in Vietnam, China, South Korea, and Africa increased purchasing, allowing US cargoes to fill the gap and gain pricing room. About 50% of US PE capacity is export-oriented, making it highly sensitive to global spot prices. However, the sustainability of the arbitrage window depends on whether the spread holds. Traders note that if prices rise more than 3 cents/lb further, arbitrage with Asia will no longer be “easy,” as larger gains would close the window. Additionally, US PE is ethane-based, with no direct cost link to crude oil, yet pricing still references the global marginal cost curve (naphtha route). Higher oil prices increase the relative advantage of US cargoes, but this advantage is cyclical. Long term, as Asia’s PE self-sufficiency rises, US cargoes may shift to a marginal balancing role, with competition focusing on logistics costs and delivery reliability. This price rally is a short-term signal from a supply shock, not a trend reversal.

headline: Fresh packaging cost shock puts consumer brands under pressure | Mint
summary_text: Plastic raw material prices have risen 15-20% in two to three weeks and are around 60% above pre-war levels, while packaging costs for brands have climbed 30-40%.(Pixabay) Summary Companies are exploring lighter packs, recycled plastic and material substitutions to contain costs, but limited alternatives and weak consumer demand are challenges. Bengaluru: Consumer goods companies are weighing another round of price increases, using less material, and reducing grammage as plastic steadily gets dearer amid US-Iran tensions, on top of the hikes they have already taken this year. The price of plastic raw material has jumped 15-20% in just the last two to three weeks and now stands about 60% above pre-war levels, said Thimmaiah Napanda, managing director and chief executive of Alternicq Ltd (formerly Manjushree Technopak Ltd), India’s largest maker of rigid plastic packaging. He estimates that packaging costs for brands have climbed 30-40%. The rise hits the plastics used in most bottles, containers and caps for food, drinks, personal care and household products. Snack makers are not spared. The plastic film used for wrappers has become 20% costlier in recent weeks and is 30-40% higher than a year ago, said Amit Kumat, managing director and chief executive officer of packaged food firm Prataap Snacks, which owns the Yellow Diamond brand. Brands have little room left to absorb this, so they are turning to lighter packaging and higher prices. “There are only a finite number of things you can do to contain costs,” said Arvind Singhal, chairman and managing director of retail consultancy The Knowledge Company. “With little expectation of raw material prices returning to pre-war levels soon, manufacturers may have to pass on more of the burden to consumers.” ... Some companies are looking to reduce their dependence on expensive fresh, non-recycled plastic and use less material wherever possible. At personal care firm Plum Goodness, the focus is on optimising packaging, including reducing bottle thickness and modifying caps where technically feasible, without compromising product quality, founder and chief executive officer Shankar Prasad told Mint. The company is also seeking to secure supplies at better prices by buying larger quantities where possible and sourcing from vendors holding existing inventory procured at lower rates. “Buying better can help us for some time, but ultimately, everybody will have to meet the market price,” Prasad said. In the FMCG category, personal care, home care, food, and beverages are most vulnerable to packaging price shocks. New Delhi-based cosmetics maker Glam21 is evaluating recyclable materials like recycled PET (rPET) for bottles, recycled HDPE for containers, glass for jars and bottles, and recyclable mono-material plastics for tubes and caps, co-founder Pradeep Goyal said. “But any switch would depend on availability and the material’s ability to protect formulations from contamination and degradation,” Goyal said, noting that such changes could take a few years to implement. ... Rigid packaging manufacturers are also seeing brands shift towards PET from other plastics such as HDPE and PP. Recycled plastic is gaining traction as well. “Recycled material is now 20-30% cheaper than virgin material. Earlier, it was more expensive,” Alternicq’s Napanda said. However, alternatives remain limited by cost, availability, and product requirements. “Plastics are far more efficient than even glass in some applications because the weight of alternatives increases logistics costs as much as 30%. Manufacturers have been working to reduce costs, but I don’t think there is much scope for new packaging substitutions in the near term,” The Knowledge Company’s Singhal said.

headline: Why are Kraft paper prices rising in India? Corrugated box makers face 25% cost surge - The Economic Times
summary_text: Why are Kraft paper prices rising in India? Corrugated box makers face 25% cost surge - The Economic Times # Why are Kraft paper prices rising in India? Corrugated box makers face 25% cost surge Why are Kraft paper prices rising in India? Corrugated box makers face 25% cost surge ET Online Last Updated: Oct 10, 2026, 04:08:00 PM IST Synopsis Kraft paper prices in India have recently increased by 22% to 25%, affecting production costs significantly. This rise has pressured corrugated box manufacturers, primarily small and medium enterprises, to seek price revisions. The Western India Corrugated Box Manufacturers Association is urging customers to support immediate price adjustments. Numerous factors contribute to this price escalation, including higher raw material costs and international market trends. Agencies Kraft paper prices in India have climbed by 22% to 25% in the past three months, putting fresh financial pressure on manufacturers of corrugated boxes. The increase, which ranges from Rs 7 to Rs 10 per kg depending on the paper grade, has raised production costs for an industry dominated by micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). The Western India Corrugated Box Manufacturers Association (WICMA) has called for an immediate price revision for corrugated boxes and greater stability in Kraft paper prices. The association represents an industry that includes around 4,000 corrugating units in western India and approximately 25,000 units across the country. Kraft paper is the primary raw material used to manufacture corrugated boxes, which are widely used to package and transport products across sectors such as food, pharmaceuticals, fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) and e-commerce. **Why are Kraft paper prices rising in India?** The recent increase in Kraft paper prices reflects a combination of higher raw material costs, international market movements, energy expenses and changes in domestic supply. According to WICMA, several factors are contributing to the rise. **1. Higher waste paper and recycled fibre costs** Waste paper and recycled fibre are important inputs in Kraft paper manufacturing. An increase in the cost of these materials, whether sourced from India or overseas, raises the cost of producing paper. When mills pay more for recycled fibre, the additional expense can put pressure on the prices charged to corrugated box manufacturers. **2. Rising international paper prices** Movements in global paper prices can influence the domestic market. Higher international prices may affect procurement costs and the pricing decisions of Indian manufacturers. This adds another layer of pressure on corrugating units that are already dealing with higher input expenses. **3. Indian mills allocating capacity to exports** WICMA has also cited Indian paper mills booking production capacity for export orders. When mills allocate capacity to overseas buyers, the amount of paper available for domestic customers can be affected. The resulting supply conditions may influence prices in the Indian market. **4. Higher energy, fuel and chemical costs** Paper manufacturing requires energy and other industrial inputs. Rising expenses related to fuel, coal and chemicals add to the overall cost of production. These increases can feed into Kraft paper prices, making it more expensive for corrugated box manufacturers to source their main raw material. **5. Transportation and logistics expenses** The cost of moving raw materials and finished paper also affects the industry's overall cost structure. Higher transportation and logistics expenses can increase procurement costs for manufacturers, adding to the pressure created by other inputs. **6. Domestic supply and demand conditions** The balance between paper availability and demand within India is another factor affecting prices. Changes in raw material availability, procurement costs and mill capacity allocation can influence the prices paid by buyers. WICMA has identified these domestic market conditions, along with international developments, as contributors to the recent escalation. **Corrugated box manufacturers struggle with rising costs** The sharp rise in Kraft paper prices has created a difficult situation for corrugated box manufacturers, many of which operate on narrow profit margins. WICMA President Shlok Kedia said the industry was struggling to absorb a 22% to 25% increase in raw material prices over such a short period. headline: Packaging paper revenues to rise 10-11%; margins to expand
summary_text: ### Packaging paper revenues to rise 10-11%; margins to expand Efficiency-focused capex and healthy accruals to keep credit profiles stable ## Domestic packaging paper manufacturers are set for another year of double-digit growth this fiscal, supported by 6-7% volume growth and 3-4% realisation gains. Demand from consumption-linked sectors, increasing adoption of recyclable packaging and a richer product mix will support growth, while efficiency-focused investments should expand operating margins by 40-50 basis points to around 9%. With capex largely funded through internal accruals, credit profiles are expected to remain stable. A Crisil Ratings study of 47 packaging paper companies, accounting for around 40% of industry volumes, underpins these expectations. This growth is reshaping the domestic paper industry. Packaging paper — comprising kraft paper, duplex board and virgin board — is expected to account for nearly two-thirds of domestic paper volumes this fiscal, up from just over half in fiscal 2022, as paper-based formats gain penetration across consumption-linked sectors and the shift towards sustainable packaging gathers pace. Says Nitin Kansal, Director, Crisil Ratings, “Two forces will drive the sector’s 10-11% revenue growth this fiscal: first, volume growth as consumption-linked sectors such as e-commerce, FMCG 1, food and pharmaceuticals increase their use of packaging paper, and second, realisation gains as the product mix shifts towards higher-value grades. The share of duplex and virgin board has risen by over 500 basis points to nearly 45% of packaging paper volumes in recent years, strengthening both growth visibility and realisations.” With wastepaper prices — the largest cost component — largely outside manufacturers’ control, investments are increasingly targeting controllable costs such as energy, labour and logistics. Waste-to-energy boilers, renewable power, agro-residue processing and debottlenecking, together with higher realisations, should partly offset input-cost pressures and lift operating profitability by 40-50 bps this fiscal. This focus is evident in recent investment patterns: 60-65% of the approximately Rs 1100 crore of incremental capex undertaken by companies rated by Crisil Ratings over the past couple of fiscals went towards efficiency-led projects rather than capacity creation. As manufacturers prioritise margin resilience and balance-sheet strength over aggressive expansion, efficiency focused investments are expected to remain central to their capex strategy. Says Gaurav Arora, Associate Director, Crisil Ratings, “The sector’s capex cycle is turning more defensive than expansionary. Nearly three-fourths of the sector's incremental spending will target process efficiency, energy optimisation and debottlenecking, helping protect margins without materially stretching balance sheets. With annual capex of Rs 500-600 crore expected to be funded largely through internal accruals, gearing should remain below 0.5 times and interest coverage around 4.5 times, supporting stable credit profiles.” That said, downside risks remain. A rise in cheaper imports could pressure domestic realisations, while supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions could raise wastepaper, energy and logistics costs. The extent to which efficiency gains offset these pressures will therefore remain a key monitorable.

headline: Corrugated box prices raised 20% as kraft paper costs surge: South Indian manufacturers’ body | Coimbatore News - The Times of India
summary_text: COIMBATORE: The South Indian Corrugated Box Manufacturers Association (SICBMA), Coimbatore chapter, has announced a 20% increase in corrugated carton box prices, citing steep and repeated hikes in kraft paper rates, higher input costs, and tighter cash flow due to GST and revised payment terms. He said the price per tonne rose from Rs 31,000 to Rs 35,000- 38,000, while 28 BF kraft paper increased from Rs 30 per kg to Rs 38.5 per kg, a jump of Rs 9 per kg in two months. He added that supply from paper mills has also declined. Kathirvelu said mills that earlier allowed 30–60 days for payments are now insisting on full payment within seven days, intensifying working-capital pressure for box makers. He flagged GST-related stress, stating that manufacturers buy inputs by paying 18% GST but sell finished boxes at 5%, leaving 13% blocked as input tax credit with the govt. He said GST refunds are pending for around seven months, pushing several units into financial strain. He said other inputs such as ink, staples and bundling tape have become costlier, while labour costs have risen from Rs 700 to Rs 1,200. Kathirvelu said the industry was compelled to consider a 25% hike but limited the increase to 20%. ... He urged buyers, including the garment and apparel sector, to accept carton pricing linked to prevailing raw material costs, and called for outstanding dues to be cleared within 30 days to ensure uninterrupted production and a stable supply chain. While mills have cited geopolitical tensions in the Middle East for the price rise, he said manufacturers have requested paper mills to rein in further increases. headline: World Packaging Day 2026: Inside India’s Packaging Boom and the Race to Build Smarter |
summary_text: From the carton protecting an online order to the pouch carrying a packet of spices, packaging has become deeply woven into everyday life. It protects food, medicines and consumer goods, supports transportation and storage, helps reduce product damage and increasingly serves as a communication channel between brands and consumers. For India, the occasion comes at a significant time. The country’s packaging industry is expanding alongside consumption, organised retail, e-commerce, quick commerce and manufacturing. According to an Avendus Capital report cited by the India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF), India’s packaging industry could reach approximately ₹8.5 lakh crore (US$92 billion) by FY30, growing at around 9% annually. That growth is turning packaging from a largely behind-the-scenes business into an increasingly important part of India’s economic story. ... Supermarket shelves are filled with packaged products. Medicines require carefully designed containers. E-commerce depends on boxes and protective materials. Restaurants and food-delivery businesses rely on packaging to transport meals safely. Behind these products is a vast network of manufacturers, printers, converters, suppliers, recyclers and technology providers. According to IBEF, India has more than 22,000 packaging units, with approximately 85% belonging to the small and medium enterprise segment. This makes packaging an important part of India’s MSME and manufacturing ecosystem, creating opportunities not only for large corporations but also for specialised smaller businesses. ... ### Flexible Packaging Remains a Major Force Flexible packaging is one of the most visible formats in India’s consumer economy. Pouches, sachets, films and wrappers are popular because they are lightweight, convenient and cost-effective. GlobalData data cited by IBEF indicates that flexible packaging represented 52.5% of India’s packaging volumes in 2025, while rigid plastics accounted for another 31.8%. However, flexible packaging is also at the centre of the sustainability debate. Manufacturers are exploring lighter structures, recyclable formats and mono-material solutions that can reduce environmental impact while maintaining the barrier properties needed for food and other sensitive products. The challenge is finding solutions that are environmentally responsible and commercially viable. ... ### Paper Packaging Is Gaining Momentum Paper and fibre-based packaging are also attracting increasing attention. India’s paper packaging market reached approximately ₹1.67 lakh crore in August 2025, according to IBEF, with further growth expected through 2030. Corrugated boxes, cartons and paper bags are already widely used in retail, e-commerce and food businesses. But sustainability is not simply a matter of replacing plastic with paper. Every material has different strengths, environmental considerations and applications. Some products require moisture resistance, high durability or longer shelf-life protection. The more important question is therefore not plastic versus paper. It is what is the most appropriate material for the job, and how can its environmental footprint be reduced? ... ### Sustainability Is Changing the Industry For India’s packaging sector, sustainability is moving from a branding conversation to a business requirement. Companies increasingly have to think about the entire life of a package — from the materials used to make it to what happens after the consumer discards it. India’s Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework has increased the responsibility of producers, importers and brand owners for managing packaging waste. For manufacturers, this means sustainability is becoming part of packaging design, sourcing and business strategy rather than something considered after production. But the transition is not easy. Recyclable packaging still needs to be collected, sorted and processed. Sustainable alternatives can sometimes be more expensive. Smaller manufacturers may not have the resources to immediately invest in new technologies. India’s packaging challenge is therefore not simply to create greener materials. It is to build a complete ecosystem around them.

headline: Packaging Moves Beyond ‘pack And Wrap’ As India Pushes Quality, Safety And Innovation - THE PACKMAN
summary_text: India’s packaging industry is entering a phase in which growth will be measured not only by volumes, but by quality, safety, sustainability and technological capability. Addressing the inaugural session of the conference at Packplus 2026, Dr. Tanweer Alam, additional director and regional officer, Indian Institute of Packaging (IIP), positioned packaging as a strategic contributor to India’s economic ambitions and called for closer collaboration among government, industry and academia. Alam cited recent industry data indicating that India’s packaging sector has crossed the USD 100 billion mark and is growing at more than 10%, compared with global packaging-sector growth of around 3.9–4%. “Packaging is the engine of growth of the Indian economy nowadays,” Alam said, arguing that the sector has moved far beyond its traditional role of simply wrapping or protecting products. The next phase of growth will demand a shift in priorities. Alam highlighted four broad areas requiring sustained attention, beginning with quality. The emphasis, he said, needs to move from mass production towards producing packaging that meets higher performance and quality expectations. This transition will increasingly influence investment decisions, product development priorities and the technologies adopted across the packaging value chain. It raises the bar for suppliers across India’s packaging market. Food and pharmaceutical packaging represent another critical area. With packaging forming an integral part of product protection, safety and regulatory compliance are becoming increasingly important. Alam pointed to the growing role of regulations from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and stressed that packaging materials must meet international compliance expectations. “Safety is non-negotiable,” he said, particularly for food and pharmaceutical applications. Innovation and sustainability form another major pillar. Alam stressed that packaging decisions should be based on scientific merit rather than an assumption that one material is inherently superior to another. Plastic, paper, glass, metal and composite materials each have advantages and limitations, and the appropriate material should be selected according to functionality and end-use requirements. At the same time, the industry must address what happens after consumption. Materials need to perform their intended packaging function while also becoming more compatible with environmental requirements at end of life. This, Alam argued, is a challenge requiring sustained scientific research. ... Paper-based packaging also needs continued technological attention. While paper offers advantages as an alternative packaging material, its sensitivity to moisture can restrict applications. Improving barrier properties and developing specialized packaging solutions will be essential, Alam said. Technology adoption represents another opportunity. Artificial intelligence, machine learning and IoT can help packaging companies improve quality, raise efficiency, reduce defects and move towards zero-defect manufacturing. He also called for stronger testing and certification infrastructure, greater industry-academia cooperation and measurable approaches to sustainability. Circularity should be considered at the design stage, with efforts to reduce material mass, volume and carbon footprint.

summary_text: The Indian pulp and paper industry stands at a decisive inflection point. With a market currently valued at ~USD 4.7 billion and projected to touch USD 11.3 billion by 2032 at 13.4% CAGR, the next decade will be defined by how the sector balances growth opportunities with structural cost challenges, sustainability mandates, and a fast-evolving consumer base. India’s per capita paper consumption remains just 15 kg against a global average of 57 kg, signalling immense latent demand even as digitalization caps traditional segments. ... Market Factors: From Commodity to Domestic-Led Packaging Growth Packaging and paperboard have decisively become the industry’s backbone, contributing 55-65% of total turnover. This shift is structural, not cyclical. E-commerce growth, FMCG expansion, organized retail, and food delivery are creating relentless demand for corrugated boxes, folding cartons, and paper-based alternatives to plastic. Government bans on single-use plastics across states have accelerated this migration, with F&B chains, QSR brands, and event organizers adopting paper cups, trays, and moulded-fibre packaging. The segment grew 8.2% YoY in FY24 and remains the primary investment magnet. However, growth is moderating. headline: Road freight green transition hits cost wall: new industry survey | IRU | World Road Transport Organisation
summary_text: ## Seven in ten operators say customers won’t pay the extra cost of greener transport, according to IRU and Trimble’s 2026 Green Compact survey. A new survey of road freight operators shows that, while they are cutting emissions, cost is now their biggest obstacle to going further, compared to last year’s survey, in which cost ranked second to infrastructure. Moreover, around seven in ten operators in Western Europe (70%), Eastern Europe (71%) and Australia (67%) say their customers are unwilling to pay the additional cost of decarbonisation. IRU Secretary General Habib Turki said, “The next phase of decarbonisation requires much greater investment. Operators cannot carry that cost alone, particularly when their customers are unwilling or unable to pay more for greener transport.” ... infrastructure Together, expensive solutions and unwilling customers form a cost wall. The price of decarbonising is high, but operators have no reliable way to pass it on. Solutions are seen as too expensive by 64% of Western European operators, 62% in Eastern Europe and 40% in Australia. The shift is clearest in alternative fuels. Last year, the lack of charging and refuelling infrastructure was the leading obstacle. In 2026, vehicle prices have become the biggest barrier in both European regions. In Western Europe, 66% of operators cite vehicle prices, up from 49% in 2025. In Eastern Europe, the figure has risen from 52% to 78%. The gap is large. An electric truck costs two to three times as much as its diesel equivalent, far more than operators’ thin margins can absorb. ... Nine in ten Western European operators (90%) take at least one measure to cut emissions, as do 87% in Eastern Europe and 55% in Australia. They start with measures that pay for themselves: routing optimisation (53% in Western Europe, 62% in Eastern Europe) and eco-driving training (42% in both). But formal commitment lags. Targets have been set by 41% of Western European operators, 31% in Eastern Europe and 11% in Australia, and only 43%, 23% and 6%, respectively, calculate their CO₂ emissions. ... Around 41% of Western European operators already use alternative fuels, against 14% in Eastern Europe and 7% in Australia. Renewable diesel (HVO), which works with existing engines, leads in every region. In Western Europe, its use is expected to rise from 29% today to 54% within five years. Battery-electric investment is planned by 29% of Western European operators, 17% in Eastern Europe and 10% in Australia, and it is concentrated where it fits best. In Western Europe, 87% of operators with turnover above EUR 100 million plan to invest, against 26% of smaller firms, and 40% of regional operators plan to invest against 17% of long-haul operators. In a sector dominated by SMEs, the divide is capital, not will. ... Beyond the operator survey, the new report also compares Brazil, China, the EU, India and the US, demonstrating how regulation is diverging. For example, China’s mix of tighter standards and strong incentives took new-energy vehicles to roughly 29% of new heavy-truck sales in 2025. The EU has the most complete framework, but operators struggle to follow it: only around one in eight say they understand a given EU policy well. Incentives also vary widely, with governments using two approaches – push and pull – neither of which closes the gap on its own. Push measures raise the cost of diesel. For example, ETS2, the EU’s new emissions trading system, will price road fuel emissions at around EUR 60 per tonne of CO₂ starting in 2028, adding an estimated 5.5% to the total cost of ownership of a long-haul truck in France. CO₂-differentiated tolls are also in place or being introduced in 11 EU countries. In Germany, higher tolls have increased costs for a Euro VI articulated truck by 83%, equivalent to around 10% of its total cost of ownership. This brings diesel trucks closer to cost parity with electric trucks, which remain exempt from tolls until 2031. Pull measures lower the cost of zero-emission vehicles. Purchase incentives exist in many EU countries but are often capped, difficult to apply for, and available only for short periods, making them poorly suited to multi-year fleet renewal plans. Toll exemptions vary widely, from Germany’s full exemption to reduced rates elsewhere. Even so, 38% of Western European operators and 44% of Australian operators still say government incentives are insufficient. ... Although slipping to second place in this year’s survey, energy supply and grid capacity also remain major challenges. A fully electric EU truck fleet would require electricity equivalent to around a fifth of the combined electricity available in Germany and Poland, according to IRU estimates. Europe currently has just 1,225 public truck-capable charging stations, compared with an estimated need for 50,000 high-power charging points. Most charging will take place at depots, where securing grid capacity typically takes one to two years. More than 1,000 transport operators from across 36 countries participated in the survey.

summary_text: There are 76,083 businesses in Italy (up-to-date figures from Unioncamere), most of which are small, if not tiny. Over the past ten years, the sector has lost more than 20,000 of them, including over 4,500 in the last two years alone. This decline has affected sole traders, whilst a trend towards consolidation has seen an increase in limited companies, which now account for 37 per cent of the total. Those in the middle ground – that is, the 33,000 small companies – have minimal profit margins, barely 2–3 per cent, at a time when the increase in traffic (which is positive in itself as it is a clear sign of economic dynamism) requires investment not only in new, technologically advanced and safer vehicles, but also in organisational platforms utilising IT systems. Concentration is synonymous with market maturity; with over one billion tonnes transported each year, the market ranks fifth after Poland, Germany, Spain and France. Not only that, but it represents both an advantage on the demand side and a challenge on the supply side of the service. The gap, however, has gradually widened. ... The sector’s turnover stands at 60 billion euros, accounting for more than half of the turnover of the Italian contract logistics sector, which the Milan Polytechnic Observatory has estimated at 112 billion euros. The pie is not divided equally. An elite group of 1,068 companies generates €17.4 billion, equal to one-third of the sector’s total, and owns 32.5 per cent of the vehicles on the road. The remaining companies share €42.6 billion, with an average turnover of €433,000 compared with €16.3 million for the major operators. Only 94 companies exceeded the €50 million turnover threshold. Brt (formerly Bartolini of Bologna) remains at the top of the rankings, with €1.9 billion in revenue, the only company to break the €1 billion mark. It is now controlled by Geopost (a subsidiary of the French postal service) and has a turnover almost four times that of the second and third-placed companies: Arcese Trasporti with €587 million and Stef Italia with €585 million, which specialises in the cold chain. Next come the Executive Group (578 million, logistics and third-party transport) and Zenit (463 million, fuel distribution), followed by a series of smaller players. It is clear that, although market concentration has increased by 46 per cent over ten years, it is still not sufficient to compete with giants such as the German firm DHL, which has a turnover of over 80 billion euros, the Danish firm DSV, which is targeting 40 billion, and the other major players: the Swiss firm Kuehne+Nagel and the Lithuanian firm Girteka – all names that motorway users see constantly on lorries. ... The road haulage sector, too, must contend with the demographic winter. Over the next five years, 86,224 Italian drivers – 28 per cent of the current workforce – will retire. To offset these retirements, over 17,000 new drivers would need to enter the market each year, but over the last two years the number of young drivers has increased by only around 2,000. “The gap between demand for and the supply of qualified drivers is emerging as one of the main structural risk factors for the sector in the coming years,” writes Federtrasporti. The other gap concerns earnings. Looking at employees, the contract for mobile staff stipulates a minimum gross salary of 2,000 euros, but the basic pay serves only as a reference point. In fact, the salary depends on job grade, driving licence, type of vehicle, and whether routes are domestic or international – and thus on travel allowances, overtime, night shifts, and company or individual agreements. What is certain is that they are not rolling in money and carry out a demanding, often gruelling job. On average, the net income is not particularly attractive, yet in the logistics sector, the issue of drivers’ wages is strategic: without reliable drivers, even efficient warehouses, advanced software and optimised planning are not enough to guarantee on-time deliveries. ... This is also one of the key points in the ongoing negotiations with the government, which have been underway for months. From 20 to 24 April, a transport strike was organised to demand changes to legislation (on safety, the Highway Code, the use of fuels and renewable energy sources) alongside financial support such as a fuel tax credit, motorway tolls and the reimbursement of excise duties.
