summary_text: Charles County Moves Forward With Employee Health Center - The BayNet # Charles County Moves Forward With Employee Health Center by Jessica Jennings October 24, 2026October 22, 2026 Source: Screenshot of Marathon Health’s presentation to the Charles County commissioners, Sept. 15, 2026. **LA PLATA, Md.** — Charles County commissioners took another step toward establishing a primary care center for county employees and their families Tuesday, Oct. 20, approving a contract with Marathon Health. The approval allows the county to move forward with planning and setting up the center. The proposed center would serve employees, retirees and family members covered by the county’s health insurance plan. The goal is to make routine care easier to access while helping control health care costs. Commissioners approved the contract after staff said it had completed legal review. The action follows a Sept. 15 presentation outlining the proposed services, staffing and expenses. Source: Screenshot of Marathon Health’s presentation to the Charles County commissioners, Sept. 15, 2026.### **What Would The Center Offer?** The September proposal calls for one full-time doctor and two full-time medical assistants, with at least 40 operating hours each week. **Proposed services include:** * Checkups and preventive care. * Treatment for minor illnesses and injuries. * Care for ongoing conditions such as diabetes. * On-site lab testing and generic medications. * Virtual medical appointments and virtual mental health care. * Work-related health services. * Help coordinating specialist referrals. Patients could use an app or online portal to schedule appointments, contact their care team, request prescription refills and view lab results. An after-hours nurse line would also be available. Pricing in the proposal was based on at least 2,650 eligible employees and family members. Source: Screenshot of Marathon Health’s presentation to the Charles County commissioners, Sept. 15, 2026. The September presentation identified $900,000 in funding through the Maryland Association of Boards of Education for startup expenses. The presentation lists $721,500 for facility setup and $198,300 in other implementation fees. Together, those expenses total $919,800. The slides do not explain how the difference would be covered. First-year operating costs are estimated at about $1.34 million, including staffing and other expenses, plus medications, vaccines and lab services billed at cost. Marathon projects the center would reduce the county’s medical and prescription claims by about $897,000 in its first year. Those savings would not fully cover the center’s operating costs, leaving a projected net cost of about $439,000 that year. Over five years, the company projects approximately $12.4 million in claims savings and $7 million in center costs, resulting in about $5.4 million in net savings. Those figures are estimates presented by Marathon, rather than savings already achieved. Source: Screenshot of Marathon Health’s presentation to the Charles County commissioners, Sept. 15, 2026. The model brings several routine health services into one setting, giving eligible employees and families another option for medical care. Marathon’s presentation described same-day or next-day appointments for urgent concerns, longer appointments and access to both in-person and virtual care. The company’s approach aims to reduce spending on outside medical services by treating illnesses earlier and helping patients manage ongoing health conditions. ### **What Happens Next?** The contract approval is a step toward establishing the center. Details about the location, opening schedule and how eligible employees would begin using it remain to be announced. Watch the Oct. 20 commissioners’ afternoon session on CCGTV. headline: Charles Approves Contract for Employee Health Clinic -
summary_text: Charles Approves Contract for Employee Health Clinic - # Charles Approves Contract for Employee Health Clinic The vote moves the county from planning to building a primary care center for workers, retirees and families on its health plan. Location, hours and opening date are still to come. by David M. Higgins II, Publisher/Editor October 22, 2026October 22, 2026 Credit: Charles County Government **LA PLATA — **Charles County government workers, retirees and their families on the county health plan are a step closer to having their own doctor’s office. The Board of County Commissioners on Oct. 20 approved a contract with Marathon Health to set up and run an advanced primary care center for people covered by the county’s health insurance. The voice vote came with no opposition and no discussion, in the first item of the board’s afternoon session. All five commissioners were present. Jake Dyer, the county’s director of fiscal and administrative services, told the board that since a presentation in mid-September, staff had worked through the legal review of the contract. Approval, he said, lets the county begin the actual next step of standing up the center. ## What the county was promised Commissioners gave consensus to pursue the clinic on Sept. 15. As **the Chronicle reported then**, county staff and Marathon representatives laid out the case using two years of the county’s own claims data. The county spends about $21.4 million a year on employee health care. Marathon projected the center would cost about $1.3 million a year in flat per-employee fees, which cover medications, lab work and vaccines. The projections presented in September were: * About $897,000 in savings in the first year * About $12.3 million in gross savings over five years * About $5.3 million in net savings over five years, after the center’s costs Those figures did not include potential savings from the center’s occupational health work, such as screenings for first responders. Marathon said it would tie performance guarantees to patient engagement, patient satisfaction, clinical results such as diabetes management, and claims savings. ## What patients would get The center would offer primary and preventive care, urgent care for minor illness and injury, on-site lab work and occupational health screenings. It would dispense roughly 150 to 200 generic medications at no out-of-pocket cost to people on the plan, and stay open at least 40 hours a week. The county would lease an existing building, with build-out costs capped at $700,000 under the plan presented in September. Employer-run clinics like this are meant to cut costs by steering routine care away from emergency rooms and urgent care centers and catching chronic conditions earlier. Marathon told commissioners it has built more than 55 such centers and that 17 operate in Maryland. ## Still to be decided The Oct. 20 approval did not settle the details residents and employees will most want to know. The contract’s total value, the center’s location, its hours and its opening date were not discussed at the meeting. In September, officials estimated the center could open about six and a half months after funding and a site are finalized, with a target of the current fiscal year, which ends June 30, 2027. Commissioners will set the center’s hours and location. With the current board’s term ending in mid-November, those decisions may fall to the board chosen in the Nov. 3 general election.

headline: Self-funded health plans: why RCM&D's broker is sounding the alarm | Insurance Business
summary_text: Ben Bohonowicz has spent 16 years watching the group health insurance market shift. Today, as a Division Director at RCM&D in Baltimore, he believes the traditional broker model is approaching a reckoning and that self-funded health plans are the clearest path forward for the mid-market employers his team serves. "The amount of double-digit increases that have come from the fully insured marketplace this year is the most I've ever seen in my career," Bohonowicz told Insurance Business Benefits US. "The starting point is around 12 to 15%, but we've gotten renewals that are 20, 30, 40, 50%." Bohonowicz oversees a team of 60 benefits professionals spanning Philadelphia to Richmond, operating as the benefits arm of RCM&D, a firm with roots going back to 1885, predominantly in the property and casualty space. The division focuses heavily on the 50-to-1,000+ employee market, a segment where self-funded and level-funded arrangements are rapidly becoming the norm. ... ## The self-funded shift is already here The numbers back his view. Self-funded administrative services only (ASO) plans now account for 43.5% of total US health enrollment - the largest single coverage segment in the country. And according to data from the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF), nearly 27% of employers with 10 to 200 employees are now self-funded. "And if you bundle level-funded on top of that, it actually becomes the majority on a nationwide perspective," Bohonowicz said. He frames the case for self-funding around three pillars for first-time employer conversations: transparency, control, and cost containment. In a fully insured arrangement, he says, employers have access to little or no claims data, no ability to shape the vendor stack, and no lever to pull when costs spike. "In the absence of [transparency and control], you will never contain cost. It will never happen. It's pure luck and hope if you end up having a good renewal from year to year." Stop-loss contracts, he notes, have matured significantly, offering levers including no-new-laser with renewal rate caps, aggregate accommodation, advanced funding, and terminal liability option (TLO) off-ramps that allow employers to capture the upside of self-funding while protecting against runaway individual claimants and cash flow volatility. ... In response, the firm built a proprietary concierge pharmacy program that targets the 20% of plan members who drive 80% of pharmacy costs - those taking multiple maintenance medications, whether generic, brand, or specialty. A dedicated pharmacy team coordinates procurement through the most cost-effective sourcing channel and delivers medications directly to members at no cost. The employer pays wholesale acquisition cost rather than PBM-negotiated prices. The program is deployed even where a full PBM carve-out is not possible, running on top of an independent PBM arrangement where it consistently outperforms standard negotiated pricing, according to Bohonowicz. For employers where pharmacy is driving outsized plan spend, he estimates that converting to self-funding, deploying the program, and fixing the PBM arrangement can reduce total plan costs by 20% to 30%. The Department of Labor's ongoing push for pharmacy benefit transparency is providing regulatory tailwind for this kind of intervention and Bohonowicz believes more is coming from the enforcement side. ... When asked to name the single biggest threat to the traditional broker model over the next two to five years, Bohonowicz did not hesitate. " Broker compensation disclosures," he said. "When people start to see where the money is going and where the incentive lies, I think it will do the same exact thing that's happened in the 401(k) space." Disclosure requirements that reshaped fee transparency in the retirement planning industry, drawing scrutiny to advisor compensation structures, are in his view poised to do the same in group health. The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2020 included broker compensation disclosure requirements for group health plans, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026 has extended and strengthened those provisions. But awareness among employers remains low. "When we ask some of the prospects we work with, 'Have you seen your broker compensation disclosure?' - like, what are you talking about?" he said. "It's not being met the way it should be. There needs to be more teeth to this."

headline: John Zabasky Urges Small Employers to Adopt Annual Benefits Checkup | DC Metrowire
summary_text: DC Metrowire Staff • October 22, 2026• Business Small employers should make an annual benefits checkup a standard part of their yearly routine, according to John Zabasky, CEO of WorXsiteHR Insurance Solutions, Inc. The review, which Zabasky says should be free, examines how a health plan is being used, where workers encounter friction, and whether the employer is still getting a fair deal on cost. Rather than waiting for a problem to arise, Zabasky recommends employers schedule the review automatically each year. "Most employers only look hard at their benefits when something breaks," Zabasky said. "I want employers checking in every year, on purpose, whether anything is wrong or not." The checkup is intended as a plain assessment of plan performance, not a sales pitch for a new plan. It should involve a walkthrough of enrollment numbers, claims patterns, and direct worker feedback with the employer. ... The concept grew out of Zabasky's experience working with lower income, part-time, and seasonal workforces through the HealthWorX Plan, where WorXsiteHR serves as the exclusive third-party administrator. "With seasonal and part-time workforces, things change fast," he said. "Turnover changes. Hours change. A plan that fit in January can be a bad fit by September, and nobody notices until renewal." ... According to Zabasky, a good annual checkup delivers three things: a plain-language summary of how the plan performed, a short list of changes worth making, and a direct answer on whether costs remain in line with what similar employers are paying. The goal is to catch small problems before they become renewal-time surprises. "I would rather flag a problem in June than have an employer find out at renewal that their workers stopped using the plan months ago," he said. ... HealthWorX is a no-cost medical plan subsidized by a non-profit, designed to give lower income, part-time, and seasonal workers access to healthcare they can actually use. WorXsiteHR administers the plan for employers who want it. Zabasky said an annual checkup habit helps employers ensure that access does not quietly erode over time. "A benefit only works if people use it," he said. "A checkup is how you make sure that stays true year after year, not just in the first year."

headline: Centene scales employee ICHRA program as big employers lead market shift | Insurance Business
summary_text: Centene Corporation is enrolling its own employees in the individual coverage health reimbursement arrangement (ICHRA) model it markets to other employers, and it’s now scaling that experiment beyond the single-state pilot it launched this year. The St. Louis-based managed care company announced that its Ambetter Health Solutions arm will extend its CHOICE Arrangements program, the federal government’s official rebrand for ICHRAs, to all Ohio- and Oklahoma-based employees for plan year 2027. The rollout follows a 2026 pilot covering more than 700 of Centene’s Indiana-based workers, which the company described as successful enough to justify the expansion. Centene is both a seller and now a scaled-up user of the ICHRA model. Its ICHRA commercial membership hit approximately 50,000 as of the second quarter of 2026, roughly two-and-a-half times its size a year earlier, according to the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call. CEO Sarah M. London has called ICHRA the “future of individual health insurance.” That context makes the internal rollout as much a market signal as a benefits decision. ... Indiana enacted the first state-level ICHRA tax credit in 2024, offering small employers up to $400 per employee in year one to adopt the model over traditional group coverage. Ohio has its own ICHRA tax credit bill advancing with bipartisan support. Ambetter also plans to add four more markets - Alabama, Iowa, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania - to its commercial ICHRA footprint in 2027. ... ## Large employers are moving faster than brokers Centene’s internal expansion sits inside a broader shift that is changing the nature of ICHRA conversations. According to the HRA Council’s 2025-2026 annual report, more than 20,000 US businesses now offer an ICHRA, a 53% jump from 2025, with covered lives surpassing 500,000. Applicable large employers, or those with 50 or more full-time equivalent employees, are now the fastest-growing segment, with adoption more than doubling year-over-year. That large-employer momentum is where the model creates direct pressure for benefits advisors. An ALE rethinking its benefits structure is a different kind of client conversation than a small business exploring ICHRA as its first benefits offering, and it requires a different level of fluency. Yet the TASC 2026 Broker ICHRA Survey found that 54% of benefits brokers have still never sold an ICHRA, up from 47% in 2025. The share of brokers who fully support the product fell from 48% to 29% in the same period. The 2026 EBRI-Morgan Health Employer ICHRA Survey, which gathered responses from nearly 1,000 benefits decision-makers, found that 77% of employers said a broker or benefits consultant recommendation would make them more likely to adopt an ICHRA. Among small employers not currently offering any health coverage, 55% were unaware that ICHRA was even an option.

headline: Maryland's FAMLI Brings New Costs, Challenges for Contractors - News | Building Congress & Exchange
summary_text: Maryland construction companies are facing a new expense that could affect everything from employee paychecks and labor rates to project bids and workforce availability. For one Baltimore-area contractor, the anticipated cost could reach $100,000 annually. Ted Bowes, president of Excell Concrete, says the additional expense will force his company to raise labor rates and adjust its contract bids. Beginning in January, the state’s new Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) program will require payroll contributions to fund paid, job-protected leave for eligible employees. While the program will provide important financial protection for workers facing serious medical or family needs, it also presents new costs and staffing challenges for employers. With a November 15 deadline approaching for companies considering private insurance plans, employers need to start making decisions now. Under FAMLI, eligible employees will be able to take up to 12 weeks of paid leave annually to care for themselves or a family member, receive up to $1,000 a week and return to their jobs when their leave ends. Employees who have worked at least 680 hours in Maryland during the qualifying period will be eligible for benefits. Although payroll contributions from employers and employees begin in January 2027, benefits will not become available until January 2028. In the meantime, employers must identify eligible employees, evaluate insurance options, register with the state and prepare their payroll and benefits systems. ... Maryland employers can participate in the state-run FAMLI program or select an approved private insurance plan. “The state plan is a simpler compliance path,” said Nicole Fender, Compliance Manager/Employee Benefits with RCM&D. “There is lower administrative burden, meaning the state is going to handle the eligibility, claims, appeals and benefit payments.” However, employers will still have some compliance obligations, such as filing quarterly wage and hour reports to the state, and handling employee-facing notice requirements. Before defaulting to the state plan, employers should consider getting quotes for private FAMLI insurance coverage spanning multiple years to evaluate potential cost savings, Fender said. Some private insurers are containing the cost of FAMLI plans, in part, by building smaller reserves than the state plan. “By using the same carrier that handles your other employee benefits, namely short-term disability (STD), you will have better integration of benefits and you may be able to negotiate some service guarantees, such as turnaround times on claims,” Fender said. Bundling FAMLI and disability policies under one carrier could generate savings since some FAMLI claims will not become short-term disability claims, and potentially reduce disability insurance premiums.

summary_text: ANNAPOLIS, Md. — Maryland approved $65.6 million in contract renewals and additional funding Oct. 7 to continue building the online system employers and workers will use for the state’s paid family and medical leave program. The Board of Public Works (BPW) approved the request without discussion, according to its meeting summary. The spending supports Maryland’s Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) program, which The BayNet previously outlined for employers. Payroll contributions begin Jan. 1, 2027, and benefits become available Jan. 1, 2028. The approval extends contracts with Nava Public Benefit Corporation and Fearless Solutions LLC through Oct. 31, 2028. It includes $31.2 million for two renewal years and $34.4 million in additional funding, bringing the combined contract ceiling, including the original two-year term, to $96.8 million. In its request to the board, Item 56-IT-OPT/MOD, the Maryland Department of Labor said the additional money would sustain approximately 100 vendor personnel through the program’s launch. The system must handle employer reporting and contributions, worker claims, payments, appeals and fraud prevention. The department said the later launch schedule allows more features to be completed before benefits begin. Funding will come from the FAMLI fund. For workers, the program will provide partial wage replacement of up to $1,000 weekly for up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave, according to the state’s program overview. Qualifying circumstances include welcoming a child, addressing a serious health condition or caring for a family member. Employers participating in the state plan will begin collecting contributions before workers can claim benefits. The initial contribution rate is 0.9% of covered wages, generally split equally between employers and employees. Employers with fewer than 15 employees are exempt from the employer share but must remit employee contributions. The first quarterly payment is due April 30, 2027. The state says collecting contributions a year before benefits begin will allow the fund to build reserves before paying claims.

headline: Q&A: Experts Share What Benefits Trends Will Shape the Next 5 Years | WorldatWork
summary_text: As the benefits landscape continues to shift and evolve, what trends, innovations or challenges should employers watch for? And, how can they prepare? To learn more, Workspan Daily (WD) spoke with the following benefits experts about their predictions and tips for HR professionals to consider as they look ahead: - Bianka Douglas, the vice president and people business leader at Prudential Group Insurance; - Laine Thomas Conway, the vice president of delivery enablement and engagement at benefit services provider Alight; and, - Robby White, the U.S. benefits business line leader at risk management and consulting firm Gallagher. ... What do you think benefits will look like in five years? And, what future benefits trends do you anticipate? Thomas Conway: I don’t expect our core benefits to change dramatically. It’s not like artificial intelligence (AI) eliminates my need to get a knee replaced or for my kid to get braces. The core benefits are the core benefits. Right now, there is an interest and openness to a new type of health plan [such as plans with up-front pricing and no deductibles]. Younger generations are more open to experimentation around plan types. It’s been well over a decade since we’ve seen something really new in the plan design space with high-deductible health plans, so we’re ripe for a new type of plan design. That can be hard because you have to teach people how to fish all over again, but it’ll be interesting to see what that next frontier is. White: Benefits will likely be more personalized, data-driven and integrated into employees’ daily experiences. Rather than annual enrollment being the primary interaction point, employees will receive ongoing guidance throughout the year based on life events, changing needs and workforce trends. Several trends appear poised to accelerate: - AI-powered benefit recommendations and year-round decision support; - Greater personalization based on life stage and household needs; - Expansion of family-building and caregiving benefits; - Increased focus on financial well-being and emergency savings; - More integrated well-being ecosystems connecting physical, emotional and financial health; - Greater use of analytics to measure outcomes and improve benefit effectiveness; - Enhanced leave programs that address a broader range of family and caregiving situations; and, - More consumer-oriented healthcare solutions designed to improve navigation and cost transparency. ... Douglas: One of the biggest challenges will be balancing greater personalization with simplicity. Employers should start by listening to their workforce, identifying where employees lack confidence and understanding the moments when additional guidance would be most helpful. Employers also will need to maintain trust as technology plays a larger role in the benefits experience, particularly when it comes to transparency, privacy and data protection. Thomas Conway: The percent of employees who regretted a healthcare decision they made in the past year is up to 67%. That number will continue to grow because I think asking AI [for healthcare advice] will become a regret. It’s dependent on you asking the right prompt and the tool not trying to please you. So, how do we harness AI in a way that people can ask it questions to gather information, but do it in a way where they’re not getting hallucinations or AI slop? We can’t put the genie back in the bottle, but we can provide a layer of trust. White: The biggest challenge will likely be balancing growing employee expectations with affordability. Personalization and effective steerage can help strike that balance by directing employees to the right resources and care at the right time, improving how benefits are used while helping control costs and limit waste.

headline: How Jennifer Schaefer Is Transforming the Employee Benefits Conversation
summary_text: Every year, the same scenario plays out for many employers. A health plan renewal arrives with a steep increase, the rate is negotiated down a few points, and the remaining cost is either absorbed by the company or passed on to employees. Then, 12 months later, the cycle begins again. After seeing that pattern repeatedly throughout her career, Jennifer Schaefer decided employers needed a better way to manage their benefits strategy. Schaefer is the founder and CEO of JS Benefits Group, an employee benefits and HR consulting firm serving employers across Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, and New York. She entered the industry in 1993 and has since worked with more than 1,200 employers. "I started the firm with a simple belief," Schaefer says. "Employers deserve an advisor who is accountable for helping them improve their results, not someone who simply manages the annual renewal." ... "We look beyond the renewal and examine the plan itself, the underlying costs, and the opportunities to improve both the employer's investment and the employee experience," she explains. Today, JS Benefits Group works with small and mid-sized businesses on group health plans, level-funded and self-funded strategies, ACA compliance, and fractional HR support. The goal is to help employers make better decisions about their benefits while improving the employee experience. "For us, success isn't simply placing a plan," she says. "It's helping a client make a better decision and being able to show the impact." ... Schaefer is focused on helping mid-sized employers get a clearer picture of what is actually driving their healthcare costs. Rather than waiting for the next renewal to reveal another increase, she wants employers to have better information throughout the year. "Too often, employers receive a renewal rate, react to the increase, and then repeat the process the following year," she notes. "They may know what they're spending, but they don't always have a clear picture of why they're spending it." Level-funded and self-funded plan structures can change that. When structured appropriately, they give employers greater visibility into the data behind their costs and more opportunity to manage the factors driving them. But Schaefer isn't advocating for a particular plan structure simply for the sake of changing plans. She sees these options as tools that can help employers understand their costs and make more informed decisions.

headline: ‘Well-Being Is in Everything’: Inside One Company’s Wellness Approach
summary_text: When Atlantic Packaging began its workplace wellness program in 2012, the company wasn’t starting with a question about how to get employees to take more steps or eat better. It was starting with a more basic problem: Some employees weren’t seeing a doctor at all. Most of the 1,260 U.S. employees at Atlantic Packaging — a manufacturing company with employees spread across roughly 25 locations — work in a warehouse, on a manufacturing floor, or on a truck. At one of its largest North Carolina locations, employees had to travel about 30 minutes to see a primary-care provider. “We knew our people just weren’t seeing a doctor,” said Becca Schusler, Atlantic Packaging’s director of wellness. “They didn’t even know their numbers.” So the company started bringing care to them. One of its first initiatives was onsite biometric screening. In 2012, Atlantic also established an onsite health center at its Tabor City, N.C., location, with the goal of making primary care more accessible to employees who otherwise might turn to urgent care or the emergency room. The visits are at no cost to employees. Having that in place allows the company to go beyond asking employees to make healthier choices and instead focus on “trying to remove barriers to care,” she said. Today, Schusler said, 84% of employees at that location have used the health center. The company’s wellness strategy has since expanded well beyond traditional workplace wellness. Employees have access to annual physicals, preventive screenings, health coaching, diabetes-management programs — as well as mental and behavioral health resources and financial coaching. The company even encourages employees to spend time outdoors through what it calls its “Nature Challenge.” ... Schusler: Our employees have to do their onsite biometric and annual physical, a preventive exam, and one health coaching visit. We offer free health coaching for all of our employees. The health coaches are registered dietitians, personal trainers, and certified health coaches. If they do those four things, then they get a reduction on their premiums or their rates. We’re able to use a 30% differential. Specialty Credential: Total Rewards ... Schusler: We do a lot of education. We have a diabetes self-management education and a Spark metabolic health program. For the diabetes self-management education program, members can get a continuous glucose monitor at no cost to them, and they can learn how to use that and how that has a big effect on managing their Type 2 diabetes. Seventy-five percent of our people with Type 2 diabetes are making progress on their A1C. As a population, we’ve actually improved 1.2 points in A1C, which is really great. ... Schusler: We know that mental and behavioral health is a big risk and issue in our population. We have partnered with a mental and emotional health provider that offers six free coaching and six free counseling visits to all our employees each year. They also have an app with self-guided exercises. We started it last year in May, and we already had 12.5% participation or engagement. EAPs [employee assistance programs] usually only see about 3% engagement.

headline: Benefits Broker Acquisitions in the DMV | Capitol Benefits
summary_text: # Three Benefits Brokers Serving This Region Have Been Acquired. What That Means for Your Account Team Key takeaways for employers - Aon agreed on August 31, 2026 to buy USI Insurance Services from KKR for roughly $17 billion, with closing expected in the fourth quarter. - Marsh McLennan Agency completed its acquisition of TriBridge Partners, a Columbia, Maryland benefits and retirement firm, on June 1, 2026. - Business Benefits Group in Fairfax joined private equity backed Patriot Growth Insurance Services back in 2022, so this is a multi-year pattern rather than a 2026 development. - Being acquired is not automatically bad for clients. What it reliably changes is who owns the relationship and how long your account team stays. - Five questions, asked before renewal, tell you whether your service model survived the transaction. If your benefits broker was acquired in the past few years, you are in a very large group, and the pace has picked up. ... ## What actually happened, and when These are public transactions. We are describing them because they are relevant to employers in this market, not to criticise the firms or the people in them. | Transaction | Announced | Why it matters here | | --- | --- | --- | | Aon acquires USI Insurance Services | August 31, 2026, expected to close in Q4 | About $17 billion, all cash, bought from the private equity firm KKR. USI joins Aon alongside NFP, which Aon acquired earlier. A very large share of the US middle market moves under one roof. | | Marsh McLennan Agency acquires TriBridge Partners | Announced April 30, 2026, closed June 1, 2026 | TriBridge is headquartered in Columbia, Maryland and advised employers on benefits, retirement and wealth. This one happened inside our own market. | | Business Benefits Group joins Patriot Growth Insurance Services | April 2022 | BBG, based in Fairfax, was one of the larger remaining independents in Northern Virginia. Patriot Growth is backed by the private equity firm GI Partners. | Two of those closed this year. The third is four years old, which is the more useful point: this is not a sudden event you can wait out. It is the direction the industry has been moving for some time. ... . Acquisitions are legitimate transactions and we are not going to claim every one of them ends badly for clients. Some employers barely notice. What we would push back on is the assumption that you have to hand over ownership of the relationship to get scale. Benefits administration technology, compliance support, claims and utilization analytics, multi-state capability, specialist expertise for the situations that do not fit a template: these are table stakes now, not a reason to be acquired. Independent firms reach them through carrier relationships and selective partnerships instead. We are independently owned and we serve more than 5,600 clients across 16 states. So the question is not whether a firm is big. It is something narrower and much less discussed: continuity. Integration means restructuring. Restructuring means reassignment. The person who knew your plan history, your difficult claim from two years ago, and exactly how much risk your CFO will tolerate is often not the person you are speaking to eighteen months later. Sometimes that is fine. Sometimes you discover it in the middle of a claim, which is the worst possible moment to be explaining your own history to someone new. ... These work whether or not your broker has been acquired, and they are more useful than asking a firm directly whether it is about to be sold. 1. Who owns the firm today, and has that changed in the last three years? A straight answer takes one sentence. Hesitation is itself informative. 2. How many times has our account team changed in the last three years? This is the single most revealing question on the list, because churn shows up here before it shows up in service. 3. Who are the named people on our account, and who covers when they are out? A firm that answers with names is describing a team. A firm that answers with a service model is describing a queue. 4. Has our compensation arrangement changed? You are entitled to this in writing. Federal law requires brokers and consultants to ERISA group health plans expecting $1,000 or more in compensation to disclose direct and indirect compensation to the plan fiduciary, and an ownership change is a reasonable moment to ask again. 5. Has our carrier access or market access changed? Larger platforms sometimes gain access, and sometimes consolidate to preferred carriers. Either can affect what you are shown at renewal. Ask which markets were approached last year and which were not.

headline: What Aon's confirmed $17B USI deal means for your benefits team | Human Resources Director
summary_text: The deal is done. Aon confirmed Monday, August 31, 2026, that it will acquire USI Insurance Services — one of the largest employee benefits and insurance brokerage firms in the United States — from KKR & Co. and other shareholders for $17.0 billion. For HR leaders at midsize U.S. employers, the announcement marks the start of a significant shift in the advisory landscape. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. When it does, more than 10,500 USI employees across nearly 200 U.S. offices will operate under the umbrella of Aon, a global professional services firm with a historically large-enterprise focus. The midmarket — where most of USI's employer clients sit — is now the explicit strategic priority for the combined organization. ... USI Insurance Services, headquartered in Valhalla, New York, provides employee benefits consulting, group health insurance advisory, retirement plan services, property and casualty coverage, and voluntary benefits solutions to employers across the country. With approximately $3 billion in annual revenue, it is the tenth-largest insurance broker in the U.S., according to Aon's official announcement. ... Aon is explicit about what it is buying: access to a segment it has historically underserved. The U.S. middle market represents more than $40 billion in insurance and benefits opportunity and accounts for more than one-third of U.S. commercial property and casualty direct written premium, according to Aon's deal announcement. USI gives Aon a ready-made platform in that segment — one with existing employer relationships, adviser networks, and benefits consulting capabilities that would take years to build organically. Greg Case put it directly: the combination will "substantially enhance our middle-market footprint." That ambition matters because it signals intent. Aon is not acquiring USI to manage it quietly — it is acquiring it to compete aggressively in the midmarket. That means investment in the platform, which could benefit employers through expanded resources, technology, and carrier access. It also means the combined firm will be a formidable competitor to the independent and regional brokerages that many midsize employers currently use. ... Rising benefits costs are already putting pressure on HR teams to extract more value from their advisory relationships. As employers tighten their grip on benefits spending amid surging healthcare costs, having a well-resourced adviser matters — but so does ensuring that adviser's incentives remain aligned with the employer, not just the acquiring firm's debt repayment schedule.

headline: Tunisia upgrades the digital backbone of higher education - Huawei
summary_text: Tunisia is positioning itself as one of North Africa’s digital innovation hubs. As part of the country’s digital transformation strategy, universities and education agencies are investing in new infrastructure to support online learning, research collaboration, and digital skills development. At the center of that effort is Khawarizmi Computing Center (CCK), a technology organization under Tunisia’s Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research. Established in 1976, CCK provides computing, networking, and digital services to universities and higher education institutions across the country. As demand for digital education services has grown, CCK has worked with Huawei to modernize the infrastructure supporting Tunisia’s higher education system. ... The rapid growth of remote learning, cloud services, AI applications, and digital research platforms has increased pressure on university networks and data infrastructure across Africa. Tunisian universities need more bandwidth, lower latency, stronger cybersecurity protection, and better tools for managing increasingly complex networks. The organization also faced challenges around data management and disaster recovery as universities expanded their digital services. According to CCK, educational institutions needed more reliable ways to synchronize data between sites, protect research information, and maintain service continuity. ... ### Building cloud and network infrastructure To support those needs, CCK and Huawei upgraded multiple parts of Tunisia’s education infrastructure, including cloud computing, networking, storage, backup, and security systems. A central component of the project is Huawei CloudStack, a platform to support virtual data centers and digital services for universities. CloudStack allows institutions to host applications including online learning systems, video conferencing, cloud desktops, and ERP services, while centralizing management and improving data protection. CCK also expanded network connectivity between universities using fiber-optic infrastructure and Huawei’s SD-WAN technology, which helps organizations manage and optimize traffic across wide-area networks. The SD-WAN platform gives network administrators greater visibility into network performance while helping improve security and reliability across connected campuses. The project also included upgrades to network security systems and introduced Huawei’s iMaster NCE-Campus platform, which allows IT teams to centrally manage and monitor campus-wide networks. The system helps administrators identify problems more quickly and optimize network performance across the campus. ... Along with the infrastructure rollout, Huawei and Tunisian universities have expanded cooperation on ICT training and cybersecurity education. Huawei has worked with local schools to establish cybersecurity laboratories and introduce specialized training programs linked to the company’s HCIA Security certification. (HCIA stands for Huawei-certified ICT Associate.) Such programs are designed to help students build skills relevant to security engineering and other ICT roles. The company has also supported student startup and entrepreneurship initiatives through programs including the Huawei ICT Competition, Seeds for the Future, and Spark Competition.

headline: New Libyan telecom firm to launch data center in 2027 - DCD
summary_text: A new private telecom firm in Libya has unveiled plans for a new data center and 5G rollout in the country. Ozone Telecommunications and Technology Group, also known as the O3 Group, officially launched operations in Benghazi this week (19 October) as Libya aims to establish itself as a regional digital hub connecting Europe and Africa. – Getty Images The company expects that its new Tier III data center currently under construction will be operational in March 2027. Once completed, the facility will provide local hosting, cloud services, and business applications to telecommunications operators, financial institutions, government organizations, and corporate clients. The Data Center Map lists eight data centers in Libya. O3 also said it wants to establish a new 5G mobile operator supported by infrastructure for international connectivity, a fiber-optic network and a data center. A pilot launch of 5G services is scheduled for Benghazi by the end of 2026, with the commercial launch set for the second quarter of 2027. ... Meanwhile, the Medusa Submarine Cable System has reportedly completed the pre-laid shore end installation in Benghazi, which is the section of cable laid in advance between the land site and the offshore connection point. The Medusa subsea cable is an open-access underwater fiber-optic communications network stretching approximately 8,760 km (with core routes around 7,100 km) across the Mediterranean Sea. It is the longest submarine cable project in the Mediterranean, designed to link Southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Libya has 13 cable landing stations along the country's north coast, but only four subsea cables connect them. O3 will focus on developing international connectivity via the Medusa submarine cable.

headline: Libya’s O3 Group Unveils Digital Infrastructure Plans After Medusa Cable Landing - TechAfrica News
summary_text: O3 Group (Ozone Group for Telecom & Technology) is a privately owned Libyan telecommunications and technology company, established in 2024 and headquartered in Benghazi. It is chaired by Dr Faisel Gergab, a former chairman of the Libya Post, Telecommunications and Information Technology Company (LPTIC), and operates under the theme “Limitless Empowerment.” The fact sheet, dated 17 October 2026, accompanies the company’s public introduction, which coincides with the first Medusa submarine cable landing in Libya at Benghazi. The company’s stated aim is to build an integrated digital infrastructure platform for the country, with its various projects at different stages of construction, deployment and development. ... The foundation of that strategy is the Medusa submarine cable, a neutral, open-access system stretching more than 8,700 km across the Mediterranean and linking Europe, North Africa and the wider region. It is designed with up to 24 fibre pairs per segment and up to 20 Tbps per pair. Benghazi received the first Libyan landing on 17 October 2026, and a second is planned for Tripoli, which would give the east and west of the country geographically diverse international connections. Norman Albi, CEO of the Medusa Submarine Cable System, is due to attend the Benghazi event. ... From the landing points, O3 plans to carry traffic across a national fibre and DWDM transmission network of roughly 12,000–13,000 km, with about 100 transmission sites and a design backbone capacity of around 1.6 Tbps. The network is meant to serve mobile operators, internet service providers, businesses, government bodies and data centres. Fibre already extends south from Benghazi toward Kufra, which O3 sees as the basis for a longer-term corridor to Chad and other landlocked African markets, positioning Libya as a transit point for digital traffic between Europe and Africa. On the domestic side, O3 is developing a Tier III data centre in Benghazi with more than 160 racks, an initial capacity of about 2 MW expandable to roughly 5 MW, and a design availability benchmark of about 99.982%. It uses N+2 power backup, N+1 precision cooling, multiple fibre routes and round-the-clock monitoring, and it holds Uptime Institute Tier III Certified Design Documents, meaning it is designed to be concurrently maintainable. The facility is aimed at carriers, cloud providers, financial institutions, government, oil and gas firms and large enterprises, and is intended to let more data and content be hosted inside Libya. For consumers and businesses, O3 Mobile is planned as a 4G, 5G and Fixed Wireless Access network of approximately 3,200 sites, designed to support more than 3.2 million users. It is still under development and will be introduced in stages ahead of wider commercial rollout. Alongside it, O3 is building enterprise and wholesale capabilities including backbone connectivity, international internet capacity, cloud and hosting, private networks, IoT, GRX, IPX, signalling and VSAT services. ... Beyond infrastructure, the company is developing two supporting initiatives in Benghazi. O3 Technology Village is a planned innovation ecosystem combining technology, education, business and public spaces for companies, entrepreneurs and researchers. O3 Academy is the training arm, with programmes in telecommunications and technology training, professional development, certification and partnerships with international education providers, plus plans for a broader initiative offering internationally recognised qualifications within Libya. ... One point worth noting is that most of the figures, including the fibre footprint, backbone capacity, data centre capacity and mobile network scale, are described as planned or design targets rather than operational achievements. The only completed milestone stated is the first Medusa landing in Benghazi.

headline: Orange Maroc signs three cybersecurity deals
summary_text: Orange Maroc partners with Fortinet, NETSCOUT and Ivanti to strengthen cybersecurity and protect critical infrastructure, networks and connected devices. Businesses, government offices and industrial sites are facing growing risks as they move more of their work online. Orange Maroc has announced three partnerships with global cybersecurity firms to help protect their systems, networks and connected devices. The telecom operator signed agreements with Fortinet, NETSCOUT and Ivanti during Morocco CyberSecurity Week 2026, which runs from 12 to 14 October in Rabat. Orange Maroc is a silver sponsor of the event and its cloud and security partner. The deals will help the company protect industrial control systems, detect threats to networks and identify and fix security weaknesses in computers and other connected devices. Orange Maroc has obtained an Operational Technology (OT) specialisation through its partnership with Fortinet. The technology is used to protect the systems that control industrial operations, including those found in energy networks, water facilities, transport hubs and factories. The agreement with NETSCOUT will expand protection beyond conventional defences against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, which try to overwhelm a website or network with traffic. The new approach will provide wider network visibility and help detect changing threats. The partnership with Ivanti will focus on managing security risks across devices. Its technology can help organisations identify equipment, detect vulnerabilities and automate fixes, including software updates that close security gaps. ... ortinet, founded in 2000 and based in Sunnyvale, California, specialises in network security, secure access service edge (SASE) technology and industrial cybersecurity. It is listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker FTNT. Its products include FortiGate firewalls and the Fortinet Security Fabric, a platform designed to bring different security systems together. In the Orange Maroc partnership, Fortinet’s expertise will focus on operational technology. This includes supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and industrial control systems (ICS), which help operate machinery and manage industrial processes. These systems are used in sectors such as manufacturing, energy and transport, where a cyberattack can disrupt physical operations as well as digital services. NETSCOUT was founded in 1984 and is based in Westford, Massachusetts. Listed on the Nasdaq under NTCT, it provides tools for monitoring network performance, examining data traffic and detecting cyber threats. Its security portfolio includes technology from Arbor Networks, which NETSCOUT acquired to strengthen its DDoS detection and protection business. The partnership with Orange Maroc will use network monitoring, traffic analysis and threat intelligence to help identify suspicious activity and protect large networks against changing attacks. Ivanti was formed in 2017 through the merger of HEAT Software and LANDESK, although the businesses behind it date back to 1985. The privately held company is based in South Jordan, Utah, and specialises in unified endpoint management, IT service management and security. Its tools allow organisations to discover, manage and secure devices from a central system. They can also help automate vulnerability detection, software patching and other corrective actions. ... In early October 2026, Orange Maroc signed separate enterprise agreements during the AUSIM convention to deploy sovereign cloud platforms backed by graphics processing unit (GPU) infrastructure. The systems are intended to support artificial intelligence processing within local enterprise environments. Orange Cyberdefense, the group’s cybersecurity business, also operates a hub in Casablanca’s Technopolis. It serves organisations in Morocco and across North and West Africa. ... The three new partnerships add industrial protection, network monitoring and device security to Orange Maroc’s business services as companies and public institutions face growing pressure to protect their digital systems. Orange Maroc serves 18.8 million customers in the country. The company says its investments are intended to support the wider digital economy as businesses and public institutions rely more heavily on connected services. ... The agreements come as Morocco pursues its Maroc Digital 2030 strategy and prepares infrastructure for major international events, including the 2030 FIFA World Cup. Industry estimates value the country’s cybersecurity market at $157.11m in 2026. It is forecast to grow by an average of 8.67% a year, reaching $238.12m by 2031. Demand is growing particularly quickly for companies that manage cybersecurity on behalf of other organisations. Managed security services, threat detection and response, and security operations centres are expanding at an estimated annual rate of more than 13.5%. One industry estimate puts the combined market for managed detection and response (MDR) and security operations centres (SOCs) at $168m in 2026. Financial services account for an estimated 25.10% of business spending on cybersecurity, making banking, financial services and insurance a major source of demand. Healthcare is expected to see the fastest growth in cybersecurity spending, at an estimated 16.74% a year, as hospitals and other providers digitise medical records and face tighter regulatory requirements. Public institutions and state-owned companies must also follow information security and infrastructure protection guidance issued by the General Directorate for Information Systems Security (DGSSI). The market is creating opportunities for telecom operators to sell more than phone and internet services. By offering cybersecurity tools and managed protection, they can help businesses defend their systems while developing new sources of revenue.

summary_text: Vertiv and Cybastion signed an MoU targeting digital infrastructure across six Northwest and West African markets, with Morocco's hyperscale and AI ambitions at the centre. ... ## 01 Why it matters - Vertiv signed an MoU with Cybastion on Monday to collaborate on digital infrastructure in Northwest Africa. - The framework covers Morocco, Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal, Burkina Faso, Chad and Gabon. - Morocco's Ministry of Digital Transition signed a separate MoU with Vertiv in July this year. - Zineb Kamri cited Morocco's ambition to become a regional digital hub attracting hyperscale and AI investment. - No contract values, capacity figures or rollout dates were disclosed. ... ## 02 The story Vertiv signed a memorandum of understanding with US-based Cybastion on Monday to create a framework for joint digital infrastructure projects across Northwest Africa, with Morocco positioned as the anchor market for hyperscale and AI data centre investment. The agreement covers six countries where both companies already have active engagement and what Vertiv calls strategic alignment: Morocco, Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal, Burkina Faso, Chad and Gabon. For Vertiv, the deal is about getting into large-scale infrastructure projects earlier. The company supplies power, cooling and critical physical infrastructure for data centres, and Cybastion brings established relationships inside government-led digital transformation programmes — a channel that matters in markets where sovereign cloud and national AI strategies drive procurement. ... ## What does the partnership actually cover? The MoU establishes a framework rather than a concrete project pipeline. There are no contract values, capacity figures or rollout dates attached to the announcement. Zineb Kamri, regional director for Northwest Africa at Vertiv, framed the agreement as a scalable structure the two companies can apply wherever joint opportunities emerge. "Cybastion has already established a strong footprint in West and Central Africa and is actively expanding into North Africa," Kamri said in a statement. "This geographic reach complements Vertiv's regional growth strategy. Morocco, in particular, represents a key market, especially given its ambition to become a regional digital hub and attract hyperscale and AI infrastructure investments." ... The announcement is an MoU, not a contract, and neither company disclosed financial terms or specific projects. The commercial substance will depend on whether national digitalisation programmes in the six named markets convert into funded data centre builds. Cybastion's leadership put the emphasis on speed of deployment. CEO Dr. Thierry Wandji said the collaboration with Vertiv "strengthens our ability to rapidly deploy the critical digital infrastructure needed to help African countries move toward digital sovereignty."

headline: NEC Africa wins $75,000 4G contract with Savannah Uganda — Telecom Gazette
summary_text: G deal with Savannah Uganda NEC Africa has landed a US$75,000 4G expansion deal with Kampala ISP Savannah Uganda, deploying Juniper MX304 routers for its 50,000 subscribers, and is targeting Uganda's banks on the back of new Bank of Uganda data residency rules. ... - NEC Africa won a US$75,000 contract with Savannah Uganda for 4G expansion in Kampala and surrounding regions. - The deployment uses Juniper Networks MX304 routing equipment. - Savannah Uganda currently serves approximately 50,000 users and is preparing for wider East African expansion. - Geoffrey Karanja, NEC Africa key account manager, confirmed additional ISP targets: Airtel Uganda, Robtelcom, Sprint and Revia. - Bank of Uganda now requires encryption systems and security infrastructure to be hosted within national borders, driving HSM demand. ... ## 02 The story NEC Africa has won a US$75,000 contract with Kampala-based internet service provider Savannah Uganda to expand 4G connectivity in the capital and surrounding districts, the vendor confirmed this week. The deal positions NEC Africa as a core infrastructure partner for an operator that currently serves roughly 50,000 subscribers and is preparing for wider East African expansion. ... ## What does the contract cover? The deployment centres on Juniper Networks' MX304 routing platform, which NEC Africa says will give Savannah Uganda headroom as its subscriber base and regional footprint grow. The MX304 is a compact edge router built for high-density 100 Gigabit Ethernet aggregation, suited to operators scaling from metro to regional traffic volumes. NEC Africa key account manager Geoffrey Karanja said in a statement on Tuesday that the vendor has also been engaging more broadly across Uganda's enterprise and financial services market. ... ## Why is the financial sector in play? A regulatory shift by the Bank of Uganda is generating fresh demand for locally hosted encryption and security hardware, Karanja explained. The central bank now requires that encryption systems and security infrastructure remain hosted within national borders — a data residency rule that has put hardware security modules (HSMs) back on bank procurement lists. NEC Africa is pitching its Utimaco HSM and encryption portfolio to banks that need to meet the new requirement while protecting customer data and transaction traffic. "Uganda is an important market for us," Karanja said. "There is a lot of traction within that market from an internet penetration point of view and a lot of development happening across Uganda from an enterprise, SME and corporate connectivity perspective." ... ## Which other ISPs are in the pipeline? Karanja named four targets beyond Savannah Uganda: Airtel Uganda, Robtelcom, Sprint and new entrant Revia. Airtel is by far the largest of the four, operating as a mobile network operator with millions of subscribers, while Robtelcom and Sprint sit in the smaller ISP tier. Revia is an emerging player seeking its first network contracts. The breadth of the list underlines how NEC Africa is pairing a small anchor deal with Savannah Uganda to a wider sales motion across Uganda's ISP ecosystem, from incumbents to greenfield entrants.

headline: Orange, Focus partner to keep data in Tunisia | ITWeb Africa
summary_text: Orange Tunisia and technology company Focus are partnering to provide Tunisian businesses with locally hosted cloud and IT infrastructure, giving companies greater control over where their data is stored and how their digital systems are managed. Announced on 5 October, the partnership will provide cloud environments hosted and operated in Tunisia to businesses of different sizes, with a focus on data control, security, performance and local technical support. The companies say the offering will give businesses greater visibility over their data and infrastructure while allowing them to scale computing resources as their needs change. The partnership comes as organisations increasingly consider data location, infrastructure management and local technical support alongside cost and computing capacity when adopting cloud services. Under the agreement, Orange Tunisia will contribute its business network and ICT capabilities, while Focus will provide its cloud infrastructure and digital transformation expertise. The companies say the combined offering is intended to make cloud adoption more accessible to local businesses. For companies modernising legacy IT systems, locally hosted cloud services offer an alternative to maintaining extensive physical infrastructure. Businesses can instead access computing resources while relying on local providers for infrastructure management and technical support. ... The emphasis on local hosting comes as African businesses and governments pay greater attention to where digital infrastructure and data are located. Keeping computing resources within national borders can give organisations greater visibility over their digital environments, although local hosting does not by itself guarantee security, regulatory compliance or protection from cyber threats. The partnership also comes as businesses adopt more data-intensive applications, artificial intelligence and digital services, increasing demand for reliable computing infrastructure and making control over underlying systems more important. ... For Tunisia, locally operated cloud infrastructure could support the development of a domestic cloud ecosystem and give businesses access to technical expertise without relying entirely on support teams based outside the country. The immediate commercial scale of the partnership remains unclear. Orange Tunisia and Focus have not disclosed investment, infrastructure capacity, customer pricing or the number of businesses they expect to serve. Its impact will ultimately depend on factors including reliability, pricing and scalability, as well as whether businesses see sufficient value in local hosting to shift workloads from established international cloud providers. The partnership nevertheless signals growing interest in locally operated cloud infrastructure as Tunisia's digital economy expands, with Orange Tunisia and Focus positioning local ownership, support and data-location control as key elements of their offering.

headline: Egypt Licenses $400M Hassan Allam Data-Center Operator
summary_text: ## ⚡ Key Takeaways On June 15, 2026, Egypt’s National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (NTRA) licensed Hassan Allam Digital Infrastructure — an arm of a major Egyptian engineering group, partnered with local VC firm A15 — to build and operate a $400 million data-center and cloud complex serving government, financial and business clients. It is the NTRA’s tenth data-center license in two years, showing a deliberate program to convert cloud demand into domestically owned capacity. Bottom Line: The sovereignty value is control, not location: local ownership keeps keys, administration and jurisdiction onshore. Algerian engineering groups should pair with domestic tech investors, design a sovereign-cloud offer around a state anchor tenant, and compete on provable sovereign control before foreign local-zones capture the localization demand. ... The interesting thing about Egypt’s newest data-center deal is who is building it. On June 15, 2026, in Cairo, Egypt’s National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (NTRA) granted a license to Hassan Allam Digital Infrastructure and Data Center Solutions, backed by a $400 million first-phase investment, at a ceremony attended by Communications and Information Technology Minister Raafat Hindi. Hassan Allam is not a foreign hyperscaler parachuting capacity onto Egyptian soil — it is an arm of one of Egypt’s largest homegrown engineering and construction groups, now moving into digital infrastructure. The customer list is the tell. According to w.media’s report on the license, the facility will serve “government entities, financial institutions, and both national and international businesses.” That ordering matches exactly the buyer profile driving sovereign-cloud demand across the region: the state first, regulated finance second, general enterprise third. Egypt is not licensing a commodity colocation shed; it is licensing a facility positioned to host the workloads a government most wants kept on domestic, supervised infrastructure.

headline: Shaping Africa’s Digital Future: Inside Nokia and Orange Egypt’s 28-Year Co-Innovation - Telecom Review Africa
summary_text: Africa’s telecom sector has entered a pivotal phase, with operators balancing continued 2G/3G legacy support against accelerating demand for 4G and 5G capacity, rising data consumption, and growing pressure to modernize operations through automation and AI. Egypt, one of the region’s largest and most closely watched markets, offers a useful lens into how these dynamics play out in practice. Increasingly, the depth and continuity of an operator-vendor relationship is shaping the pace and direction of this evolution. In an exclusive interview with Telecom Review Africa, Dr. Ayman Amiri, CTIO of Orange Egypt, and Mikko Lavanti, President of Nokia Middle East & Africa, reflected on a partnership that spans nearly three decades of joint work, from GSM through 5G, and how that foundation is now guiding operational modernization efforts with implications beyond Egypt’s borders. ... Orange Egypt’s mobile journey has been closely intertwined with Nokia’s, with the partnership spanning 28 years and supporting successive generations of mobile technology and network evolution. For Dr. Ayman Amiri, continuity is imperative. “Together, we have successfully navigated every major technology transition—from GSM to 3G, 4G, 5G, and today’s network modernization,” he explained. This long-standing collaboration has enabled Orange Egypt to build a resilient network while continuously improving coverage, capacity, and customer experience. The result, he argued, is more than a well-maintained network, noting that, “More importantly, it has established a strong foundation for future-ready, software-driven, and AI-enabled networks.” ... That appetite for innovation is most visible today in Orange Egypt’s internal transformation program, known as ‘Make Orange Great Again’, a strategic initiative centered on operational excellence, network modernization, and sustained improvements in customer experience. According to Dr. Amiri, the program rests on three pillars: network modernization and automation, maximizing value, and operational excellence. “By leveraging AI-driven optimization, predictive maintenance, automation of operational processes, and targeted capacity expansion, we have significantly improved network availability, reduced congestion, accelerated incident resolution, and increased operational efficiency,” he explained. Overall, these pillars have translated into a more reliable and consistent customer experience. ... Reflecting this partnership approach in tangible terms, Orange Egypt and Nokia collaborated on a solar energy trial at the KS-HK-BATTAH site, which has since emerged as a reference model for more sustainable telecom infrastructure across the region. The project brought together teams from both organizations—across network, energy, operations, rollout, and project management—to design and implement an integrated renewable energy solution that enables the site to run on 100% solar power, supported by lithium battery storage, without any compromise to network performance or service continuity. The conventional 27 KVA diesel generator was switched off entirely, reducing fuel consumption by approximately 55 to 60 liters per day and eliminating generator maintenance requirements altogether.

headline: Nokia Bets on AI to Power Africa's Next Telecom Era - Tech Orijin
summary_text: Nokia is betting big on artificial intelligence. As Africa’s telecom industry enters a new phase, the Finnish technology giant wants a leading role. It once dominated Nigeria’s mobile phone market. Now it’s positioning itself as a key player in Africa’s AI-driven network future. For decades, Africa’s telecom story centered on basic connectivity. Towers went up. Fibre cables stretched across the continent. Operators rolled out 4G and, eventually, 5G. Today, AI is changing what these networks must deliver. Instead of simply moving data, networks now need to process it and act on it in real time. ... Africa’s telecom market is currently worth $66 billion. By 2030, it’s projected to reach $90.3 billion. That growth is drawing fresh investment from global tech giants like Meta, Google, and Microsoft. These companies are pouring money into subsea cables, cloud infrastructure, and AI systems. As a result, they’re gaining growing influence over the digital backbone that will power Africa’s next stage of development. For Nokia, the pressure is real. It must carve out a role in this emerging AI economy. Otherwise, it risks becoming a low-value connectivity vendor. ... Nokia still leans on 4G and 5G as the foundation of its African business. The company works with major operators, including Airtel, Orange, Vodacom, Safaricom, and Maroc Telecom. It also has active 5G deployments in Angola, South Africa, and Ethiopia. But Nokia wants more than connectivity revenue. Its Artificial Intelligence Radio Access Network platform, known as AI-RAN, blends existing telecom infrastructure with GPU-based computing. This brings AI workloads directly into the network. Nokia launched the commercial version of this platform on July 15, 2026. This shift matters a lot. Nokia has largely exited the consumer phone business. So it needs new revenue streams beyond hardware sales. That need is even more urgent as lower-cost rivals like Huawei keep expanding across the continent. ... Meanwhile, economics may prove tougher than technology. AI-RAN infrastructure is expensive. GPU-accelerated processing at centralized hubs can cost tens of thousands of dollars per node. In some cases, it exceeds $100,000. Power consumption adds another layer of cost. This is especially significant in markets already burdened by high electricity, generator, and diesel expenses. As a result, analysts expect AI-RAN to first take hold in high-traffic urban areas and enterprise environments, where returns are easier to justify. ... Still, practical use cases are already emerging. For example, Mausoof pointed to a Nokia deployment during the Hajj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia. There, AI-powered automation managed between 10,000 and 15,000 network changes during peak demand. This kind of automation reduces energy use and maintenance needs. Because of that, it may offer a more realistic path forward for African markets than widespread GPU deployment. ... Looking ahead, trials in Africa are expected to begin as early as the first quarter of 2027. Further announcements will likely follow at Mobile World Congress 2027. Full commercialization is targeted for 2028. Even so, Mausoof expects broader adoption across the continent to extend well beyond 2030. That’s because technology maturity and infrastructure readiness vary widely from one market to another.

headline: Disty Technologies : Quatre ans de transformation
summary_text: Entrée sur le marché en juillet 2022 avec la promesse de financer une nouvelle phase de développement, la société affiche aujourd’hui une activité et une rentabilité en nette progression. Le distributeur IT mise désormais sur l’intelligence artificielle, la cybersécurité, le cloud et les infrastructures numériques pour prolonger cette trajectoire. ... Il y a quatre ans, Disty Technologies faisait figure de pionnier. Le distributeur de produits et solutions informatiques devenait, le 20 juillet 2022, la première PME à rejoindre le marché alternatif de la Bourse de Casablanca. L’opération, d’un montant de près de 172 MDH, avait été réalisée au prix de 284 DH par action et portait sur un flottant de 61%. Depuis, l’entreprise a changé de dimension. En 2025, son chiffre d’affaires s’est établi autour de 638 MDH, en hausse de plus de 16% sur un an. L’Ebitda a atteint 38,1 MDH, en progression de 18,7%, et le résultat net a bondi de 33,6%, à près de 25,9 MDH. Sur une période plus longue, la transformation est encore plus perceptible avec un chiffre d’affaires qui est passé de 496,6 MDH en 2022 à 637,4 MDH en 2025 et l’Ebitda de 21,1 à 38,1 MDH. Dans le même temps, la marge nette est remontée de 0,8 à 4,1%. ... Disty a parallèlement travaillé sur son outil opérationnel. La société a obtenu la certification ISO 9001 en 2024 et le statut d’Opérateur économique agréé auprès de la douane. Elle a déployé des outils de Business Intelligence permettant de suivre les ventes, les stocks et les balances âgées et a renforcé l’interconnexion entre ses systèmes logistiques et son ERP. Pour 2026, elle prépare les certifications ISO 14001 et ISO 45001. IA et cybersécurité, nouveaux relais La prochaine étape se jouera davantage sur la composition de l’activité. Au-delà de la distribution classique de PC, imprimantes et équipements, Disty vise les segments à plus forte valeur ajoutée, à savoir le cloud, la cybersécurité, le gaming, l’affichage dynamique, l’intelligence artificielle et les infrastructures de data centers. En 2025, l’entreprise a notamment conclu un partenariat avec PNY/NVIDIA comme distributeur à valeur ajoutée de solutions destinées à l’IA et aux centres de données au Maroc. Le management estime disposer d’une marge de progression significative. Disty travaille déjà avec quelque 1.600 professionnels de l’informatique sur un marché estimé à environ 2.000 acteurs. Le potentiel de croissance est donc non négligeable, avec à la clé plusieurs moteurs, dont le renouvellement des équipements acquis pendant les années Covid, l’arrivée de PC intégrant des fonctionnalités d’IA et les investissements publics liés à la transformation numérique, notamment dans l’éducation et la santé. ... Un marché IT en pleine recomposition Le marché IT marocain accélère sa mutation sous l’effet du cloud, de la cybersécurité, des data centers et de l’IA. Casablanca accueille déjà plus de 25 data centers, avec de nouvelles capacités en développement. DC Market Insights évalue le marché marocain des data centers à 489,7 millions de dollars en 2025 et le projette à 965,8 millions en 2035. La cybersécurité suit la même tendance. Selon Mordor Intelligence, ce marché passerait de 144,6 millions de dollars en 2025 à 238,1 millions en 2031, soit une croissance annuelle moyenne de 8,67%. À cela s’ajoutent les ambitions dans l’IA. Le gouvernement vise une contribution de 100 MMDH supplémentaires au PIB d’ici 2030, avec notamment le développement du cloud et de data centers souverains.

headline: Maroc : le cloud et l’IA au cœur d’un accord avec l’américain Vertiv - We are Tech
summary_text: Alors que les projets liés à l’intelligence artificielle et aux data centers se multiplient au Maroc, le royaume renforce son écosystème d’infrastructures numériques en s’alliant à de nouveaux partenaires internationaux. Le ministère de la Transition numérique et de la Réforme de l’administration du Maroc et Vertiv, une entreprise américaine spécialisée dans les infrastructures numériques critiques, ont signé, le lundi 27 juillet à Rabat, un Mémorandum d’entente (MoU) portant sur le développement des infrastructures numériques, du cloud computing et de l’intelligence artificielle (IA). Le document a été paraphé par la ministre déléguée chargée de la Transition numérique et de la Réforme de l’administration, Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni (photo, à droite), et le Managing Director de Vertiv Africa, Wojtek Piorko (photo, à gauche). L’accord prévoit notamment des échanges d’expertise, la réalisation d’études techniques, l’identification de projets structurants et l’exploration de solutions adaptées aux besoins du Maroc. La coopération couvre également le calcul à haute performance, les centres de données ainsi que les solutions électriques et de refroidissement nécessaires à leur fonctionnement. L’accord inclut également des réflexions relatives au développement du centre de données souverain de 50 MW à Rabat, destiné à renforcer les capacités nationales en matière de cloud souverain, d’hébergement des services publics numériques, d’IA, de calcul intensif et de cybersécurité. Vertiv apportera son expertise technique sur les infrastructures de centres de données, les solutions électriques et de refroidissement ainsi que les technologies nécessaires au développement d’infrastructures cloud intensives. ... Le partenariat avec Vertiv s’inscrit par ailleurs dans la mise en œuvre de la stratégie Digital Morocco 2030, de la feuille de route « AI Made in Morocco » et de la feuille de route nationale pour le développement du cloud 2025‑2030. Il intervient alors que le Maroc engage plusieurs projets dans les domaines des centres de données, du cloud et du calcul à haute performance, sur fonds de développement des usages de l’intelligence artificielle et de numérisation des services publics. Depuis le début de l’année, le Royaume a notamment signé des accords avec Nexus Core Systems, ALTEN, Capgemini et Huawei dans différents domaines liés au numérique et à l’intelligence artificielle. Le partenariat avec Vertiv porte, pour sa part, sur un volet plus directement lié aux infrastructures qui soutiennent ces technologies, avec un accent sur les centres de données, le calcul haute performance et les systèmes électriques et de refroidissement.
