summary_text: AECI Specialty Chemicals has officially announced its appointment as the South African agent for Prime Evolue Singapore and their premier EVOLUE™ metallocene linear low-density polyethylene (m-LLDPE) range # AECI Specialty Chemicals introduces Prime Polymers’ EVOLUE™ bimodal metallocene polyethylene THE South African flexible packaging sector is undergoing a rapid evolution, driven by the demand for higher production efficiencies, superior film performance and sustainable design. To help local converters meet these challenging market requirements, AECI Specialty Chemicals has officially announced its appointment as the South African agent for Prime Evolue Singapore and their premier EVOLUE™ metallocene linear low-density polyethylene (m-LLDPE) range. This partnership brings world-class polymer technology directly to local manufacturers, supported by AECI’s dedicated team of technical professionals. ... Redefining processability and strength: the bimodal advantage Historically, film extruders have faced a difficult trade-off between the outstanding mechanical properties of metallocenecatalysed resins and the ease of processing associated with conventional low-density polyethylene (LDPE). Conventional mono-modal LLDPE resins often struggle with processing constraints, while mono-modal metallocene grades can require higher extrusion pressures and specialised equipment. EVOLUE™ overcomes this historic bottleneck by combining a state-of-the-art metallocene catalyst with Mitsui Chemicals’ proprietary bimodal process technology. The bimodal process utilises two cascaded reactors to produce polymers with precisely controlled composition and molecular weight distributions (MWD). By carefully tailoring the polymer structure, EVOLUE™ features a narrower MWD than conventional polyethylene, resulting in a significantly reduced presence of problematic low- and high-molecularweight components. The reduction of low-molecular-weight components directly addresses blocking and odour issues. Simultaneously, reducing the high-molecular-weight components enhances both fi lm clarity and heatsealability. Crucially, because bimodal EVOLUE™ maintains a broader MWD than monomodal metallocene grades, it delivers exceptional ease of processing, higher extrusion outputs and lower melt temperatures without sacrificing mechanical strength. In many co-extrusion and blending applications, this advanced processability can even eliminate the need to blend in LDPE, offering converters substantial cost savings. ... Outstanding physical and optical performance For convertors producing high-performance flexible films, EVOLUE™ provides a step-change in mechanical properties: • Unrivalled puncture and dart impact strength: Key grades such as SP1520, SP1510, and SP0510 exhibit outstanding dart impact performance, reaching the maximum nonbreak test limit of over 1500g on a 40 micron blown film. Puncture strength and pinhole resistance are also superior to other standard m-LLDPE grades of similar densities, offering exceptional package integrity during transport. This outstanding strength profile opens significant opportunities for down-gauging (thickness reduction) to reduce raw material consumption and total cost. • Extremely low gel count: Gels (or “fish eyes”) are a common cause of printing defects and film structural weakness. EVOLUE™ is specially designed to maintain a very low gel count, which guarantees a flawless printing surface, improves aesthetic appearance, and minimises web wastage during high-speed printing and converting. • Low odour and low taste transfer: Using a specialised treatment to minimise volatiles, EVOLUE™ achieves an incredibly low odour index of 31.1. This is significantly lower than conventional C4-LLDPE (36.1), conventional LDPE (36.2), and competitor metallocene C8-LLDPE (41.9), ensuring that the original taste and flavour of packaged food and liquids remain entirely unaffected. ... Tailored grades for diverse applications The EVOLUE™ portfolio imported and stocked by AECI Specialty Chemicals includes specialised grades tailored for specifi c converting processes. In blown film applications, the range includes SP2020, SP2320, and SP2520, which are highly recommended for liquid standing pouches due to their balance of stiffness and sealing integrity. For liquid sachets, frozen foods, and bag-inbox (BIB) packaging, grades like SP0510 and SP1520 act as excellent strength and heat-seal modifiers. When low-temperature heat sealing and rapid hot tack are required for high-speed form-fi ll-seal (FFS) lines, SP0820 and SP0510 excel. Additionally, SP3010 and SP3210 are optimised for heavy-duty industrial shipping bags that demand maximum tensile and tear strength. ... For cast film extrusion and extrusion coating, AECI offers grades such as SP0540, SP2040, and SP1071C, expanding the technology to lamination and polypropylene (PP) modifi cation. ... A bridge to circular and sustainable packaging Beyond performance, EVOLUE™ provides a practical pathway for South African brand owners and converters to achieve their Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and sustainability goals. The resin is highly compatible with mechanical recycling streams and can be blended with recycled PE or PP to improve the physical properties of post-consumer resins. Crucially, EVOLUE™ enables the design of high-barrier, fully recyclable mono-material structures. By using EVOLUE™ for both the printing substrate (such as BOPE or MDO films) and the high-performance sealant film, converters can replace non-recyclable multi-material laminates with fully recyclable all-polyethylene packaging. Furthermore, the global portfolio extends to chemical recycling options and renewable feedstocks under the bio-circular Prasus™ brand, reflecting Prime Polymers’ commitment to protecting life and resources on this planet. ... Partnering with AECI Specialty Chemicals As local polymer markets navigate supply challenges and technical transitions, AECI Specialty Chemicals stands ready to support convertors with its technical expertise. By partnering with global leaders like Prime Polymer, AECI ensures that South African technical industries have reliable access to high-performance polymers that meet the highest international standards. AECI’s experienced technical sales team is available to assist with formulation optimisation, trial support, and grade selection to optimise processing efficiency and final film performance.

summary_text: Caparol signs strategic partnership with Nasib Industrial Products to accelerate Africa expansion | ZAWYA Growth in Kenya has been fueled by Caparol’s Africa product assortment, developed to combine German quality standards with the requirements of African markets. Image Courtesy: Caparol ## Agreement strengthens supply across East Africa and lays the groundwork for expansion into West Africa DUBAI and NAIROBI: Caparol, the German premium paints and coatings brand, has signed a strategic agreement with Nasib Industrial Products Ltd in Kenya and, together with its local partners, will double production capacity in the country to meet rising demand across East Africa. The agreement expands Caparol’s local production, distribution and market presence, and positions Kenya as a manufacturing and supply hub for neighbouring markets. It builds on the dedicated Africa office Caparol opened in 2025, which has led the company’s regional business development since. “Africa represents one of the most exciting long-term growth opportunities for Caparol. The development we have seen in Kenya over the past year has exceeded our expectations and clearly demonstrates the potential for our brand and product portfolio across the continent,” said Dirk Schilmoeller, Managing Director Middle East & Africa, Caparol. **Demand driven by a range built for Africa** Growth in Kenya has been fueled by Caparol’s Africa product assortment, developed to combine German quality standards with the requirements of African markets. The range has gained traction in both professional and retail channels, and Caparol has secured a growing number of major residential, commercial and hospitality projects across the country. “Our strengthened partnership with Nasib Industrial Products Ltd is an important milestone in this journey. We are building a scalable business platform that allows us to grow beyond Kenya, expand our reach across East Africa and, in the next phase, explore opportunities in West Africa. Our ambition is to establish Caparol as a leading premium paints and coatings brand across key African markets.” **Investing ahead of demand** The planned capacity increase will support continued growth in Kenya and allow more efficient supply to neighbouring East African countries. Local manufacturing will also improve product availability and shorten supply chains. “The decision to significantly increase our production capacity reflects our confidence in the long-term potential of the African market. We are investing ahead of demand to ensure that our infrastructure, product availability and local capabilities can support the next phase of our expansion,” Schilmoeller added. **Next stop: West Africa** While East Africa remains the immediate focus, Caparol is evaluating opportunities in West Africa. Its approach is to build strong regional partnerships, develop locally relevant product portfolios and expand production and distribution step by step in selected markets. Alongside this, the company continues to invest in technical training, architect and consultant engagement, specification support, retail development and customer service. “Our vision goes well beyond individual markets. We see tremendous opportunities to bring Caparol’s German quality, innovation and technical expertise to a much broader African customer base. With the right local partners, strong products and continued investment, we are creating the foundation for sustainable growth across the continent,” concluded Schilmoeller.

headline: Training Day boosts customer awareness, product value
summary_text: Recognising a growing need among customers for direct access to technical expertise, application best practice and the latest industry innovations, specialised chemicals, adhesives and sealants manufacturer Henkel South Africa launched its first Training Day on August 17. Held at the Birchwood Hotel and the OR Tambo Conference Centre, in Johannesburg, the event brought together customers from a range of industries that rely on adhesive technologies, including manufacturing, packaging, consumer goods, industrial assembly, maintenance and engineering. The day was designed to bridge the gap between product knowledge and practical implementation, helping customers maximise performance, efficiency and reliability in their operations, says Henkel Adhesives South Africa head Natasha Naidoo. While professionals from different industries created opportunities for knowledge sharing and cross-industry learning, the versatility of Henkel’s technologies, with its “commitment to supporting customers across multiple sectors with tailored expertise” was also demonstrated. The initiative enabled attendees to explore how Henkel’s solutions could be optimised for a specific application, as products deliver their “utmost value” when customers understand how to apply them effectively in their own environments. “Without technical guidance, customers may miss opportunities to improve performance, reduce downtime, increase efficiency or achieve greater sustainability outcomes,” she adds. ... Real-World Challenges The Training Day was led by Henkel’s application engineers. Customers typically engage with them when operational, maintenance, reliability, productivity or infrastructure challenges impact on their business performance, says Naidoo. These range from broad objectives, such as reducing downtime, extending asset life, improving efficiency or lowering maintenance costs, to specific technical issues affecting individual components or applications. Naidoo says application engineering acts as a bridge between research and development, sales and customers, consequently translating market needs into technical innovations. This enables Henkel to validate performance through testing and trials, thereby reducing risk before full-scale implementation, in addition to co-innovation with customers﻿ helping to develop tailored solutions﻿. Application engineers demonstrated real-world applications during Training Day, which familiarised customers with the way in which Henkel’s solutions address challenges before they disrupt production. “We wanted to provide a platform for open dialogue, allowing us to better understand our customers’ challenges and work together on tailored solutions. It was a win-win for both sides,” Naidoo says. The demonstrations covered Henkel’s Loctite, Pattex and Tangit ﻿brands, with application engineers highlighting ﻿their ﻿uses﻿. Loctite is suited to applications where equipment, vehicles or infrastructure suffer recurring failures, owing to components loosening, leaking, wearing down, corroding or breaking. The application engineers help identify the root cause of these failures and recommend solutions that improve reliability, reduce unplanned downtime, extend equipment life and lower maintenance costs. During the event, Henkel also demonstrated how Loctite adhesives reduce assembly time, improve production efficiency and replace traditional mechanical fasteners. Pattex is typically ideal for building, repairing, fixing, mounting or sealing applications. The application engineers help ensure that the right product is selected for the specific materials, conditions and performance requirements, consequently enabling end-users to complete jobs efficiently and achieve professional-quality results without specialist equipment, Naidoo explains. Tangit is designed for leaking, damaged or poorly performing plastic piping systems in water, sanitation, irrigation, building and industrial applications. Engineers recommend the appropriate joining, sealing and repair solutions to improve system reliability, prevent water loss, ﻿and help build resilient infrastructure. Across all three brands, application engineers work closely with customers to understand their specific operational challenges to create practical solutions. Knowledge Partner Dedicated application engineering teams operate at customers’ facilities, supported by innovation centres that enable Henkel to test, validate, customise and co-develop solutions. This brings the company closer to customers and accelerates innovation and implementation. “Manufacturers have a responsibility to share knowledge, not just products. As technologies become more advanced, customers increasingly need support to apply them effectively and safely,” Naidoo elaborates. Consequently, Henkel ﻿offers technical training, ﻿best-practice sharing and guidance to help customers unlock more value. It also provides insights into technologies, sustainability trends, process innovations and industry best practice, which helps its customers improve their competitiveness. This creates a continuous feedback loop, during which customer challenges inform future innovation and new technologies are developed with real-world applications in mind, Naidoo says.

headline: The evolving role of inks and coatings - Packaging And Print Media
summary_text: ## PACKAGING in South Africa is undergoing significant technological change. As converters face shorter print runs, increasing SKU complexity, tighter quality expectations and pressure to reduce waste, the role of printing inks and coatings has evolved. Ink now contributes to the overall packaging solution, not just colour. 29 September 2026 in Acquisitions & evolutions At Siegwerk South Africa, this means working closely with converters to understand the application, substrate, press conditions, filling lines and end user or brand owner requirements before developing or recommending the most appropriate ink or coating. ‘Technology cannot simply be copied from another market and expected to work in South Africa,’ says Ashvika Harisunker, head of technology at Siegwerk. ‘It needs to be adapted to local press conditions, substrates, supply chains and customer requirements. That makes technical collaboration critical.’ ... #### Migration and curing flexibility In food, pharmaceutical and hygiene packaging, migration control is one of the most important technical considerations. Siegwerk’s global low-migration portfolio includes technologies such as SICURA Nutriflex 10, SICURA Nutriflex LEDTec and SICURA Nutriplast 2 New. These solutions are designed for suitable low migration in indirect food packaging while maintaining printability, adhesion, colour strength and production efficiency. The series covers UV- and LED-curing solutions for flexographic and sheetfed applications. Dual-cure technology is another area of interest, offering converters greater flexibility when moving between conventional UV and LED-UV curing. Siegwerk’s SICURA Flex Dual Cure series supports this flexibility while offering formulations aligned with the German Printing Ink Ordinance (GIO). ... #### Chemistry for a circular economy Sustainability is also influencing ink chemistry. Globally, Siegwerk has expanded its NC-free toolbox, including solutions for both lamination and surface printing on flexible polyolefin structures. In 2025, the company introduced NC-free surface-printing solutions for PE and PP in flexographic and gravure applications, supporting packaging designs that improve recyclability. ‘South African converters are adjusting packaging constructions in response to Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) requirements and circular-economy objectives,’ says Ashvika. ‘This is influencing packaging design, material selection and how waste is managed.’ One notable global development is the growing use of functional coatings. Siegwerk’s CIRKIT portfolio is designed for circular packaging and includes barrier coatings, heat-seal lacquers and other functional technologies. These coatings can provide oxygen, moisture and grease resistance, support recyclable mono-material structures, reduce reliance on multilayer constructions and enable the move to fibre-based packaging. Recent developments include CIRKIT OXYBAR WHITE, which combines oxygen-barrier functionality with white ink in a single printable layer, and CIRKIT NOVASEAL, a heat-seal lacquer portfolio for fibre-based and selected flexible packaging. ‘For South Africa, these technologies open opportunities in areas such as paperisation, flexible packaging, foodservice packaging and mono-material structures, where maintaining barrier and sealing performance is a key technical challenge,’ Ashvika notes. ... #### Beyond colour Colour management is becoming more closely linked to productivity and waste reduction. Siegwerk offers expanded colour gamut (ECG) technologies across UV-curable, solvent-based and water-based inks, using a fixed extended ink set that includes CMYKOGV. COLORWERK FastMatch Cloud, developed with X-Rite Pantone, integrates formulation, colour correction and quality control into a cloud-based platform. Across South Africa’s diverse mix of substrates and printing equipment, from new-generation presses to legacy machinery still in operation, technical support is important for successful implementation. Current technology projects include formulation optimisation, root-cause analysis, customer-specific ink development, colour consistency, sustainable label solutions and the evaluation of alternative packaging structures. ‘The objective is to understand the complete printing process and help the converter achieve the right combination of quality, productivity, regulatory compliance, cost-effectiveness and sustainability,’ says Ashvika. Siegwerk’s global portfolio reinforces this approach. It includes low-migration systems, NC-free inks, renewable and water-based technologies such as UniNATURE and CIRKIT functional coatings, with innovation focused on addressing packaging challenges.

headline: Moving with the market - Packaging And Print Media
summary_text: ## As recycled content, tightening regulations and digitalisation reshape the plastics industry, SAPY is responding with a combination of technical development, closer collaboration and continued investment in its people and systems. 21 September 2026 in Efficiencies The plastics industry is dealing with a more complicated brief than it did a few years ago. Customers want greater recycled content. Packaging requirements are tightening. Regulations are evolving across global markets. And manufacturers are expected to improve traceability, efficiency and product consistency at the same time. For SAPY, the response is not to treat these as separate challenges. Instead, the masterbatch manufacturer is building its approach around collaboration – with suppliers, converters, recyclers and customers – supported by investment in technology, regulatory knowledge and product development. ‘We don’t believe compliance should be approached in isolation,’ says Tracy Sinclair, head of market strategy and sales at SAPY. ‘Regulations continue to change, and understanding what is actually required means working with our suppliers, looking carefully at our own formulations and then sharing the relevant information with our customers.’ ... #### Compliance before the deadline The European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), heavy metals and food-contact requirements are increasingly part of the conversation for plastics and packaging companies, particularly those supplying export markets. SAPY’s approach is built around understanding these developments before they become an urgent customer requirement. The company works directly with established raw material suppliers, supported by its internal systems and ISO 22000:2018 food safety management system, to assess the implications for its formulations and the applications in which they are used. PFAS provides a practical example. SAPY has supplied a locally manufactured PFAS-free processing performance additive (PPA) to the South African market for more than 18 months. Developed using an active ingredient containing no fluorine compounds, the product is already in commercial use, with further independent testing underway to provide additional supporting data. At the same time, SAPY continues to supply its established PPA where it remains appropriate under applicable regulations. The appropriate solution depends on the application and destination market, says Tracy. ‘It isn’t simply about replacing one product with another,’ she says. ‘We need to understand the application, where the finished product is going and what requirements apply.’ Knowledge sharing is a significant part of the process. Regulatory developments are incorporated into SAPY’s internal training, equipping its business development team to discuss not only products, but the regulatory considerations surrounding their use. ... #### Making recycled polymers work The growing use of post-consumer recycled material presents a different, but equally technical challenge. South Africa’s recycling industry produces increasingly sophisticated PCR material, supported by sorting, processing and quality controls. Yet recycled polymer is fundamentally different from virgin material. Its previous lifecycle and the composition of the recovered stream can introduce variation that affects colour, appearance and processing. For converters, that variability makes consistency the challenge. SAPY works with converters and recycled-material suppliers to develop solutions suited to the specific material and end use. The company supplies masterbatches containing up to 100% PCR carrier and also develops solutions for applications containing high levels of recycled content. ‘Our approach is collaborative,’ says Tracy. ‘We work with converters and their material suppliers to understand the substrate, processing conditions, application and required outcome and then formulate accordingly.’ ... The technical solution must also make commercial sense. SAPY combines its formulation expertise with direct sourcing, purchasing volumes and manufacturing scale to keep solutions competitively priced. ‘It’s about finding the right balance,’ Tracy says. ‘We want to provide a masterbatch that works effectively with the material and application, while remaining commercially practical for our customer.’ ... SAPY is applying the same thinking to digitalisation. Its SAPY Live system has been part of the business since 2016. That experience has now led to SAPY Live V2, a bespoke platform supported by significant hardware and software upgrades. Rather than adapting the business to a conventional ERP or MRP system, SAPY has continued developing technology around its own operational requirements. ‘Our requirements, refined over more than 30 years of business, are extremely specific,’ says Tracy. ‘Rather than trying to make the business fit a system, we have continued developing a system around the way our business actually operates.’ ... The system is progressively extending across functions including warehouse management, CRM and R&D. QR code-driven, real-time information improves visibility and traceability, while integrated quality controls and operational data provide greater scope for identifying trends and improving decision-making. ... Majid has since obtained his Commercial Pilot Licence – Helicopter (CPL-H), while SAPY is building on the programme through a new brand ambassadorship with Enstrom Helicopter Corporation. A new helicopter will be based at the plant as part of the next phase of the initiative. ... The common thread is collaboration, and the recognition that navigating a changing industry requires suppliers, manufacturers and customers to work more closely together.

headline: How a Paint Business from Soshanguve Won R1 Million | SME South Africa
summary_text: A business that started in a five-square-metre structure in Soshanguve has grown into a paint manufacturing company with plans to expand local production. That business is Maduwa Paint World, founded by Rodney Maduwa, who was named the winner of the 2026 Standard Bank Kasi SME National Pitch Challenge and walked away with a R1 million prize. His win comes after years of building industry experience, growing his business and identifying an opportunity within South Africa’s paint manufacturing value chain. ... Maduwa registered his business in 2013, initially selling cleaning detergents before moving into paint manufacturing. The business started from a five-square-metre structure in Soshanguve and has since grown into a company producing decorative and industrial coatings across several provinces. ... ## The Winning Idea Maduwa’s winning pitch focused on more than selling paint. He plans to produce acrylic emulsion locally, a key raw material used in paint manufacturing. A significant portion of this input is sourced from outside South Africa. Producing it locally could help reduce costs, strengthen supply chains and support local manufacturing. Maduwa’s business growth has also created opportunities for others. He has trained more than 200 young people in professional paint application skills. Some of these businesses now purchase products directly from Maduwa Paint World. This has created a wider network around the company, linking skills development, employment and entrepreneurship. ... Held under the theme “Commercialising Kasi: Unlocking Competitive Township Businesses”, the summit brought together entrepreneurs, industry leaders, policymakers and business development partners. This year, 10 entrepreneurs from all nine provinces competed for the R1 million prize. ... The judges looked beyond a strong business story. They assessed customer value, sustainability, profitability, scalability, governance, compliance, competitive advantage and the ability to adapt to changing market conditions. ... The Standard Bank Kasi SME National Pitch Challenge forms part of the bank’s broader Enterprise and Supplier Development programme. Through the programme, a qualifying majority of Black-owned businesses receive support through funding, mentorship, business development and market access. For Maduwa, the R1 million pitch competition prize provides capital to take his Soshanguve-based business into its next phase of growth.

headline: Adhesive 'shortage' reaction
summary_text: # Adhesive 'shortage' reaction Published: 7th Nov 2022 Author: Tony Dickson - S&V Editor Eric Marzoppi, managing member of Royal Adhesive Industries cc, complained about the article in last week's newsletter under the headline 'Adhesives - yes, there's a shortage, for some'. He wrote: "The information contained in the article is a poor portrayal of the adhesive market and we would like to request for it to be retracted, corrected and an apology / explanation on the correct facts to be sent on every platform whereby the original content was published. "Whilst the manufacturer in question has valid points and one cannot dispute the difficult trading conditions we all find ourselves in, to imply that there is an adhesive shortage is false and misleading. The article has given a false perception to adhesive stakeholders surrounding a non-existent 'adhesive shortage' and this false information has large potential to negatively impact the market, and thus adhesive suppliers, clients, and all stakeholders within the market. We would like for you to understand the potential gravity and trepidation articles such as the one referred above may have on the market, and the effects that these have on further adhesive suppliers." The background to the article is that a well-known component supplier, who often gives S&V information on news in the industry, sent me a message reading: "A customer mentioned [an adhesive shortage] to me in Pmb and the next day a Jhb customer mentioned the same." When he gave me the information, he asked that his name not be used, and he didn't name his customers. Why they were having a problem procuring adhesives, I don't know. It appears clear that our assumption to a shortage of adhesives, has been misleading and false and if we instigated any panic or unnecessary concern it is regretted.

headline: From a German detergent maker to a global adhesive tech leader | News24
summary_text: This year marks a defining milestone for Henkel South Africa as the company celebrates 75 years of operating in South Africa, alongside Henkel’s 150th global anniversary. More than a celebration of longevity, the dual anniversary reflects a legacy of innovation, resilience and partnership that has helped shape industries, support local manufacturing and contribute to South Africa’s economic development for three quarters of a century. headline: R10bn hit to economy forecast if Sasol exits coal-to-liquids
summary_text: A study by University of Cape Town (UCT) researchers into Sasol’s prized Secunda plant, which converts coal, supplemented by limited natural gas, into synthetic liquid fuels and chemicals, has warned that decarbonising such a system could either entail a rapid shutdown or present a complex transition challenge. The academics Nosaibeh Nosrati-Ghods, Bryce McCall, Harro von Blottnitz, Bruno Merven, Imrah Kamedien, Joseph Masenda, and Andrew Marquard note that Sasol’s coal-to-liquids (CtL) complex in Secunda, which is responsible for about 12% of national greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, illustrates tensions in the country’s just transition plans, where rapid or unplanned shutdown could impose substantial economic and energy security risks. “A rapid and unstructured transition away from the Secunda CtL operations could reduce South Africa’s GDP by R9.9bn, result in approximately 24,900 job losses, and increase reliance on imported liquid fuels,” the study reads. “If instead the transition is understood as a structured transformation pathway, this implies that existing assets are progressively reconfigured to align with long-term climate targets, including national net-zero emissions by mid-century.” ... The giant Secunda plant is Sasol’s biggest money-maker and biggest environmental headache, accounting for nearly 84% of its scope 1 and 2 carbon emissions. Sasol has over the years had several run-ins with environmentalists and authorities over its emissions, second only to Eskom. President Cyril Ramaphosa last week visited the plant alongside Sasol CEO Simon Baloyi, where the president hailed the facility and its contribution to South Africa’s industrial base. ... The Secunda complex’s construction commenced in 1976 and remains a jewel in South Africa’s industrial crown. It is the sole manufacturer of most of South Africa’s petrochemicals and plastic raw materials based on ethylene and propylene, as well as ammonia, for fertiliser and explosives. Economic research firm Trade & Industrial Policy Strategies (TIPS), established 30 years ago for industrial policy, has said generating the necessary green hydrogen to replace Secunda’s current production would demand 18,000MW of continuous renewable electricity, representing nearly 51% of South Africa’s entire current peak electricity demand. The capital expenditure required to construct such huge infrastructure is estimated to exceed R1-trillion. ... UCT examined three scenarios for Secunda’s just transition. The baseline, which pencils in no transition, reflects current operations under existing policies, including the legislated carbon tax and the phase-out of imported natural gas from Mozambique by 2034. Under this scenario, Secunda CtL operations continue under coal-based configurations, with units retired only when they fall below operational thresholds. The second scenario incorporates Sasol’s 2030 decarbonisation measures, including renewable electricity procurement, process-efficiency improvements, and product slate adjustments relative to 2017. The third scenario introduces a binding long-term emissions constraint, consistent with South Africa’s long-term emissions constraint (LTEC). Under this constraint, CtL capacity is maintained independently of age-based retirement, subject to system-wide optimisation. “Across all scenarios, technology adoption is determined endogenously through least-cost optimisation, without predefined commissioning schedules. Assets are retired when uneconomic or displaced by cost-competitive alternatives. “The three scenarios are designed to reflect increasing levels of policy stringency, defined as the degree of binding constraints imposed on the facility’s emissions and technology choices. “The baseline scenario represents the least stringent case, incorporating only the existing carbon tax trajectory and the confirmed phase-out of Mozambican gas imports, with no binding emissions ceiling.” ... Sasol has been in the hydrogen game for more than 70 years, but the hydrogen of the future — clean, green hydrogen — is still not mainstream and far from cheap to produce. ... Sasol has 3.5-million tonnes of grey hydrogen, used primarily in making ammonia, fertiliser and refining oil.

The product is also highly malleable and conformable, allowing for easy application to irregular substrates and complex concrete profiles. This flexibility simplifies installation on site and supports quality workmanship across a wide range of project conditions. ... The waterstop system is designed to withstand hydrostatic pressure of up to 70 metres and delivers a minimum volumetric expansion of 100%, making it particularly effective in high water table environments and critical civil engineering applications. As part of Chryso Southern Africa’s broader waterproofing and construction chemicals offering, ADCOR® 500S reinforces the company’s focus on delivering advanced, fit-for-purpose solutions that enhance the performance and longevity of infrastructure assets across the region.

The scheme provides for the launch of a new WAF1 rotation and the extension of WAF3, WAF5 and WAF6 coverage. The amendments must come into force in the region as of the third week of December. They aim to develop connections via the ports of Algeciras, Spain, and Tangier Med, Morocco, to several African markets. > The new WAF1 service will provide a link between Algeciras, Tangier and Dakar, according to the rotation Algeciras–Tanger–Dakar–Algeciras. This organization should facilitate the transport to Senegal of goods from Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, through connections with the Maersk international maritime network. The WAF5 service will also be reorganized around a new rotation between Algeciras and Tangier to Monrovia, Liberia, Abidjan and San Pédro, Côte d'Ivoire, Takoradi, Ghana and Lagos, Nigeria, before returning to Algeciras. The other two services will be expanded. The WAF3 will integrate the ports of Tema, Ghana, Onne, Nigeria, and Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo. WAF6 will also serve Cotonou, Benin. These adjustments concern several markets in the Gulf of Guinea and Central Africa, with new possibilities for connecting African ports with the Western Mediterranean. Maersk points out, however, that the timetables are still subject to change. This regional reorganisation takes place while the shipowner also adjusts certain intercontinental services of its Gemini network, operated with Hapag-Lloyd. A new line, AE18, has to interconnect several Asian ports to Algeciras and Tanger Med from November 2026, while the rotations AE2, AE11 and AE19 will be modified. These separate changes relate to the links between Asia and the Mediterranean and may affect the connections available for goods to West Africa.

headline: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa | SSATP
summary_text: The International Maritime Organization (IMO), the Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP), and the World Bank, in partnership with the Ghana Maritime Authority, convened a regional workshop in Accra from October 19 to 23, 2026, to accelerate the digitalization of ports across nine West and Central African countries. Opened on October 19 by a representative of Ghana's Ministry of Transport, the five-day workshop aimed to: - Promote the adoption of the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, which sets out how shipping and port data are structured and shared electronically to streamline communication; and - Scale up the implementation of Maritime Single Windows (MSWs) and Port Community Systems (PCSs), which are integrated digital platforms that streamline vessel and cargo clearance, reduce bureaucratic delays, and strengthen Africa's competitiveness in global maritime trade. ... The workshop convened a broad coalition of regional and international institutions committed to translating policy into action, including the Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA), the African Development Bank (AfDB), the African Harbour Masters' Committee (AHMC), and the African Alliance for Electronic Commerce (AAEC). Bringing together 55 participants, including 15 women, from maritime administrations, port authorities, and customs authorities in Cabo Verde, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Sierra Leone, the workshop was structured around both knowledge sharing and practical capacity building. Sessions highlighted the strategic benefits of MSW implementation and the need to align with the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business. The program shared lessons and good practices from regional IMO needs assessment missions, including analyses of ship and cargo clearance systems, key challenges, and recommendations for effective MSW deployment. Participating Member States also presented their port systems, fostering peer learning on progress, challenges, and opportunities. ... The workshop also explored potential synergies between PCSs and MSWs to further enhance port efficiency and trade facilitation. A central principle of the workshop was that MSWs are not standalone digital solutions but core elements of a broader, regionally harmonized trade facilitation ecosystem. By deepening participants' understanding of the Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic (FAL Convention), strengthening coordination among port stakeholders, and clarifying the financing and policy requirements for MSW implementation, the workshop helped equip countries with the practical knowledge needed to accelerate MSW deployment. The workshop also drew on the previous International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH)–World Bank study, Port Community Systems: Lessons from Global Experience. ... The initiative aligns with SSATP's Fourth Development Plan (DP4), which prioritizes digitalization of transport and trade corridors across Africa. MSWs are widely acknowledged as essential for reducing logistics costs, improving efficiency, and strengthening port competitiveness.

headline: Airfreight in Africa booming, thanks to disrupted ocean shipping services - The Loadstar
summary_text: African airfreight is seeing something of a boom from the disruption in ocean freight across the Middle East, but forwarders remain sceptical as to whether it will provoke long-term structural benefits. Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express’s Sub-Saharan Africa operations, told The Loadstar the shift from ocean services had left airfreight the only viable alternative to keep goods moving. “When people run into trouble from a seafreight point of view, the alternative becomes airfreight, becomes express, and that is a notable trend across African airfreight’s growth momentum at the moment,” Mr Heymans told The Loadstar. For DHL Express, the timing has proved particularly useful, coinciding with the launch of its Heavy Weight Express service, allowing its customers to ship consignments of up to 3,000kg, with individual pieces of up to 1,000kg. Expanding beyond smaller parcels, the new service is designed for automotive, energy, engineering, machinery, and pharmaceuticals, Mr Heymans noting the significant cost implications delays place on these sectors. “The timing of the launch worked out quite well, which makes the conversation a lot easier, and a lot more comfortable for those customers seeking these sorts of services,” explained Mr Heymans. However, he did not disclose how much additional volume DHL Express had gained as a result of shipping disruption, nor how much of the growth in airfreight was a result of transference from ocean freight over underlying growth patterns. Anecdotal evidence from forwarders active on the African west and south coasts indicates that the continent is experiencing an uptick in demand for capacity, with overall volumes growing, but none was able to tell The Loadstar how the present situation should be assessed. One forwarder said: “There’s definite growth in demand for capacity in and out of certain countries around the continent – Nigeria, South Africa, and Ghana are big lanes for us – but if it is specific modes, we can only say that uptick in airfreight bookings is transference.” Others believe there are long-term prospects on the airfreight side for the continent’s major players, with forwarders noting that the chaos in the Middle East, issues with the US, and looming threats in Asia were leading all to reconsider their supply chain make-up.

headline: West Africa port congestion: new surcharges from 22 October
summary_text: ## What happened Congestion at West and Central African ports has not eased going into the last quarter of the year, and major container lines are now passing the cost on to shippers. Everstream Analytics’ port congestion report of 14 October puts the average vessel wait at Conakry, Guinea, at about 12.5 days, where berths are allocated first-come, first-served and limited to one vessel per shipping line. Tema in Ghana averaged around 5.8 days, and reefer plug use there has reached 100%. Cotonou in Benin and Pointe-Noire in the Republic of the Congo were each close to four days, with Pointe-Noire’s yard reported to be about 95% full and fixed berthing windows suspended. Against this background, carriers have announced new peak season surcharges. From 22 October 2026, cargo from China to West and Central Africa faces a surcharge of US$350 per TEU for Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Benin, Equatorial Guinea, Ghana and Togo, and US$550 per TEU for ranges that include Angola, Congo, DR Congo, Gabon, Cameroon, Senegal, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea-Bissau. An existing Guinea-Conakry surcharge stays at US$200 per TEU. From 25 October, a further US$800 per TEU surcharge applies with another major line on cargo from Asia and Oceania to Luanda, Lobito, Cabinda, Pointe-Noire, Matadi, Boma, Libreville, Port-Gentil, Kribi, Douala, Walvis Bay, Bata and Malabo. Analysts quoted by The Loadstar blame the problem on vessel capacity and cargo volumes growing faster than yards, roads and inland transport: Drewry found that Douala ran at 102% of capacity last year. ... ## What this means for shippers Exporters and forwarders shipping from Pakistan, China and the rest of Asia to these ports should expect longer and less predictable transit times for the rest of 2026. The surcharges mostly hit short-term and spot bookings, so check your quotation and booking confirmation for a PSS line before the cargo is loaded rather than finding it on the freight invoice. Importers buying on CFR or CIF terms should expect suppliers to pass on the increase. Delays also put documents at risk. The cargo tracking note for the destination, such as the Cameroon BESC/ECTN, the DR Congo FERI or the Guinea cargo tracking certificate, has to match the final bill of lading. When congestion leads a carrier to roll a booking, change the vessel or discharge at a different port, the BL details change and the certificate may need to be amended. Cargo that arrives without valid, matching paperwork can be held at the port. At terminals that are already full, that quickly adds up to demurrage, storage charges and possible penalties.

headline: Airfreight in Africa: the battle for hubs to open up the continent - Air Cargo Week
summary_text: - African airfreight growth is constrained by high costs, ageing aircraft, limited cargo infrastructure and indirect routes, with outdated bilateral agreements and slow implementation of the Single African Air Transport Market restricting intra-African connectivity. - Competing strategies are emerging, with Aglow Air targeting short-haul West African routes using ATR freighters, while Kenya Airways Cargo and TAAG develop Nairobi and Luanda as regional hubs; Ethiopian Airlines remains the dominant player. - Rising China–Africa trade, e-commerce and demand for perishables, pharmaceuticals and industrial cargo offer significant growth potential, but sustainable expansion depends on regulatory reform, direct routes, improved handling facilities and reliable cold-chain infrastructure. ... While intra-African trade struggles to take off, air freight is emerging as a strategic lever. Yet, the continent’s skies remain largely underutilised, hampered by outdated infrastructure, regulations inherited from the colonial era, and prohibitive costs. Faced with this reality, several players are trying to develop competing solutions. On one side, Aglow Air is betting on ATR cargo aircraft to connect short-haul West African routes. On the other, Kenya Airways Cargo and TAAG are focusing on regional hubs in Nairobi and Luanda to capture long-haul traffic, with the ambition of competing with the Gulf hubs. Air Algérie/Tassili, currently consolidating, represents another state-owned model. Different strategies, but one shared challenge: making African air freight viable, profitable, and self-sustaining. ... Connectivity remains incomplete The potential is immense, but it runs up against a persistent reality: goods shipped from one African country to another take an average of three to five days in transit, with mandatory stopovers in Europe or the Middle East. “Rates are extremely high, unaffordable for many exporters,” explains Cathy Kayitesi, Sales Director at Africa Global Logistics. “Many turn to sea freight and only use air freight as a last resort, for perishable, special, or high-value products.” Adding to this economic obstacle is a fleet problem: many of the aircraft used on the continent are over thirty years old, with frequent breakdowns leading to delays and uncertainty. “Connections remain a major challenge,” adds Ms. Kayitesi. “In the absence of direct flights, goods must transit through external hubs before reaching their final destination.” ... Two competing models To address this situation, two strategies are emerging. On the one hand, Aglow Air is relying on ATR cargo aircraft to cover short-haul routes in West Africa, taking a niche approach. On the other hand, Kenya Airways Cargo and TAAG are developing their regional hubs in Nairobi and Luanda to capture long-haul traffic, with the ambition of competing with the Gulf hubs. Aviation expert Samba Thiam observes that “the most underserved routes are between West Africa and Southern and Central Africa: Abidjan-Luanda, Accra-Lusaka, Dakar-Nairobi.” According to him, TAAG is rapidly filling this gap thanks to its North-South corridor and new routes to Lusaka, Abidjan, and Accra. Kenya Airways Cargo, for its part, remains a key player for East-West and Horn of Africa connections, even though its Nairobi hub is sometimes bypassed by traffic from Europe or the Gulf. ... The weight of political legacies But beyond strategic choices, regulation is hindering the growth of air freight. The current African air network is the product of bilateral agreements inherited from the colonial era, designed to connect capital cities to European metropolises, not African cities to each other. Despite the existence of the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM), signed by 38 states, its implementation remains hesitant. “Governments continue to block traffic rights, particularly fifth freedom rights, to protect their often underperforming national airlines,” Thiam lamented. As a result, fragmentation prevents the creation of direct links and forces freight to transit through external hubs, increasing costs and delays. This is compounded by inadequate airport infrastructure, as more than half of African airports lack suitable cargo facilities, warehouses, or cold chain infrastructure, which severely penalises perishable goods. ... Hubs in operation Despite these obstacles, hubs are emerging. Ethiopian Airlines dominates the market with a 35 percent share, far ahead of Kenya Airways and Royal Air Maroc (25 percent combined). Its cargo capacity has increased from 266,000 tonnes in 2016 to 715,000 tonnes in 2023, with 16 cargo aircraft and a target of 37 by 2035. Kenya Airways Cargo, for its part, boasts an annual capacity of 380,000 tonnes and is strengthening its Nairobi hub. The Abidjan hub is also cited as a serious contender to become a major gateway to West Africa, with the potential for 25 to 35 new routes and an estimated 25 to 30 percent reduction in fares thanks to increased competition. As for Luanda, its geographic location, at the crossroads of Southern Africa, South America, and Europe, makes it a rising star. ... Demand driven by e-commerce and sensitive goods Justin Nbeye, an international trade expert, points out that “trade between China and Africa reached a record US$348 billion in 2025.” With the extension of zero-tariff treatment to all African countries, agricultural exports (coffee, flowers, fresh fruit) are boosted, while e-commerce driven by platforms like Temu and SHEIN is experiencing growth of over 20 percent per year, creating sustained demand for air freight. At the same time, pharmaceuticals, industrial freight, and mining remain promising segments, but demanding in terms of cold chain and reliability.

headline: Cotonou port rebounds but faces growing competition in West Africa - Africa Business Insight
summary_text: The Port of Cotonou has recovered from a sharp decline in cargo traffic linked to a diplomatic dispute with neighbouring Niger, but mounting competition from regional rivals is putting pressure on Benin’s main maritime gateway to strengthen its commercial position. The port handled more than five million additional tonnes of cargo in 2025, while container traffic exceeded 500,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), according to port authorities. After volumes fell from 12 million tonnes to nine million tonnes in 2024, the Port of Cotonou Authority (PAC) is targeting a further increase of around two million tonnes in 2026. But the rebound comes as ports in Côte d’Ivoire, Togo and Ghana expand their capacity, while Nigeria invests in modernising its maritime infrastructure. Cotonou is investing nearly 500 billion CFA francs (US$855 million) in infrastructure improvements, seeking to restore traffic and attract new customers. The challenge is considerable. Abidjan handled 46.6 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, including 1.69 million TEUs, while Ghana’s Tema port recorded 31 million tonnes and 2.2 million TEUs. Lomé handled 2.4 million TEUs. Cotonou’s recovery has therefore done little to close the gap with its larger regional competitors. ... Infrastructure race intensifies Regional ports are investing heavily to capture additional cargo and strengthen their links with landlocked countries. Tema is pursuing a development programme worth around US$1.5 billion through a public-private partnership involving the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority, Meridian Port Services, APM Terminals and Africa Global Logistics. In Togo, an investment programme led by Mediterranean Shipping Company has brought more than €500 million (US$559 million) into Lomé’s port infrastructure. Nigeria is also emerging as a more formidable competitor. The country opened the Lekki deep-sea port in 2023 and is investing US$1 billion in modernising its main facilities at Apapa and Tin Can Island. In September, Nigerian authorities announced a further modernisation programme covering the ports of Calabar, Delta, Onne and Rivers. Proposed deep-sea port developments at Badagry and Ogun have also returned to the government’s agenda. Competition extends beyond terminals to the transport corridors linking ports with inland markets. Ghana is developing a 1,102-kilometre railway intended to connect Tema with Burkina Faso’s capital, Ouagadougou, while Côte d’Ivoire already has an established rail connection to the Burkinabe city. Nigeria is also seeking to improve its access to Niger through the planned Kano-M aradi railway, expected to be completed by the end of 2026. Such links can influence the choice of port for traders serving landlocked economies, where transport costs and the reliability of inland freight routes are important considerations. ... ### Digitalisation offers an advantage Cotonou is seeking to compete through operational efficiency as well as infrastructure investment. The port authority says its digitalisation programme has improved vessel processing and cargo handling, reducing delays for importers and freight operators. The final stage, covering the digitalisation of cargo collection, is still under development and could become operational in March 2027. Charles Bennett Fayomi, the PAC’s director of port operations and security, said container waiting times had fallen considerably. “In Cotonou, things have changed considerably. For a container, the wait is now 36 to 72 hours,” he said during the second edition of PAC Media Connect. The authority also says excessive roadside inspections and police extortion along transit corridors have largely disappeared in recent years. These improvements could help Cotonou attract customers seeking predictable delivery times, even as competing ports handle substantially larger volumes. ... Abidjan combines a substantial domestic market with transit services to countries including Burkina Faso and Mali. Lomé has developed into a major container transshipment hub, while Tema serves Ghana’s domestic economy alongside international shipping routes. Cotonou, meanwhile, has yet to establish an equally clear commercial specialisation. One option under discussion is to attract shipping companies that are expanding in Africa but have a less entrenched presence in competing ports. Chinese operators, including COSCO Shipping, have been identified as potential partners as trade between China and African markets grows. However, attracting new carriers would require reliable services, competitive infrastructure and strong inland connections. Excessive dependence on a small number of shipping companies could also expose the port to changes in their commercial priorities. The PAC is targeting annual cargo traffic of 25 million tonnes within a decade, although regional competitors are also planning substantial increases in capacity.

headline: West African port congestion exposes gaps beyond terminal gates - The Loadstar
summary_text: Congestion along West Africa’s coast is exposing infrastructure that appears dramatically ill-suited to the region’s rapidly developing container market, with concerns that the level of investment, and its intended developments, are not where they need to be. Last year, Drewry recorded a 19.4% year-on-year upturn in regional container throughput, reflecting the introduction of larger vessels on Asia-West Africa services, and The Loadstar’s reporting indicates developing trade between West Africa and Latin America. Eirik Hooper, Drewry’s ports and terminals specialist, told The Loadstar: “The congestion appears to be the result of a mismatch between rapidly expanding vessel capacity, growing volumes and the ability of terminals and supporting logistics systems to process that cargo.” He believes the source of this pressure is linked to introduction of 24,000 teu vessels on MSC’s Africa Express service, which began last April, and by May was calling at Lomé, Tema, Abidjan, and Kribi, although he warned problems vary considerably across ports. According to Drewry, Doula operated last year at 102% utilisation, with volumes rising 48% year on year, while Conakry, Dakar, Lomé, and Pointe-Noire hovered between 81% and 84%. But pointing to Tema, Mr Hooper said simply seeing this as a terminal issue would not help. ... The Ghanaian gateway experienced congestion of between four and seven days during the summer peak and is still hovering around the six-day mark, despite the country’s transport minister noting there had been significant improvements in terminal capacity this year. But Mr Hooper said this came “without corresponding improvements to its supporting transport infrastructure”, adding: “The Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority had already identified imports, empty containers and road congestion as principal contributors to delays. ... DP World chief executive and managing director for Africa, Mohammed Akoojee, seems to see a relatively obvious solution: combining terminal expansion with investment across the wider African supply chain. Mr Akoojee told The Loadstar: “Addressing these challenges requires more than expanding terminals. Investment in modern equipment, deeper berths, roads, rail and inland logistics networks must go hand in hand to ensure cargo moves efficiently through the supply chain.” For its part, DP World has invested $340m in modernising its Dakar terminal, increasing throughput from 265,000 teu in 2008 to 850,000 teu in 2025, with the operator noting that this has seen vessel wait times plummet from 35 hours to near zero. However, he said that “even highly productive terminals” eventually encountered physical constraints, with this particularly true in cases where opportunities for further expansion are limited. “Our $1.2bn investment in the new deepwater port of Ndayane builds on this progress, providing capacity for larger vessels and future trade growth. Ndayane will have an initial annual container-handling capacity of 1.2m teu in the first phase,” Mr Akoojee said. This project forms part of a wider wave of port development across the region, including new terminals at Pointe-Noire, Banana, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and projects in Nigeria, alongside expansions at San Pedro in Ivory Coast, Takoradi in Ghana, and Luanda. “With African trade expected to grow and shipping evolving, continued integrated investment in port and logistics infrastructure are essential; needs vary by market, but our focus remains developing capacity, improving efficiency and strengthening inland connectivity,” he added.

headline: Growing trade driving congestion and delays at West African ports - The Loadstar
summary_text: Strong volume growth along the West African coast growth is proving the double-edged sword some had warned of, with many of the ports that had been reaping rewards now subject to heavy and intensifying congestion. Ghana, Guinea, and Sierra Leone are among the countries most affected by delays sprouting up along the coast, all three rapidly approaching similar volumes to those handled in the entirety of 2025. Forwarders active on West African trades told The Loadstar they too had observed the congestion hobbling many of the ports’ ability to function effectively, one expressing concern over looming temperature-controlled cargo due for delivery. A forwarder with volumes destined for Temam in Ghanam told The Loadstar: “CMA CGM has announced a congestion charge of $400 per teu for these shipments. This means an additional cost of $800 for each 40ft refrigerated container.” Hapag-Lloyd has also announced a $250 surcharge on reefer shipments destined for Tema, which became applicable for shipments sailing as of yesterday, adding to the worries of cargo owners. The carrier has warned customers to expect delays of 10 days for discharging and loading goods, although Portcast claims that the situation at the Ghanian port may be improving, average waits having fallen below the four-day average, an improvement on last week. Instead, it singles Conakry and Freetown as the ports to be concerned about, congestion delays at both exceeding 10 days – a rapid deterioration at the Sierra Leone capital’s gateway saw delays increase by four days, week on week, and by more than a day at Conakry. Only a month ago, Sierra Leone Ports and Harbours Authority director general Yankuba Askia Bio claimed a “decongestion” effort, led by multiple stakeholders, had succeeded, resulting in Freetown being removed from a list of congested African gateways. Efforts at Conakry to mitigate the worst of the congestion have seen trucks operating around the clock at Guinea’s main gateway to keep cargo flowing, and ensure the backlog does not worsen. While at Tema, the Ghana Shippers’ Authority said last month it was working with the port authority, shipping lines, and terminal operators to increase vessel calls to accelerate empty-container evacuation. But there is growing recognition across the sector that against a backdrop of surging volume growth, the ports are delaying what will inevitably be needed if they are to avoid a catastrophic collapse in supply chains – investment and expansion in infrastructure.

headline: AGL drives warehouse hubs around African ports to capture the regional trade boom | Africa Insights
summary_text: On 23 April 2026, the convention signed between the Gabonese state and Africa Global Logistics (AGL) for the deep‑sea port of Kobe‑Kobe summed up a broader shift: new mineral, container or multipurpose terminals are now conceived together with their logistics zones, warehouses and evacuation corridors, rather than as isolated quays. The agreement gives AGL a global mandate to build and operate the port and to develop the Belinga–Kobe‑Kobe railway axis, a central component of an integrated logistics platform along Gabon’s Atlantic seaboard. This integration of the hinterland is becoming strategic as shipping lines and investors bet on an African port boom in which logistics services – warehousing, pre‑carriage, inland distribution – weigh as heavily as handling capacity. AGL now highlights an end‑to‑end supply‑chain offer, combining port concessions, warehouses and rail services to ease trade along several African corridors. On Cameroon’s coast, this shift is already visible. AGL Cameroon is investing CFA 2.6 billion in the Kribi Logistics Hub, which is to cover nearly 7 hectares with modern warehouses, optimised storage areas and infrastructure sized to support an increase in throughput towards about 1 million TEU per year. The hub aims both to capture maritime container flows and to serve as a consolidation point for a still under‑equipped Central African hinterland. ... Around major coastal metros such as Abidjan or Lagos, logistics platforms now sprawl well beyond port fences. In Côte d’Ivoire, the Ministry of Transport reports that the Port of Abidjan handled more than 40.1 million tonnes of cargo in 2024 versus 34.7 million tonnes in 2023, a rise of about 15.6 %, driven in part by investment in new terminals and extended logistics zones. This step‑up strengthens operators’ interest in warehouse parks connected to the city ring road and to corridors toward Mali, Burkina Faso or Niger. On the Nigerian seaboard, the same logic leans heavily on special economic zones. Within the Lekki Free Zone, TY Logistics Park is developing grade‑A warehouses and third‑party logistics services (3PL) less than 20 minutes from the Lekki deep‑sea port, with an offer that integrates storage, cross‑docking and last‑mile distribution for the Lagos market and the broader West African region. The stated goal is to turn this park into a regional redistribution hub, at a time when legacy urban ports still struggle with congestion. ... Beyond terminal concessions, AGL increasingly presents itself as an architect of logistics ecosystems. The company’s institutional communication highlights an integrated offer combining port handling, warehousing, multimodal solutions and value‑added services for mining, oil, agricultural and fast‑moving consumer goods sectors. Its portfolio now covers several major port platforms where associated warehouses and inland depots are designed to cut transit times and support industrial localisation in Africa. ... In large hubs such as Lagos or Abidjan, this search for a competitive hinterland also intersects with digital and documentary‑flow issues. Nigeria’s Ports Authority is rolling out a Port Community System and a National Single Window to strengthen port logistics competitiveness, in parallel with reconstruction and modernisation projects at existing terminals. Without these integration layers – information systems, organised truck parks, inland depots – new port‑adjacent warehouses risk reproducing inland the very bottlenecks that used to form at the quayside.

headline: DP WORLD AND TGI GROUP PARTNER TO STRENGTHEN LOGISTICS CAPABILITIES IN NIGERIA
summary_text: ## Partnership combines DP World's global logistics expertise with TGI Group's strong market presence to expand logistics capabilities and support trade growth in Nigeria and across West Africa LAGOS, NIGERIA, 1 October 2026 – DP World and Nigeria-based Tropical General Investments (TGI) Group have joined forces to strengthen logistics capabilities in Nigeria, leveraging their combined expertise to support trade and unlock future growth across West Africa. DP World's Nigeria entity, DP World Logistics Limited, will continue to serve its customers and partners without interruption, maintaining existing services, operations and customer commitments as it builds additional capabilities. The company has a substantial footprint in Nigeria, particularly in market access across the healthcare and consumer sectors, alongside a growing logistics presence. Combining DP World’s global logistics and supply chain expertise with TGI Group's strong market presence, extensive distribution network and operational experience, the business will be able to deliver a broader range of integrated supply chain solutions. While initially focused on Nigeria, the collaboration also creates a platform for expansion across West Africa. Through DP World Logistics Limited, the business will continue to provide services across Nigeria, including road freight and contract logistics, while enhancing these capabilities and exploring new offerings, including fourth-party logistics (4PL) solutions. It will also help connect Nigerian businesses to regional and global markets through the group's wider network. DP World will also provide logistics and operational support services to TGI Group, helping improve supply chain efficiency and optimise operations. Mohammed Akoojee, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, DP World Africa, said: “Nigeria is one of Africa’s most important economies and a critical market for the future of trade on the continent. This partnership marks another important step in our journey and we look forward to welcoming TGI into the DP World family. headline: SACO expands West African network with Nigeria office | World Ports Organization
summary_text: SACO Shipping has expanded its West African presence with the opening of a new office in Apapa, Lagos, and a branch in Port Harcourt. The Nigerian operation would provide LCL import services through the ports of Lagos and Onne, said SACO Shipping West Africa director Ian Treder. Clients will also have access to FCL import solutions and global airfreight import services through SACO’s wider group. The airfreight services will be provided through the Air Cargo Group and SACO Air, according to Treder. Lagos would receive direct bi-monthly sailings from Hamburg, Antwerp, Durban, Mumbai and Ningbo, while Onne would be served by a bi-monthly sailing from Hamburg, he said. Cargo originating in markets including the United States, Australia, Italy and France could also be routed into Nigeria through SACO’s international network, said Treder. The company established a presence in Nigeria in response to growing demand for neutral and reliable consolidation services. “Nigeria is a strategic hub for West African trade, but infrastructure constraints, market volatility and fragmented consolidation services have historically presented challenges for freight forwarders,” Treder said. The new operation would give forwarders access to more predictable groupage schedules and direct connections with Europe, Asia and southern Africa, reducing dependence on routes involving multiple transhipments, he added. It will operate as a neutral LCL consolidator, serving freight forwarders without competing with them for shipper business. The Nigerian offices would connect with SACO’s South African operations in Durban, Cape Town, Johannesburg and Gqeberha, as well as its West African network in Abidjan, Tema, Dakar, Cotonou and Conakry, said Treder. “This will strengthen the connections available for LCL cargo moving between southern and West Africa and link Nigeria more closely with SACO’s wider global network,” he said.

headline: HMM presents in Valencia its MA2 connection between Algeciras and West Africa | El Estrecho Digital
summary_text: HMM has presented in Valencia its MA2 service between the Mediterranean and West Africa, a connection that has been operating since last July with Algeciras as the head of a rotation that includes stops in Tangier Med, Dakar, Tema, Lekki, and Abidjan. The meeting was attended by representatives from HMM, Sea & Ports Group, and the port and logistics sector. From Algeciras, Nicolás Martínez Andión, head of the Business Development and Marketing Area of the Port Authority of Algeciras Bay (APBA), and Maribel Grau, commercial director of TTI Algeciras, were present. El Estrecho Digital already reported on April 19 about the announcement made by HMM to initiate this connection with West Africa, whose operation was scheduled for July. The shipping company later communicated that the MA2 would start from Algeciras on July 7 and complete each rotation in 35 days. The line is jointly operated by HMM and Ocean Network Express (ONE). The South Korean company markets it under the name Mediterranean-West Africa Service (MA2), while ONE uses the name Mediterranean Africa Express Service (MAX). ... The rotation established by both companies comprises Algeciras, Tangier Med, Dakar, Tema, Lekki, and Abidjan, with a subsequent return to Algeciras. HMM announced five container ships with an individual capacity of 2,800 TEU and a complete cycle of 35 days for this operation. ONE, for its part, communicated a weekly frequency for the MAX. Algeciras also serves as a connection point for the MA2 with other maritime services of HMM. In its commercial communication prior to the start of the line, the shipping company detailed that goods coming from Asia could link to the MA2 through the FE3 and FIM services in Algeciras, while the MP2 performed this function via Tangier Med. ONE also identifies Algeciras and Tangier Med as the two Mediterranean connection points for this line. The company notes that MAX allows linking West Africa with markets in the Far East, northern Europe, the Indian subcontinent, North America, and Latin America through its network of international services. This structure is complemented by the feeder connections disseminated by APBA from Algeciras to Bilbao, Vigo, Lisbon, Leixões, Valencia, Barcelona, and Casablanca. ... The MA2 is part of the expansion of the regional network announced by HMM in April. When announcing the service, the company informed that it had secured 24 feeder ships during the previous six months. That set consisted of ten units of 2,800 TEUs commissioned to HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, two ships of 1,900 TEUs purchased in the market, and twelve units between 1,800 and 2,700 TEUs contracted earlier.

headline: U.S. software firm Pigee to acquire 55% stake in Nigeria’s ShipAfrica - Africa Business Insight
summary_text: U.S. logistics technology company Pigee has agreed to acquire a controlling 55-percent stake in Nigerian logistics startup ShipAfrica, expanding its presence in one of West Africa’s largest markets. The transaction will give Pigee an established operating base in Nigeria as it seeks to build its logistics network across Africa. The deal will be completed in three stages over 18 months and financed through a combination of cash and equity, Pigee chief executive Leroy Lawrence told TechCabal. The value of the transaction has not been disclosed. ShipAfrica will continue to operate under its existing name following the acquisition, while its founder and chief executive, Walter Isoko, will remain at the helm. The deal gives Pigee access to ShipAfrica’s existing infrastructure and local network, which the U.S. company plans to use to support international trade and logistics operations across the continent. Lawrence said the terms of individual acquisition tranches could change depending on how much capital Pigee raises during the 18-month acquisition period. The acquisition comes as technology companies and investors increasingly target Africa’s logistics sector, where fragmented transport networks, high delivery costs and limited cross-border infrastructure have created opportunities for digital platforms. Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country and one of its largest economies, is viewed as a key market for companies seeking to build regional logistics and commerce networks. For Pigee, taking control of ShipAfrica provides a local platform from which to expand its transportation software and logistics services rather than building an entirely new operation in the market. The company aims to use ShipAfrica’s Nigerian presence to simplify international trade and reduce operating costs, according to the announcement. The transaction also reflects a broader trend of international technology companies seeking partnerships and acquisitions that provide immediate access to local infrastructure, customers and market knowledge.

headline: Billionaire Baba Danpullo takes 10% stake in AGL Cameroon

However, AGL Cameroon’s post-recapitalisation share capital stood at CFA10.621 billion ($17.8 million), divided into 315,750 shares with a nominal value of CFA33,639 each. CCML’s 31,575 shares therefore represent exactly 10 percent of the company, with a combined nominal value of about CFA1.06 billion. That figure reflects the accounting value of the shares, not the price Danpullo’s company paid for them. ... The investment gives Danpullo’s business group a direct position in Cameroon’s logistics infrastructure at a time when the sector is becoming increasingly important to the country’s trade ambitions. AGL operates across logistics, port terminals, maritime services and rail transport in Africa. AGL Cameroon is the former Bolloré Africa Logistics business. The group now operates across several African markets and remains a major player in the continent’s supply chains.

headline: ITF puts co-ordinated port pricing on the table as two operators handle two-thirds of West Africa's boxes | Container Management
summary_text: Four carriers — Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), Maersk, CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd — made nearly 80% of West African port calls in 2024, up from 54% in 2014. Two operators move two-thirds of the boxes crossing Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria and Togo. They are partners as well as competitors, sharing joint ventures on Ivorian and Ghanaian terminals, including Côte d'Ivoire Terminal in Abidjan, and Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA), a shareholder in Meridian Port Services at Tema alongside both groups, is the last major public stevedore left in the Gulf of Guinea.
