headline: Nigeria’s Cargo Corridor: How Layered Taxes, Offshore Insurance Are Quietly Eroding Air Freight Competitiveness – Independent Newspaper Nigeria
summary_text: A single pallet of Nigerian produce bound for Europe now carries the weight of a tax code, a fragmented insurance market and a currency in flux; as industry data suggests the toll is getting heavier, not lighter. Follow one consignment of fresh produce from a Lagos warehouse to a European tarmac, and the cost stack tells its own story. Before the goods even reach the aircraft, they pass through cargo registration fees, export charges, courier and tarmac levies, landing charges and trans-shipment costs, a sequence airline operators say has ballooned into one of the most burdensome fee regimes in West Africa. Professor Obiora Okonkwo, Chairman of United Nigeria Airlines and spokesman for the Airline Operators of Nigeria (AON), has put a number on the ticketing side of that burden: airlines are charged around 18 separate taxes on a single ticket, with roughly 70 per cent of the fare flowing to government agencies rather than the carrier. Cargo shippers face an equivalent maze of registration, extension and demurrage charges layered by regulators including the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA). The financial strain is visible in the results of Nigeria’s two dominant ground handlers. Combined revenue at Skyway Aviation Handling Company (SAHCO) and Nigerian Aviation Handling Company (NAHCO) rose from roughly N53.4 billion to N58.4 billion between 2025 and 2026, yet combined cost of sales jumped by almost 40 per cent over the same period, far outpacing revenue growth. SAHCO’s net profit margin fell from about 38.6 per cent to 16.7 per cent despite higher turnover, a pattern analysts attribute partly to rising operational levies rather than falling demand. That is why SAHCO’s Managing Director, Adenike Aboderin, has publicly renewed calls for tax relief. “Overheads are rising, inflation is high, forex is unpredictable,” she said, arguing that “tax waivers and government support will go a long way to help ground handlers remain competitive.” ... Freight forwarders echo the concern from the trade side. Seyi Adewale, Managing Director of Mainstream Cargo, estimates Nigeria may be forfeiting between 30 and 40 per cent of potential government revenue to inefficiencies across the cargo value chain, a figure he says outweighs the damage caused by having multiple regulatory agencies at the ports. He also notes that air freight now accounts for more than 80 per cent of total logistics costs in many Nigerian export transactions, meaning naira depreciation against dollar-denominated freight rates compounds every other charge in the stack. ... The Insurance Leak Layered on top of taxation is a second, less visible cost: offshore insurance placement. Because Nigeria’s underwriting capacity for aviation and cargo risk remains thin, a large share of premiums bypasses the domestic market entirely. Industry estimates cited ahead of the country’s insurance recapitalisation deadline suggest roughly 70 per cent of high-value premiums from specialised assets – including aviation – continue to flow to brokers and reinsurers in London and other global centres, rather than staying within the Nigerian financial system. Incoming Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA) chairman Ebelechukwu Nwachukwu has made domestic underwriting expansion a priority of her administration, as the industry grapples with what analysts describe as significant “underwriting capacity leakage” – an estimated 70 per cent of high-value premiums in aviation and other specialised risk categories still flow to reinsurers in London and other offshore centres. ... The scale of what is at stake is considerable: aviation insurance premiums in Nigeria are projected to approach $2 billion annually, yet airlines argue they are effectively forced into double coverage because aircraft lessors will not recognise domestic policies, pushing carriers back offshore even where local content rules require otherwise. headline: Un terminal à conteneurs à Touba pour rapprocher le dédouanement des bassins de consommation - APS
summary_text: Diourbel, 17 août (APS) – La Direction générale des Douanes, le Conseil sénégalais des Chargeurs (COSEC) et Focus Investment Group (FIG) annoncent avoir signé un protocole d’accord tripartite portant sur la création, l’aménagement, l’opérationnalisation et l’exploitation d’un terminal à conteneurs de destination à Touba, cité religieuse du centre du Sénégal. Cette infrastructure constitue l’une des composantes majeures de Touba Terminal, un projet développé sur près de 350 hectares et bénéficiant du statut de zone économique spéciale (ZES), précise un communiqué parvenu lundi à l’APS. Selon le texte, elle vise à rapprocher les opérations douanières et logistiques de la destination finale des marchandises et des principaux bassins de consommation. Implanté sur environ 40 hectares, le terminal aura une capacité initiale de 100.000 EVP par an, extensible à 200.000 EVP à terme. Il comprendra notamment des entrepôts de stockage sous douane, des silos pour le vrac et une gare de gros porteurs pouvant accueillir jusqu’à 200 camions par jour. Le projet prévoit également une zone industrielle et logistique de 200 hectares destinée à accueillir des infrastructures de production ainsi que des plateformes de stockage et de distribution dédiées au “last mile”. Il prévoit, en outre, une centrale solaire d’une capacité de 50 MW et une Bourse agricole destinée à mieux organiser, stocker et valoriser la production nationale. Cette organisation devrait contribuer à fluidifier les opérations de dédouanement, à réduire les ruptures de charge et les délais logistiques, à améliorer la traçabilité des marchandises et à renforcer la compétitivité des corridors reliant le Sénégal aux marchés de la sous-région, selon les promoteurs du projet. Les flux destinés à Touba et aux autres régions de l’intérieur du Sénégal, ainsi qu’une partie des marchandises en transit vers l’hinterland, pourront ainsi être réceptionnés, stockés, contrôlés et distribués au plus près des zones de consommation, indique le communiqué. Le projet représente un investissement estimé à 110 milliards de francs CFA. Il ambitionne de générer, à terme, plus de 300 milliards de francs CFA de flux commerciaux annuels et de contribuer à la création de plus de 70.000 bénéficiaires directs et indirects sur sept ans. Le démarrage des premiers travaux est prévu au premier semestre 2027, signale la même source.

headline: African Airfreight Outperforms Global Market - Air Cargo Week
summary_text: - Africa’s air cargo market is outperforming global trends, with projected growth of 6 percent and demand rising 7 percent in March 2026. The Africa-Asia corridor is driving much of this momentum, while geopolitical disruption is redirecting freight away from Middle Eastern hubs towards West African gateways. - Senegal is positioning Dakar’s Blaise Diagne International Airport as a West African airfreight hub, with first-quarter 2026 volumes up 21.4 percent year-on-year and plans for a new cargo terminal, warehouses and storage facilities capable of handling 80,000 tonnes annually by 2028. However, declining regional transit traffic shows the hub still has ground to cover. - Mauritania is pursuing a more specialised hub strategy around Nouadhibou, leveraging its fisheries industry and redirected regional trade flows. A new cold-chain facility provides a foundation for seafood exports, but gaps in pharmaceutical and hazardous cargo infrastructure, alongside customs delays, remain obstacles to wider hub development. ... While the global air cargo market is experiencing stagnation, Africa is posting an impressive performance, with projected growth of 6 percent, significantly exceeding global forecasts. This is more than a short-term rebound; it reflects a broader trend that is increasingly reshaping the global logistics landscape. The figures are striking. Against a backdrop of sluggish global economic conditions, the African continent continues to demonstrate strong momentum in the airfreight sector. This growth is being driven by the convergence of several powerful market dynamics. ... Following a detailed analysis of Dakar’s Blaise Diagne International Airport (AIBD), logistics expert Hadime Thiam confirms that airfreight activity in Dakar did not decline in March 2026. On the contrary, volumes increased sharply. “In the first quarter of 2026, AIBD recorded 11,700 tonnes of freight, representing a 21.4 percent year-on-year increase,” he states. IATA data supports this trend across the continent, with African air cargo demand rising by 7 percent in March, although the pace moderated following increases of 18.2 percent in January and 21 percent in February. Discussing trade corridors, Thiam explains: “The conflict in the Middle East has reshaped freight flows. The Africa-Asia corridor, the most dynamic, recorded a 22.6 percent increase in March. Conversely, routes linked to the Middle East have collapsed, with Middle East-Asia traffic down 58.6 percent. As for the Morocco-West Africa corridor, including Dakar, it remains structurally under pressure due to heavy reliance on passenger aircraft belly capacity and a declining supply of freighter services on the Casablanca-Dakar route.” ... Thiam also notes that the Senegalese government is determined to position the country as the leading airfreight hub in West Africa, with concrete signs of progress visible through infrastructure development and policy initiatives. New cargo terminal project The government plans to build a new cargo terminal, warehouses, and storage facilities, with a target handling capacity of 80,000 tonnes annually. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2026, with completion expected in 2028. Reforms and political commitment A strategic development plan for the air hub covering the 2021-2025 period has been approved, followed by the Programme for the Reconstruction of Senegal’s Airports (PRAS). In addition, cargo-focused workshops are being organised to develop a long-term strategic roadmap for the sector. Nevertheless, growth ambitions still face challenges. In 2024, AIBD handled 39,922 tonnes of cargo. While the government described this performance as positive, officials also acknowledged that it remains below the country’s potential. Regional transit traffic continues to decline, indicating that the hub has not yet reached full operational maturity. ... Regarding investment, Hamed explains: “As an airline operator, I can confirm that concrete investments are underway to make Nouadhibou a hub for the fisheries sector, even if there is still a long way to go.” He points to the infrastructure already in place. A refrigerated terminal has been developed at Nouadhibou International Airport with support from the World Bank. The facility includes a 600 sq m warehouse, a 245 sq m cold storage room, a refrigerated shipping area, an analysis laboratory, handling equipment including a freight scanner and pallet jacks, and a racking system for 120 pallets, providing storage capacity for 85 pallets of fresh fish. “The fisheries potential is immense. Nouadhibou is Mauritania’s leading fishing port, and the country is the world’s second-largest exporter of seafood products after Japan. Developing this air hub is therefore a strategic priority,” he adds. ... In Nouadhibou, the airport still lacks dedicated facilities for pharmaceutical and hazardous cargo, while customs procedures can be slow. The runway was also closed in 2023 for repairs. However, the Nouadhibou Free Zone and a series of ongoing development projects demonstrate a clear commitment to establishing the city as a major logistics hub. In Senegal, despite ambitious plans and significant infrastructure investment, the decline in regional transit traffic highlights the intense competition among West African gateways. Operational capabilities will need to continue expanding if the country is to achieve its hub ambitions.

summary_text: ## Korea Pavilion at WHX in South Africa; 32 companies take part Diagnostic kits and portable X-ray equipment showcased Korean medical devices tested at five local hospitals in pilot projects With Africa heavily reliant on imports for medical devices, Korean diagnostic and imaging equipment companies are seeking to enter local markets using South Africa as a base. Demand for diagnostic devices and testing equipment for early diagnosis and disease management is also growing amid population aging and an increase in chronic diseases. The population aged 60 and over in sub-Saharan Africa rose from 43 million in 2010 to 67 million in 2025, and is projected to reach 163 million by 2050. This year's WHX brought together around 600 companies from more than 60 countries and attracted more than 8,000 medical professionals. Attendees included global manufacturers such as Siemens Healthineers and Roche Diagnostics, as well as hospitals, testing institutions, and medical device distributors and buyers from across Africa. ... The Korea Pavilion showcased in vitro diagnostic (IVD) kits and portable X-ray equipment. Twelve companies working with the Korea International Trade Association sent product samples to the region and promoted their products and held buyer consultations through KOTRA. The Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) is seeking faster government approval to replace aging laboratory equipment, according to a Modern Ghana report. The Authority has not publicly identified the specific instruments at issue, the funding sought, or the procurement timeline targeted in the available coverage. The appeal sits at a familiar junction for national standards bodies. Reference instruments carry uncertainty budgets that rest on manufacturer-stated service life, controlled environments, and regular calibration. Once equipment passes that service-life envelope, drift, contamination, or mechanical wear widens the claimed accuracy — and certificates issued to industry carry confidence intervals that drift from achieved performance. ... ## What kind of aging drives the appeal? Modern Ghana did not enumerate the equipment affected. Three categories typically drive replacement cycles in any standards-setting laboratory: - Mechanical comparators and dimensional probes, where wear introduces systematic bias that calibration alone cannot eliminate - Optical, chromatographic, and spectroscopic systems, where detector and source aging degrades sensitivity, selectivity, and detection limits - Electronic references, where component-level drift gradually exceeds the absolute-accuracy claims the manufacturer specifies within the first decade of service Each category ages differently, but all require capital procurement to replace — not service contracts to repair. ... Public-sector capital expenditure above defined thresholds generally requires multi-stage clearance. Lead times for laboratory instruments sourced internationally — including import waivers, vendor qualification, and on-site commissioning — often extend over many months. The metrological consequence resembles a missed calibration interval: measurements continue, but the chain of traceability weakens each quarter the replacement is deferred. ... The Authority's remit, as suggested by its statutory name, covers the development and promotion of standards, including laboratory testing and calibration services that anchor trade, health, and industrial compliance. The full range of instruments in question — and the specific approval stage at which the appeal is held up — was not stated in the public reporting. ... The unresolved question is whether the country's measurement infrastructure will continue to meet the uncertainty budgets claimed on issued certificates. Funding through donor programs, regional cooperation via AFRIMETS, or a dedicated domestic capital grant are typical financing pathways for national standards bodies in the region. Which channel the government authorizes will determine whether the Authority's stated accuracy classes align with achieved performance through the next budget cycle.

Donkor, the GPOL is a place where students will develop the knowledge and skills to further real-world applications of optics and photonics in the West African region. ... SPIE is invested in the long-term advancement of optics and photonics in Ghana. Chief Engagement Officer Allison Romanyshyn, Board Members Daewook Kim and Samuel Achilefu, and 2025 President Dr. Peter de Groot, who also serves as Chair of the GPOL Advisory Board, attended the celebration. headline: Standards Bureau laboratory to resume full operations after years of inadequacy
summary_text: The National Bureau of Standards (NBS) says its central laboratory is expected to resume full operations tomorrow after years of limited capacity caused by inadequate equipment and the need for repairs. The laboratory has faced operational challenges since 2017, when it received equipment from Trademark East Africa, some of which was not functioning. The facility tests and certifies the quality and safety of imported and locally manufactured food, consumer goods and other products. Speaking to journalists in Juba on Wednesday morning, Central Laboratory Director Wilson Wani Leju said the facility had undergone renovation and was now being prepared to resume full testing services. “For years, the laboratory was in poor condition. We have now completed the renovation and installed the necessary signage, so it is ready for testing,” Leju said. He said the laboratory received equipment from Trademark East Africa in 2017, but some of the equipment was not functioning. “Some of it was not working, but it has since been repaired, and all but one item is now operational. The remaining item needs repair. We have also recently received equipment from the FAO and installed it,” Leju said. Leju said most of the donated equipment and technical support came from Trademark East Africa and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). The equipment is intended for use in the Chemistry, Microbiology, Mechanical Metrology, Paper and Textile laboratories at the National Central Laboratory. “Our technicians are currently working with colleagues from the metrology laboratory to commission it. The microbiology laboratory is fully operational, with no major obstacles. In the chemistry laboratory, some equipment is still being commissioned. We expect to begin full operations tomorrow,” he said. The director said the improved equipment would allow the laboratory to conduct tests that were previously difficult or impossible to perform. “Previously, we didn’t test for heavy metals such as arsenic, mercury, and lead. Now, we can test for pesticides and measure substances like caffeine in soft drinks and coffee,” Leju said. He warned that limited testing capacity could allow harmful substances in food and other consumer products to go undetected, potentially exposing consumers to health risks. “If harmful contaminants are present in products and go undetected, they may pose health risks, including cancer, even if the effects don’t appear immediately,” he said. Leju also highlighted improvements in the testing of cereals for aflatoxins, toxic substances produced by certain types of fungi that can contaminate food. “We also test cereals for aflatoxins. In the past, testing may have measured only total aflatoxins; now, it identifies specific types, such as B1, B2, and M1,” he said. ... Despite the new equipment and renovations, Wani said the bureau still faced gaps in its testing capacity. “The bureau still lacks adequate advanced testing equipment to detect harmful substances, poisons and chemical additives in some parts of the country,” he said. The laboratory’s return to full operations is expected to strengthen the country’s capacity to verify the safety and quality of imported and locally manufactured products and help identify potentially harmful substances before they reach consumers.

For us, it starts with building capacity at home. What we are doing now is taking that experience to the next level. We are improving our manufacturing capabilities, strengthening our engineering and technology divisions, and moving from simply supplying laboratory equipment to delivering complete scientific infrastructure. But manufacturers also have a responsibility. We cannot ask for local patronage and then compromise on quality. We must invest in our people, equipment, processes, certification and quality management. At Finlab, for example, we have invested in quality systems and achieved ISO 9001:2015 certification. For me, that is the balance we need: the government creates opportunities for credible local manufacturers, and Nigerian manufacturers commit themselves to internationally acceptable standards. ... headline: SU provides remote access to X-ray diffraction lab for African scientists | Stellenbosch University
summary_text: ## SU provides remote access to X-ray diffraction lab for African scientists Wiida Fourie-Basson Media officer, Faculty of Science 09 September 2026 - The next cohort of African scientists will soon receive hands-on training to “remotely” access a state-of-the-art X-ray diffraction laboratory in Stellenbosch University’s Department of Chemistry and Polymer Science. This is part of the UNESCO’s Remote Access to Lab Equipment initiative (UNESRALE) and aims to increase the use of crystallography on the African continent. The next cohort of African scientists will soon receive hands-on training to “remotely” access a state-of-the-art X-ray diffraction laboratory in Stellenbosch University’s Department of Chemistry and Polymer Science. This is part of the UNESCO’s Remote Access to Lab Equipment initiative (UNESRALE) and aims to increase the use of crystallography on the African continent. Crystallography is the science of studying how molecules and atoms are organised in crystals. This knowledge is useful in fields such as geology, chemistry, physics, biology, and materials science. One important aspect of crystallography is using X-ray diffraction to determine the arrangement of atoms and molecules in a crystal. This helps scientist to understand why materials have the properties they do, enabling them to develop new materials with improved properties for particular applications. Prof. Delia Haynes, an expert in crystallography in the supramolecular research group in SU’s Department of Chemistry and Polymer Science and coordinator of the project, says crystallography is key to many research questions of direct importance to Africa: “Efforts to increase the use of crystallography on the African continent are hampered by lack of access to this highly sophisticated equipment. X-ray diffractometers are also prohibitively expensive and require a stable power supply,” she explains. SU is home to one of the best-equipped X-ray diffraction laboratories on the African continent, along with several of Africa’s top researchers in this field. Scientists from the University of Lorraine in France first piloted the concept in 2022 through the AFRAMED project, training scientists from six African countries in handling high-performance and modern measuring devices. This pilot project was supported by the International Union of Crystallography, UNESCO and the National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) in France through their International Research Network programme, and has since trained a total of more than 15 researchers ... The Stellenbosch team hosted a week-long introductory crystallography school in 2023, attended by 46 students and researchers from Botswana (2), Zimbabwe (4) and South Africa (40). The course focused on the theory of X-ray diffraction and how to use the relevant software to solve and refine crystal structures. Participants were also given a tour of the laboratory facilities with a demonstration of a single-crystal X-ray diffraction data collection. During 2025, under the auspices of the Stellenbosch University Crystallography Remotely Accessible Lab (SUNCrystAL) initiative, another 28 participants from Botswana (3), Ghana (1), Kenya (3), Nigeria (2), Zimbabwe (2) and South Africa (17) attended the school. Afterwards, eight researchers from Zimbabwe, Botswana, Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana received intensive hands-on training in the X-ray diffraction laboratory. Over only two weeks they were trained in how to choose and mount a crystal, how to collect and process data, and how to operate the diffractometer over a remote connection. ... According to Prof. Bertie Fielding, Dean of the Faculty of Science, these workshops are about more than training and building capacity: “Through these workshops, we are also building strong partnerships across the African continent, which is an important strategic priority for the Faculty of Science.” ... The next SUNCrystAL event is planned for December 2027, associated with the 5th Pan-African Conference on Crystallography, which will be held in Stellenbosch. For more information contact Prof Haynes (dhaynes@sun.ac.za).

summary_text: The government is proposing new regulations that would make the calibration of specified measuring equipment mandatory while requiring calibration service providers to obtain licenses. "PURSUANT to section 8 of the Statutory Instruments Act, the Cabinet Secretary for Investments, Trade and Industry notifies the general public that Regulatory Impact Statements on the proposed Standards (Product Certification) Regulations, 2026 and the Standards (Scientific and Industrial Metrology) Regulations, 2026 have been prepared to assess the impact of the Regulations on the community and businesses," the notice read in part. ... Under the proposed regulations, KEBS would prescribe the categories of equipment that must undergo mandatory calibration, meaning businesses and institutions using such equipment could be required to have it regularly checked to ensure it provides accurate measurements. Calibration involves checking measuring equipment against recognised standards to verify its accuracy. The proposed regulations would also establish a licensing framework for companies and institutions offering calibration services. According to the proposals, KEBS will also get a new role, where it will be designated as Kenya's National Metrology Institute, with the regulations providing for the designation of other institutes to offer metrological traceability services. Under the new rules, offenses for violations will also be introduced, paving the way for enforcement against persons or businesses that fail to comply with the requirements once the regulations are in force. ... Following the new proposals, the government, through the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investments, invited members of the public and businesses likely to be affected by the regulations to submit their views. Businesses have been given 14 days to review and submit their views through a written memorandum to KEBS. ... is, therefore, to request all persons likely to be affected by the proposed Regulations to submit written memorandum on the proposed Regulations to the Managing Director within fourteen (14) days from ... At the same time, the government has proposed separate Standards (Product Certification) Regulations, 2026 that seek to establish product certification marks, provide a framework for their administration and enhance the quality and safety of goods. The product certification rules are also intended to prevent deceptive practices and facilitate regional and international trade. If the proposed rules are effectively passed and come into force, businesses using equipment covered by the regulations would be required to have it regularly calibrated to ensure accurate measurements, while calibration service providers would need to obtain licences from KEBS.

headline: Kenya turns to mobile labs to take advanced diagnostics to remote areas - The Standard Health
summary_text: Rabak Sami Ahmed, representative of Egyptian molecular diagnostics manufacturer Remedy, ... health stakeholders ... the Kenya Health ... 2026 in Nairobi on August 19, 2026. [Noel N ... wa, Standard] Kenya is exploring the use of portable and locally manufactured medical diagnostic technologies to reduce the cost of healthcare and bring specialised services closer to patients, particularly those living in underserved and remote areas. The technologies, showcased during the Kenya Health Summit 2026 at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) in Nairobi, include mobile molecular laboratories capable of conducting advanced diagnostic tests outside conventional hospital laboratories. For patients in remote areas, accessing specialized diagnostic services often means travelling long distances to referral hospitals, increasing both the financial and logistical burden of seeking care. Mobile diagnostic platforms could help bridge this gap by taking testing services closer to communities. In Baringo County, a mobile molecular laboratory has been deployed to communities with limited access to healthcare and unreliable electricity. Residents were screened for Hepatitis B, with those who tested positive undergoing molecular testing to determine their viral load. The approach demonstrates how mobile technology can support early detection while reducing the need for patients to travel to major urban centers for specialized tests. Rabak Sami Ahmed, a technical representative of Egyptian molecular diagnostics manufacturer Remedy, said decentralizing diagnostic services is critical to achieving universal health coverage. “Health has to reach the people where they are,” Ahmed said. He said the company is seeking partnerships with county-level hospitals and other health institutions to expand access to molecular diagnostics, particularly in remote parts of the country. Ahmed said the company's experience in Egypt shows that affordable diagnostic technologies can help lower the cost of testing, noting that its solutions have reduced diagnostic costs by about 40 per cent. “If we replicate this in Kenya, we will be able to achieve diagnostics at a much more affordable price,” he said. Osama Ismail, Remedy's representative in Kenya, said the company is also interested in working with the Ministry of Health and research institutions to strengthen the country's diagnostic capacity. However, expanding molecular diagnostics beyond major towns will require more than purchasing and distributing equipment. Health facilities will need reliable electricity, affordable reagents, skilled laboratory personnel, equipment maintenance and quality assurance systems. Sustainable financing will also be critical to ensuring that patients can afford the tests once the technology reaches local facilities. Without these supporting systems, there is a risk that sophisticated diagnostic equipment will remain concentrated in urban hospitals, leaving rural communities dependent on distant referral laboratories.

headline: Pack Expo 2026: PACK CHAT from show floor, Day 3 - PKN Packaging News
summary_text: N presents Pack Chat from Pack Expo, proudly supported by Heat and Control, bringing you packaging innovations that caught our eye on day three of the show. ... Watch the video here: ... SUMMARY TRANSCRIPT: At CAMA Group, Alessandro Rocca showed me the new MTL monoblock, which forms, loads and closes cartons in one machine – at 80 cartons a minute, handling up to 450 products a minute. It features a cabinet-free design, plus AI-driven monitoring of temperature and vibration. Alongside it is CAMA’s new Machine Enhancement Program: a cobot that loads carton blanks from the pallet into the magazine, and a cobot mounted on an autonomous mobile robot that can change its head and move between machines – loading reels or handling materials, 24 hours a day. Right-sizing specialist Packsize has just closed its acquisition of Italian automated packaging company Panotec, extending its global reach. Adam Fray says brands now see right-sized, on-demand boxes as a way to fund wider warehouse automation – less corrugate, lower freight and labour costs on every box. Its X5 Nozomi, developed with EFI, adds full-colour, edge-to-edge printing, so every right-sized box can carry unique branding. In Australia, Packsize partners with Visy. Plastic replacement is the big theme at Graphic Packaging International. Its Boardio paperboard canister – now commercial for coffee and Mentos gum – uses 90 per cent less plastic than the containers it replaces, and ships flat to be erected on the filling line. Its EnviroClip paperboard carriers replace plastic rings on bottles and cans, and are already commercial with Pepsi.And for cans, EnviroClip on a rounded-corner paperboard tray locks multipacks together like a brick, so no shrink film is needed. Technology Excellence Awards finalist Greiner Packaging is showing its Click In Sealing Lid. Instead of a heat-sealed aluminium foil and a plastic overcap, a single lid is sealed ultrasonically inside the rim – in partnership with Telsonic Ultrasonics. The lid reseals with a click, keeps the same line speed as heat sealing, and removes the foil layer, the pack’s biggest contributor to its carbon footprint. Paired with Greiner’s square CUBO cup, it makes a mono-material pack. It’s now moving towards commercialisation with customers in Europe. And finally, another Technology Excellence Awards finalist: Colorcon’s OneLock puts three functions into one closure for pharmaceutical and nutraceutical bottles. Arianna Keller showed me how it’s child-resistant – push down and turn – and tamper-evident: the first time it’s opened, a disc pops off the top. Underneath, the desiccant lives in the cap itself, so there’s no need for a separate canister dropped into the bottle, and no heat-induction liner either. It fits standard 38mm bottles, so it can drop straight onto existing lines. Thanks for watching Pack Chat. headline: Kicking the can on plastic | The Post
summary_text: Documents released under the OIA show Ministry for the Environment officials drafted a paper that advised matching European Union rules on PVC and rigid polystyrene food containers. 123rf.com ... Environment minister Nicola Grigg planned to bring a paper to Cabinet setting a new 2030 deadline for a hard-to-recycle plastic packaging ban – only to abandon the proposal after meeting with industry lobbyists. Documents released under the Official Information Act show Ministry for the Environment officials drafted a paper that advised matching European Union rules on PVC and rigid polystyrene food containers. Then-environment minister Penny Simmonds had told industry stakeholders in February of her intention to seek Cabinet agreement in late July for the January 2030 deadline. Grigg took on the portfolio in April. Her intention to proceed was reaffirmed as late as June, when she met the Packaging Forum at Parliament. Talking points prepared for the meeting said: “I intend to take a proposal to Cabinet shortly, aligning timing with the EU (from 1 January 2030), which industry feedback suggests is workable.” Documents show the Forum lobbied for an Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme where companies pay a levy or fee for using hard-to-recycle plastics. They also wanted timelines that matched rules in other export markets such as Australia, which is yet to set a phase-out deadline. Shortly after the meeting, the July Cabinet paper was pulled. The Post revealed in August that the Government had shelved work on the ban. “No paper went forward to Cabinet and therefore no decisions have been made on proposed phase-outs,” Grigg told the Sunday Star-Times this week. “I decided further work was needed. I hope to progress this in future. A decision will be a matter for a future government.” ... PVC (polyvinyl chloride) cling film is widely used in supermarkets and butcheries for wrapping meat, poultry, fish, and deli products. Christel Yardley ... ## The pay-to-pollute push The draft Cabinet paper targeted four main packaging uses: PVC cling film on fresh meat, poultry, and deli items; rigid polystyrene sushi trays, meat trays, and bakery containers; expanded polystyrene food packaging; and single-serve rigid PVC butter and condiment tubs. Officials told Grigg that setting a 2030 deadline was critical not just for domestic waste targets, but to protect exporters from non-tariff trade barriers. They warned that under the European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, non-compliant packaging faces a ban in Europe from 2030, meaning exporters who fail to transition risk losing access to key European retail networks. But they also noted that while alternatives exist for domestic retail uses, industry transition costs were a primary point of friction. Under an EPR scheme, packaging producers pay levies based on the volume and recyclability of materials placed on the market. That creates financial incentives to eliminate problematic plastics and fund collection infrastructure. Packaging Forum chief executive Craig Miller confirmed he met with Grigg to discuss regulatory settings, but denied encouraging the minister to shelve the paper. ... The Packaging Forum did not encourage Minister Grigg to defer or withdraw the draft Cabinet paper on hard-to-recycle plastics,” ... said. “However, ... have recommended that alignment with Australia and the EU is an important consideration to take into account, particularly from an exporter's perspective.” ... The battle with plastic waste began in earnest in 2018, when the government announced a nationwide ban on single-use shopping bags, giving retailers a year to prepare. Over the next few years, the government introduced bans on single-use produce bags, plates, bowls, cutlery, and certain straws, alongside plans for compostable produce labels. But progress stalled on phase three: difficult-to-recycle plastics used for meat, produce and deli goods, including PVC, polystyrene and PVdC. Originally set for mid-2025, the coalition scrapped the target date in late 2024. Simmonds ignored official advice to set a manageable mid-2026 deadline, which left retailers and packaging firms in limbo. ... When Grigg took over the portfolio, officials prepared a fresh Cabinet submission aimed at providing regulatory certainty by locking in the 2030 phase-out date. ... They also provided her with unresolved sector requests, including an update briefing from dairy giant Fonterra. The documents revealed Fonterra’s trial runs to replace hard-to-recycle plastics had hit major product-safety failures. The co-operative said efforts to swap out PVC in its exported butter mini-dishes for recyclable PET failed because the replacement plastic caused light-strike oxidation, a process where light exposure spoils the dairy product. Fonterra warned officials there were no proven alternative materials on the market capable of protecting the exported frozen butter dishes. Fonterra also reported delays in replacing rigid polystyrene (PS) in multi-pack yoghurt and culinary pottles. Switching materials would require multi-million dollar retrofits or replacing processing machinery, a process Fonterra said was delayed by ongoing global supply chain bottlenecks. To prevent export disruption, Fonterra asked for a multi-year transition extension past the original mid-2025 deadline for yoghurt pottles, alongside an explicit export exemption for PVC butter dishes while testing continues. ... headline: The ANZPAC plastics pact will wind down. Its last scorecard had one of four 2025 targets on track · The Print Register
summary_text: The ANZ ... The Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation, which runs the Australian, New Zealand and Pacific Islands Plastics Pact, says ANZPAC will begin an orderly wind-down process. For a printer or converter the short answer is that no obligation changes: the pact was voluntary, and the Covenant and the NEPM still apply. What goes is the region’s member-reported scorecard on plastic packaging. Its last edition, published in December 2024, found one of four 2025 targets on track, and as at 7 October 2026 the pact had published nothing on the 2025 target year. ... APCO’s notice, headed Update on the future of ANZPAC, carries no date. The Internet Archive first captured it on 9 September 2026. It gives four reasons: a decline in membership and a number of external challenges, including delays to the United Nations Global Plastics Treaty, reduced regional funding opportunities and continuing regulatory uncertainty in Australia. Together, it says, they made the program in its current structure increasingly difficult to sustain. On what comes next, the notice says APCO is actively exploring opportunities to transfer the ANZPAC brand and foundational work to a suitable partner that can build on its legacy in the region, that APCO will provide product stewardship support through its Stewardship team, and that Further updates on the wind-down process will be provided during the remainder of 2026. It names no partner and no end date, and it does not say what happens to the pact’s published guides and specifications. ... The Australian “regulatory uncertainty” is the story this masthead has followed all year. On 8 September APCO said a new Commonwealth packaging scheme would not come this term, and on 18 September environment ministers routed reform back through the Covenant instead. ... ANZPAC set four regional targets for 2025. Its most recent impact report, version 1 dated December 2024 and covering members’ 2023 data, said plainly: Only one of the four regional targets (Target 3) is on track to be met by 2025. The figures behind that line, from the report’s own summary table: ANZPAC 2025 targets against reported progress. Targets 1, 2 and 4 are aggregated member reporting; Target 3 is the regional recyclability assessment. | Target | Baseline | 2023 | 2025 goal | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1. Eliminate problematic and unnecessary plastic packaging | 9,194 t on market, 2,237 t eliminated (2021) | 4,844 t on market, 960 t eliminated | 0 t on market | | 2. Plastic packaging reusable, recyclable or compostable | 63% (2021) | 71% | 100% | | 3. Plastic packaging collected and effectively recycled, region | 216,340 t (2020) | 278,380 t | +25% in each geography | | 4. Average recycled content | 7.5% (2021) | 15% | 25% | The recycled tonnage rose 29% between 2020 and 2023 (our check: 278,380 against 216,340 is 28.7%). The report says Target 3 was met in Australia and the Pacific Islands and was close in New Zealand. On the other three, the 2023 numbers sit well short: 71% designed for recovery against 100%, and 15% recycled content against 25%. Scale matters when reading those numbers. Members reported placing 461,415 tonnes of plastic packaging on the region’s markets in 2023, against an estimated 1,575,900 tonnes in total, which the report calls around 30% of the total. The scorecard described the members, not the market. ... membership ... report ... member ... : ... 1 ... 2 ... pact ... and ... governments ... Nothing you are obliged to do changes. ANZPAC sat alongside regulation, not inside it; its own report described its work as voluntary initiatives by ANZPAC and its Members. The obligations are elsewhere, and APCO’s 8 September statement put them in one line: Obligations under the NEPM continue to apply, and the Covenant remains the pathway through which most Australian businesses meet them. If your business was a member, APCO’s notice points questions to its stewardship team, and further updates are due before the end of 2026. ... If you use the pact’s resources, save the ones you rely on now. The pact’s resources page carries, among others, a set of 12 Australian industry-agreed specifications for recycled polymer materials and its circular design principles for packaging. The notice’s plan is to transfer the brand and foundational work to a partner, and it does not say whether the documents stay where they are.

headline: Manufacturing trial puts Australian recycled polypropylene into KitKat packaging - Australian Manufacturing
summary_text: Australian manufacturing capability for recycled plastics is being demonstrated through a trial that has produced locally manufactured recycled polypropylene for use in a limited run of Nestlé KitKat wrappers. The trial builds on a 2022 collaboration between Viva Energy and Nestlé that introduced recycled soft plastic packaging for KitKat 4 Finger bars. The latest project aimed to demonstrate whether the supply chain, from refinery processing through to food-grade packaging, could be completed domestically. Viva Energy said more than 9.5 tonnes of plastic pyrolysis oil was processed at the Geelong Refinery in 2025 as part of the proof-of-concept. The company said its refinery and polymers plant provide the only Australian facility currently capable of chemically recycling used soft plastics into food-grade plastic feedstock. ... Viva Energy Executive General Manager Energy ... Infrastructure Bill ... the project demonstrated the potential of existing manufacturing infrastructure ... Geelong ... is Australia ... s ... this level of refining ... capability ... only ... Patterson ... We have proven the use of soft ... oil as ... how existing industrial ... adapted to support a circular ... economy ... Nestlé Oceania General Manager Confectionery Andrew Lawrey said the limited production run was intended to test new approaches to soft plastic recycling. ... “This collaboration demonstrates what’s possible when industry works together to tackle packaging challenges and accelerate the transition to a more circular economy,” Lawrey said. The companies noted that the trial was a single batch rather than an established ongoing manufacturing supply chain. They also said pyrolysis oil used in the project was imported because suitable local supply is not yet available at scale. Viva Energy said further development of domestic circular supply chains would require policy support for soft plastic collection, sorting and recycling, as well as investment in recycling and advanced manufacturing infrastructure. headline: Nestlé Tests Mass-Balance Recycled Feedstock in KitKat Wrappers - ThePackHub
summary_text: Nestlé Oceania has produced a limited run of KitKat 4 Finger wrappers using polypropylene attributed to recycled soft plastic feedstock through a mass-balance system. Featured in ThePackHub’s Innovation Zone, the Australian proof of concept explores a route for converting difficult-to-recycle flexible plastic waste into feedstock suitable for polypropylene intended for food-contact flexible packaging. The project involved Viva Energy, Taghleef Industries and Amcor, with the resulting material used for a bespoke production run of seven million KitKat wrappers in Victoria. ## Converting soft plastic waste into polymer feedstock At the start of the process, plastic pyrolysis oil was processed by Viva Energy at its Geelong Refinery in Victoria and used as a feedstock for polypropylene production. More than 9.5 tonnes of pyrolysis oil were processed during the proof of concept. This was followed by five tonnes of recycled polypropylene being supplied into the downstream packaging production process. Nestlé then worked with Taghleef Industries and Amcor to convert the material for the KitKat wrapper run. The development is significant because it focuses on flexible plastics that can be difficult to recycle through conventional mechanical recycling routes. Rather than attempting to turn collected flexible packaging directly back into new film, the process converts the waste into a feedstock that can enter polymer production. For food packaging in particular, the project demonstrates a potential route for incorporating feedstock derived from previously used flexible plastics into polypropylene intended for food-contact applications while maintaining the functional requirements of the wrapper. ... The KitKat wrappers use ISCC PLUS-certified recycled material allocated through a mass-balance system. Mass balance is a chain-of-custody approach in which recycled and conventional feedstocks can be mixed during polymer manufacturing. The amount of recycled input entering the process is tracked and attributed to a corresponding quantity of finished material. This distinction is important when considering recycled-content claims. It does not mean that each individual KitKat wrapper physically contains a defined percentage of molecules originating from recycled soft plastic. Instead, the recycled feedstock is accounted for and allocated through the certified production system. For packaging buyers and converters, this approach offers a different route to introducing recycled feedstock into applications where material performance and food-contact requirements can make the direct use of mechanically recycled polymers more challenging. ... The project does not substantially alter the familiar flexible wrapper format. Its focus is instead on the feedstock entering the polypropylene production system. That makes the trial particularly relevant to the wider challenge of finding further outlets for used flexible plastics while retaining the performance required of food packaging. ThePackHub’s view is that the project offers a potential way to turn difficult-to-recycle soft plastics into feedstock for new food-grade wrappers, while keeping the existing packaging format largely unchanged.. The development remains at pilot-testing stage, but the production of seven million wrappers provides a sizeable demonstration of how a mass-balance approach can be applied within an established confectionery packaging supply chain.

headline: Recorp enters Australian beverage can market - PKN Packaging News
summary_text: ## New Zealand-owned aluminium can manufacturer Recorp has expanded into Australia, offering beverage companies access to a range of can formats manufactured at its South Auckland facility. Recorp is positioning manufacturing flexibility, lower minimum order quantities and high recycled content as its main points of difference. The company will supply Australian customers from its 16,000-square-metre plant in Manukau, South Auckland. Opened in November 2024 following an investment Recorp puts at NZ$115 million, the facility has capacity to manufacture about 550 million cans annually. Its production line operates at up to 1850 cans a minute and incorporates eight bodymakers, dual decorators and equipment designed for relatively rapid changes between can heights and diameters. For Australian beverage companies, the range includes 250ml Slim, 330ml Sleek and Classic cans in 330ml, 375ml, 440ml and 500ml formats. Classic cans can be manufactured with either 200 or 202 diameter ends. Recorp says the flexibility of its plant allows it to accept lower minimum order quantities and shorten lead times, helping smaller beverage producers and larger companies testing new products avoid substantial initial inventory commitments. The company has not disclosed its minimum order volumes. Founder and chair Rob Fyfe said this capability was built into the plant from its inception. ... Recorp is also introducing ReCan85, its beverage can it says is manufactured with 85 per cent recycled aluminium. The company describes it as being among the highest recycled-content beverage cans available in Australasia and says the level is above the 60–65 per cent it regards as the international industry average. The recycled material includes post-consumer aluminium recovered from used beverage cans. Under Recorp’s New Zealand supply model, collected cans are processed offshore before the aluminium is returned to its Auckland facility for manufacture into new cans. The ReCan85 enters an Australian market in which other manufacturers are also raising recycled content. Visy, for example, began an 18-month trial in 2025 of an aluminium beverage can containing an average of 83 per cent recycled content, produced at its Yatala plant in Queensland. Parton said Recorp’s broader objective was to grow aluminium’s share of the single-serve beverage market, particularly in categories currently using plastic and glass bottles. While the company describes the Australian entry as a “launch”, no Australian manufacturing facility has been announced. The immediate development is the extension of Recorp’s New Zealand production and customer service operation to Australian beverage brands.

headline: AICC slams new containerboard price hikes
summary_text: The association said there have been three separate price rise announcements from the main containerboard producers within five months. ... 11, 2026 The association said the increases are not supported by current raw material costs or wider economic data. Credit: Richard Peterson / Shutterstock.com. Independent packaging association AICC has objected to the latest containerboard price rise announcements, saying that the “increases are without merit”. The group said there have been three separate price rise announcements from the main containerboard producers within five months. The latest came from PCA, which announced a $140/tonne increase for liner and medium from 1 September 2026. International Paper set out an $80/tonne rise for the same date while Smurfit Westrock announced a $100/tonne increase. AICC noted that the three latest announcements were made within a three-day period. In its statement, the association said the hikes are not supported by current raw material costs or wider economic data. The association highlighted that producers have pointed to economic pressures, high operating rates and factors such as inflation, fuel, labour and insurance, as well as tight supply to justify the increase. However, AICC said it is “skeptical” of those explanations in the present containerboard and corrugated market. It argued that the moves may instead point to a “small group of producers having market dominance”. According to AICC, PCA, Smurfit Westrock and International Paper together account for about 63% of the containerboard and linerboard supply market. It said PCA is 95% vertically integrated, meaning only 5% of its mill capacity is sold on the open market. International Paper and Smurfit Westrock have significant open-market sales, although AICC said independent operators represent only 10% to 12% of the market. The association also outlined producers’ prices have increased over the past five years in down market, and that the announced hikes disproportionately affect independent box manufacturers. ... AICC said three price rises in one ... are “unusual, but not unprecedented” pointing to 1994 and 2010.

headline: Packaging reform needs a clear destination - PKN Packaging News
summary_text: ## As Europe’s PPWR comes into effect this week, Australia’s packaging sector is still waiting for the regulatory certainty needed to turn circularity commitments into investment. On 12 August, the European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation begins to apply across its 27 member states. It is an important milestone, although not the end of the regulatory process. Many of the PPWR’s detailed requirements and targets will be introduced progressively, and businesses are still working through what implementation will mean in practice. Even so, Europe has established a direction. The regulation creates a binding framework covering packaging design, minimisation, recyclability, recycled content, reuse, labelling and producer responsibility across the EU market. The contrast with Australia is difficult to ignore. Australia’s packaging reforms remain under development, following consultation on options that included mandatory packaging requirements, an extended producer responsibility scheme and stronger administration of the existing co-regulatory framework. In the meantime, the current arrangements remain in place, and industry continues to operate without certainty about the final shape, timing or cost of reform. On an alarmingly regular basis, PKN is publishing call after call for clarity, certainty, direction on reform, including recycled content mandates and EPR. ... I do not pretend to have the answers to how Australia’s future packaging framework should be designed. But through PKN’s sustained coverage of the reform debate, a clear and consistent message has emerged from packaging manufacturers, recyclers, brand owners and industry groups: voluntary ambition cannot deliver circularity without the policy settings and market conditions to support it. It is equally apparent that Australia cannot afford much more delay. ... Industry is not simply asking for more regulation. What businesses need is a coherent, nationally consistent framework that defines responsibilities, creates viable end markets and gives companies confidence to invest. That distinction matters. Packaging businesses make decisions about manufacturing equipment, material development, recycling infrastructure and supply contracts over long timeframes. Investment becomes difficult when policy settings remain uncertain or differ between jurisdictions. ... Australia does not need to replicate PPWR. Our geography, population distribution, collection systems, processing capacity and markets are very different from Europe’s. But the PPWR demonstrates the value of setting a clear regulatory destination, even when the pathway towards full implementation extends over several years. ... The need for certainty is particularly apparent in Australia’s recycled plastics market. Recent pressure on the domestic resin and recycling sector has exposed the gap between building processing capacity and creating reliable demand for its output. Recyclers can invest in plants and packaging companies can develop formats incorporating recycled polymers, but those investments remain vulnerable when locally produced recyclate must compete with low-cost virgin resin and imported material. ... As industry participants and recycling organisations have repeatedly argued, mandatory minimum recycled-content requirements would create a level of demand that voluntary targets have failed to secure. They would also give recyclers and packaging manufacturers a firmer basis for investment, while reducing the commercial disadvantage faced by businesses already incorporating recycled material. The detail would matter enormously. Mandates would need to account for material availability, food-contact requirements, technical performance and the different challenges associated with individual polymers and packaging formats. But those complexities are an argument for carefully designed regulation, not for indefinite delay. ... Extended producer responsibility is another recurring theme in industry submissions and commentary. Pact Group has argued that a mandatory EPR framework is needed to support domestic recycling, stimulate demand for recycled content and ensure producers take greater responsibility for the packaging they place on the market. For EPR to make a material difference, it will need to do more than collect and redistribute fees. It should reward packaging designed for circularity, impose higher costs on difficult-to-recover formats, and direct funding towards the collection, sorting and reprocessing systems required to keep materials in circulation. It must also help connect the different parts of the system. A recyclable package has limited value if it is not collected. Collected material will not become a resource without sorting and reprocessing capacity. Recyclate will not support a circular economy unless manufacturers have both the incentive and the confidence to use it. ... There is already broad agreement about many of the problems. Australia sends substantial volumes of packaging to landfill, recycled-content uptake remains uneven, and fragmented rules add cost and complexity without necessarily delivering better environmental outcomes. What remains unresolved is how responsibility will be allocated, which requirements will become mandatory and when businesses will be expected to comply. Europe’s PPWR will face its own implementation challenges. Its existence does not guarantee that every target will be met or that collection and recycling systems will operate consistently across all member states. Nor does it provide Australia with a policy template that can simply be imported. ... a clear ... , an ... strong enough ... give ... the confidence ... invest ... it.

headline: Leno Mesh Bag Capacity Expands | Pope Textile Bag & Packaging

headline: New era for paper and packaging as APIA becomes APPIA - ProPack
summary_text: The Australasian Paper Industry Association has rebranded to the Australasian Paper and Packaging Industry Association (APPIA) The Australasian Paper Industry Association (APIA) has rebranded as the Australasian Paper and Packaging Industry Association (APPIA), reflecting the rapid growth of the fibre-based packaging sector across Australia and New Zealand. The name change signals the association’s expanded focus as fibre-based packaging continues to gain momentum, marking a new chapter for the industry and aligning the organisation with the evolving needs of its members. In addition to the evolution of the sector, the association said the change in name also reflects increasing regulatory obligations and the expanding role of international mills and fibre-board substrate manufacturers within the regional supply chain. ... ## Market analysis shows high growth for fibre-based packaging APPIA said industry research and market analysis show that fibre-based packaging categories in Australia have experienced over 50 per cent growth in the past decade, as demand for recyclable and renewable packaging formats accelerates globally. APPIA executive director Kellie Northwood said the name change is recognition of a fast-growing sector Northwood said APPIA’s expanding membership now includes paper manufacturers, international mills, packaging converters, fibre-board substrate suppliers, merchants, recyclers, and associated supply chain stakeholders across the A/NZ region. “The packaging landscape today is deeply interconnected with international manufacturing, fibre-board substrates, global pulp markets and circular economy frameworks,” she said. APPIA is now strengthening industry engagement with Responsible Wood and PEFC certification systems, supporting certification expansion beyond pulp and paper production, into manufacturing and broader supply chain operations. Ongoing engagement continues with Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation (APCO) and the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment, and Water across consultations relating to kerbside recyclability frameworks, packaging guideline reforms, and broader circular economy policy development. As well, APPIA now holds a seat on the APCO Materials Stewardship Committee, providing technical insights into fibre-based packaging reforms for the Australian industry. ... As part of the transition, APPIA has released a new brandmark and confirmed a new industry website will be launched in the coming quarter, including technical guidance materials, compliance advisory notes, regulatory updates, and industry resources to support members navigating increasingly complex legislative and environmental obligations.

headline: AIP partners with Packaging Cockpit in Australasia - ProPack
summary_text: The Australasian Institute of Packaging (AIP) is partnering with the Packaging Cockpit to bring global packaging specification management software to the Australasian region, including Australia, New Zealand, and parts of Southeast Asia. AIP executive director Nerida Kelton said, “The Packaging Cockpit is a tool that calculates the technical recyclability – as well as the life cycle assessment – of packaging systems and scientific calculations, and it enables data interface with suppliers and brands”. Kelton said the Packaging Cockpit is ideally suited for Australasian companies which are exporting into Europe, as the system is intuitive, comprehensive, and supported by leading European retailers and brands. “If your business needs to meet the Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulations, complete Declarations of Conformity, Technical Documentation and access your packaging suppliers’ specifications, then the Packaging Cockpit is the answer,” she said. Kelton added the team behind the Packaging Cockpit want to help make the recyclability of packaging systems transparent and help companies make the right decisions when optimising their packaging portfolio. ... “The Packaging Cockpit is intended to be applied both internally within companies and to entire supply chains,” said Kelton, adding that it integrates a scientific database and scientific methods into the software that is suitable for mass data. “Not only can the Packaging Cockpit fulfill PPWR regulations, but also other Extended Producer regulations across all corners of the globe. One system for the entire supply chain. The calculations can be performed for different countries, allowing country-specific evaluations. In addition, further management functions of the packaging portfolio can be performed. “The Packaging Cockpit can intuitively manage your packaging worldwide, and most importantly the basic version is available free of charge, which enables brands, packaging suppliers and manufacturers to be able to build their datasets and digitalisation of their specifications, in readiness to be able to then undertake their reporting and regulatory requirements. “Brands can work with their packaging suppliers to access their data through the Packaging Cockpit.”

headline: Moving beyond recycling: improving Australia's approach to packaging sustainability | The Canberra Times | Canberra, ACT
summary_text: When Australians talk about food packaging, the conversations almost always end up being around its environmental impact and the need to recycle. For many years, policy debates, environmental campaigns, and consumer efforts have treated packaging primarily as an end-of-life waste problem that needs to be minimised or recycled. But according to experts across the food supply chain, this narrow focus on material recovery is causing us to miss opportunities to strengthen Australia's food system security with improvements in packaging sustainability and to also solve the important problem of food waste along the supply chain. They're urging an increase in focus and investment on the 'critical middle' - the processing, packaging, storage, and distribution stages of the system - to reduce food waste and emissions, and improve resource efficiency, rather than on recycling alone. "Many people just think of packaging as a cause of waste and environmental impacts that needs to be minimised, when in fact its main role is to enable secure and resilient food systems," says Boris Munster, Managing Director of food processing and packaging leader Tetra Pak Oceania. Boris Munster. Picture supplied "Packaging is critical infrastructure, it's a supply chain enabler that ensures food travels through supply chains safely as well as preserving products and extending shelf life. While recycling is important, a narrow focus on material recovery can unintentionally increase food waste and emissions elsewhere in the supply chain." ... In ... the critical ... , the complex network of processing, packaging, and ... that keeps ... 's ... supply moving at scale and underpinning some of our biggest food industries. ... Each year around 7.6 million tonnes of that food is wasted across the Australian food system, during production and transport and in households, the equivalent of 312 kilograms per person. It costs the economy $36.6 billion When food spoils in transit, on shelves or in homes, it means the water, fuel, and energy used to produce it is wasted. This is where high-performance packaging acts as a key supply chain enabler: preserving nutrition, ensuring food safety, and extending shelf life. ... Mr Munster said that Australia's more than $10 billion dairy industry is a prime example of how food handling processes combined with the latest long life beverage cartons can bypass the need for cold-chain storage. "Australia is a big country," he said. "Imagine what savings you can make by eliminating the need for refrigerated transport travelling across thousands of kilometres, cutting both freight costs and emissions." ... While recycling remains an important piece of the circular economy puzzle it shouldn't be viewed as the only solution for reducing emissions. Mr Munster said Tetra Pak's research showed that recycling contributes only two per cent to the reduction in emissions. "Ninety-five per cent is defined by the choice of materials and the way it's produced which is why we believe by making the right decisions along the value chain can create a better outcome for everybody," he said. "There is an opportunity to build a framework that is broader that will also create sustainable innovations and sustainable food solutions. Having a regulatory framework that encourages material diversity brings resilience. It allows the industry to innovate using renewable, fibre-based materials that can cut lifecycle emissions by up to 65 per cent by 2050, compared to far more limited gains available through plastic recycling." ... Protecting ... A tougher regulatory focus on certain packaging types such as the aseptic packaging used for long-life products doesn't only affect food on grocery aisles - it threatens Australia's export capacity. Australia exports roughly 30 per cent of its total dairy production, with nearly a third of those exports shipped as liquid milk. For overseas markets such as Asia, long-life carton packaging is currently the only viable technology that allows Australian liquid dairy to arrive safely without spoiling. Restricting or penalising these material formats jeopardises critical export revenues for regional processing hubs and dairy farming communities. To help bridge the gap between high-level policy and practical supply chain solutions, industry partners are stepping up. In July, RMIT University and End Food Waste Australia launched a new agency to provide smaller Australian food producers with science-based tools to optimise their packaging, cut food waste, and improve supply chain efficiency. The new Food and Beverage SME Packaging and Machinery Solution Centre is a collaboration that also includes Tetra Pak, the Australian Packaging and Processing Machinery Association and the Australasian Institute of Packaging. ... "If you look at the large enterprises, the Nestles or the Coca-Colas of the world, they have a lot of knowledge in-house that smaller businesses don't have access to," said Mr Munster. "They are missing that support and opportunities to look at their value chain to make optimisations to their systems, and increase sustainability."

headline: Pact Group and Aldi give plastic waste new life
summary_text: Pact Group and Aldi give plastic waste new life. headline: European Paper Faces Costlier Path to Net Zero
summary_text: ## Europe’s pulp and paper industry has cut direct CO2 emissions by approximately 30% since Cepi launched its first decarbonisation roadmap in 2011, but reaching net zero by 2050 will require a more complex and increasingly costly mix of technologies and infrastructure, according to a new industry outlook. The 2050 Decarbonisation Outlook, prepared by Vision Hunters for Cepi, concludes that the sector has exceeded the climate ambition established in the 2011 roadmap. Past reductions have been driven primarily by replacing fossil fuels with biomass and other renewable energy sources, improving energy efficiency and modernising production assets. Structural changes in the European paper market have also contributed. Since 2011, European paper and board production capacity has declined by approximately 9 million metric tons, while demand and production have fallen by about 13 million and 14 million metric tons, respectively, the study estimates. Closures of older graphic paper mills have contributed to lower sector emissions alongside investments in efficiency, fuel switching and newer production assets. Looking ahead, the report identifies a credible route to net zero through further asset modernisation, process optimisation, fuel switching, electrification and the deployment of technologies including carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), bio-CCUS, advanced drying systems and hydrogen applications. The updated outlook projects cumulative emission reductions of 19.2 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent between 2025 and 2050, compared with 14.0 million metric tons anticipated under the earlier roadmap. The study expects electrification to become the dominant decarbonisation lever after 2030 as fossil-free electricity becomes more widely available and new technologies mature. Access to competitively priced electricity will therefore become increasingly important to the sector’s ability to meet its climate targets. The remaining challenge varies significantly by mill type. Stand-alone recycled-fibre and virgin-fibre paper mills, many of which continue to rely on natural gas, account for more than 55% of sector capacity and nearly 75% of current greenhouse gas emissions, according to the study. These facilities represent a significant opportunity for further reductions through electrification, heat pumps and the replacement of fossil-fuelled equipment. Integrated chemical pulp and market pulp mills could play a different role. Cepi estimates that capturing and storing biogenic CO2 from these operations could deliver an additional 2.5 million to 10 million metric tons of annual CO2-removal potential by 2050. ... Future reductions, however, are expected to be more difficult and expensive than those achieved during the past 15 years. Investment requirements are projected to rise substantially, with spending needs peaking between 2030 and 2040 as the industry moves from relatively mature efficiency and fuel-switching measures toward more capital-intensive electrification and emerging technologies. Mill-level investment alone will not be sufficient. The transition also depends on access to competitively priced fossil-free electricity and heat, expanded power grids, CO2 transport and storage infrastructure, sustainable biomass and a policy framework capable of supporting industrial investment. Many of the most significant breakthrough technologies are not expected to reach large-scale deployment until after 2030. The outlook comes as European pulp and paper producers face rising energy and carbon costs as well as growing international competition. The report says global overcapacity and intensifying competition are increasing the risk of carbon leakage and could affect the sector’s long-term competitiveness if European producers face decarbonisation costs that are not matched in competing regions. The study concludes that the technologies and pathways required to reach net zero are increasingly identifiable. Their deployment, however, will depend not only on investments by pulp and paper producers but also on the availability of energy, infrastructure and policy conditions extending well beyond individual mills. ... Cepi is the European association representing the pulp and paper industry. Through its 19 national associations, it represents about 480 companies operating 856 mills across Europe and directly employing more than 175,000 people. Based in Brussels, Cepi represents the sector before European institutions and other stakeholders.

headline: European Commission Reiterates Serious Concerns about UPM and Sappi Graphic Paper JV
summary_text: To address the Commission's concerns, UPM and Sappi are planning to submit proposals for specific remedies, but given the rationale of the transaction, not divestments. Oct. 5, 2026 (Press Release) - UPM and Sappi have received a Letter of Facts from the European Commission stating that it continues to have serious concerns about the proposed graphic paper Joint Venture. The parties are in the process of analyzing and responding to the Letter of Facts. UPM disagrees with the Commission's preliminary assessment and will continue to engage with the review process. UPM continues to believe that the proposed Joint Venture would support the long-term competitiveness, sustainability and resilience of the European graphic paper industry. To address the Commission's concerns, the parties are planning to submit proposals for specific remedies, but given the rationale of the transaction, not divestments. ... The proposed Joint Venture is being assessed at a time when the European Commission is updating its approach to competition policy to better reflect Europe's changing economic and strategic environment in a more fragmented world. The Commission leadership has rightly called for merger assessment which — besides safeguarding effective competition — would give appropriate weight to resilience, innovation and investment as well as longer-term market dynamics. That direction is now reflected in the Commission's draft revised Merger Guidelines published on April 30, 2026. ... A dynamic, forward-looking approach in merger control review is particularly critical in structurally declining markets. Due to digitalization, the demand for graphic paper in Europe has more than halved over the past two decades and is projected to decline further in the coming years. The proposed Joint Venture represents a rational response to these market realities and would enable a more orderly adjustment of industry capacity while maintaining reliable customer supply and generating significant efficiencies. Without the Joint Venture, the outlook for the European graphic paper industry is likely to become increasingly challenging: European producers would be under increasing pressure, accelerating further capacity closures in a manner which would make customers dependent on imports already in the short term due to drastically narrowed paper grade portfolios. Continued market decline and overcapacity would make it increasingly difficult to maintain a competitive and reliable European supply base. ... UPM and Sappi announced the planned Joint Venture in 2025 and signed the definitive agreement on the transaction in May 2026. The transaction requires among other conditions merger control approvals, and most jurisdictions, including China, South Africa and the U.S., have already approved the transaction. The European Commission's final decision is expected by year-end or shortly thereafter. The Joint Venture would become operational upon closing. ... On May 28, UPM announced that it signed a definitive agreement to form a graphic paper Joint Venture with Sappi, and the parties have secured financing arrangements that will provide a robust financial standing for the Joint Venture.
