headline: UPM-Sappi paper venture advances
summary_text: UPM and Sappi have cleared another regulatory hurdle in their planned combination of European graphic paper operations. South African competition authorities have approved the transaction without conditions, according to Bloomberg. The decision advances the deal, but the European Commission’s review remains decisive. The two companies plan to combine their graphic paper businesses in a new independently operated company owned equally by UPM and Sappi. ## EU raises competition concerns The proposed transaction would create a major European producer in a market already characterised by declining demand and repeated capacity cuts. The European Commission opened an in-depth investigation earlier this year and in August issued a Statement of Objections outlining preliminary concerns that the deal could reduce competition in parts of the graphic paper market. UPM has stressed that the document is part of the regulatory process and does not constitute a final decision. Reports by Reuters and Helsingin Sanomat in September suggested that the Commission could move to block the transaction, but no final decision has yet been announced. ... Despite the uncertainty, UPM and Sappi are continuing preparations for the new company. Gunnar Eberhardt has been nominated as chief executive officer and Stephen Blyth as chief financial officer. Other senior positions are also expected to be filled by executives from the two existing organisations. All appointments remain conditional on regulatory approval and completion of the transaction. Until then, UPM and Sappi will continue to operate separately. ... ## Industry under pressure The planned joint venture comes as Europe’s graphic paper market continues to shrink. Digitalisation has reduced demand for newsprint, magazine paper and other printing grades for years, prompting producers to close machines, reduce capacity and concentrate production at their most competitive mills. UPM and Sappi argue that combining their operations would create a stronger and more efficient business. For competition authorities, the key question is whether consolidation would leave customers with too few suppliers or give the new company excessive market power. South Africa’s unconditional approval is therefore only one part of the regulatory process. headline: EU challenges UPM and Sappi’s planned paper venture
summary_text: The European Commission has reached the preliminary conclusion that the proposed joint venture between Finland’s UPM and South Africa’s Sappi could restrict competition in the European printing paper market. Brussels fears that the transaction could enable the new company to raise prices or reduce product quality. The Commission has outlined its concerns in a statement of objections sent to the two forest industry groups. The document represents a formal step in the EU’s competition investigation and does not prejudge the final outcome of the case. According to Finnish public service broadcaster Yle, the planned joint venture would become the market leader in several categories of graphic paper across the European Economic Area, or EEA. Printing paper is used in products including magazines, catalogues, advertising material and books. Demand has been declining for years as information, publishing and advertising have increasingly moved to digital channels. The downturn has resulted in mill closures, production cuts and extensive restructuring across the European paper industry. ... The proposed company would combine UPM’s graphic paper operations in Europe and the United States with Sappi’s European business in the same sector. Selected parts of Sappi’s speciality paper activities and related operations would also be included. The European Commission’s concerns focus primarily on the markets for coated mechanical paper and coated woodfree paper. Its preliminary assessment indicates that the joint venture could obtain a sufficiently strong position to reduce competitive pressure. Greater market power could allow the company to raise prices or lower product quality to the detriment of customers. A highly concentrated market could also reduce customers’ choice of suppliers and weaken the incentive for producers to develop their products and services. The assessment is particularly significant because the transaction would combine two of Europe’s largest graphic paper producers. The Commission must now determine whether competition from other manufacturers and alternative products would be sufficient to constrain the new company. The investigation comes as European paper producers are already adjusting to a structurally contracting market. Companies argue that consolidation may be necessary to maintain efficient production, while customers remain concerned about the consequences of having fewer suppliers. ... The Finnish forest industry group remains confident that the companies can address the ... According to UPM, the joint venture is a necessary step to safeguard long-term supplies of graphic paper to European customers. The company also argues that the transaction would help strengthen a European paper industry facing declining demand, high energy and raw-material costs, and excess production capacity. ... The companies’ case rests largely on the rapid transformation of the market. Structural demand for graphic paper has fallen for many years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain profitable production and sufficient capacity at European mills. The Commission must nevertheless assess whether the claimed industrial benefits outweigh the risk of customers having fewer suppliers from which to choose. ... UPM and Sappi signed the definitive agreement to establish the graphic paper joint venture in May 2026. UPM’s entire Communication Papers business would be transferred to the new company. Sappi would contribute its European graphic paper operations, selected speciality paper activities and associated functions. UPM and Sappi would each own 50 per cent of the joint venture. Neither company would therefore have sole control over the business. Sappi operates the Kirkniemi paper mill near Lohja in Finland. The facility is a major producer of coated paper used in magazines, advertising materials and other printed products. UPM, meanwhile, has extensive graphic paper production operations in Europe and the United States. The transaction would bring the companies’ mills, sales organisations and related activities together within one of the market’s largest producers. The parties now have an opportunity to respond to the Commission’s objections, provide additional evidence and propose measures to address the identified competition concerns. Possible remedies could include the sale of assets or other binding commitments. It is not yet known whether UPM and Sappi intend to offer concessions. The European Commission’s continued investigation will determine whether the joint venture can be approved in its current form, cleared subject to conditions or prohibited.

headline: EU raises objections to UPM-Sappi giant joint venture - Timber Industry News
summary_text: UPM says it can address competition concerns raised by the European Commission over its planned €1.42 billion graphic paper joint venture with Sappi, keeping one of the largest restructurings of Europe's paper industry on course despite a deeper regulatory challenge. headline: EU Details Concerns Over UPM-Sappi Paper Venture
summary_text: ## The European Commission has issued a Statement of Objections outlining its preliminary competition concerns over the planned graphic paper joint venture between UPM and Sappi. According to the Commission, the proposed transaction could reduce competition in the European markets for coated mechanical paper and wood-free coated paper. These grades are widely used for magazines, books and promotional materials. The Commission’s preliminary assessment indicates that the joint venture could gain sufficient market power to increase prices or reduce product quality. The regulator also remains unconvinced that the cost savings, environmental improvements and supply-resilience benefits presented by the companies would offset the potential harm to competition. A Statement of Objections is a formal step in an in-depth merger investigation and does not prejudge the final outcome. UPM and Sappi can submit a response, examine the Commission’s case file and request an oral hearing. UPM said it is reviewing the document with Sappi and will respond in due course. The company remains confident that it can address the Commission’s preliminary concerns. UPM also maintained that the venture is needed to secure reliable supplies for European graphic paper customers and strengthen an industry facing declining demand, structural overcapacity and high operating costs. The Statement of Objections marks the latest development in a review whose timetable was suspended on May 26 while regulators awaited requested information. The Commission now has until November 11 to issue a final decision. The proposed 50-50 venture, valued at €1.42 billion, would combine the entire UPM Communication Papers business with Sappi’s European graphic paper operations. The two businesses will continue operating independently until the transaction receives the required regulatory approvals and closes.

headline: PaperShell secures €40.3M EU grant to build its first full-scale factory
summary_text: The Swedish deeptech company has signed a Grant Agreement with the European Commission under the EU Innovation Fund, unlocking €40.3M of a €83M project to expand its Tibro plant to 23,000 tonnes per year capacity by 2030. The material is already NATO-approved and shipping to customers in construction, defence, electronics and transport. PaperShell makes a composite that looks and sounds improbable on paper, which is apt, because it is essentially made of it. The Swedish company presses layers of kraft paper, impregnated with a bio-binder derived from agricultural waste streams, into load-bearing components that the company says are stronger than plastics, lighter than aluminium, and more versatile than glass fibre composites. Its pilot plant in Tibro, Sweden, has been running since 2023 and has shipped more than 150,000 components. The total investment ofapproximately EUR 400 million makes it the single largest investment in NorskeSkog's history. At the same time, Norske Skog willremain a reliable supplier of high-quality publication paper products," saysGeir Drangsland, CEO of Norske Skog.Deliveries of containerboard to customers will start during the second quarterof 2025. Capacity utilisation is expected to reach 50-60% towards the end of2025 and full utilisation of 95% during the first half of 2027. The productionwill be fully based on recycled paper. headline: Mondi reports Q3 EBITDA of €196m amid rising input costs
summary_text: Mondi reported third-quarter underlying EBITDA of €196 million, down from €223 million a year earlier. Higher energy and raw-material costs—including wood costs in Central and Eastern Europe—continued to weigh on performance, while competitive pressure and delays in passing through paper-price increases constrained Corrugated Solutions margins. Mondi said stronger packaging-paper prices and announced increases across several grades should support results toward the end of 2026 and into 2027, although input-cost pressures remain.

headline: Finland’s Paper Industry Cuts Fossil CO₂ Emissions by 85 Per cent
summary_text: Figures from the Finnish Forest Industries Federation indicate that Finland’s pulp and paper industry has reduced fossil CO₂ emissions by about 85% since 1990 and landfill waste by 97% since 1992. The reported progress reflects long-term investment in cleaner production technologies, energy efficiency and greater use of industrial by-products—useful context for suppliers and buyers assessing the sector’s decarbonisation trajectory.

headline: Positive investment decision at Saugbrugs
summary_text: Norske Skog approved an investment of up to approximately NOK 850 million to rebuild paper machine 6 at its Saugbrugs site in Halden, Norway. The machine is designed for flexible annual production of up to 300,000 tonnes of TMP-based kraftliner or 230,000 tonnes of SC magazine paper, with start-up expected in the first half of 2028. The kraftliner option would expand the company’s fibre-based packaging offering; once PM6 starts, production on the existing PM4 and PM5 machines is planned to end.

headline: Finland wins 12 ScanStar awards
summary_text: Finnish firms won 12 of 18 awards at the 2026 Nordic ScanStar packaging competition, with 30 entries from Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark. Recognised solutions included packaging intended to reduce plastic use, improve logistics and enable reuse of fibre-based materials. The results highlight Nordic suppliers’ continued innovation in fibre packaging and provide examples of alternatives for packaging procurement.

headline: Mondelēz International replaces PET cookie trays with FSC-certified paper
summary_text: Mondelēz said it is replacing rigid PET trays with FSC-certified paper trays for more than 115 cookie products across eight brands and 25 European markets, including Nordic countries. The change covers around 28,000 tonnes of biscuits annually and is presented by the company as a major European bakery-packaging sustainability initiative. For fibre-based packaging suppliers, the transition signals substantial branded demand, while procurement teams will need to assess performance and supply requirements against the displaced plastic format.

headline: EU challenges UPM and Sappi’s planned paper venture
summary_text: The European Commission reached a preliminary view that the proposed UPM–Sappi joint venture could restrict competition in the European printing-paper market. Sappi’s Kirkniemi mill in Finland is among the assets expected to be included. The regulatory scrutiny puts a major structural deal—and its potential effects on supplier choice and market concentration—under review.

headline: Metsä Board Kemi to modernize board machine winder
summary_text: Metsä Board planned to modernise the board-machine winder at its Kemi mill during the site’s October–November annual maintenance shutdown. The finishing-line investment is a targeted mill upgrade intended to improve board-production operations; the work is scheduled alongside the planned outage.

headline: Kemi mill shutdown affects Finland's wood market
summary_text: Metsä Fibre planned a six-week production stoppage at its Kemi bioproduct mill during October and November for a cooking-system modernisation coordinated with annual maintenance. The outage is expected to temporarily reduce the mill’s pulpwood demand, affecting forest owners, logging contractors and transport providers in northern Finland. The report also notes uncertainty for the regional wood market related to Stora Enso’s proposed permanent closure of the nearby Veitsiluoto sawmill.

headline: Stora Enso plans to centralise sawmill production in Northern Finland
summary_text: Stora Enso proposed moving pine-timber sawing from its Veitsiluoto sawmill in Kemi to other northern Finnish sawmills, particularly Oulu and Kalajoki. If implemented, the plan would permanently close Veitsiluoto and affect about 60 employees; negotiations were to precede a final decision. The proposed consolidation reflects the company’s focus on efficiency and profitability and could affect local suppliers and wood procurement patterns.

headline: Stora Enso Confirms Gruvön CLT Closure
summary_text: Stora Enso has confirmed the permanent closure of its cross-laminated timber (CLT) production unit at Gruvön in Sweden by the end of 2026. The decision, announced on October 22 following negotiations, will affect approximately 80 positions. Sawmill operations at the site will continue. The closure follows a proposal announced in September, when the company initiated negotiations over the future of its Gruvön CLT operations. Stora Enso cited slower-than-expected market growth, rising wood costs and relatively high fixed production costs as factors that have continued to undermine profitability.

headline: Essity Sees US Restaurants Cutting Back On Paper Towels
summary_text: Essity Sees US Restaurants Cutting Back On Paper Towels. Essity, a Swedish hygiene-products maker, says US restaurants are pulling back faster than European ones, and that is showing up in weaker demand for its Tork paper towels and other "away-from-home" supplies. What does this mean ? Essity CEO Ulrika Kolsrud told Reuters on Thursday that fewer Americans are going out to eat, a big deal because the US generates about 40 % of revenue in the company's professional hygiene unit. In the third quarter, that division saw sales fall, with both volumes and prices down at the same time as costs of goods sold rose.

headline: Essity Q3 2026 slides: cash flow strong as margins compress
summary_text: Essity presented its third-quarter 2026 results on October 22, showing a company navigating significant cost headwinds while maintaining strong cash generation and pursuing strategic acquisitions. The Swedish hygiene and health products maker reported net sales of SEK 36.1 billion, up 4.1 % from the prior year, though organic growth slipped 0.3 % as volume and price/mix effects remained slightly negative. The presentation, led by CEO Ulrika Kolsrud and CFO Fredrik Rystedt, emphasized resilience in challenging market conditions, with operating cash flow reaching SEK 5.8 billion and the company maintaining a solid balance sheet with net debt at 1.0 times EBITDA. However, profitability metrics came under pressure, with the EBITA margin excluding items affecting comparability declining to 13.1 % from 14.6 % in the year-earlier quarter. Essity shares traded at $ 273.5 following the presentation, down 1.08 % and reflecting investor concerns about margin compression despite the company's strategic progress.

headline: Norske Skog Q3 2026 slides: property gain lifts profit amid cost pressure
summary_text: Norske Skog ASA (OSE: NSKOG) presented its third quarter 2026 results on October 22, revealing a complex picture of transformation progress shadowed by operational challenges. The Norwegian paper and packaging producer reported EBITDA of NOK 448 million and pre-tax profit of NOK 251 million, but investors responded cautiously, sending shares down 3.87 % to $ 40.95 as markets digested the impact of a substantial one-time gain that masked underlying operational pressure. The quarter's headline results were significantly boosted by a NOK 338 million gain from the sale of property to Norwegian Nuclear Decommissioning (NND) at the company's Saugbrugs facility. This transaction, which closed in early October with NOK 770 million in proceeds, strengthened liquidity and enabled debt reduction but complicated assessment of the company's core operational performance during a period of elevated energy costs and production challenges at its flagship Golbey mill in France. Financial Performance Highlights.

headline: Billerud Q3 2026 slides: margin recovery accelerates to 10%
summary_text: Billerud presented its third-quarter 2026 results on October 22, showcasing a significant profitability recovery as the Swedish packaging and paper maker delivered a 10 % adjusted EBITDA margin alongside strong cash generation. The company reported net sales of 10,166 SEKm, marking a return to positive growth in both its European and North American markets, while cash conversion reached 127 % and leverage declined to 2.0x. The presentation, led by President & CEO Ivar Vatne and CFO Andrei Krés, highlighted sequential margin improvement of more than 50 % from the prior quarter's 7 % level, signaling progress in the company's recovery from a weak start to 2026. The results come as Billerud advances its strategic transformation in North America while navigating mixed market conditions across its key end-use segments. Quarterly Performance Highlights.

headline: Essity reports Q3 volume decline despite margin beat
summary_text: Investing.com - Essity AB posted third-quarter results that showed weaker-than-expected volumes alongside a stronger margin performance, with organic sales declining 0.3 % against analyst expectations of 1.2 % growth. The Swedish hygiene and health company reported volumes fell 0.1 % in the quarter, missing the consensus estimate of 1.3 % growth. Pricing and mix declined 0.2 %, contrary to expectations of a 0.3 % increase, despite previously announced price increases in Consumer Tissue. EBITA reached SEK4,725 million, representing a margin of 13.1 %, approximately 90 basis points above the consensus estimate of 12.2 %. The result was 7 % ahead of analyst expectations of SEK4,414 million.

headline: Finnish Pulp and Paper Cuts Fossil CO₂ Emissions 85%
summary_text: Fossil CO₂ emissions from Finland's pulp and paper industry fell from 5.88 million tonnes in 1990 to approximately 900,000 tonnes in 2025. Fossil CO₂ emissions declined by around 85 % both in absolute terms and relative to production, supported by improved energy efficiency and the replacement of fossil fuels with bioenergy. Other air pollutants have also decreased substantially.

headline: International Paper confirms Capital Markets Day ahead of planned DS Smith separation
summary_text: International Paper has confirmed that its EMEA Packaging Business will hold a Capital Markets Day in London on 3 November 2026, as preparations continue for its proposed separation into an independent, publicly traded company operating as DS Smith plc. The event will take place from 13:00 to 17:00 GMT and will be hosted by Tim Nicholls, future Chief Executive Officer of DS Smith plc, and Vincent Bonnot, future Chief Financial Officer, alongside other senior leaders from the EMEA business. Presentations will cover the proposed company's business model, growth strategy and financial outlook following the separation, providing investors with further details of its planned position in the European packaging market. International Paper expects to complete the separation through a spin-off, with DS Smith plc listed on the London Stock Exchange and a Level II American Depositary Receipt (ADR) programme listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The proposed transaction remains subject to several conditions, including final approval from International Paper's Board of Directors, the effectiveness of a registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) , and publication of a prospectus approved by the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

Its performance improvements follow a headbox investment announced in December 2025 for paper machine 6 (PM6) , aimed at improving fiber formation, sheet uniformity and strength. headline: Chemicals in Q3 2026: Where the industry stands
summary_text: Chemicals total shareholder returns (TSR) have outpaced the broader market so far in 2026, even as demand growth remains uneven and supply disruptions continue to shape trade ... ## What we are seeing in October 2026 - Chemicals TSR performance has outpaced the broader market but has been volatile. Chemicals TSR rose 14 percent through mid-September 2026, compared with 10 percent for the broader world index (Exhibit 1). Most of the sector’s outperformance occurred in January and February 2026, before the Middle East supply constraints emerged, and TSR has been broadly flat since. This follows several years of the chemicals sector lagging behind the overall market, with a CAGR of 5 percent since the start of 2023, compared with 21 percent for the world index. 1 - Electronics and data center exposure is driving the strongest TSR contribution. Chemical companies serving electronics and data centers have generated TSR of about 48 percent so far in 2026, compared with 14 percent for the chemicals industry overall (Exhibit 2). Their enterprise-value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) multiples increased by roughly four to five turns during the year. Aside from electronics-related businesses, valuations across the chemicals industry have been fairly consistent in 2026. - The Middle East disruption continues to play out, but its effects on petrochemical markets have been more limited than a previous McKinsey analysis estimated. Supply and shipping constraints continued into the third quarter of 2026. 2 Petrochemical prices have so far moved broadly in line with feedstock costs, and the pricing effect has been more limited than earlier market commentary indicated. 3 Imports into Asia and improving global availability have helped moderate the impact. Approximately 8 million metric tons per annum (MTA) of global ethylene capacity came online from April through July 2026. - Chemical companies are shifting from cost transformations to structural change. With demand recovery outside of Asia no longer assumed for sectors other than electronics, players are looking for ways to change their positioning, including through M&A. Many are focusing on portfolio moves, consolidation, asset rationalization, and reducing capital projects. On AI, discussions are shifting from pilots and productivity gains to embedding AI in core processes. 4 ... - Profitability is rebounding sharply for petrochemical players. Based on equity analyst estimates, EBITDA for the largest-revenue public petrochemical companies is expected to nearly double from 2025 to 2026—an estimated 106 percent increase—with total EBITDA in line with 2019, 2020, and 2022. 5 - Industry free cash flow is expected to recover through 2027, as capital intensity continues to decline and operating cash flow rebounds. Capital expenditures among the top chemical companies have fallen from approximately $80 billion in 2023 to an estimated $60 billion in 2026—the lowest level in seven years. Higher free cash flow could support balance sheets, based on equity analyst estimates. - Petrochemical players have seen a negative impact on industry returns over the past several years. Base-chemical market cap outside of Greater China is down approximately $110 billion since the start of 2023, while market capitalization of Greater China base chemicals is up about $25 billion (Exhibit 3). - Large-scale M&A activity is continuing. headline: Why Did US Diacetone Alcohol Prices Remain Unchanged in Late September 2026?
summary_text: The US Diacetone alcohol (DAA) market remained largely stable in late September 2026 as balanced supply, cautious downstream purchasing and mixed feedstock signals prevented a clear price direction. Diacetone Alcohol, widely used as a solvent in paints, coatings, inks, adhesives and other industrial applications, entered the end of the month with buyers largely covering routine requirements rather than building substantial inventories. At the same time, developments in the upstream acetone market and broader US manufacturing environment provided competing signals, keeping the market range-bound. ... US Diacetone Alcohol prices held unchanged through late September, following a firmer first half of 2026. Market data showed North American Diacetone Alcohol had gained earlier in the year as acetone costs increased and solvent demand remained relatively constructive. By late September, however, the market had lost some of that momentum. Acetone prices had softened after the August settlement declined from July, while significantly higher US acetone imports increased supply flexibility. Bulk cargoes from Europe and Asia added to availability and reduced the likelihood of immediate feedstock-driven cost pressure. ... Demand was steady but lacked the strength required to push Diacetone Alcohol prices higher. Paints and coatings remained important outlets, while adhesives, industrial solvents and cleaning applications provided a baseline level of consumption. Buyers were nevertheless cautious about holding excess stocks as the peak summer construction period passed. This encouraged procurement mainly against immediate requirements rather than aggressive spot accumulation. The broader US economy continued to show resilience in September, although construction was among the sectors reporting contraction in the latest survey, reinforcing the mixed demand environment. ... Supply conditions remained comfortable enough to prevent significant upward pressure. The US acetone market benefited from additional imports and stable production availability, while feedstock propylene was described as well supplied. Full operation of major propane dehydrogenation units and soft derivative demand contributed to downward pressure on upstream propylene economics. This combination gave Diacetone Alcohol producers less room to push through higher offers despite elevated costs elsewhere in the chemical supply chain. ... The US Diacetone Alcohol market is likely to remain range-bound in the near term, with the balance between acetone costs and downstream solvent demand determining the next move. A sustained recovery in coatings, adhesives and industrial activity could strengthen buying interest, while comfortable acetone availability and cautious inventory management could continue to cap gains. Higher logistics and energy costs remain an upside risk, particularly as US businesses report increasing supply-chain and fuel-cost pressures.

summary_text: Korea Alcohol Group is shifting its portfolio toward semiconductor materials, moving the focus from ethanol and commodity chemicals to higher-value semiconductor materials. It began as an ethanol producer in 1984 and entered the electronic materials market in 1999 after completing an electronic-grade normal butyl acetate plant in Ulsan. Normal butyl acetate is an organic solvent used to control the dissolution performance and volatility of semiconductor thinners. Semiconductor materials accounted for more than 80% of PURIT's sales in the first half of this year, at 66.8 billion won. ... They now account for about 65% of total semiconductor-related sales. The company supplies thinners, etchants, strippers, cleaning solutions, monomers and polymers used in semiconductor photolithography and etching processes. Semiconductor materials sales have recently increased, led by hydrofluoric acid (HF)-based etchants that the company has successfully localized. ENF Technology's official materials describe its portfolio as including process chemicals for semiconductor and display manufacturing. ... The group has established a structure linking the businesses of its affiliates from raw-material sourcing and distribution through basic chemical materials, advanced semiconductor materials, and recycling and resource circulation. KC&A sources chemical raw materials in South Korea and overseas, while Korea Alcohol Industrial and PURIT produce high-purity electronic-grade solvents. ENF Technology uses those materials to make semiconductor process products such as thinners. PURIT also operates a waste organic-solvent recycling business using waste generated during manufacturing processes. KC&A describes its role as supplying raw materials to affiliates including Korea Alcohol Industrial and ENF Technology. ... The group is also building a large production hub bringing together its major materials affiliates. Korea Alcohol Industrial, ENF Technology and PURIT are establishing an integrated campus in the Yesan 2 General Industrial Complex in South Chungcheong Province, with a combined investment of 450 billion won. headline: Two Countries Ship Nine Tenths of Your Ethyl Acetate · Capacity Ledger
summary_text: # Two Countries Ship Nine Tenths of Your Ethyl Acetate INEOS mothballed Europe's largest ethyl acetate line on September 22, and the American drum barely felt it, because Britain had already fallen to 1.1 percent of the US import book. Mexico and South Africa carry 90.5 percent of what's left, the tightest that book has been in seven years, and the largest domestic plant spent this spring in Chapter 11. INEOS rates the ethyl acetate line at Hull at 200,000 tonnes a year. America's entire annual ethyl acetate import book is 39,945 tonnes. One European plant, five times everything the United States buys from the rest of the world put together. INEOS mothballed it on September 22 along with the acetic acid and acetic anhydride units beside it, and the honest read on what that does to your drum price is close to nothing. Britain was 1.1% of the book last year. ... #### The Book Is Two Lanes Mexico and South Africa, and it has been those two for as long as the series runs (chart below). Mexico declared 21,792.7 t into the US in 2025 and South Africa 14,349.9 t. Together that is 90.5% of the year's 39,945.3 t, the highest concentration in the seven years we pulled, against a low of 81.8% in 2020. Everyone else divides 3,382.8 t. India took 4.0%, Brazil 2.6%, Britain 1.1%, Korea and China under a point each. All of Europe, every EU member plus the UK, came to 488,426 kg, or 1.22% of the book. Worth knowing about the two lanes you actually depend on: - The South African volume comes out of Sasol's Secunda solvents complex, Unit 590, which makes ethyl acetate by dehydrogenating its own ethanol rather than from acetic acid. Different feedstock, different cost curve, no exposure at all to the gas-versus-methanol economics that shut Hull. - Secunda's own 2025 air licence lists Unit 590 as running "Intermittent" where the solvent units next to it are listed "Continuous." The licence publishes the production-rate table with the numbers blank, so nobody outside Sasol has a nameplate to work with. - Mexico's lane is the bigger one and the more opaque. The desk could not verify from public sources which Mexican site or sites fill it, which is its own answer about how much of this you can diligence. ... The UK lane peaked in this series at 4,008.1 t in 2020, a tenth of that year's book. By 2023 it was 461.5 t. Last year, 419.9 t. Call that 0.21% of Hull's published nameplate. American buyers walked away from that plant years before the gas bill closed it. Now, the lane was rebuilding on its way out the door. January through June 2026 brought 577.6 t from Britain, 2.9 times the same months of 2025 and already more than the whole of last year. So the sliver of Hull that America had started buying again is exactly the sliver that stopped in September. ... #### The Domestic Answer Went Through Chapter 11 The obvious hedge against a two-country import book is a domestic plant, and the largest one in the country spent 2026 being sold for parts. Viridis Chemical ran the ethyl acetate plant at Columbus, Nebraska, making the solvent from corn ethanol instead of coal or methane derivatives, work the EPA gave a Green Chemistry Challenge Award in October 2024. ICIS put the line at 52,000 t/y from the end of 2022, by a distance the biggest in the US. The company spent 2025 moving it to a BioUrja site near Peoria, Illinois, and the move is what killed it. Payments to the construction contractor hit roughly $21.5m against a $14.9m contract, 44.3% over, inside a project budgeted at $26.7m all-in. The ethyl acetate-to-ethanol spread contracted 26% in the second half of 2025 while that was happening. Viridis and four affiliates filed Chapter 11 on March 8, 2026 in the Southern District of Texas, case 26-90393, and ran a fast section 363 sale of the stalled Peoria plant. The court signed off on the liquidation plan after the assets went. The Nebraska plant had never really carried the load anyway. Court filings describe it running in "limited operations" after its 2019 completion because the adjacent ADM ethanol plant could not supply input of sufficient quality. ... #### Final Thoughts The pricing news right now is friendly. H1 2026 import volume ran 7.8% above H1 2025 and the average declared unit value fell 24.0%, from $1.130/kg to $0.859/kg, which is the same weak spread that bankrupted the domestic producer showing up on your side of the invoice. The exposure is the shape of the book, not the level of the price. Ninety percent of a solvent that goes into your coatings, your adhesives, your pharma washes and your printing inks arrives from two countries, one of which publishes nothing about the plant and the other of which the desk cannot even locate. Hull was the headline this month. Secunda and whatever is behind the Mexican border are the numbers.

headline: Chemists struggle to ditch hazardous solvents — even after decades of ‘green’ efforts | Nature
summary_text: An analysis of 1.3 million chemical reactions listed in patents over four decades has shown that chemists still depend heavily on hazardous solvents, despite a nearly 30-year campaign to make chemistry ‘greener’ using safer, more sustainable alternatives. The survey is the largest and most comprehensive of its kind. Solvents are workhorse liquids used to dissolve chemical substances during reactions; chemists also use them to extract and purify reaction products. Some of the most common solvents, such as dichloromethane (DCM), are known to have health risks, or are hazardous in other ways — for instance, many are flammable. Almost all of them are derived from oil or natural gas, giving them a substantial environmental footprint. The patent survey, published this month in Angewandte Chemie 1, found that solvents classed as hazardous were used in about 60% of reactions mentioned in patents in 1976, but that by 2016 that proportion had risen to above 70% (see ‘Hazardous solvents persist’). “I was disappointed, rather than surprised,” says Helen Sneddon, a sustainable-chemistry researcher at the University of York, UK, who co-authored the analysis with Maarten Dobbelaere, a researcher who applies artificial intelligence to chemistry at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. ... The survey not only shows that hazardous solvents such as DCM continue to be favourites among chemists, but also finds that when government regulations restrict the use of a toxic solvent, chemists are more likely to switch to another hazardous liquid than to choose a greener or safer alternative. Furthermore, it shows a substantial rise in the use of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), which is key to the synthesis of popular peptide drugs. By some definitions, TFA is a ‘forever chemical’, one of the many persistent per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) increasingly found in waterways, soils and living creatures. ... Still, the analysis might not have captured some areas of progress. The database ends in 2016, so doesn’t include changes after that. Neither does it measure the quantities of solvents involved in these reactions, for example, so it’s possible that a trend towards scaling down, or miniaturizing, reaction set-ups in laboratories could be helping to drive down overall solvent use. And whereas the patents mostly record early-stage research, scaled-up manufacturing processes often weed out hazardous solvents such as DCM, Sneddon says.

Oxea cited changing global supply and demand dynamics and current market conditions. The increases apply in North America and Mexico, South America and the rest of the world; no European prices were listed. The rest-of-world increases of USD 250 to USD 300 per metric tonne on n-propanol, n-butanol and isobutanol are the steepest per-tonne rises in the 18 September list. On 28 August, it told customers it would raise carboxylic acid prices from 1 September because of changes to United States Section 301 measures on forced labour signed by the U.S. administration on 23 July. ... Butanols are used as gasoline blending components, and isobutanol is approved as an oxygenate. n-Propanol and the acetate solvents on the 18 September list — n-propyl, n-butyl and isobutyl acetate — go mainly into coatings, printing inks and cleaning products, with little direct lubricant use. ... Oxea is not integrated back into olefins. Its main site, the Ruhrchemie industrial park in Oberhausen, Germany, receives propylene and ethylene by pipeline from the Rhine-Ruhr petrochemical network, and buys synthesis gas and hydrogen from a partial oxidation plant that Air Liquide operates on the site under a contract renewed in May 2026 to run to 2038. Oxea also produces at Marl, Germany, at Bay City and Bishop, Texas, U.S.A., and at Nanjing, China, its only production site in Asia. The raw material and energy costs it cites are therefore largely those of purchased feedstocks. ... For Asian buyers, most of whom are supplied from Germany or Texas, the relevant figures are the rest-of-world prices, quoted in U.S. dollars. headline: Prasol Chemicals sees ₹3,200 crore revenue potential as capacity utilisation improves | Latest News Updates | 7Globe
summary_text: Speciality chemicals manufacturer Prasol Chemicals sees revenue potential of around ₹3,200 crore over the long term as it expands capacity and improves utilisation, company executives said after the firm’s ₹500-crore initial public offering (IPO) opened for subscription. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of around ₹80 crore and an offer for sale worth ₹420 crore. Nishith Rajnikant Shah, Chairman & Whole-time Director, and Dhaval Nalin Parikh, Joint Managing Director, said the company has enough room to scale operations using its existing assets before undertaking another round of expansion. CNBC-TV18 estimated that Prasol could scale revenue potential to around ₹3,000-3,200 crore through higher utilisation and future capex. Responding to the calculation, Shah said, “It is more than fair. A fair assumption.” ... Capacity expansion to support future growth Prasol is currently operating at around 44% capacity utilisation, leaving room to increase production without significant new investments. Shah said the company typically begins expansion once plants reach 80% utilisation, instead of waiting until they are fully occupied. “Normally, when we reach 80% of the plant capacity, we look for expansion. We never go to 100%,” he said. The company has already acquired 20-25 acres of adjoining land at both its Mahad and Khopoli manufacturing facilities for future expansion. Shah added that the company has sufficient internal cash generation to fund expansion plans. ... Shah said Prasol expects profitability to improve as it manufactures a larger share of products instead of distributing them. The company converts acetone into higher-value speciality chemical derivatives, which carry better margins. “As you go up, your margin increases, and also with time, your utilisation goes up,” Shah said. He added that the company is replacing part of its distribution business with manufacturing, which should further support margins through operating leverage. Focus remains on speciality chemicals Parikh said Prasol’s products are designed for specialised industrial applications rather than commodity markets. The products are supplied to customers in agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, home and personal care, mining and lubricant industries, where the company develops customised formulations with strict quality specifications. Parikh said Prasol competes with global companies such as Arkema, Solvay, Lubrizol and Chevron, although no single player manufactures the company’s entire product portfolio. Raw material sourcing to improve The company currently imports about 70% of its acetone requirement, while phosphorus is fully imported. Shah said India’s domestic acetone supply is expected to improve with additional production capacity coming on stream, which could strengthen raw material availability for the company in the coming months.

headline: ECHA Tightens REACH Disclosure for Extraction Solvents
summary_text: On August 2, 2026, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) issued an emergency revision of the REACH Registration Technical Guidance v5.3 that changes how certain extraction solvents used in pharmaceutical and agricultural active ingredient processes must be documented. For exporters, registrants, downstream formulators, and supply-chain teams serving the EU market, the immediate issue is not only the new disclosure requirement itself but also its effect on dossier completeness, customs clearance timing, and customer acceptance after mid-August. ... ## What the emergency update changes According to the provided event summary, ECHA released an emergency revision of REACH Registration Technical Guidance v5.3 on August 2, 2026. The update requires all solvents used for extracting pharmaceutical and agricultural active ingredients, including ethyl acetate, acetone, isopropanol, and certain Eco-hydrocarbon Solvents, to disclose in registration dossiers all organic components present at or above 0.1% and their Threshold of Toxicological Concern (TTC) values. The requirement is stated to take effect from August 15, 2026. headline: Raw Material Supply Shortage! INEOS Phenol Declares Force Majeure on Phenol and Acetone Operations - Latest News | Plas.com
summary_text: INEOS Phenol, a global leader in the production of phenol and acetone, has declared force majeure on supply of both products and implemented sales allocation measures to manage limited supply to customers. The force majeure was triggered by a disruption in feedstock supply to its European phenol production operations. The incident was sparked by a fire at the BP refinery in Gelsenkirchen, western Germany, on the evening of July 15, 2026. The fire occurred at the Scholven plant site during a heatwave affecting the region. This integrated refining and petrochemical complex processes approximately 12 million tons of crude oil annually and supplies fuels and feedstocks to the chemical industry in Germany and across Europe. It is this feedstock linkage that connects the refinery fire to the phenol shortage. Gelsenkirchen is a key source of benzene and cumene for INEOS. Benzene from the BP refinery feeds the INEOS cumene unit in Marl, and this cumene is subsequently converted into phenol and acetone at INEOS's plant in Gladbeck. When the fire disrupted these upstream supplies, INEOS could no longer secure sufficient feedstocks to maintain contracted production volumes of phenol and acetone, leading to the force majeure declaration and the implementation of sales allocations. ... The Gladbeck plant is central to this event. It is the world's largest single‑line phenol production unit and one of the largest phenol production sites globally, with a phenol capacity of approximately 650,000 tons/year and an acetone capacity of about 400,000 tons/year. In June 2026, INEOS confirmed that the Gladbeck plant would continue operating beyond 2027 and remain its primary production hub in Europe. This decision followed the postponement of the restart of its idled Doel plant near Antwerp, Belgium. As a result, Gladbeck now accounts for an even larger share of regional supply, meaning any disruption at this plant has a significant impact on European supply. ... The timing of this event is particularly challenging because European phenol and acetone markets were already tight before the fire. From 2025 to 2026, production capacity in the region has declined further as producers cut capacity or closed assets due to high energy costs, carbon‑related expenses, and competition from low‑cost imports. At the start of 2026, the market absorbed the bankruptcy of DOMO Chemical's Leuna plant in Germany and further capacity reductions, while acetone prices had already been rising. Now, INEOS's force majeure lands on a market with almost no spare buffer. ... Downstream, the buyers most affected are producers of bisphenol A, phenolic resins, polycarbonate resins, and solvents. These materials are used in automotive components, construction products, electronics and circuit boards, wind turbine blades, and coatings, among other applications. Under the allocation scheme, these customers receive reduced supplies and may need to draw down inventories, import from Asia or the United States, or slow their own production under the current circumstances. ... As of July 27, 2026, the force majeure remains in effect, and the allocation scheme is still active. The duration depends on how quickly BP can restore normal operations in Gelsenkirchen and how soon feedstock supply to Marl and Gladbeck returns to normal levels. INEOS has not yet announced a specific date for full supply resumption. Buyers and analysts are closely monitoring whether feedstock supply has stabilized, at which point INEOS could lift the allocation and restore normal supply.

The justices gave no clear signs of how the court will rule, but over the course of two hours of questioning, they did demonstrate unison on one point: It is a hard and consequential task to identify who is legally liable for the impacts of climate change. Although Boulder's case was first filed in Colorado courts, oil and gas companies asked the Supreme Court to step in, arguing that important climate change matters should n't play out at the state level.

headline: Sibos 2026: Fragmentation in trade tech and payments in LatAm
summary_text: Latin America attracted $194.233 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, but fragmented regulations and limited interoperability continue to hinder integration. AI could expand financial inclusion, improve credit access for underserved communities, and optimise infrastructure investment across Latin America. Growing demand for structured trade finance, stablecoins, and digital payment solutions presents opportunities for local banks to strengthen regional connectivity. Latin America (LatAm) received $194.233 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) in 2025. With a booming cryptocurrency market and global leadership in stablecoin adoption, the FDI figures testify to investor interest in LatAm’s innovative finance market. While connections between LatAm and global markets are booming, these markets remain domestically insulated; investment corridors are narrow, with limited opportunity for cross-border financial engagement across LatAm. Mexico and Brazil dominated inflows, accounting for 62% of all FDI, while the US accounted for 35% of incoming finance. Patchwork regulations and a lack of interoperable infrastructure further hinder financial relationships between LatAm countries. ... ## Regulation needs a regional outlook The speed of stablecoin adoption across the region has surprised the world – financial regulators have their jaws on the floor and their lawbooks left in the 2010s. Many countries across LatAm lack regulatory guidelines for digital assets, relying on legislation designed to target fintechs or the early bitcoin boom. Mexico remains reliant on a 2018 Fintech Law that bars regulated financial institutions (FIs) from offering virtual-asset services directly to customers, while until 2024, Bolivia banned cryptocurrencies altogether. The bigger problem is that cross-country regulatory alignment is lacking, complicating the development of financial pathways. Brazil and Colombia both have thriving real-time payment systems with high domestic market penetration: Pix in Brazil and Breve in Colombia. Those systems, administered in organised regulatory environments, are backed by national central banks. However, they currently lack interoperability – payments cannot be sent between the rails. Fragmented financial systems echo across LatAm, nowhere more so than in Central America, which struggles with lower FDI and patchwork financialisation. “We want to develop a long-term vision for our region, and it has to be led by the ministers of finance,” one speaker said. But designing a streamlined regulatory environment is far easier said than done. ... ## Innovation and integration The COVID-19 Pandemic, tariffs, and the war in Iran have upended the traditional banking order. Trade finance vehicles, designed to handle more volatile international environments, are in their heyday. Indeed, the widespread adoption of instruments such as letters of credit (LCs) in AI capital expenditure (CapEx) launches as risk-management tools testifies to their growing industry reputation. “We have seen an uptick in demand for structured financial solutions for trade. From LCs to international factoring, reverse factoring, and receivables financings, we’ve had to become more creative because of geopolitical tensions,” explained one panellist. The advantage for LatAm is that building from the ground up lets banks standardise trade and finance vehicles across the region. AI is demanding a more innovative, customer-facing approach from banks, forcing banks to remap processes like capital allocation. However, as highlighted by the panel, not everyone trusts AI to make their financial decisions yet. This disparity – between those more and less confident entrusting AI – drives the differences in how banks need to serve their clients. AI’s divisive nature is likely to split user habits, with some customers demanding automation and agentic decision-making processes. In contrast, others will hold out for more traditional service-sector skills, and FIs are already thinking in split-levels.

headline: The Guide to Mergers & Acquisitions - Seventh Edition - Private equity and institutional investors in Latin America: the defining developments of 2026 - Latin Lawyer
summary_text: After a slow and uneven 2024, the year 2025 saw a reactivation of significant interest in private equity and institutional capital in Latin America, and the momentum has carried into 2026. Regional M&A activity climbed on two key counts in 2025: the number of announced deals increased by roughly 12% year on year, and aggregate deal value rose by approximately 40%, surpassing $114 billion. [1] Private equity was a principal engine of that rebound. Buyout and growth transactions in the region totalled roughly $19.8 billion in 2025. This is more than double the prior year’s figure, even though the number of deals fell to 189 – a clear sign that capital is being deployed in fewer, larger and more carefully underwritten transactions rather than spread across a broad pipeline. [2] That pattern, fewer deals but bigger deal values, has defined 2026. Brazil’s first-quarter deal count fell 29% year on year to 154 transactions, yet aggregate value rose by 47% to $16 billion. [3] Mexico’s total capital mobilised surged by more than 70% to around $28 billion. [4] Most market participants describe the 2026 environment as selective and bifurcated: well-capitalised sponsors and strategics are willing to pay up for scarce, high-quality assets in energy, infrastructure and financial services, while mid-market transactions face a tighter fundraising and financing backdrop, and volumes remain well below the peaks of 2021 and 2022. [5] Three developments stand out as the most consequential of the past year: - Brazil enacted a sweeping tax reform that, from 1 January 2026, ends three decades of dividend tax exemption for foreign investors and reshapes how funds structure cross-border holdings; - Latin American private capital continued to institutionalise rapidly, evidenced by record global general partner (GP) stakes and continuation-fund activity, deepening sovereign wealth fund participation and a fast-growing private credit market; and - a set of political inflection points – most notably Colombia’s election of a market-friendly president after a term marked by threats to investment treaty protections, and Mexico’s continuing struggle to reassure investors after its judicial overhaul – will shape capital allocation decisions in the region for years to come. ... headline: LexLatin | Seguros en América Latina: finanzas abiertas, inteligencia artificial y nuevos competidores en Colombia, México y Perú
summary_text: Las reglas para el intercambio de datos, el uso de algoritmos y automatizaciones, junto con la protección de datos personales y la gestión de riesgos climáticos están redefiniendo el sector asegurador en América Latina. Un análisis de las novedades regulatorias en tres países de la región revela oportunidades de negocio y nuevos desafíos de cumplimiento para las compañías. Fecha de publicación: 16/10/2026 La regulación del sector asegurador evoluciona en distintos frentes, desde la protección de datos personales y el uso de inteligencia artificial hasta la gestión de riesgos climáticos y la entrada de nuevos competidores. En Latinoamérica, los cambios tienen alcances distintos según cada jurisdicción. En Perú, las finanzas abiertas y los seguros paramétricos modifican el entorno regulatorio y abren nuevas posibilidades de distribución; en México, la protección de datos y las propuestas legislativas sobre seguros médicos marcan parte de la agenda; y en Colombia, la gestión de riesgos climáticos y tecnológicos adquiere relevancia regulatoria. Según el boletín Actualidad Iberoamericana de Seguros, correspondiente al tercer trimestre de 2026, la inteligencia artificial está transformando procesos clave del sector asegurador, desde la tarificación y la evaluación de riesgos hasta la gestión de siniestros y la detección de fraude. El documento advierte que la implementación de la IA plantea nuevos desafíos regulatorios relacionados con la transparencia, la discriminación y la supervisión de los sistemas automatizados. A su vez, analiza novedades regulatorias, análisis jurisprudenciales y artículos sobre el mercado asegurador y reasegurador en España, Portugal, México, Colombia y Perú. ... En Perú, los cambios regulatorios abarcan el intercambio de información, la autorización de nuevas compañías y el desarrollo de productos. Rafael Corzo, socio de Pérez-Llorca, identifica las finanzas abiertas, el ingreso de nuevos competidores y la incorporación de nuevos productos y líneas de negocio. En materia de finanzas abiertas, la Superintendencia de Banca, Seguros y AFP (SBS) publicó el 5 de octubre de 2026, para comentarios, un proyecto que comprende los primeros cuatro títulos del Reglamento General del Sistema de Finanzas Abiertas. La propuesta establece las bases para el funcionamiento del sistema, incluidos los datos comprendidos, las responsabilidades de los participantes, la habilitación técnica y la gestión del consentimiento. Corzo explica que la propuesta contempla la participación de las aseguradoras en el intercambio de información para distintas actividades del negocio. El proyecto de Reglamento General del Sistema de Finanzas Abiertas, publicado por la Superintendencia de Banca, Seguros y AFP (SBS) para comentarios mediante la Resolución SBS N.º 02433-2026, contempla la participación de las aseguradoras en el intercambio de datos con autorización de los clientes. La propuesta prevé que esa información pueda utilizarse en procesos como la cotización, la suscripción de riesgos y la atención de siniestros, además de establecer obligaciones de intercambio para las entidades en una etapa posterior. > > > “El segundo cambio es la llegada de nuevos competidores. La SBS ha facilitado el ingreso al mercado: creó una ventanilla única para las nuevas entidades, la Coordinación Ejecutiva de Organización de Empresas (Resolución SBS N° 00935-2026), e incorporó nuevas modalidades de autorización, entre ellas una dirigida a filiales de grupos aseguradores internacionalmente activos (Resolución SBS N° 02133-2026). Los primeros resultados ya son visibles: Nacional de Seguros S.A., especializada en caución y fianzas, cuenta con sus autorizaciones de organización y de funcionamiento, mientras que Sanitas Seguros S.A., enfocada en el ramo de vida, obtuvo la autorización de organización y se encuentra a la espera de la de funcionamiento”, sostiene Corzo. ... México: protección de datos y presión legislativa En México, la agenda regulatoria incluye diversas iniciativas sobre seguros de gastos médicos mayores. Entre los asuntos planteados en propuestas legislativas figuran límites a los incrementos de primas, portabilidad de pólizas sin perder antigüedad ni periodos de espera cumplidos, mayor transparencia en las tarifas hospitalarias y posibles beneficios fiscales para personas mayores de 60 años. Las medidas deben distinguirse según la iniciativa o el dictamen en el que se plantean, pues no constituyen una única reforma aprobada. Fátima Eizaguirre, asociada de Pérez-Llorca, señala que, según datos de la Asociación Mexicana de Instituciones de Seguros (AMIS) citados en el análisis del sector, entre el 15 % y el 20 % de las aseguradoras mexicanas utilizan inteligencia artificial en sus operaciones, principalmente en la detección de fraude, la suscripción de riesgos, la gestión de siniestros y la atención al cliente. El país no cuenta con una ley general específica de inteligencia artificial. Sin embargo, las compañías deben considerar las obligaciones derivadas de otras normas, en particular de la Ley Federal de Protección de Datos Personales en Posesión de los Particulares, publicada el 20 de marzo de 2025. La reforma modificó el marco institucional de supervisión y trasladó las funciones correspondientes a la Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno.
