headline: KPMG: el momento idóneo para que la banca y las aseguradoras peruanas potencien su crecimiento, eficiencia e innovación - AmCham News
summary_text: Con más de dos décadas de trayectoria asesorando a las principales entidades financieras de Europa y América Latina, Pablo Vaño, socio líder de Financial Services Consulting de KPMG España, visitará el Perú desde el próximo 19 de octubre para fortalecer la propuesta de valor y las capacidades estratégicas de KPMG en el mercado local. En un contexto global marcado por la volatilidad y la transformación tecnológica, el experto indica que las instituciones financieras y aseguradoras del país deben alinear su gestión hacia cinco riesgos clave que definirán la competitividad en los próximos años. Cinco riesgos claves en el sector financiero Vaño ha señalado que los directorios de la banca y las aseguradoras peruanas enfrentan una matriz de riesgos interconectados que no pueden gestionarse de manera aislada, sino integral. Son los siguientes: 1. El riesgo físico y climático: El clima ha dejado de ser una variable externa para convertirse en un factor determinante del riesgo de crédito y de negocio. Las previsiones apuntan a que fenómenos cíclicos como El Niño podrían llegar a impactar significativamente el PBI peruano. En este escenario, especialmente el sector asegurador peruano enfrenta un desafío mayúsculo: la alta exposición a riesgos físicos exige el diseño de productos especializados y una mayor agilidad en la gestión de pólizas, superando la mera suscripción tradicional para ofrecer un valor añadido que fortalezca la vinculación con el cliente. 2. La calidad del crecimiento crediticio: El crédito en el Perú muestra un dinamismo importante, impulsado con fuerza por el consumo de retail y el segmento de las pequeñas y medianas empresas (pymes). Si bien esto representa una gran oportunidad comercial, conlleva implícitamente un reto de control sobre el riesgo de crédito que requiere sistemas de monitoreo avanzados. 3. Ciberseguridad, fraude y blanqueo: La digitalización acelerada de los servicios financieros incrementa la exposición a delitos cibernéticos, riesgos de externalización y exigencias crecientes en materia de cumplimiento y prevención. 4. La disrupción de los modelos de negocio: La irrupción de nuevos competidores tecnológicos (fintechs, startups) y el cambio en los hábitos de los usuarios obligan a la banca tradicional a reinventar sus canales digitales para mantener la cercanía y la vinculación con los clientes en entornos virtuales. 5. Geopolítica y volatilidad financiera: Las tensiones internacionales, la fluctuación en los precios de los combustibles y las presiones inflacionarias inciden directamente en los costos de financiación tanto para las entidades como para los usuarios finales. ... Frente a este escenario, una de las principales tesis que Vaño comparte con los ejecutivos peruanos es la necesidad de capitalizar el actual ciclo de bonanza económica. «Perú es hoy un mercado de alto crecimiento y alta rentabilidad, a diferencia de Europa, un entorno mucho más maduro en el sector financiero, donde la eficiencia de costos se ha vuelto una prioridad absoluta», señala Vaño. La experiencia europea demuestra que en los periodos de expansión se suele perder el foco en la optimización de procesos. Por ello, recomienda utilizar el momento actual para integrar soluciones basadas en inteligencia artificial y analítica de datos, construyendo un colchón de resiliencia operativa antes de que el crecimiento crediticio se desacelere. Asimismo, subraya que la adopción de la inteligencia artificial en la admisión de riesgos debe entenderse como un acelerador del juicio experto humano para evitar sesgos algorítmicos. ... El valor diferencia de KPMG en Perú Para acompañar a las instituciones de banca y aseguradoras en esta hoja de ruta, KPMG consolida en el Perú un modelo diferencial que combina la fortaleza de un equipo local experto con el respaldo de su red global. Esta dualidad permite realizar análisis comparativos (benchmarking) y aplicar lecciones aprendidas en jurisdicciones complejas –como la adaptación a normativas internacionales de capital y requerimientos prudenciales– con una visión holística que abarca desde la tecnología y la ciberseguridad hasta el negocio y la sostenibilidad.

headline: How Latin America's technology capital is faring - BNamericas
summary_text: Tech venture capital in Latin America remains selective – which, in itself, is not news. Funding rounds in recent quarters have generally been fewer, with capital concentrated in a handful of large checks. But it's not all a drought. Fintechs and credit solutions, artificial intelligence applied to local problems and healthtech are the verticals attracting investors. Depending on the business case, HRtechs, lawtechs and other innovative models also feature. The use of debt and FIDCs (Brazilian receivables investment funds) in place of traditional equity is also growing, as the figures and the latest deals show. According to the Open Innovation and CVC Ecosystem in Brazil report by Sling Hub, with support from ABVCAP (the Brazilian private equity and venture capital association), Alya Ventures and EY, Brazilian startups raised US$629mn in 66 rounds in the third quarter of 2026. That is the lowest quarterly volume since early 2025, down 63% from the second quarter and 50% year-on-year. The number of rounds fell 20% quarter-on-quarter and 61% year-on-year. Equity declined 21% to US$325mn, with the remainder going to credit and hybrid deals. Three deals accounted for 46% of the total: Kesh Bank's US$108mn raise, UME's US$98.4mn FIDC and Decade's US$85mn seed round, the largest ever in Latin America at that stage. Rounds with corporate participation totaled US$202mn. That is 32% of volume, versus 4% in the previous quarter, and the jump was driven by financial institutions. Itaú, Bradesco, XP and Credit Saison invested in UME's FIDC. Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, XP and ABN AMRO, among others, took part in A5X's US$69.9mn Series D. In M&A, the quarter saw 27 acquisitions, three of them by corporates: Alymente (C6 Bank), Int6 Tech (Harmonic) and Cobmais (Vela LatAm, part of the Constellation Software group). The previous quarter had been stronger. ... Highlights Among recent highlights, fintechs and credit deals dominated fundraising over the past month. In Mexico, Kapital, an AI-powered financial services unicorn, raised US$125mn from Tru Arrow Partners and Fasanara Capital, with participation from Cervin Ventures, Niya Partners and Overlook Capital. The company will accelerate growth in Mexico, Latin America, the US and Europe. Also in Mexico City, Nelo secured a US$100mn credit line from Victory Park Capital to move beyond consumer lending and become an AI-powered commerce platform. Kontempo, a B2B trade credit company operating in Mexico with Argentine roots, raised US$10.5mn in a Series A round led by Portage and IGNIA, with participation from Tectonic and MS&AD. In Brazil, Asaas, based in Joinville, Santa Catarina state, raised R$300mn (US$60mn) in its third FIDC to fund card receivables prepayment for its clients. The total comprised R$280mn in senior quotas, rated AAA by S&P, and R$20mn in subordinated quotas retained by the company. São Paulo-based NG.CASH, which targets young people, raised US$15mn in a round led by Blockchain Capital. The investment brings total funding since its founding to more than US$65mn, and the company will expand its credit offering and prepare to expand in the region.

headline: ‘Creative’ Laws Underpin LatAm’s Fintech Expansion | Global Finance Magazine
summary_text: Strong regulation and dynamic regulators are helping nurture a fintech boom across the region. This article appears in the October issue of Global Finance Magazine. The number of fintech startups in Latin America has grown by 340% over the past six years as these companies take a leading position in areas such as financial inclusion, cross-border payments, and instant payments. Nubank reached a milestone in January, becoming the largest private bank in Brazil with over 112 million users, according to the Central Bank of Brazil. The instant payment system Pix now accounts for more than half of transactions in the country and has some 170 million users, with 80% to 95% of the country using the service. “Creative laws are not always good laws. So you can have very creative regulation that is not necessarily very good regulation,” said Eduardo de Los Heros, legal manager at Bitso, a Mexican cryptocurrency trading service and fintech. “Brazil has very advanced regulation for digital payments, and El Salvador has made Bitcoin its calling card to position itself as the crypto regional hub.” ... Brazil, Colombia, and Mexico account for about 57% of all Latin American fintechs, with remittances, loans, and financial management the main segments. In Mexico, the arrival of Mercado Libre and its subsidiary Mercado Pago, as well as Nubank, has forced traditional banks to offer their own digital alternatives. “Mexico and Brazil, as the biggest economies, are pushing towards regulation. El Salvador is small but dynamic and has a fantastic regulatory sandbox,” said Daniel Leiva, partner at Torres Legal in El Salvador. “Then there are countries that are also pushing forward, like Colombia and Argentina. Argentina is fighting to integrate fintechs into the economy.” ... With a Fintech 2.0 Law due in Mexico, the market is starting to mature as adoption of digital banks and payment schemes increases across the region. Mexico now has over 1,000 fintech companies, second in the region only to Brazil. “This famous law has the objective to develop open finance as well as public access to user data of Mexican financial projects,” said de Los Heros, “creating clear regulations for virtual actors, tokenization, and stable coins.” That would not be a minute too soon, as Mexico’s rapid fintech expansion has outstripped the Comisión Nacional Bancaria y de Valores (CNBV)’s ability to regulate, Leiva said. ... With one regulator, the National Commission of Digital Assets (CNAD), working in tandem with the Central Bank of El Salvador, the focus has been on neutral laws; CNAD regulates certain types of activities, like crypto, without marrying the law to specific technologies. A broader scope allows for quicker adoption and avoids delays in achieving regulatory consensus on specific blockchain models, for example. This enables distributed technologies and similar models to be regulated more effectively. ... Colombia’s instant payment system, Bre-B, was launched by the Banco de la República last October. Bre-B aims to connect traditional banks, fintechs, and digital wallets through a single public digital platform. By August, it had recorded 1.51 billion transactions and more than 35 million users; 171 financial institutions had integrated by then. Those numbers could be even better if the bank had been less passive and restrictive over the past couple of years, according to Leiva. Eduardo De Los Heros, Bitso That said, Colombia’s fintech sector is at a crossroads, with rapid uptake butting up against a new regulatory framework. The Banco de la República and the Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia have instituted new regulations to protect consumers, ensure financial stability, and combat money laundering. Fintechs now have to adhere to the same standards as traditional banks, including rigorous know-your-customer protocols.

headline: Magnar aporta no Brasil com IA jurídica adaptada ao direito latino-americano após captar US$ 8 milhões - Brasil Inovador
summary_text: A startup latino-americana Magnar, especializada em soluções de inteligência artificial aplicadas ao setor legal, anunciou o início formal de suas operações comerciais e institucionais no Brasil em setembro de 2026. A expansão para o mercado brasileiro, combinada com a entrada simultânea no México, marca o movimento de consolidação regional da legaltech. Pouco mais de doze meses após a sua fundação, a empresa reporta atender uma base de aproximadamente 30 mil usuários e mais de 300 escritórios de advocacia espalhados pela América Latina. O plano de crescimento em território nacional é impulsionado pelo fechamento de uma rodada de investimentos Série A no valor de US$ 8 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 44 milhões), liderada pela gestora 6 Degrees Capital. A captação financeira será direcionada para a instalação de escritórios físicos, contratação de equipes comerciais e técnicas locais e aceleração do desenvolvimento de software adaptado às peculiaridades normativas do país. A plataforma desenvolvida pela empresa atua na automação de pesquisas jurídicas, na análise preditiva e estruturada de grandes volumes de dados processuais, além do auxílio na redação e revisão de peças e contratos. Liderada pelo CEO e cofundador Andrés Arellano, a empresa busca diferenciar-se ao integrar sua inteligência artificial diretamente aos fluxos de trabalho já utilizados pelos profissionais do direito, estabelecendo conectividade nativa com ferramentas como Microsoft Word e Outlook. ... O mercado de prestação de serviços jurídicos na América Latina passa por uma transformação profunda impulsionada pela necessidade de eficiência operacional e redução de custos. Países de tradição jurídica fundamentada no direito romano-germânico (civil law), como o Brasil e o México, apresentam um volume documental e processual substancialmente superior àqueles regidos pela common law. No contexto brasileiro, o sistema judiciário lida com um acervo que supera 80 milhões de processos em tramitação, gerando uma demanda crônica por automação técnica nos escritórios de advocacia e nos departamentos jurídicos corporativos. ... A proposta tecnológica da Magnar fundamenta-se na estruturação de bases de dados locais e atualizadas em tempo real com diários oficiais, doutrina, súmulas e julgados dos tribunais superiores e estaduais brasileiros, incluindo o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e o Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ). Diferente de assistentes virtuais de propósito geral, a ferramenta fornece rastreabilidade completa das fontes consultadas, permitindo que cada trecho de minuta ou parecer gerado venha acompanhado dos links e citações normativas correspondentes. Esse mecanismo de validação cruzada minimiza os riscos de erros técnicos e assegura que a decisão final permaneça sob total controle do profissional humano responsável. ... Além da 6 Degrees Capital, a rodada Série A contou com a participação do fundo mexicano Hi Ventures, da aceleradora Platanus e de um grupo estratégico de escritórios de advocacia regionais, entre os quais se destaca o escritório chileno Carey. A presença direta de organizações do próprio ecossistema legal na estrutura societária atua como um validador de produto (product-market fit), garantindo que as atualizações do software respondam a demandas reais de eficiência, governança corporativa e segurança da informação, alinhando-se aos ditames da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD).

headline: China-Latin America trade in services: How much potential is there? - CGTN
summary_text: Since its launch in 2012, CIFTIS has developed into an important international platform for China's trade in services and a window through which global businesses can observe the opening up of China's services sector and explore market opportunities. The 13th CIFTIS brings together participants from more than 90 countries and international organizations, along with over 1,800 companies. Over decades, much of the world came to know "Made in China." At this year's CIFTIS, however, a different trend is worth watching: China is increasingly looking to turn its service capabilities – in finance, tourism, education, healthcare, culture, information technology and professional consulting, as well as digital services and artificial intelligence – into something that can be taken to international markets. After 'Made in China' goes global, what comes next? A dedicated zone for promoting services that support companies going global has been set up at this year's CIFTIS, bringing together services such as finance, legal affairs, accounting, advertising and human resources to provide one-stop support for companies expanding overseas. At first glance, this may simply look like a way to provide companies with the practical support they need to "go global." But viewed from another angle, it points to a broader change in how Chinese companies are entering overseas markets. 2026 CIFTIS debuts China Services Case Exhibition, September 9, 2026. /VCG In the past, when a company expanded overseas, the first priority was often to sell its products. Today, the questions are becoming much more complex: Who will build the brand in the local market? Who will handle legal and tax matters? Who will manage local marketing? Who will build digital sales channels? Who will provide payment, logistics, customer service and after-sales support? As a result, what enters an overseas market is increasingly a broader service ecosystem built around a Chinese-made product. This is one of the most interesting changes at this year's CIFTIS: the focus is expanding from helping "companies go global" to helping "services support companies going global." As Chinese companies enter overseas markets, finance, digital services, marketing, technology and professional services are becoming important parts of the support system, working alongside products such as automobiles, appliances and electronics in the expansion into international markets. ... When discussing trade between China and Latin America, people most readily think of energy, minerals, agricultural products, automobiles, household appliances and infrastructure. These areas remain important pillars of China-Latin America economic and trade cooperation. But as the digital economy and trade in services continue to grow, the scope of that cooperation is also expanding, with both sides exploring opportunities in digital services, technology applications and professional services. What may emerge is a different combination: you have the market, I have the technology; you have the application scenarios, I have the services; you have local experience, I have global tools. Chinese companies can bring digital payments, e-commerce, cloud computing, AI, logistics and marketing services to Latin America. Latin American companies, meanwhile, can draw on their knowledge of local languages, cultures and markets to help Chinese businesses establish themselves in the region. ... Foreign trade in Latin America and the Caribbean has faced new uncertainties over recent years. The impact of US tariff policies has further highlighted a need to reduce dependence on individual markets and diversify trade partners. In its International Trade Outlook for Latin America and the Caribbean 2025, the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean noted that US tariff policies had increased uncertainty in global trade, and recommended that countries in the region deepen economic and trade ties with partners including China, the European Union, India and ASEAN, while strengthening intra-regional cooperation. At the same time, the report projects that exports of goods from Latin America and the Caribbean will grow by 5% in 2025, while exports of services will increase by 8%. As the global trade landscape undergoes rapid changes, trade in services is becoming an increasingly important avenue for Latin American countries to diversify their international economic and trade relations, explore new markets and seek new sources of growth. This is creating new opportunities for Chinese companies in Latin America, where traditional trade in goods is increasingly being complemented by exchanges in services and capabilities. A Latin American company may need more efficient digital services, while a Chinese company may need local market knowledge and cultural expertise. An e-commerce system entering a new market needs to adapt to local consumers, while a digital service crossing borders must also bridge differences in language and culture.

headline: Grupo Financiero Inbursa Adopts Harvey Across Its Legal Organization – Unite.AI
summary_text: Grupo Financiero Inbursa, one of Mexico’s largest financial institutions, has deployed Harvey’s legal AI platform across its legal team, Harvey announced on September 7, 2026. The rollout covers the group’s litigation operations first, with further legal workflows scheduled to follow as adoption widens across the organization. The Mexico City-based financial group is using the platform to modernize legal operations and enable its lawyers to work more efficiently across complex legal matters, according to the announcement. Harvey said the deployment is intended to help the legal team build more systematic, scalable operations while allowing attorneys to spend more time on strategic judgment and higher-value work. ... ## Litigation Workloads Lead the Rollout Inbursa’s litigation team is the first internal group to use the platform. The team is applying Harvey to help manage thousands of court and regulatory notices each year, analyze litigation matters, and prepare for oral proceedings, the announcement states. As adoption expands across the legal organization, Harvey is expected to support additional workflows. These include M&A due diligence, regulatory analysis, contract review, and other high-impact legal work, according to the company. The deployment followed in-depth workshops with Inbursa’s legal team in Mexico City. Those sessions were used to identify the highest-impact opportunities across the organization before the platform went into production use. ... Alongside the Inbursa deployment, Harvey said it is expanding its team in Mexico City as the company continues to grow across Latin America. The expanded local team is intended to work more closely with customers across the region. Harvey builds domain-specific AI for legal and professional services. According to its company page, its products cover workflows including contract analysis, due diligence, compliance, and litigation, and the platform is used by more than 2,400 customers in more than 70 countries, including more than 75 AmLaw 100 firms. Harvey lists Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, GV, the OpenAI Startup Fund, Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz, and EQT among its investors.

headline: Claudia Camargo: convirtiendo una consultora de impuestos en un motor para América Latina - Semana
summary_text: # Claudia Camargo: convirtiendo una consultora de impuestos en un motor para América Latina La contadora pública bogotana que escaló desde consultora hasta CEO en dos firmas internacionales ahora apuesta por convertir a Colombia en el referente regional de transformación digital en servicios profesionales. Redacción Semana 27 de agosto de 2026 a las 2:52 p. m. La disciplina es la filosofía de vida de Claudia Camargo Foto: A.P.I. Disciplina como filosofía de vida, así se podría resumir la trayectoria de esta contadora pública de la Universidad Santo Tomás, primera contadora de su familia, que construyó su carrera con una convicción clara: el bilingüismo sería su diferencial. Esa decisión la llevó a Inglaterra, en 2007, y la devolvió a Bogotá para trabajar en PwC, una multinacional de servicios profesionales en la que, en 12 años, ascendió de consultora a directora del área tributaria. En 2017, llegó a la firma especializada en auditoría BDO para liderar la unidad de impuestos, que entonces contaba solo con dos personas; ocho años después, Camargo aumentó a 90 el número de colaboradores y logró 4 millones de dólares en ingresos. Actualmente, dirige la oficina más grande del grupo BDO Interaméricas, un bloque que une a ocho firmas de esa consultora en la región con Colombia como motor. Desde su llegada ha impulsado dos apuestas que lo dicen todo sobre su visión: B-Women, programa para fortalecer el liderazgo femenino dentro de la firma y dotarlas de herramientas de marca personal y networking, y una transformación en inteligencia artificial que ya tiene al 70 por ciento de las áreas con proyectos propios en marcha. Madre de dos voleibolistas adolescentes que encontró en los horarios y la disciplina la fórmula para no tener que elegir entre el trabajo y la familia, su siguiente propósito apunta hacia afuera: aportar al país y ser un motor constante para sus hijas.

headline: Alster lanza nuevo servicio de outsourcing para agilizar la gestión contractual de las empresas de Latam | Derecho Práctico
summary_text: (En la imagen, Andrés Jara, fundador de Alster, durante la presentación del lanzamiento). Alster anunció el lanzamiento de un nuevo servicio de outsourcing para la revisión de contratos orientado a mejorar la gestión contractual de grandes compañías mediante la combinación de procesos, tecnología y talento especializado. La propuesta busca reducir ineficiencias y liberar capacidad de los equipos legales en un área donde una mala gestión puede erosionar, en promedio, un 8,6% del valor de los contratos, según World Commerce & Contracting. El lanzamiento se realizó en el marco del Alignment Lab una instancia de trabajo organizada por Alster que reunió a equipos de Legal y Procurement de reconocidas empresas del mercado chileno, tales como CCU, Río Tinto, Transelec, Colbún, Kinross, Carozzi e ISA Energía, para analizar los principales puntos de fricción que surgen a lo largo del ciclo de vida de los contratos. Durante el encuentro se abordaron desafíos que Alster ha identificado de manera recurrente en organizaciones de Latinoamérica: demoras en aprobaciones, el exceso de revisiones, falta de estandarización de documentos y criterios, la dependencia de abogados para tareas recurrentes y dificultad para medir el desempeño de la gestión contractual. ... Frente a estas dificultades, el servicio plantea externalizar parte de la gestión contractual mediante procesos estandarizados, tecnología y equipos especializados “ Esta propuesta recoge aprendizajes de mercados más desarrollados y los lleva a la realidad de las grandes compañías. Estructuramos y diseñamos procesos, estandarizamos la documentación y trabajamos bajo una lógica de mejora continua, para que la relación entre Legal y Procurement fluya de una manera que permita realmente acelerar los negocios e impactar el crecimiento de la organización”, señaló Jara. El modelo clasifica los contratos según su complejidad y nivel de riesgo, permitiendo externalizar tareas específicas hacia abogados especializados, mientras el equipo legal interno se libera de procesos operativos para enfocarse en decisiones estratégicas. Este proceso se complementa con una etapa de optimización y la creación de playbooks de negociación, garantizando consistencia y agilidad. Los resultados respaldan esta metodología: durante un programa piloto ejecutado entre 2021 y 2026 para el área de Abastecimiento, se gestionaron más de 5.100 contratos y 16.300 tareas. Gracias a este enfoque, la capacidad de resolución aumentó un 88% sin elevar el presupuesto, reduciendo el tiempo por tarea en un 36% y liberando más de 2.300 horas de trabajo que antes se perdían en revisiones innecesarias.

headline: Thomson Reuters integra CoCounsel en HighQ y suma IA… | Revista Mercado
summary_text: La compañía incorporó su tecnología de inteligencia artificial dentro de la plataforma de colaboración y gestión legal para acelerar contratos, *due diligence* y notificaciones regulatorias en América Latina, con foco en trazabilidad y control, en un contexto de mayor presión regulatoria para los equipos legales en Argentina 19 de agosto de 2026 Thomson Reuters incorporó CoCounsel, su tecnología de inteligencia artificial (IA), dentro de HighQ, su plataforma de colaboración y gestión legal. La integración busca que profesionales y equipos legales completen trabajos complejos con mayor rapidez, al aplicar IA generativa a la gestión de contratos, procesos de due diligence y notificaciones regulatorias, con “confianza, trazabilidad y control”. El despliegue en la región apunta a ampliar el uso de IA dentro del trabajo legal, al pasar de herramientas que asisten tareas puntuales a capacidades que permiten completar procesos dentro de flujos de trabajo ya existentes. En ese marco, la integración permite abordar procesos legales de extremo a extremo, con extracción automática de información clave y generación de insights accionables que activan tareas y workflows de forma automática. ... CoCounsel está basada en el estándar de Fiduciary Grade AI, o IA de grado fiduciario, y está diseñada para profesionales con funciones regulatorias de cuidado y supervisión. Actualmente, la tecnología es utilizada por 1 millón de usuarios en 107 países y territorios en sectores altamente regulados. Entre los procesos que la integración permite impulsar se incluyen la gestión de contratos, con identificación de impactos regulatorios y cláusulas desactualizadas; las notificaciones regulatorias, con registro automático, clasificación, análisis de datos para direccionar el caso y control de plazos; el due diligence, con organización, clasificación y análisis automatizado de documentación; y la atención a clientes externos, mediante portales de autoservicio con acceso rápido a información confiable y menor carga operativa. La integración de HighQ y CoCounsel en América Latina amplía el portafolio regional de soluciones de Thomson Reuters para profesionales legales, junto con Legal One, Westlaw y CoCounsel Core.

headline: Teknei acelera su expansión en Latam con la adquisición del negocio de BPO de Indra - La Nota Económica
summary_text: - La operación fortalece la oferta de Teknei en México, Colombia y Perú, integrando experiencia operativa con capacidades de automatización, analítica avanzada e inteligencia artificial. La compañía potenciará sus servicios de BPO combinando su agilidad e innovación tecnológica con la experiencia y solidez del negocio adquirido. Teknei, empresa líder en soluciones tecnológicas y transformación digital, anuncia oficialmente la integración y el lanzamiento de sus nuevos servicios de Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) en el mercado latinoamericano. La adquisición responde a la creciente demanda de servicios de externalización inteligentes en Latinoamérica, donde las organizaciones buscan mejorar su eficiencia operativa, acelerar su transformación digital y optimizar costos mediante tecnologías avanzadas. El anuncio llega en un momento de fuerte expansión del sector. El mercado global de BPO se estima en torno a los 222.000 millones de dólares en 2026 y se proyecta que crezca a una tasa compuesta anual cercana al 6% durante la próxima década. En Latinoamérica, el segmento de contact center y BPO prácticamente duplicará su tamaño —de unos 11.500 millones de dólares en 2024 a cerca de 20.400 millones en 2030—, impulsado por los modelos nearshore, el talento multilingüe y una migración acelerada hacia operaciones más técnicas y especializadas apoyadas en inteligencia artificial. Tras la exitosa adquisición del negocio de BPO de Indra, Teknei no solo integra una sólida cartera de clientes e infraestructura operativa en la región, sino que permitirá evolucionar los modelos tradicionales de BPO hacia operaciones más inteligentes, apoyadas en automatización, analítica avanzada e inteligencia artificial. ... La propuesta de valor de Teknei integra capacidades avanzadas de hiperautomatización, automatización robótica de procesos (RPA), inteligencia artificial y analítica avanzada para transformar operaciones, incrementar la eficiencia y mejorar la experiencia de clientes y personas usuarias. Todo ello respaldado por una sólida trayectoria en sectores como banca, seguros, telecomunicaciones, energía y administración pública, que permite desarrollar soluciones adaptadas a los desafíos regulatorios y operativos de cada mercado. Esa trayectoria se refleja en la confianza de más de doce marcas globales que ya trabajan con Teknei, entre ellas BBVA, Santander, HSBC, Banamex, Scotiabank, Movistar, Sabadell, Mazda, Kavak, Walmart, Cinemex y Grupo México. Los clientes actuales seguirán contando con la misma calidad de servicio y la máxima continuidad operativa durante todo el proceso de integración. La transición ha sido diseñada para garantizar la estabilidad de las operaciones, el cumplimiento de los estándares establecidos y una experiencia fluida.

headline: Multinacional de origen suizo Alpadis adquiere la uruguaya Gardien para desembarcar en América Latina
summary_text: Foto: Leonardo Mainé La estabilidad democrática y financiera de Uruguay sigue atrayendo a inversores internacionales. Alpadis, multinacional suiza de servicios fiduciarios, corporativos y planificación patrimonial para empresas e instituciones -se estima que los activos vinculados a las estructuras que administra el grupo ascienden a varios miles de millones de dólares-, concretó la adquisición mayoritaria de la uruguaya Gardien, especializada en servicios corporativos, planificación patrimonial y asesoramiento a clientes privados y empresariales. Martín Rubio, director ejecutivo de Gardien -ahora Alpadis Uruguay- y cofundador de la firma junto a Ricardo Sánchez, director general, destacó que la operación marca el desembarco de la multinacional en la región. «Creamos la empresa en 2019 junto a mi socio español Ricardo Sánchez, que tiene experiencia en JP Morgan y en bancos grandes en Luxemburgo y Suiza. Desde Alpadis se acercaron hace dos años porque buscaban poner un pie en Latinoamérica, empezamos a ver una sinergia y hace dos meses firmamos para ser parte del grupo. Esto le permite a Alpadis ingresar a América Latina a través de nosotros. Montevideo será en la base inicial del grupo para desarrollar sus actividades en el Cono Sur y avanzar posteriormente hacia otros mercados de América Latina», explicó. ... Para Rubio, la elección de Uruguay por la firma suiza respondió a una combinación de la estabilidad y seguridad del país y las características que familias y empresas de alto patrimonio buscan al momento de estructurar sus activos. «Tenemos un sistema tributario de base territorial, con imposición limitada sobre rentas del exterior, una moderna ley de fideicomisos, regímenes de zonas francas consolidados, un régimen atractivo de residencia fiscal, libre movilidad de capitales sin controles cambiarios y vehículos societarios flexibles, dentro de un marco alineado con estándares internacionales de transparencia (OCDE, GAFI), que distingue a Uruguay de las jurisdicciones puramente offshore», resaltó. ... ### Duplicar negocios Desde ahora, dijo Rubio, la firma local pondrá el foco en captar el creciente movimiento empresarial entre América Latina, Europa y Asia, que genera una mayor demanda de servicios corporativos, cumplimiento regulatorio, planificación internacional y estructuración patrimonial. El empresario detalló que desde Montevideo se atenderán a clientes uruguayos y regionales, principalmente de Perú, Argentina, Brasil, Chile, Paraguay. Hoy, Alpadis Uruguay tiene unos 30 clientes de alto patrimonio -el 80% del exterior- y la meta es duplicar el tamaño de la operación en los próximos dos años. «Esto será tanto por una mayor cartera de clientes regionales, como por el aumento del volumen de servicios prestados desde Montevideo y una ampliación progresiva de la capacidad del equipo local», apuntó. Con ese objetivo, la oficina local sumará la experiencia y el alcance de Alpadis en mercados asiáticos donde tiene una sólida presencia. «Por ejemplo, tras la entrada en vigor del acuerdo entre el Mercosur y Singapur, el 1° de marzo de 2026, a los clientes regionales les podemos brindar acceso a nuestros profesionales ubicados en ese país», indicó. También incorporará procesos, herramientas tecnológicas y estándares internacionales utilizados por el grupo. «Los clientes mantendrán su vínculo con el equipo uruguayo, pero contarán con el respaldo de una organización internacional con experiencia en mercados financieros y empresariales de Europa, Asia y Medio Oriente», concluyó.

headline: La Cámara - La revista digital de la Cámara de Comercio de Lima
summary_text: # BDO Perú proyecta un crecimiento anual superior al 10 % impulsado por el outsourcing y la IA 27.07.26 Outsourcing e inteligencia artificial impulsan las proyecciones de crecimiento de BDO Perú. Empresa: BDO Perú / Código de asociado CCL: 00056190.0 La transformación digital y la adopción de inteligencia artificial están redefiniendo el mercado de los servicios empresariales en el Perú. En este contexto, BDO Perú, firma que este año conmemora 32 años de operaciones en el país, proyecta mantener un crecimiento anual superior al 10 % durante los próximos años, respaldado por la mayor demanda de servicios de Business Services & Outsourcing (BSO) y por el desarrollo de soluciones tecnológicas orientadas a mejorar la eficiencia y la toma de decisiones en las organizaciones. En declaraciones de Walter Suni, socio director de la línea de servicio de Business Services & Outsourcing de BDO Perú, la evolución de la firma ha estado marcada por una estrategia de diversificación e innovación. La organización se incorporó a la red internacional BDO en julio de 1994, cuando la entonces firma Pazos López de Romaña Rodríguez inició una nueva etapa enfocada inicialmente en auditoría financiera y asesoría tributaria. A finales de la década de 1990 amplió su portafolio hacia consultoría y servicios de tercerización de procesos contables y de nómina. Uno de los principales hitos fue la creación de BDO Outsourcing S.A.C. en 1999, especializada en servicios de outsourcing. Según Suni, esta decisión fortaleció el crecimiento de la firma y permitió consolidar esta línea de negocio, que actualmente representa más del 40 % de sus ingresos. Posteriormente, desde 2010, la organización orientó sus esfuerzos a incorporar tecnologías digitales en la prestación de sus servicios para desarrollar procesos más eficientes, escalables y adaptados a las necesidades del mercado. ... Respecto a las tendencias que marcan el sector de Business Services & Outsourcing, el ejecutivo explicó que la automatización y el uso de bots han dado paso a una nueva etapa liderada por la inteligencia artificial. “La inteligencia artificial está acelerando exponencialmente ese proceso y redefiniendo la forma en que se conciben y ejecutan los servicios empresariales”, señaló. Añadió que este cambio no solo mejora la eficiencia operativa, sino que también transforma los perfiles profesionales, al exigir nuevas capacidades relacionadas con el análisis de información, la interpretación de datos y el apoyo a la toma de decisiones mediante sistemas inteligentes. Suni sostuvo que el procesamiento inteligente de transacciones será una práctica habitual en el corto plazo, por lo que las empresas del sector deberán actualizar de manera permanente sus modelos de negocio, invertir en nuevas tecnologías y fortalecer las competencias de sus equipos para mantener su competitividad. Mathew came in the state's landmark Cambridge Analytica case against Facebook for violations of New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act. It is the largest penalty against the tech giant to date. The judge's order followed a civil case in September in which jurors found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. The company was accused of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica used Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.

headline: Meta Ordered To Pay $25 Billion Over Misleading Claims, User Data Scandal
summary_text: New Mexico's attorney general initiated legal proceedings against Meta in 2021 after reports emerged that Cambridge Analytica had collected data from up to 87 million Facebook accounts through a third-party application without users' permission. The state alleged that Meta had misrepresented its data-sharing practices, its handling of hate speech and misinformation, and other internal policies to Facebook users in New Mexico. According to the state's case, Meta was aware that external parties had extensive access to users' personal information and allowed hateful or harmful material to remain on its platforms when doing so served its commercial interests. On September 25, jurors determined that 26 of the 29 statements made by Meta and its executives on these matters were misleading. They also concluded that the company had violated New Mexico's consumer protection laws more than 43 million times.

headline: US dairy processors invest $15 billion in manufacturing expansion across 23 states | New Food
summary_text: US dairy processors are betting big on future demand, with more than 85 manufacturing projects planned or underway through 2030. IDFA map of US investments US dairy processors are investing more than $15 billion in manufacturing capacity across 23 states, as companies expand production to meet domestic demand and pursue international export opportunities. A new analysis from the International Dairy Foods Association (IDFA) identifies more than 85 projects planned or underway through 2030, including new processing plants, factory expansions, additional production lines and equipment upgrades. “America’s dairy industry is investing for growth,” said Michael Dykes, President and CEO of IDFA. “More than $15 billion in new capacity and modernized facilities and economic opportunity for communities across 23 states. Dairy companies are putting capital to work because they see growing demand for dairy foods in the US and around the world.” ... The investment comes as US dairy manufacturing is forecast to grow faster than the broader manufacturing sector over the next decade. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that inflation-adjusted dairy manufacturing output will increase by nearly 30 percent between 2025 and 2035, rising from $138.5 billion to $179 billion. Employment in dairy product manufacturing is also expected to grow by 5.6 percent over the same period, compared with 3.5 percent across total US employment and just 0.6 percent in manufacturing overall. Recent trade figures provide further context for the expansion. According to the US Dairy Export Council, US dairy exports increased by 9 percent on a milk-solids-equivalent basis in the first half of 2026, while export value rose by 12 percent to $5.31 billion. Cheese exports grew by 24 percent over the same period. ... ## Milk and cheese attract largest investment IDFA’s analysis shows that milk and cream processing accounts for the largest share of investment, at $5.63 billion, followed by cheese manufacturing at $3.76 billion and yoghurt and cultured dairy products at $3.07 billion. Butter and powder production accounts for a further $1.86 billion, while ice cream manufacturing represents $745 million. New York leads investment by state, with $2.8 billion in projects, followed by Texas ($1.7 billion), Michigan ($1.43 billion), Wisconsin ($1.4 billion) and Pennsylvania ($1.4 billion). US dairy processors are betting big on future demand, with more than 85 manufacturing projects planned or underway through 2030 to expand capacity and tap into growing domestic and international markets.

headline: U.S. Dairy Processing Invests $15 Billion In Manufacturing Across 23 States - IDFA
summary_text: # U.S. Dairy Processing Invests $15 Billion In Manufacturing Across 23 States More than 85 projects underscore dairy’s position as a bright spot in American manufacturing WASHINGTON, Oct. 20, 2026— America’s dairy processors are investing more than $15 billion in new and expanded manufacturing capacity across 23 states, with more than 85 projects planned or underway through 2030, according to a new analysis from the International Dairy Foods Association (IDFA). The investments span nearly every major dairy category and include new plants, facility expansions, additional processing lines and modernization projects. They reflect strong confidence in the future of U.S. dairy as companies add capacity to produce more high-protein, nutrient-dense dairy foods to meet growing domestic demand and expand export opportunities. ... The investment comes as dairy manufacturing is projected to outpace the broader manufacturing sector in both employment and output growth over the next decade. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects dairy product manufacturing employment will increase 5.6% from 2025 to 2035, compared with 3.5% growth for total U.S. employment and just 0.6% for manufacturing overall. Inflation-adjusted dairy manufacturing output is projected to rise nearly 30% over the same period, from $138.5 billion to $179 billion over the same period. Food manufacturing is the nation’s largest manufacturing sector by employment and is projected to add approximately 84,000 jobs between 2025 and 2035—more employment growth than any other major manufacturing sector. Dairy is positioned to contribute to that growth through continued investment in production capacity, technology and innovation. That makes dairy a particularly strong example of the innovation, investment and economic contribution celebrated during Manufacturing Month each October. The U.S. dairy manufacturing industry includes approximately 1,200 processing plants supplied by nearly 24,000 American dairy farms. Across the broader dairy economy, the industry supports more than 3.05 million jobs, generates $197.6 billion in wages, contributes $779.45 billion in overall economic impact and generates more than $83 billion in state and local taxes. summary_text: ## Insight Focus Milk powder and whey prices rose as supplies remained tight. The USDA lowered milk production forecasts for 2026 and 2027 while raising its 2027 all-milk price forecast. Strong demand and limited supplies supported gains in nonfat dry milk, whey and cheese, while rising powder premiums raised export concerns and butter prices remained under pressure. ... ## Milk Powder Markets Strengthen as Availability Tightens Nonfat dry milk prices strengthened as robust domestic and Mexican demand, coupled with limited production, tightened spot availability. Western dryers operated at capacity, with some production already committed into 2027. Scarce high-heat powder pushed buyers beyond their typical sourcing regions. The widening premium for US nonfat dry milk over international skim milk powder prices began to raise concerns about export competitiveness. Elevated diesel costs continued to complicate distribution. ... ## Strong Cheese Demand Contrasts with Weak Butter Market Cheese prices climbed sharply despite heavy cheddar inventories. headline: Milk, Dairy and Grain Market Commentary
summary_text: Protein reigns supreme over the dairy complex. In the GLP-1 era, consumers are hungry for protein in all forms, and dairy delivers. Whey proteins are particularly desirable thanks to their neutral flavor. Food processors covet whey powders, protein concentrates (WPCs), and protein isolates (WPIs) as they seek to improve nutritional labels without sacrificing on taste or texture. Demand for WPC with at least 80% protein has faded as prices have climbed high enough to push buyers to alternative sources, including milk protein concentrate. But food makers continue to snap up WPC-34 and WPIs. ... Whey processors can’t concentrate the entire whey stream, and dry whey output is up 8.3% for the year to date. Whey powder isn’t tight, per se. Manufacturers’ stocks of food-grade whey powder reached 67.4 million pounds on July 31, up 37.4% from the year before. But demand is massive at home and abroad. Prices are rising in the U.S., but they’ve climbed faster in Europe, and the U.S. is winning exports. Impressive demand pushed CME spot whey powder to 80.5ȼ per pound, up 2.5ȼ on the week. That marks the highest spot whey powder value since February 2022, and it’s within a hairsbreadth of the highest price ever in whey’s eight-year tenure on the CME spot market. ... Cheese processors are keeping their vats full in order to run their plants efficiently and to capitalize on whey sales. Whey prices are so high that potential market signals to produce less cheese are muted. For many cheese varieties – especially mozzarella – demand is keeping pace with output. But Cheddar blocks are abundant. Despite record-shattering exports, cheese stocks climbed counter-seasonally in August. They reached 1.44 billion pounds, up 2.3% from the year before. ... In the West, dryers are running hard. But in the East, Midwest, and Southwest, other dairy processors are using up most of the milk, and there are very few trucks lined up at milk powder facilities. Meanwhile, demand for dairy protein remains strong and buyers are apparently undeterred as prices near the eye-popping spring highs. CME spot nonfat dry milk (NDM) jumped 9ȼ this week to $2.17.

headline: Cottage cheese went viral, and now the dairy industry is scrambling to keep up
summary_text: Cottage cheese went from diet-food punchline to a frequently scarce item in parts of the dairy aisle within just a few years. Dairy cooperatives are committing hundreds of millions of dollars to cultured-dairy expansions, and some producers are selling future capacity before new equipment is even online. Making cottage cheese is measured in hours, not the minutes of a sudden demand spike, and producers are still racing to catch up. Photo credit: Depositphotos. Good Culture fans have compared the hunt for a tub of cottage cheese to the “Hunger Games.” Organic Valley said its cottage cheese was selling faster than it could produce it. National brands and dairy cooperatives are responding with new partnerships, equipment upgrades and plant expansions, and the factories needed to fix the shortage cannot be built on demand. ... U.S. cottage cheese retail sales topped about $2.2 billion in the year ending July 2026, up 16.7% over the prior year. Per-capita consumption reached about 2.4 lbs in 2024, the highest level since 2009. Yogurt grew rapidly after that, particularly after Greek yogurt became mainstream, while cottage cheese declined for decades, becoming the default food of joyless dieting. The current resurgence has not yet reached those historic highs. However, Dairy Farmers of America has reported that what began as a high-protein trend has since broadened into a wider consumer movement, with younger audiences driving new usage occasions across the category. ... Westby Cooperative Creamery says its former cottage cheese process took about 16 hours, and the specialized equipment it needed to modernize carried a 50-week lead time. Westby says it is Wisconsin’s only cottage cheese manufacturer, a farmer-owned cooperative operating since 1903. For most of that time, the former process relied on open vats and substantial manual labor, with workers standing over vats to stir ingredients, shovel fresh curd and drain whey by hand. In August 2025, the creamery announced a $14.1 million modernization project to install four enclosed vats with upgraded refrigeration and HEPA-filtered air environments. The creamery’s sales team said publicly that it had already sold all existing capacity and that new inquiries were arriving every week. The new system cuts production time from 16 hours to eight and adds 7 million pounds of annual capacity. Westby pre-sold every pound of that additional capacity within six months of the project announcement. When the creamery held its ribbon-cutting ceremony this September, the new capacity was already spoken for. ... Upstate Niagara Cooperative, now operating as UNC Dairy, is committing $250 million to the largest capital project in the cooperative’s history, according to the company. The West Seneca, New York, cooperative is owned by more than 230 upstate New York dairy farms. The project was initially estimated at $150 million in 2024 before UNC Dairy increased the investment to $250 million in 2025. The goal is to expand capacity for cottage cheese, Greek yogurt, sour cream and milk to meet what the company describes as “insatiable” demand. Construction is underway, with completion expected in late 2026 or early 2027, according to project reporting. Organic Valley said its cottage cheese sales rose more than 30% in the first half of 2025 from a year earlier. Good Culture, whose dollar sales have nearly quadrupled over the past three years, partnered with Michigan Milk Producers Association to produce its products at MMPA’s Remus, Michigan, facility, which held its grand-opening ceremony on June 16, 2026. Producers are adding capacity, but Westby’s experience suggests that at least some new output is being committed before it even comes online.

headline: Whey suppliers racing to catch up with protein demand | Food Business News
summary_text: CHICAGO — The US whey protein ingredients business is experiencing record high prices because of demand. In response, there is an unprecedented amount of growth in investment to manufacture more, said Mike McCully, president of McCully Consulting, South Bend, Ind., during a Sept. 21 presentation at the International Whey Conference taking place in Chicago. “Nearly one-third of foods in the grocery store now contain some sort of protein,” he said. “Whey is in salad dressing, Pop-Tarts and Doritos.” To produce more, dairy processors need to increase cheese production, as whey is a side stream of making cheddar, mozzarella and other cheeses. “Today, cheese has become the byproduct of whey production,” McCully said. “The US dairy industry’s investments will grow new cheesemaking capacity by more than 500,000 tonnes by early 2027.” He emphasized the net increase in capacity will be less due to lost capacity from the closure of older cheesemaking plants. Also, it represents capacity and not production. That will take longer. In addition, drying facilities are converting capabilities from producing lower-value whey products, such as whey protein concentrate (WPC) with less than 80% protein content and sweet whey powder to producing WPC 80 and whey protein isolate (WPI), which has at least 90% protein content. The converted plants often have flexibility to produce both WPC 80 and WPI. Production of WPI in 2025 was up 11% compared with 2024, while WPC 80 production was up 9%, McCully said. “Still, the supply is very tight and will continue to be very tight,” he said. “We are going to continue to see high prices. There’s only about a month of inventory on hand. It’s an exciting time to be in the whey protein business, but very challenging from buyers’ and end-users’ perspectives. “It was not that long ago when cheese makers’ net profit came 80% from cheese and about 20% from whey processing,” McCully said. “Today, over 50% of net profit in the US comes from whey production.” ... Part of the reason new cheesemaking capacity will not immediately translate to increased supply of WPC 80 and WPI is domestic demand for cheese is not growing. Per capita consumption of natural cheese in the United States totaled 39.9 lbs in 2024, down from a record high of 40.2 lbs in 2023 and the lowest level since 39.6 lbs in 2021, according to the US Department of Agriculture. One theory for the decrease is the reduction in out-of-home eating because of inflation. Pizzas, burgers and nachos are all carriers for large amounts of cheese. “The US is going to continue to see cheese production growth because there’s just not enough whey proteins out there,” McCully said. That means exports also need to continue to grow. In July 2026, about 144 million lbs of cheese was shipped out of the United States. The record-breaking amount of cheese exports equated to more than 10% of US production, according to the USDA.

headline: State of the Industry | Functional favorites fueling demand for cultured dairy | Dairy Processing
summary_text: The cultured dairy category encompasses a wide range of products, including dips, sour cream, cream cheese, cottage cheese, kefir, yogurt and other fermented dairy foods. While yogurt remained the category leader in per-capita consumption over the past year, cottage cheese and kefir continued to post some of the strongest growth, fueled by continued consumer interest in protein, gut health and functional nutrition. The USDA reported that per-capita yogurt consumption increased 6% in 2024, rising from 13.8 lbs per person to 14.5 lbs. During the past 20 years, yogurt consumption has climbed 58%, reflecting the category’s ability to evolve with changing consumer preferences while maintaining its reputation as a nutritious, convenient food. Retail sales data from Circana, Chicago, shows an 11.6% increase in yogurt sales from July 2025 to July 2026, with $13.6 billion in total retail sales. Growth across cultured dairy is being driven by more than just traditional health messaging. Consumers are increasingly seeking foods that naturally deliver protein, probiotics and other nutrients without relying on highly processed ingredients or supplements. At the same time, manufacturers are repositioning cultured dairy beyond breakfast, introducing snack-sized portions, drinkable formats and products designed for post-workout recovery, meal preparation and on-the-go lifestyles. Cottage cheese has emerged as one of the category’s biggest success stories. Consumption rose to 2.4 lbs per person in 2024, the highest level since 2009. Retail sales data suggest the resurgence has staying power. Sales increased 16.7% over the past year, with overall sales exceeding $2.2 billion, according to Circana. “What’s been most surprising [this past year] is how the resurgence of cottage cheese has continued to build rather than taper off,” said Rebecca Heagney, senior director of marketing-dairy brands, Dairy Farmers of America, Kansas City, Kan. “What started as a high-protein trend has evolved into a much broader consumer movement, with younger audiences embracing the category and driving new usage occasions. Culture and social media have played an important role in keeping the momentum going, with platforms like TikTok continuing to reintroduce a legacy product in fresh ways by highlighting its versatility, creativity and nutritional benefits.” ... Kefir is another cultured dairy product benefiting from consumers’ growing interest in digestive wellness and functional foods. Long recognized for its naturally occurring probiotics, kefir is increasingly attracting shoppers looking for convenient ways to support gut health while also delivering protein and other nutrients. As awareness of fermented foods continues to grow, manufacturers see significant opportunity to introduce the category to new consumers. “One of our greatest accomplishments has been continuing to expand household penetration and introduce kefir to new consumers across the country,” said Julie Smolyansky, president and chief executive officer, Lifeway Foods, Morton Grove, Ill. “In many ways, we’ve been preparing for this moment for a long time. We’re proud to see kefir becoming a staple in more households than ever before.” For nearly 40 years, Lifeway Foods has focused on bringing the benefits of cultured dairy and probiotics to more consumers while continuing to innovate within the category. This year, the company launched a probiotic beverage with collagen and expanded into sports nutrition. “We also introduced MuscleMates, the world’s first cultured dairy product formulated with creatine, addressing growing consumer interest in protein, strength, healthy aging and metabolic health,” Smolyansky said. ... “The biggest trend shaping the dairy category today is the growing consumer focus on functional nutrition, particularly protein, gut health and fiber,” said Rafael Acevedo, president and general manager-dairy yogurt, protein shakes and kids’ nutrition, Danone USA, Broomfield, Colo. “At the same time, there is a meaningful opportunity to modernize offerings for families within the kids’ nutrition category.” That opportunity extends well beyond the traditional yogurt cup. Manufacturers are introducing drinkable yogurts, refrigerated snack packs, frozen cultured dairy treats and other portable formats that fit today’s on-the-go lifestyles. The goal is to deliver the nutrition consumers expect from cultured dairy in products that are convenient, enjoyable and appropriate for every eating occasion. ... “In general, we see the cultured products category becoming much more snack-driven,” said John McGuckin, chief executive officer, Clio Snacks. “Yogurt has always had strong credibility around nutrition, but the next wave of growth will come from products that translate those benefits into formats that fit more naturally into people’s everyday routines. The brands that win will be the ones that make cultured products feel less like a health food and more like a snack people genuinely look forward to while still offering functional benefits.” Category innovations • MULU Cottage Cheese from Dairy Farmers of America is formulated with a proprietary two-layer whey-and-casein protein system, delivering 18 grams of complete dairy protein per serving. • Danone USA reformulated Danimals smoothies and low-fat yogurt pouches to now be a good source of three key nutrients many children aren’t getting enough of: calcium, vitamin D and fiber. The smoothies now also contain 25% less total sugar than the prior smoothie recipe. • LALA Plus is a new lactose-free drinkable yogurt smoothie line. A 7-oz bottle provides 150 calories, 11 grams of protein, 4 grams of fiber, 0.5 grams of fat, real fruit and active probiotics. • Alexandre Family Farm is rolling out A2/A2 Organic Probiotic Sour Cream, a European-style cultured dairy product containing 25% milkfat. It is made from milk that comes from grass-grazing cows that convert rich pasture into high milkfat, nutrient-dense dairy.

headline: Canada’s 2026 Retaliatory Dairy Tariffs: What Is Tariffed, What Moves, and What It Means for U.S. and Wisconsin Milk Prices – Farm Management
summary_text: ## Key Findings - Both countries have put new tariffs on each other’s dairy. Since August 19, 2026, the United States has charged 50% on Canadian whey products, milk proteins, lactose, casein, and milk powders. Canada’s answer takes effect September 8: 50% on the same kinds of U.S. ingredients and 25% on all U.S. cheese. Neither country tariffed butter, fluid milk and cream, yogurt, or ice cream. On September 15, the United States added Canadian cheese to its 50% list. On September 29, the United States banned imports of Canadian whey products. - Canada’s tariffs apply to product inside the import quotas. Since the USMCA took effect, U.S. dairy entering within Canada’s tariff free quotas has paid no tariff. Now it will. The old over quota tariffs of roughly 241% to 298% are unchanged and are not being paid; they stop trade above the quotas. - U.S. dairy sales to Canada were about $1.3 billion in 2025, 14% of U.S. dairy exports. The tariffed products that can be measured at customs value total about $255 million. Butter, the largest single sale at $228 million, is not tariffed in either direction. - Filling Canada’s quotas completely would change U.S. milk prices very little. The cheese, butter, and cream quotas already fill; the skim milk powder quota is empty because there is no price difference to earn. Filling every quota would add roughly $30 to $120 million per year of exports, about $0.01 to $0.05/cwt. - The price effect comes through cheese and whey prices. Each $100 million of lost exports is about $0.04/cwt spread across U.S. milk. The Class III price is calculated from cheese and dry whey prices, the two products Canada tariffed: a $0.01/lb drop in cheese lowers Class III about $0.10/cwt, and in dry whey about $0.06/cwt. Scaling the closest published model to a Canada only action, with the arithmetic shown in the paper, gives an anchor estimate of roughly $0.20 to $0.35/cwt for a sustained action, inside a wider planning range of $0.10 to $0.50/cwt. - Wisconsin is more exposed than other states. The tariffs land on cheese and on the whey made from cheese. The anchor estimate equals roughly $65 to $113 million per year across Wisconsin farm milk sales, about $51 to $90 per cow; the wider planning range is $32 to $162 million. - The size of the effect depends on duration and relief. Dairy imported into Canada for re-export is not automatically exempt; relief must be applied for. All figures here are before relief. ... The United States acted first. On July 20, 2026, the President signed proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows tariffs of up to 50% on goods from a country the President determines is discriminating against U.S. commerce. The dairy proclamation states that Canada discriminates in how it hands out the USMCA cheese quota: Canadian retailers cannot hold USMCA cheese quota but can hold quota for European cheese (The White House, 2026a). That is a U.S. determination, not a trade panel ruling; the last USMCA panel on the subject, in November 2023, sided with Canada. The tariffs were set to take effect August 19. On August 18, the President suspended them for three days after Canada committed to remove the discrimination. Canada did not, and the tariffs took effect August 22 (The White House, 2026b). The products on each list are shown in Table 1 and in its note; the two lists are close copies. Both put 50% on protein ingredients and powders (milk powders, whey and whey protein, milk protein concentrate, casein) and left butter, fluid milk and cream, yogurt, and ice cream alone. Cheese was the one difference at first: Canada put 25% on U.S. cheese, while the United States initially left Canadian cheese off its list even though cheese quota administration is the stated reason for the U.S. action. On September 15, the United States added Canadian cheese to its 50% list (The White House, 2026c).

headline: US Cheese Exports Remain Strong, Says US DEC - Dairy Industries International
summary_text: Year-on-year (YOY) US dairy exports fell for the second straight month in July in a mixed bag of category-by-category results, the US Dairy Export Council (US DEC) reports. While products such as cheese and butterfat extended their growth streaks, tight exportable supplies of dairy proteins continued to limit US participation in whey protein concentrate (low- and high-protein WPC) and nonfat dry milk/skim milk powder (NFDM/SMP) markets. Total US exports fell 5% in milk solids equivalent (MSE) terms compared to the previous July, while YOY export value jumped 16% to $984 million (€846.6m). The July numbers put year-to-date MSE export volume up 9% and value up 12%. US cheese shipments continued to soar. July exports rose 25% to 65,256 metric tons (MT), a new monthly high. All major destinations posted double-digit gains: Mexico +28% (+4,914 MT); South Korea +34% (+2,052 MT); Australia +59% (+2,006 MT); South America +70% (+1,553 MT). Smaller markets expanded similarly. Exports to the UAE recorded the largest YOY decline in July (-86%, -427 MT), but US suppliers continue to find alternative paths to market, primarily through Saudi Arabia. A YOY 89% increase (+713 MT) to Saudi Arabia helped lift cheese exports to the Middle East by 19% (+327 MT). ... YOY low-protein whey exports increased 19% (+8,419 MT), as dry whey shipments remained strong. The low-protein whey category comprises three HS Codes: dry whey, low-protein WPC, and modified whey. US low-protein WPC exports have struggled all year as processors opted to make higher protein products (WPC80+) to satisfy US and global demand. YOY low-protein WPC exports fell 28% in July (-3,719 MT). (And even with manufacturers prioritizing high-protein whey production, increased domestic demand is similarly limiting US WPC80+ exports, which fell by 11% (-774 MT) in July and were down 19% year to date.) Dry whey, however, remains on track to surpass a 15-year-old annual record. YOY shipments of dry whey soared 76% in July (+12,328 MT), and year-to-date shipments were up by more than 50% (greater than 120,000 MT). In July, YOY exports to China doubled (+6,042 MT); shipments to Canada rose 353% (+4,171 MT); and exports to Japan jumped 508% (+971 MT)

headline: Gov Shapiro Secures Historic $1.2 Billion Investment from Chobani | Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
summary_text: # Governor Shapiro Secures Historic $1.2 Billion Investment from Chobani to Establish its First Dairy Operation in Pennsylvania and Create 900 Jobs, the Largest Single Investment in Agriculture in Commonwealth History September 01, 2026 Chobani’s acquisition of a Lehigh Valley facility will create more than 900 jobs and at full scale, source more than 3 billion pounds of Pennsylvania milk annually — equivalent to approximately 30 percent of the milk produced in the Commonwealth today. With Chobani’s growth and shared focus on family farms and rural communities, their decision to expand into the Commonwealth signals confidence in Pennsylvania’s dairy farms to meet consumer demand with great dairy products. ... Schnecksville, PA – Today, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Department of Agriculture (PDA) Secretary Russell Redding, Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) Secretary Rick Siger, and Department of Revenue Secretary Pat Browne announced the Commonwealth has secured a historic $1.2 billion investment from Chobani to establish its first dairy product manufacturing operation in Pennsylvania. This major project — the largest ever private investment in Pennsylvania’s agriculture industry — will create 900 full-time jobs over the next five years in the Lehigh Valley and greatly expand markets and opportunities for more than 4,000 dairy farmers in Pennsylvania. ... Chobani will assume operations of Keurig Dr Pepper’s (KDP) manufacturing facility, equipment, and related infrastructure, where Chobani plans to manufacture innovative food products beyond yogurt. The 1.5 million-square-foot facility, located at 7356 Industrial Boulevard in Upper Macungie Township, will accelerate Chobani’s ability to innovate and produce the next generation of better, more wholesome foods while creating new opportunities for Pennsylvania workers, farmers, and suppliers. When fully operational, the facility is expected to process more than three billion pounds of Pennsylvania milk annually — equivalent to approximately 30 percent of all milk currently produced in the Commonwealth — the largest increase in demand for Pennsylvania dairy in the state’s history. The project will create a significant new market for the Commonwealth’s family dairy farms, helping them grow and strengthen their businesses for generations to come. ... Production under Chobani is expected to begin in 2027.

headline: Mascoma Community Development Supports Meister Cheese Company with $15MM in New Markets Tax Credits - Mascoma Bank
summary_text: Mascoma Community Development (MCD) today announced the closing of $15 million in New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) financing to support a major expansion and modernization of the manufacturing operations of Muscoda Protein Products, LLP, an affiliate of Meister Cheese Company, LLC, located in Muscoda, Wisconsin. The transaction will help finance a $100M+ multi‑phase investment designed to significantly increase cheese production capacity, support quality jobs, and strengthen the regional dairy supply chain in a rural, low‑income community. ... The project will include construction of a new high-capacity milk intake facility, expanded cold and dry storage, a new cheesemaking plant with advanced processing lines, upgrades to whey processing and evaporation systems, and expansion of on‑site wastewater treatment infrastructure. Collectively, these investments will nearly double Meister Cheese’s milk processing capacity and position the company to meet continued growth in demand from national foodservice, private‑label, and branded customers. Founded in 1916, Meister Cheese Company is a fourth‑generation, family‑owned manufacturer and a long‑standing economic anchor in Muscoda. The expansion is expected to retain approximately 220 existing permanent jobs and create 29 new full‑time positions, the majority of which will be accessible to low‑income persons, while also supporting 188 family‑owned dairy farms that supply milk through cooperative agreements.

headline: $13 Billion Bet: Why Dairy Processors Are All-In on America's Protein Future - Dairy Herd
summary_text: The number is staggering: $13 billion. That’s how much U.S. dairy processors are spending on new and expanded manufacturing capacity across 19 states — the largest investment wave the industry has seen in decades. It’s a bet on a future where global consumers are hungry for dairy protein, and it’s reshaping the landscape of American agriculture. “The important story here is that processors are investing, committing billions of dollars to new plants, expansions and modernization projects because they have confidence in the long-term outlook for dairy,” Michael Dykes, president and CEO of the International Dairy Foods Association (IDFA) said. This unprecedented investment is preparing the industry to process 15 billion more pounds of milk by 2030 — enough to fill more than 1.7 billion gallon jugs. But where will all that dairy go? The answer lies in surging domestic demand and a fundamental shift toward export markets. ... The $13 billion in processor investments isn’t spread evenly — it’s concentrated in regions where production, infrastructure and market access align. The top five states by investment: 1. New York: $2.8 billion 2. Texas: $1.5 billion 3. Wisconsin: $1.1 billion 4. Idaho: $720 million 5. Iowa: $701 million Investments by product category: - Cheese: $3.2 billion - Milk/Cream: $2.9 billion - Yogurt and Cultured Dairy: $2.8 billion - Butter and Powders: $1.6 billion - Ice Cream: $530 million The cheese investment alone — $3.2 billion — reflects both domestic appetite (Americans now consume twice as much cheese per capita as they did 50 years ago) and growing export opportunities. U.S. cheese is increasingly competitive in global markets, and processors are building capacity to meet that demand. The yogurt and cultured dairy investment ($2.8 billion) speaks to the high-protein food trend. These aren’t just traditional yogurt plants — many are designed for Greek yogurt, Icelandic skyr, high-protein drinks and other products that appeal to health-conscious consumers. ... These aren’t just bigger plants — they’re smarter ones. Many investments focus on automation, sustainability features, and flexibility to produce multiple product types. This positions U.S. processors to compete globally not just on volume, but on quality, safety and innovation. ... “Looking ahead towards the end of the decade, we anticipate exports will be a critical growth engine for U.S. producers, and their importance is likely to rise over time,” said Will Loux, senior vice president of global economic affairs at the U.S. Dairy Export Council and National Milk Producers Federation. The recent data underscores that importance: Of the new cheese produced over the last two years, more than 60% has gone into international markets. “There is unlikely to be a ‘magic’ percentage to guarantee healthy milk prices, but ultimately, the faster we can grow demand – at home and abroad – the better milk prices will be,” Loux said. The USDA projects that exports on a skim-solids basis will increase from 21.5% of U.S. milk production in 2027 to 25.2% by 2035. That’s not just incremental growth — it’s a fundamental shift in dairy’s role in the global food system. ... But the U.S. isn’t alone in eyeing these markets. The European Union, New Zealand, Australia and increasingly South American producers are all competing for the same customers. So what’s the U.S. competitive position heading into 2030? “The United States remains incredibly well positioned to succeed in global markets over the next five years,” Loux said. “However, success will not come easily. Other suppliers are unlikely to willingly cede market share.” The U.S. has several distinct advantages that position it for export success: - Resilient and growing milk production: While other major exporters face production constraints, the U.S. is positioned to grow. - Significant investment in state-of-the-art processing capacity: The $13 billion in processing investments gives the U.S. modern, efficient facilities capable of producing the products global markets demand. - An unparalleled food safety system: U.S. dairy’s reputation for safety and quality opens doors in premium markets. - Impressive product innovation increasingly geared towards global customers: U.S. processors are developing products specifically for international tastes and preferences, not just exporting domestic products. ... summary_text: The July Federal order Class III benchmark milk price was announced at $15.52 per hundredweight (cwt.), down 46 cents from June, $1.80 below July 2025, and the lowest Class III since February. The seven month average stands at $15.85, down from $18.76 a year ago, and compares to $17.33 in 2024. Thursday's futures settlements portend an August price at $16.70; September, $17.22; October, $17.52; November, $17.55; and December at $17.58 per cwt. The July Class IV price is $18.34, down $2.62 from June, 55 cents below a year ago, and also the lowest since February. The seven-month Class IV average is $18.66, down from $18.87 a year ago, and compares to $20.33 in 2024. You’ll recall June milk production was up 2.3% from a year ago, leaving plenty to process. Starting with cheese, USDA’s latest Dairy Products report shows production hit 1.231 billion pounds, down 4.1% from May, but 1.1% above June 2025.
