YTD Cheddar hit 2.0 billion pounds, up 0.3% from a year ago. Butter production dropped to 208.2 million pounds, down 16.1 million pounds or 7.2% from May, but up 16.4 million pounds or 8.5% from a year ago. YTD, 1.3 billion pounds had been churned, up 6.0% from a year ago. Yogurt production totaled 446.3 million pounds, up 2.2% from a year ago, with YTD output hitting 2.8 billion pounds, up 5.5%. Hard ice cream came in at 68.7 million pounds, up 5.2% from a year ago, with YTD output hitting 381.6 million pounds, up 3.9%. Dry whey production slipped to 80.9 million pounds, down 1.3 million pounds or 1.6% from May, but was up 5.5 million pounds or 7.3% from a year ago, due to the higher cheese output. YTD 463.6 million pounds had been produced, up 6.9%. Whey stocks grew to 65 million pounds, up 1.9 million or 3.1% from May, and up 7.7 million pounds, or 13.5% from a year ago. Nonfat dry milk output fell to 164.9 million pounds, down 8.4 million pounds or 4.8% from May, but was up 20.5 million or 14.2% from a year ago. YTD output hit 997.6 million pounds, up 8.5%. Stocks slipped to 243.2 million pounds, down 1.8 million or 0.8% from May, and down 900,000 pounds or 0.4% from 2025. Skim milk powder production dipped to 28.7 million pounds, down 800,000 pounds or 2.7% from May, and down 25.2 million or 46.8% from a year ago. ... U.S. dairy farmers can be mighty grateful for the export market as 547.8 million pounds left our shores in June, though it was down, 4.6%, from the near all-time high in May, according to HighGround Dairy. Exports to China were down 37%. Cheese exports totaled a record 142.4 million pounds, up 23.9% from June 2025, and up 89.9% year to date. Mexican cheese imports were up 49% in June. Butter exports, at 19.2 million pounds, were up 35.4%, and up 89.9% year to date. HighGround points out “Butter exports slipped to their lowest mark since October 2025, but historically speaking, were still quite impressive.” Imports dropped from May, but were well above the prior year and moving back toward the big volumes seen in second half 2024. The overall export decline came from nonfat dry milk (NFDM) and skim milk (SMP), whey protein concentrates, and lactose. NFDM/SMP shipments, at 105.8 million pounds, were down 19.1% and down 3.0% year to date. These sales would have been booked in March and April, says HGD, when U.S. prices were “wildly out of sync with world prices and global buyers shopped elsewhere.” Dry whey exports totaled 56.5 million pounds, up 47.3% from a year ago, and up 54.1% year to date. ... In politics, the National Milk Producers Federation’s (NMPF) fight for labeling integrity got a boost this month as a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers sent a letter to FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Dimantas urging the agency to enforce its standards of identity for dairy products and stop plant-based imitators from co-opting terms like “milk,” “cheese,” “yogurt” and “butter.” The letter was signed by the original sponsors of the DAIRY PRIDE Act, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-WI, Sen. Jim Risch, R-ID, Rep. John Joyce, R-PA, and Rep. Josh Riley, D-NY, and makes a point NMPF has raised for years: FDA’s own guidance admits that consumers don’t understand the nutritional differences between real dairy and plant-based alternatives. Despite that admission, the agency has continued to rely on a voluntary labeling approach that simply hasn’t worked, says NMPF.

headline: Bongards Bets Big: $135 Million Expansion Signals Confidence in Process Cheese Future - Dairy Herd
summary_text: In an era when dairy consolidation dominates headlines, Bongards’ Creameries is making a different kind of statement: a $135 million vote of confidence in the future of U.S. dairy manufacturing. The Minnesota-based farmer-owned cooperative announced plans in August to dramatically expand its process cheese facility in Bongards — one of the largest capital investments in the co-op’s 118-year history. When construction wraps in early 2028, the facility will produce an additional 180 million pounds of process cheese annually, backed by 120,000 square feet of new space including state-of-the-art processing lines and a 70,000-square-foot automated warehouse. For an industry navigating margin pressure, shifting consumer preferences and an increasingly concentrated production base, the investment represents a strategic bet on where dairy demand is headed — and who will be positioned to capture it. ... The expansion targets four key markets: foodservice, retail, industrial ingredients and exports. Each represents distinct growth opportunities as consumer eating habits shift, convenience-focused products gain traction and international appetite for U.S. dairy strengthens. ... The new facility will feature advanced processing technology designed to improve manufacturing efficiency, enhance product consistency and provide flexibility to meet evolving customer specifications. The 70,000-square-foot automated warehouse represents a significant operational upgrade, enabling faster order fulfillment and greater inventory management precision. For a cooperative that processes hundreds of millions of pounds of cheese and whey annually across three facilities in Minnesota and Tennessee, operational efficiency isn’t just about cost management — it’s about reliability and responsiveness in an increasingly competitive marketplace. ... Today, Bongards’ member-owners are based in Minnesota and North Dakota, representing a geographically concentrated but strategically positioned milk supply. The cooperative operates as a vertically integrated cheese supplier, producing natural cheese, process cheese and whey that flow into some of the country’s largest foodservice operators, food manufacturers and retail channels. The $135 million expansion reinforces the cooperative’s ability to provide stable, long-term markets for member milk — a critical value proposition as dairy farm consolidation accelerates and producers face increasing pressure to secure reliable outlets.

headline: Association insights: IDFA prioritizing dairy's strong future | Dairy Processing
summary_text: America’s dairy industry is sending a clear and powerful message: the future is strong. Across the country, US dairy companies have announced more than $12 billion in new processing capacity and modernization investments — one of the most significant investment periods in the industry’s history. These investments reflect far more than short-term market conditions. They signal long-term confidence in dairy’s expanding role in nutrition, food policy, innovation and the global food system. ... Consumers at the core Dairy’s momentum begins with consumers. Today’s shoppers are looking for foods that deliver protein, nutrition, convenience and value. Dairy is well positioned to meet that demand, offering high-quality protein and 13 essential nutrients across products families rely on every day. Weight management trends, including the rapid growth of GLP-1 medications, are also reshaping how people eat. As consumers look for protein-rich, nutrient-dense foods in smaller portions, dairy products like yogurt, cottage cheese, cheese snacks and milk-based beverages are well positioned for growth. That demand is driving innovation throughout the dairy industry. Companies are investing heavily in lactose-free products, functional beverages, probiotic-rich cultured products, convenient snacking formats and protein-forward innovations tailored to evolving consumer preferences. Innovation forward Innovation is also transforming how dairy is produced and delivered. Across farms, processing facilities and distribution networks, the industry is using automation, precision technologies, data-driven operations and advanced manufacturing systems to improve efficiency, strengthen supply chains and produce more dairy with fewer inputs. Together, these advances are creating a more resilient and sustainable dairy supply chain and strengthening long-term global competitiveness. Across the country, companies are modernizing facilities and expanding capacity for higher-value products and ingredients. These investments are strengthening rural economies, supporting American manufacturing, creating jobs and building a more efficient and resilient dairy supply chain. ... Exports and policy Global demand is also creating new opportunities. US dairy exports are approaching $10 billion annually, and demand continues to grow for dairy proteins, butterfat and other high-value ingredients used in sports nutrition, healthy aging products, foodservice and international food manufacturing. To sustain that growth, the industry must continue advancing trade policy and market access. At the same time, the policy environment surrounding dairy is improving in meaningful ways. In Washington, policymakers are increasingly recognizing dairy’s essential role in nutrition and public health. Efforts to restore whole and reduced-fat milk options in school meals through the Milk for Healthy Kids Act reflect growing alignment between modern nutrition science and federal nutrition policy. Broader discussions around the Dietary Guidelines for Americans are also reinforcing dairy’s role in healthy dietary patterns.

Increasing production of a by-product “One of the biggest challenges is that whey is a byproduct of cheese manufacturing,” ... Analysts expect the whey protein market to remain relatively structurally tight in the near term, particularly for WPI90. However, they express caution about assuming today's record prices are sustainable indefinitely. “The inventory figures we are seeing suggest the market may not be as physically tight as current prices imply,” Badger said. “One area worth watching is reformulation into alternative dairy proteins, particularly milk protein concentrates (MPC),” Badger added. Unlike whey proteins, MPC can be produced directly from milk without relying on cheese manufacturing. Although not an ideal substitute in every application, the price difference is prompting manufacturers to explore MPCs as a possible option. Flexibility will also be increasingly important. “Processors need to be careful about making long-term investment decisions based solely on today's exceptionally high prices,” said Badger. Diversifying protein sources, adjusting formulations or reconsidering protein inclusion levels can help manage changes in demand and pricing across the market.

headline: Dairy Trends: whey markets are struggling but skim values up - 14 October 2026 Premium
summary_text: Wed 14 October 2026 10:00 PM Whey products are back, but skim milk powder has had a good week. Over the last month, whey products – the most valuable products in the dairy portfolio – have been struggling. Products such as whey protein isolate (WPI-90) and, in particular, whey protein concentrate (WPC-80) have suffered from easing demand. Less than two months ago, both products were riding the crest of a wave, trading at €30,500/tonne (t) for WPI-90 and close to €27,000/t for WPC-80. Today, those values have dropped to €28,500/t and €22,500/t respectively. Market analysts had suggested there would inevitably be pushback against such high prices, but reductions of this scale weren’t on anyone’s bingo card. More and more dairy processors across the world have invested in plants to process whey, which has been the shining light of dairy markets in recent years. Further price reductions would undoubtedly be a concern for those who have made significant investments in this area. In terms of the main dairy commodities including butter, cheese and powders, European markets have been more positive this week. Butter is the only one of the four commodities to record a decline, falling by €75/t. Skim milk powder is bullish this week, rising by €150/t to €3,500/t. Whole milk powder and cheddar are also steady but positive.

headline: Whey is expensive, scarce and more important than ever in sport nutrition
summary_text: Whey is expensive, scarce and more important than ever in sport nutrition # Whey is expensive, scarce and more important than ever in sport nutrition By Eric Royer, Global Business Development Executive, GIRACT 13-Oct-2026 Last updated on 13-Oct-2026 at 10:43 GMT Protein is set to remain a core component of many food supplement and nutrition products. (Getty Images) ## For European sports nutrition companies, protein sourcing has become a more serious commercial issue. Whey prices have risen sharply, supply remains tight and manufacturers are having to think harder about where they use whey, which grade they need and where another protein can do part of the job. The interesting point is that this has not weakened whey’s position. If anything, it has reinforced it. Whey still sets the benchmark for amino acid quality, leucine content, digestibility, functionality and consumer recognition. The challenge is no longer to find “the next whey” but to decide where whey is essential and where a blend or alternative can deliver the required result at a better cost or with a different consumer story. ### Demand outpacing production, alternatives emerging GIRACT estimated European whey protein demand at around 256,500 tons in 2024. Functional foods accounted for about 66,000 tons, with demand forecast to reach around 75,400 tons by 2029 at the time. That is significant when sports nutrition is now competing with high-protein dairy, medical nutrition, healthy aging and weight-management products for the same raw material streams. The supply pressure is visible across the industry. Most manufacturers admitted in 2026 that global whey demand was still outpacing production despite new capacity and that industry players were increasingly looking at hybrid protein strategies to manage cost and availability. The market is therefore becoming less about whey versus alternatives and more about how to use each protein where it makes most sense. Clear protein is one of the clearest examples. Clear whey has already changed the way protein can be consumed. Instead of another creamy shake, it creates a lighter, fruit-flavored drink closer to a sports beverage or flavored water, often in sugar-free, low-calorie RTD formats. What is changing now is that clarity is no longer a dairy-only proposition. In 2026, several companies launched hydrolyzed clear plant protein designed to tackle familiar plant-protein issues such as grittiness, off-notes and opacity. Overall, clear pea, rice and even yeast proteins are also being developed for refreshment-style drinks. That could be important for European formulators. GIRACT forecasted pea protein demand in European functional foods to grow from 19,300 tons in 2024 to 27,100 tons in 2029. The opportunity is no longer simply vegan protein powder; improved solubility and flavor are allowing plant proteins into formats where they previously struggled. ## Broadening positioning and stretching whey Another development worth watching is partial substitution rather than full replacement. Collagen is a good example. It should not be presented as nutritionally equivalent to whey for muscle protein synthesis. Its amino acid profile is different, but it can make sense alongside whey, especially when a product also wants to address mobility, connective tissue, beauty or healthy aging. Commercially, that can be attractive. A whey-collagen system can reduce the amount of whey required while broadening the finished product’s positioning. GIRACT’s European retail research has already identified a clear protein product providing 10 g of whey protein isolate and 10 g of collagen peptides per serving. Yeast protein is at an earlier stage, but it deserves attention for the same reason, and several of the manufacturers have committed to increase capacities. Within functional foods, the forecast growth rate is expected to be above 10% per year. The volumes are small, but the technology is moving quickly. Several companies positioned yeast protein for high-protein beverages in 2026, while their own research had explored combinations of yeast and whey protein. These supplier studies should not be treated as independent consensus, but they show where formulation work is heading: using yeast not necessarily to remove whey but to stretch it. ## Protein recovery and supply diversification Europe also has an interesting circular-economy angle. Most yeast extract producers have developed a process to recover protein, and beta-glucan from the same base material and are targeting applications including sports nutrition and functional foods. Fermentation-derived protein can therefore provide a new supply stream that is not tied directly to milk availability. Milk protein should not be overlooked either. When whey gets expensive, the obvious alternative is not always plant protein. Milk protein concentrate, milk protein isolate and micellar casein can offer useful nutritional and functional properties while keeping a dairy positioning. These proteins can be relevant in shakes, bars, meal replacements and sustained-protein concepts where the rapid absorption profile of whey isolate is not essential. Casein’s slower digestion, for example, gives it a natural role in evening and satiety products. Further ahead, precision fermentation is starting to look less like a sustainability experiment and more like a supply-diversification technology. There was a significant increase in the alternative-protein investment scene in 2026 compared to the previous year, with fermentation driving much of the growth. The number of deals also fell, suggesting investors are becoming more selective and concentrating capital on technologies with a clearer path to scale. None of this means fermentation-derived whey will solve the current shortage quickly. Cost, regulation, scale and consumer acceptance remain real questions. But scarcity gives the technology a clearer business case than it had a few years ago. ## The evolving consumer and the formulation opportunities The consumer side is changing at the same time. Sports nutrition is becoming active nutrition. Protein products are now being developed not only for athletes but also for older consumers, recreational exercisers and weight-management users. The recurring topics of energy, recovery, healthy aging are also growing as increasingly important themes. For brands, this broadens the opportunity but also makes formulation more complicated. Protein quantity alone is no longer enough. Taste, format, protein quality, claims, price and supply resilience all have to work together, and it is very tough. Whey is unlikely to lose its position at the center of European sports nutrition. What will change is how carefully it is used. Clear plant proteins will take some applications. Collagen and yeast can become useful partners in blends. Milk proteins may gain more attention, and precision fermentation could eventually add another source of high-quality dairy proteins.

headline: FrieslandCampina announces major investment programme to accelerate growth in high-value whey proteins – Food Engineering & Ingredients
summary_text: ### FrieslandCampina has announced an investment programme of more than 90 million euro to strengthen its global position in high-value whey proteins and further optimise its ingredients production network in the Netherlands. These investments include upgrades at the production sites in Bedum, Veghel, and Workum. With this programme, the business group FrieslandCampina Ingredients is expanding its capacity to convert internally sourced whey – a natural by-product of cheese production – into premium protein ingredients for performance and active nutrition, early life nutrition, and medical nutrition. It includes technological upgrades across multiple production sites to support the manufacture of advanced protein products such as WPC80, instantised whey proteins, and FrieslandCampina’s specialty Nutri WheyTM ProHeat microparticulated whey. These ingredients are used by food manufacturers in, among other applications, high-protein drinks, bars and yoghurts. ... Global demand for high-value whey proteins continues to grow across sports nutrition, lifestyle nutrition and specialised medical applications. This dedicated investment programme positions FrieslandCampina and its Ingredients business group to respond to this growth by increasing capacity and strengthening the flexibility of its whey valorisation chain. ... These investments strengthen FrieslandCampina Ingredients’ position as a leading supplier of high-value whey proteins, expand the company’s capacity to support customers worldwide with advanced nutrition solutions, and ensure that FrieslandCampina’s facilities in the Netherlands remain competitive, technologically advanced and aligned with future market and customer needs. In doing so, FrieslandCampina is also putting its Doing Dairy Right motto into practice through focused choices for growth, stability and value creation across the value chain. ... #### Sustainability and operational excellence The investments also contribute to FrieslandCampina’s broader environmental ambitions. The programme includes state-of-the-art energy- and water-efficient technologies and the phase-out of older production lines. As a result, Scope 1 greenhouse gas emissions are expected to be reduced by approximately 16 kilotonnes CO2e, while ensuring continued compliance with Dutch and EU environmental standards. #### Timeline FrieslandCampina will phase the investments over the coming years and expects to reach full operational capacity in 2028. The Works Councils will be kept informed in line with the usual processes as the interventions at the various locations are further developed.

headline: Arla invests in Skyr and cottage cheese as high-protein dairy demand grows
summary_text: Protein is becoming less of a specialist nutrition proposition and more of an everyday food choice, with dairy among the categories benefiting most from the continued shift. Skyr and cottage cheese, in particular, have moved well beyond their traditional niches as consumers look for convenient foods that combine protein, taste, and versatility. The acceleration in Skyr and cottage cheese demand is increasingly being reflected on the supply side. One of the latest developments is Arla Foods investing more than €63 million (US$74 million) to expand Sskyr and cottage cheese production in Germany and Sweden, adding capacity to two categories that have recorded strong growth across its European markets. The cooperative is putting €35 million (US$39.5 million) into Skyr production at its Upahl site in Germany and a further €28.3 million (US$32 million) into cottage cheese production at Falkenberg in Sweden, with both projects due to come on stream progressively through 2028. Arla says Skyr volumes across its European markets have increased by more than 33% over the past three years, while cottage cheese volumes have risen 25%. The figures point to a broader change in how consumers are using dairy: products once associated with particular eating occasions or demographics are increasingly being positioned as convenient, protein-rich components of everyday meals and snacks. ... The trajectory is particularly notable for cottage cheese, which has undergone something of a category revival. F&B innovators are also exploring upcycled ingredients to develop alt-cottage cheese to meet growing demand. ... Arla has been expanding its own position in the segment on several fronts. In May, the company announced the acquisition of Australian cottage cheese producer Brancourts, pointing to a market there that had grown by more than 40% amid interest in health and protein-focused foods. The move followed further investment in Swedish production and now sits alongside the latest expansion.

headline: WPC80 Prices Have Nearly Sextupled as Supply Lags Demand
summary_text: The price of whey protein concentrate containing 80% protein has risen to $32,000 per tonne, from about $5,500 in 2023. Demand is expanding across sports nutrition, GLP-1 users and everyday foods, while whey-processing capacity and raw whey volumes are growing more slowly. Whey protein concentrate with 80% protein, known as WPC80, reached $32,000 per tonne, or $14.50 per pound, according to figures compiled by commodities-intelligence platform Vesper and cited by NutraIngredients. During the same period in 2023, the price was about $5,500 per tonne, equivalent to $2.49 per pound. Rabobank recorded a sharper increase over a shorter period. Its figures show WPC80 rising from roughly €12,500 per tonne in October 2025 to €27,500 in July 2026, an increase of 120% in nine months. ... ## Processing capacity grows faster than supply Alan Johnstone, owner of Nutrilution UK, said that protein-processing capacity is increasing by about 4% a year, while the volume of raw whey produced by cheese-makers is growing by only 1.5% annually. Producing more whey requires producing more cheese, linking the availability of the ingredient to cheese output. FrieslandCampina has announced a €90m investment to expand its whey-protein production. The industry has not identified a direct replacement with the same combination of amino-acid profile, digestibility, taste and functionality. Collagen can be used in some formulations, but has a different nutritional profile. Precision-fermented whey protein is advancing as a technological option, although its economic viability at large scale remains unresolved.

headline: Protein boom boosts demand for milk powder and whey | DCA Market Intelligence
summary_text: The DCA benchmark for skimmed milk powder in Northwest Europe has risen to its highest level since 2022. Since the summer, the price has increased by around 25%. Compared with a year ago, it is now more than 40% higher. Whey powder prices have also risen sharply. Depending on whether the product is intended for food or animal feed, DCA benchmarks are currently around 59% to 94% above their levels of a year ago. The protein trend is not the only factor behind today’s high prices, but it is adding to demand for dairy proteins in a market where available supply is already relatively tight. From milk powder to chocolate bars Milk powder and whey may sound like specialist products, but consumers encounter them in many everyday foods. Skimmed milk powder is used as an ingredient in products including chocolate and other confectionery, ice cream, dairy drinks, bakery products and prepared foods. ... Whey is a by-product of cheese production. The liquid can be dried into whey powder or processed further into highly concentrated proteins such as whey protein concentrate and whey protein isolate. These ingredients are now best known for their use in protein shakes and sports nutrition, but they are also found in products such as protein bars, yoghurt, desserts, infant formula and medical nutrition. Broad demand for milk powder Demand for skimmed milk powder is currently strong, both within Europe and from export markets, says Wouter Baan, Dairy Market Specialist at DCA Market Intelligence. ... Baan also points to the high prices for milk powder and whey powder used in animal feed. “Normally, feed product trade below powder intended for human consumption. In week 37, that price gap had almost disappeared. This shows just how broad and strong demand is for available protein-rich ingredients.” A similar pattern is visible in whey powder. Whey also in strong demand The link with the current protein trend is particularly clear in whey. Standard whey can be processed further into concentrated proteins with a much higher protein content. These high-value ingredients are widely used in sports nutrition and in products to which manufacturers want to add extra protein. Prices for these concentrated proteins are on a very different level from standard whey powder. The DCA benchmark for WPC80, a product containing around 80% protein, stood at EUR €23,250 per tonne in week 38. WPI90, which has an even higher protein content, was priced at EUR €28,835 per tonne. After strong increases earlier this year, these prices have declined in recent weeks. At such elevated price levels, buyers are becoming more selective and food manufacturers are also looking more closely at alternative protein sources. __ For media enquiries, interviews or data requests: media@dcami.com

headline: Arla Foods Ingredients & Valio target GLP-1 and healthy aging needs with dairy proteins
summary_text: ## Key takeaways - GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are driving demand for small-format whey products that prevent muscle loss and support digestion. - Advanced dairy processing, such as fractionation and hydrolysis, enables targeted benefits for cognitive health, performance, and healthy aging. - Strict claims regulations hinder packaging messaging, while price sensitivity and supply chain risks create broader market pressures. As the global appetite for high-quality dairy protein surges, functional ingredient leaders are innovating with next-generation proteins designed to address evolving health trends — from GLP-1 companion nutrition to multifunctional healthy aging solutions. Nutrition Insight sits down with representatives from Arla Foods Ingredients and Valio to discuss GLP-1-driven weight-loss nutrition, high-purity whey innovations, advanced milk fractionation, and navigating global regulatory and supply chain hurdles. ... The advent of GLP-1 medications is driving the development of nutritional companion products to support muscle mass during rapid weight loss. Arla Foods Ingredients has developed application suggestions for great-tasting, high-protein, lactose-reduced options tailored to the GLP-1 market. “Our latest concepts feature our Lacprodan BLG-100 and Nutrilac ProteinBoost whey protein solutions and include a water-based high-protein shot, a fermented shot, and fermented drinking and spoonable yogurts,” Holm details. “They deliver all the essential amino acids vital for muscle health in small formats that appeal to reduced appetites. They also incorporate probiotics or cultures to additionally support digestive well-being. Catering to this segment with a range of different formats makes whey a trusted nutritional friend, both while consumers are on GLP-1 medication and also when they come off it and want more ‘normal’ food formats.” ... According to Lammi, Valio sees “new age dairy” as the combination of advanced dairy science, targeted nutrition, and scientifically supported consumer benefits. “Our current innovation focus includes high-protein dairy ingredients, advanced protein processing and hydrolysis, and milk fractionation technologies that allow us to develop solutions for increasingly specific nutritional needs,” she highlights. “For example, our clinical research has shown promising results for high-protein dairy products rich with milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in supporting physical performance and cognitive well-being during aging.” She adds that the company has also demonstrated that protein-hydrolyzed lactose-free milk produced with Valio technology can improve digestive tolerance among people with functional gastrointestinal disorders or milk intolerance. ... Even while the rise of GLP-1 medications, active aging trends, and social media discussions around protein have further increased health literacy and awareness, Arla Foods Ingredients’ Holm sees a growing disconnect between what consumers are ready to understand and what food manufacturers are allowed to communicate on pack. “While scientific evidence consistently shows that not all proteins are nutritionally equivalent, regulatory frameworks generally allow only broad protein-related claims, such as ‘protein contributes to the growth and maintenance of muscle mass.’” “These claims apply to protein as a category and do not differentiate between protein sources,” she underscores. Beyond sports nutrition, whey protein is growing in prominence in the healthy aging category. This creates a challenge for communicating the value of whey protein. “Current regulations focus on approved health claims linked to protein overall rather than differences in protein quality between sources,” notes Holm. “As a result, consumers increasingly understand that protein matters, but they receive limited information about which proteins may be most effective for specific outcomes. This leaves a significant communication gap between nutrition science and consumer understanding.” ... Lammi at Valio notes that an increasingly fragmented consumer demand offers another major challenge. “Some consumers are willing to pay for premium products, while others remain highly price-conscious. This creates a need for more targeted solutions rather than one-size-fits-all offerings.” “Geopolitical tensions, trade uncertainty, and economic changes also affect global dairy markets, supply chains, and investment decisions,” she continues. “At the same time, climate-related challenges, extreme weather, and animal health risks can increase volatility in milk production.” “For the dairy industry, the challenge is therefore twofold: remaining agile and competitive in an uncertain operating environment while continuing to improve the sustainability and resilience of food production.”

headline: Whey squeeze: FrieslandCampina builds capacity as experts map replacement trade-offs
summary_text: Whey protein demand is running ahead of supply, according to the USDA, and ingredient suppliers are answering on two fronts. They are adding high-value capacity and helping formulators work around the proteins that are in shortest supply. FrieslandCampina Ingredients has doubled whey protein isolate (WPI) capacity at its Borculo plant in the Netherlands and committed €90 million (~US$104 million) to three more Dutch sites. Guus Aerts, global director of marketing and product strategy at the company, says its build-out follows continuing structural demand and not the current whey protein squeeze. Meanwhile, Aerts says tight supply is pushing companies to reformulate, and Pratishtha Verma, dairy ingredients and applications specialist at the Center for Dairy Research (CDR) at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (UW-Madison), US, says whether that works depends on the product they are reformulating. ... From decision to commissioning, Aerts says the timeline turns on engineering, equipment lead times, permitting, and the work of expanding a running plant. New lines must be tested and qualified before they supply commercial volumes. He adds that acquisition creates a different path. “Our acquisition of Wisconsin Whey Protein provided established whey protein capacity in North America, giving us access to existing production capabilities and a regional customer base without the lead time of a new build,” says Aerts. “We use both approaches depending on the market opportunity, capacity requirements, geography and capabilities we are looking to add.” He says the Borculo plant shows the build-out route. FrieslandCampina announced the expansion in October 2023 and it began commercial operation in March 2026. The plant doubled the company’s WPI and MFGM capacity. The expansions of the plants in Bedum and Workum, along with an optimization of the Veghel plant, are scheduled to be finished in 2028. “We are building flexibility into the network as well, because customer requirements will continue to evolve,” says Aerts. “The Bedum and Workum investments add scale and flexibility, while the upgrade at Veghel supports the wider utilization of the whey stream as we increase protein production.” Guus Aerts says FrieslandCampina plans whey capacity around structural demand, not short-term tightness. ... Aerts says FrieslandCampina Ingredients plans around structural demand rather than current market tightness, citing an aging population and the influence of GLP-1 medications on appetite and eating patterns as longer-term shifts in how people eat. “Nearly 60% of global food and beverage consumers say they are deliberately increasing their protein intake, while the whey market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 6.6% through 2030,” he says. “Demand is moving toward more technically demanding applications, including ready-to-drink and clear beverages, medical nutrition, and high-protein powders, where high-purity proteins such as WPI are important.” Aerts notes that the way customers approach suppliers has shifted as well. He says conversations that once opened on price and specification now open on reliability and long-term supply. At the same time, he says application teams spend more time matching the right protein to a given formula. “Our technical and application teams work with customers to understand the product they are trying to create and identify the protein or combination of proteins that will deliver the required functionality, taste, and nutritional profile,” says Aerts. “That can sometimes open up alternatives to a constrained ingredient without compromising product performance.”

headline: Expensive whey increasingly bypasses pigs - Milk Analysis | Boerenbusiness. Nl
summary_text: Figures from the Circular Feed Association show that sales of whey and milk products to the animal feed sector fell by nearly 20% last year to 500.000 tonnes. This marks an accelerated continuation of the downward trend of recent years. Since 2022, there has been a decline of 40%. In the years prior, the trend was more fluctuating. Protein trend The rapidly declining sales of whey as pig feed are linked, alongside the shrinking livestock population, to the increasing popularity of whey. Liquid whey is increasingly being processed into regular whey powder and high-quality WPCs, for which there is high demand worldwide. Due to the protein trend, food manufacturers are increasingly adding protein to their products in order to be able to include nutritional and protein claims on the packaging. ... Liquid whey as pig feed was already a squeezed-out stream. Wim Thielen The Netherlands produced 8,9 million tonnes of liquid whey last year, according to figures from Eurostat. This was offset by sales of 500.000 tonnes of whey and milk products to the animal feed sector. "This shows that sales of liquid whey to the pig sector were already a squeezed stream," Wim Thielen, secretary of Circular Feed, stated when asked. According to him, the whey still being sold to the pig sector mainly comes from small cheese factories and local dairy producers who have no use for it. In addition, a small portion of the liquid whey is fermented, for example in the event of quality problems. The major dairy factories have long found high-value applications for whey, for example as an ingredient for baby food and for the production of lactose, says Thielen. Moreover, large dairy companies such as FrieslandCampina and Arla are investing in additional processing capacity for dairy and whey ingredients. As a result, competition for liquid whey as a raw material is increasing further, especially if the milk supply dries up. ... Whey concentrate significantly more expensive With this, the days when liquid whey was sometimes sold to the animal feed sector almost for free seem to be over. The increasing demand for whey concentrate is also evident from price developments. The DCA benchmark for whey concentrate rose to €1.500 per ton in early September, the highest level ever. Since the beginning of this year, there has been an increase of nearly 120%. In the coming years, the supply of liquid whey available for sale to the animal feed sector is very likely to decline further. In addition to the tighter availability of liquid whey, ever-increasing prices are also making the product increasingly less attractive as animal feed.

headline: Irish dairy companies poised to benefit from global protein boom
summary_text: The leading position of Irish companies has been acknowledged in a report on the global whey proteins market. Tirlán, Glanbia Nutritionals, Kerry Group, and Carbery Group are listed among the major participants in the whey proteins market by Analytical Market Research, which values the market at €7.7 billion in 2025, and projected to reach €11.6 billion by 2030. The Irish milk processors are competing side-by-side with huge multinationals such as Arla Foods Ingredients, Lactalis Ingredients, Fonterra Co-operative Group, and FrieslandCampina Ingredients. The report says that Fonterra, Glanbia and Lactalis command the broadest global distribution reach, through extensive manufacturing and co-operative networks. ... The cheese or casein manufacturing generates liquid whey as a co-product. This is filtered, concentrated and dried by integrated dairy co-operatives or specialised ingredient manufacturers, into concentrate, isolate, or hydrolysate form, then sold either directly to large food, beverage and nutrition brand owners, or through ingredient distributors serving smaller regional manufacturers and contract producers. According to Analytical Market Research, vertical integration, particularly ownership of both the raw milk supply and downstream drying and fractionation, is emerging as a meaningful competitive advantage, insulating manufacturers from the raw milk price volatility which puts pressure on pure-play ingredient processors. ... Demand is no longer confined to sports nutrition. Whey protein concentrate, isolate and hydrolysate now appear in infant formula, clinical nutrition products, ready-to-drink beverages, bakery systems and functional foods aimed at aging populations, weight-conscious consumers, and everyday snackers seeking added protein. ... Manufacturers are also benefiting from continued innovation in functional whey ingredients, including powders that dissolve cleanly in beverages, and hydrolysed formats engineered for infant formula and rapid-absorption sports products. Each of these innovations expands the use of whey protein beyond its historical base. Plant-based protein alternatives continue to compete for shelf space, in categories such as ready-to-drink beverages and meal replacements, though whey retains a functional and sensory advantage in most applications. ... Emerging market urbanisation, rising disposable income, and growing gym membership, across Asia-Pacific and Latin America represent the clearest volume opportunity for suppliers willing to invest in regional distribution and certification infrastructure, according to Analytical Market Research. Clean-label, organic and grass-fed positioning allows premium pricing, while clinical and infant nutrition continue to reward suppliers who can meet the highest regulatory and quality thresholds. Whey protein suppliers are also increasingly evaluated on the consistency of functional performance and supply security, rather than price alone, which favours integrated dairy co-operatives and manufacturers with diversified sourcing. ... North America leads the global whey proteins market with an estimated 36% share, underpinned by mature sports nutrition retail infrastructure, a dense concentration of dairy processing capacity, and high per-capita protein supplement consumption. Europe follows at around 26%, with the Analytical Market Research report saying the market in Europe is supported by the “strong dairy co-operative infrastructure in Ireland, Germany and France, alongside stringent clean-label and organic demand”. But Asia-Pacific, with an estimated 23% market share now, is identified as the fastest-growing region for sales, increasing by around 9.2% annually, driven by a rising fitness culture in China, Japan, South Korea, India and Australia, alongside expanding infant and clinical nutrition manufacturing capacity. Latin America and the Middle East and Africa together account for the remaining 15% of the market, with Brazil and the Gulf states emerging as the most active growth pockets within their respective regions.

headline: Will FrieslandCampina lose out to Arla? - Milk analysis | Boerenbusiness. Nl
summary_text: Rival Arla Foods appears to have beaten FrieslandCampina this time with its operating results for the first half of 2026. In the meantime, Arla Foods has also become slightly larger than FrieslandCampina, but that is not really the point. In terms of profit margin, the Northern European group is performing slightly better. At Arla, it was 2,8% and rising, while at FrieslandCampina it was 2,0% and declining. However, FrieslandCampina will continue to pay a slightly better milk price for the time being. The question is where the difference in performance comes from. The entire dairy sector suffered from a large milk supply and an overcrowded market in the first half of 2026. Arla, however, had fewer problems than FrieslandCampina in processing the large milk supply. The former's infrastructure seems better equipped to handle these kinds of phenomena than FrieslandCampina's production apparatus, which has become quite 'well-tuned' over the years. Fortunately, there were still the Milcobel factories, previously deemed partly redundant; otherwise, the challenges for RFC would have been even greater. ... FrieslandCampina is more reliant on the export market and other products, and although a number of sales markets, such as Nigeria and Pakistan, performed somewhat better this time, the company still felt the pressure. For the positive results over the first half of this year, which were also present, both cooperative companies rely heavily on their ingredient divisions. Arla seems to be reaping the most benefit from this, as the company has long been strong in whey processing. It has a large mozzarella production and consequently a large supply of whey. Moreover, it acquired the British whey processor Volac at the end of 2024. As of June 1st of this year, DMK subsidiary Wheyco was also added, but this addition has had barely any effect on Arla's half-year figures yet. Nevertheless, the company is well-positioned to fully benefit from the high-protein explosion in the dairy market. Revenue from Arla's ingredients division rose by nearly 20%, and the profit margin can presumably have grown even faster, but Arla does not provide figures on this. It may also suffice to mention that the price of WPC80, for example, has more than doubled in a year's time to approximately €27.000 per ton in June/July of this year. ... FrieslandCampina's ingredients division appears to be underperforming, but the question is whether this is accurate. In any case, FrieslandCampina has a larger ingredients department, divided into two branches: Ingredients and Specialised Nutrition. The latter division primarily produces infant formula, something Arla does little to nothing of. This division, which also makes extensive use of whey, is smaller than Arla's ingredients division (revenue nearly €870 million in the first half of this year) with a turnover of nearly €740 million, but saw sales rise by 24,4%. The operating result of €180 million was €40 million lower than in the first half of 2025, but remains very good. FrieslandCampina's core ingredients division generated revenue of over €925 million, which is more than Arla Ingredients and also outperformed this segment in terms of revenue growth (+22%). However, the operating result could have been better, as FrieslandCampina itself acknowledges. This is partly due to DFE Pharma incurring a loss. This company, now partly owned by CVC Capital, faced significant setbacks caused by disrupted logistics, particularly to India, and an exploding price of lactose, one of the primary raw materials. Otherwise, FrieslandCampina Ingredients is benefiting well from the enormous increase in demand for high-protein products, but, like Arla, is awaiting the successful integration of a new acquisition. For FrieslandCampina, this is Wisconsin Whey Product; for Arla, it concerns the aforementioned Wheyco. Both are strong in the market for WPCs and WPI products. Both dairy companies have more activities, but the aforementioned business units are currently receiving the most attention. headline: AFI invests in reducing Videbaek carbon emissions - Dairy Industries International
summary_text: Arla Foods Ingredients (AFI) is taking a major step towards reducing its carbon dioxide emissions at a dairy level. headline: Global whey shortage puts pressure on the food industry | Mejerimedier
summary_text: Rising demand for whey is coinciding with low availability of the raw material, and European dairy companies are now competing to secure enough of the scarce resource. Arla and FrieslandCampina compete for the raw material Whey is a by-product of cheese production and is widely used in the food industry as a protein source. According to FødevareWatch, both Arla Foods and FrieslandCampina have for some time invested heavily in securing the raw material, and both companies have purchased large volumes on the European market. The industry has looked at alternatives such as casein-based proteins, but according to the article, these can only partially replace whey’s properties. This leaves doubt as to whether the European market in particular has the capacity to absorb the extra demand from companies seeking alternatives to American whey.

headline: WPC80 keeps sliding as buyers refuse to step in
summary_text: European WPC80 prices continued to fall as buyers delayed purchases and bids remained far below offers, leaving trading thin. The article describes greater pressure on sellers and widening differences by product specification. Food-grade sweet whey was a contrasting tight spot, particularly at higher specifications, as processors direct whey into higher-value proteins.

headline: Can plant proteins help ease the whey squeeze?
summary_text: High protein demand and constrained whey supplies have led food manufacturers to consider hybrid dairy–plant formulations. Despite some easing from summer highs, European whey protein prices remained far above year-earlier levels. The article discusses supplier options including soy and pea proteins, and the formulation trade-offs involved in matching whey’s nutrition, taste and functionality.

headline: Dairy Trends: whey markets are struggling but skim values up
summary_text: The article reports that high prices had dampened demand for premium whey ingredients. European WPI-90 was reported at about €28,500 per tonne, down from €30,500, while WPC-80 fell to about €22,500 per tonne from close to €27,000. Other European dairy commodity markets, including powders, were firmer during the week covered.

headline: Whey is expensive, scarce and more important than ever in sport nutrition
summary_text: The article examines the commercial challenges facing European sports-nutrition companies amid high whey prices and limited availability. It highlights the need to select whey grades carefully and diversify sourcing or formulations. Dairy alternatives such as milk protein concentrate, milk protein isolate and micellar casein may offer useful nutrition and functionality when whey is expensive.

headline: European whey protein splits from milk protein
summary_text: Vesper reported divergent European dairy-protein price movements: WPC-80 fell 18.5% over a month while MPC-85 rose 8.6%. Both remained substantially higher year over year. The article attributes WPC-80 weakness to additional production and buyers postponing or limiting purchases while awaiting more supply.

headline: Protein boom boosts demand for milk powder and whey
summary_text: DCA reported that Northwest European skimmed milk powder and whey powder prices were markedly higher than a year earlier, amid protein-led demand and relatively tight supply. Its week-38 benchmark placed WPC-80 at €23,250 per tonne and WPI-90 at €28,835 per tonne, with both premium products easing after strong earlier increases. The article notes buyer selectivity and consideration of alternative protein sources at elevated price levels.

headline: Whey squeeze: FrieslandCampina builds capacity as experts map replacement trade-offs
summary_text: FrieslandCampina Ingredients has doubled whey protein isolate capacity at its Borculo plant in the Netherlands, with the expansion entering commercial operation in March 2026. It also committed €90 million to projects at Dutch sites Bedum, Workum and Veghel, with work scheduled to complete in 2028. The article also covers formulation options such as combining whey with casein, noting that nutritional, functional and processing effects vary by application.

headline: GLP-1 nutrition trend fuels premium whey demand
summary_text: Strong demand for protein-rich products, including nutrition associated with GLP-1 use, has kept premium whey markets tight in Europe and North America. EU WPC-80 prices were reported more than double their year-earlier level despite a recent correction. The article notes that capacity expansions take time and that whey production is linked to cheese output, complicating supply growth and competition between the regions.

headline: FrieslandCampina completes milk and whey upgrades at Gerkesklooster
summary_text: FrieslandCampina completed milk-reception and whey-processing upgrades at its Gerkesklooster cheese site in the Netherlands. The upgraded process enables production of higher-quality whey suitable for further processing into infant-formula ingredients at the company’s Borculo operation. The projects were part of a previously announced €20 million investment programme and connect cheese-site whey streams with the company’s specialised nutrition network.

headline: Arla Foods Ingredients invests €8.3m in Denmark plant to cut CO2 emissions
summary_text: Arla Foods Ingredients completed an €8.3 million heating-system investment at its Danmark Protein whey-processing facility in Videbæk, Denmark. Production Tower 4 can switch between the site’s steam system and a new electric heater, reducing gas use and potentially saving 2,500 tonnes of CO₂ annually. A similar project is planned for Tower 5; the company says both projects could deliver up to 5,200 tonnes of annual savings and improve energy flexibility.

headline: Could soaring whey prices make infant formula even more expensive?
summary_text: Using Rabobank figures, the article reports sharp year-on-year increases in whey powder, WPC-80 and WPI prices through July 2026. It argues that the main constraint for high-protein ingredients is processing capacity to convert liquid whey into concentrates and isolates, rather than simply the availability of raw whey. The reported assessment is that infant-formula price effects may be limited or moderate, while products more dependent on highly processed whey proteins face greater exposure.

headline: Glanbia announces next chief financial officer
summary_text: Glanbia has announced its next chief financial officer who will take on the role from March.

headline: Glanbia raises outlook on nutrition growth
summary_text: Glanbia has raised its full-year earnings outlook after reporting revenue and volume growth across Performance Nutrition, Health and Nutrition, and Dairy Nutrition during the first half of 2026. Revenue reached $ 2.1 billion for the six months ended 4 July, an increase of 7 % on a constant-currency basis and 7.9 % as reported. EBITDA before exceptional items rose by 14.1 % to $ 275.4 million, while adjusted earnings per share increased by 30 % to 81.24 US cents. The group now expects constant-currency adjusted earnings-per-share growth of 17 % to 20 % for the full year, compared with previous guidance at the upper end of a 7 % to 11 % range. It also raised expectations for its two main growth divisions and increased the annual savings target attached to its transformation programme from $ 60 million to $ 70 million by the end of 2027.

headline: Glanbia Hikes Profit Guidance As Protein Products Demand Booms
summary_text: Nutrition supplement maker Glanbia hiked its full-year profit forecast following bumper demand for its protein products, including from customers using them in tandem with weight-loss drugs. The Irish company expects adjusted earnings per share growth of 17 % to 20 % at constant currencies this year after EPS jumped 30 % in the first half. It had guided in late April that it would hit the upper end of a 7 % to 11 % range. Shares in the Irish company, which have almost doubled in price in the last year, were 6.1 % higher at €23.9 at 11:00 GMT. Glanbia now sees higher-than-expected revenue growth across all three of its nutrition divisions, led by its main Optimum Nutrition brand, where first-half sales rose 25 % even as it hiked the price of products twice since November.

headline: Arla highlights calcium-rich whey permeate bone health findings
summary_text: Arla Foods Ingredients is developing food applications for calcium-rich whey permeate after a Danish clinical trial found that the dairy-derived supplement could maintain bone mineral density in postmenopausal women. The company revisited the findings on 20 October, alongside work on a compact dried fruit bar containing a targeted 265mg of calcium per 10g serving. The underlying RENEW study was published online in May, making the new development an ingredient and product-formulation opportunity built on existing clinical evidence. The 12-month randomised, double-blind trial compared four approaches: a placebo, calcium carbonate, calcium-enriched permeate and the same permeate combined with inulin. The three active groups each received 800mg of calcium daily in two doses, while all participants received 20 micrograms of vitamin D per day.

headline: Fiji warns farmers against supplying unapproved sugarcane varieties, sets deadline for phase-out - ChiniMandi
summary_text: Fiji’s sugar industry continues to grapple with production and productivity challenges, with significant quantities of unapproved sugarcane varieties still being delivered to mills during crushing seasons, reported FBC News. Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna has warned growers against supplying unauthorised cane varieties, stating that the practice violates the Master Award agreement and allows mills to reject such deliveries. Farmers were earlier given three years to replace unapproved varieties, and the current crushing season will be the last in which mills accept these cane types, Tunabuna said. He stressed that the country’s average sugarcane yield of around 50 tonnes per hectare was insufficient to ensure the long-term viability of the sector. Raising productivity to at least 65 tonnes per hectare is necessary to improve farm profitability and strengthen the industry, he added. Tunabuna said low production levels were creating financial challenges for both farmers and sugar mills. The Labasa Mill, which has an annual crushing capacity of more than one million tonnes, is currently operating at approximately half its potential capacity. He said the mill needs a minimum cane supply of 7 lakh tonnes to reach its break-even level and operate more efficiently. Industry stakeholders believe that improving cane quality, increasing farm productivity and adopting modern agricultural practices will be essential to strengthening Fiji’s sugar sector and addressing the economic and climate-related challenges facing the industry.

headline: Wilmar forms Myanmar sugar venture to expand push into sweetener
summary_text: Wilmar International, the largest sugar cane miller in Australia, agreed to form a Myanmar venture with a local partner as it builds on a four-year push into sugar production in Asia. The Singapore-based company will hold 55% in the venture with Great Wall Food Stuff Industry Co. after buying all of the local company’s sugar-manufacturing capacity, Wilmar said today in a statement. Wilmar will use its own funds for the investment and the venture will not have a “material impact” on this year’s earnings per share, the company said. “Everybody’s been talking about Myanmar, so getting the foot in the door is probably worth doing,” said Carey Wong, an analyst at OCBC Investment Research Pte. in Singapore. “If you look at the spending power, it’s actually one of the biggest economies in Asia that’s left untapped.” ... The investment comes less than two months after Wilmar announced plans to take joint control of India’s largest sugar refiner Shree Renuka Sugars Ltd. in a deal valued at about US$200 million ($250 million). The Singapore company, which is also the world’s top processor of palm oil, entered the sugar business in 2010 when it bought Australia’s Sucrogen and then added assets in New Zealand, Indonesia and Morocco. Great Wall and its associates own 2 mills with potential daily capacity of 4,000 metric tons of sugar cane and an annual production capacity of 65,000 tons of sugar, Wilmar said. The joint venture will also take over Great Wall’s bio- ethanol plant and an organic compound fertilizer facility as part of the deal that requires approval from regulators including the Myanmar Investment Commission, the Singapore company said. Wilmar didn’t specify the amount of the investment being made. ... Sugar accounted for 7.5% of Wilmar’s pretax income last fiscal year ended Dec. 31, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

headline: Philippine sugar industry pushes for protection as artificial sweeteners cut into demand
summary_text: The Philippine sugar industry is seeking greater government protection as growers grapple with pest outbreaks, drought risks and rising production costs, while competition from artificial sweeteners further erodes demand for locally produced cane sugar. ## The Philippine sugar industry is seeking greater government protection as growers grapple with pest outbreaks, drought risks and rising production costs, while competition from artificial sweeteners further erodes demand for locally produced cane sugar. - The Philippine government steps up support for sugar producers facing pests, drought and rising costs. - Artificial sweeteners now account for 18.4% of the market, contributing to weaker sugar demand. - Industry groups are pushing for tighter sweetener rules and tax incentives for local cane sugar. Domestic sugar producers have urged policymakers to adopt measures that would help safeguard both production and consumption as sector faces pressures on multiple fronts. In particular, the sector is dealing with an infestation of red-striped soft scale insects (RSSI). In response, the government has deployed financial assistance, chemical controls, drones and biological measures against the pest, particularly in the Visayas. RSSI is an invasive sap-sucking pest that feeds on sugarcane and promotes the growth of black sooty mould. By coating the leaves and blocking sunlight, the mould reduces photosynthesis, stunts plant growth and lowers both cane yields and sugar content. ... Agriculture Secretary Francisco P. Tiu Laurel Jr. highlighted the ongoing cooperation between the Department of Agriculture (DA) and the Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA), which has produced new policies aimed at strengthening the sector. ... ### Artificial sweeteners add to industry pressures Meanwhile, industry organisations are calling for policy changes to address declining sugar demand caused by the growing use of artificial sweeteners and alternative sweetening ingredients. A unified industry manifesto was submitted to the DA and SRA urging tighter regulation of artificial sweeteners. Tiu Laurel acknowledged the issue, describing sugar substitutes as an “extraneous force” influencing domestic sugar demand and said government agencies would examine potential policy responses. Artificial sweeteners accounted for 18.4% of the market in the 2024-25 crop year, equivalent to 503,117 metric tonnes, while demand for refined sugar fell 13.89%, according to industry data. The figures point to a shift away from conventional sugar consumption, with industry stakeholders arguing that the growing use of sweeteners is eroding demand for Philippine-produced sugar and threatening the sector’s long-term viability. ... As of July, RSSI had affected 93,898 hectares of the country’s 421,606 hectares planted to sugarcane during the current crop year. Nearly all affected areas, or 92,295 hectares, were located in the Visayas, particularly on Negros Island and in Western Visayas, with more than 12,700 farmers impacted. The DA said it had earmarked PHP35m for chemicals and drone operations, with an initial target of 25,000 hectares and the option to expand coverage to more than 45,000 hectares depending on the severity of the infestation. Both the DA and SRA have acknowledged that the RSSI infestation was “likely to become a recurring threat”.

General manager Bob Olayo told the Herald: “Formula Foods purchased thaumatin in good faith from a long-established supplier and relied on the specifications, certificates and quality documentation provided with the product”. “When concerns were identified, Formula Foods worked with the supplier, customers, MPI regulators, local labs and even universities to investigate the issue as rapidly possible, trace affected material and manage the required response. headline: Muscovado Moves from Premium Sweetener to Functional Bakery Ingredient - Asia Pacific Food Industry
summary_text: Muscovado and other specialty unrefined sugars are finding opportunities beyond conventional sweetening as bakery manufacturers look for ingredients that can contribute flavour, colour, texture and moisture alongside sweetness. According to a report by Future Market Insights, fine grades are estimated to account for 38% of muscovado and specialty unrefined sugar demand by type in 2026, while bread and rolls are expected to represent 31% of application demand. Powdered dry formats are forecast to hold 39% of the form category. ASEAN bakery manufacturers may find that the ingredient’s potential lies in its ability to provide a distinctive molasses character and influence finished-product texture and moisture. These attributes could support premium breads, buns, biscuits and other baked products seeking differentiation from standard formulations. However, specialty sugar comes with formulation and commercial considerations. Fine grades can offer faster dispersion during industrial mixing, while manufacturers must control crystal size, molasses content, storage conditions and moisture exposure to achieve consistent results. Future Market Insights analyst Nandini Roy Choudhury said: “Industrial bakeries treat muscovado as a functional sugar only after trials confirm how molasses solids affect color, moisture and mixing behavior. The premium survives repeated purchasing if processors control crystal size and flavor intensity and protect the product from humidity during storage.” The commercial challenge is particularly relevant as manufacturers simultaneously face pressure to reduce added sugar. Specialty grades therefore need to deliver a clear sensory or functional benefit that justifies their higher cost. The report identifies Tate & Lyle, Ingredion, Roquette, BENEO, Südzucker, Nordzucker, ASR Group, Cargill, Ragus Sugars and ADM among key players. For ASEAN producers, specialty unrefined sugars could consequently become targeted formulation tools rather than broad substitutes for conventional sucrose.

Registrar of the Tribunal and Industrial Commissioner Timothy Brown presented the update while delivering the Sugar Industry Tribunal’s 2021 Annual Report to the Standing Committee on Economic Affairs. Brown adds that the 2026 forecast relies on expected sugar and molasses sales, projected harvest volumes, and anticipated sugar production. He says the Tribunal estimates total sugar and molasses revenue at $152.8 million. After costs and deductions, approximately $147.3 million remains, with growers set to receive 70 percent. “That is divided, and then, from the growers’ share, they also pay a one-third contribution for SHRIF. That’s the Research Institute. So that’s taken out. And they also have bundle insurance. They have growers that is taken off the top for any issues, burnt houses, and deaths. They have bundle insurance for that.” He adds that under the Master Award, the base price is reduced by 15 percent to absorb exchange-rate fluctuations. He says that growers initially receive 60 percent of this adjusted price, followed by a second payment roughly six weeks later. Standing Committee member Premila Kumar emphasised that farmers are demanding greater transparency regarding forecast calculations, overseas sales volumes, and realised export prices. “And unfortunately, from that time, with few amendments, we are still carrying on the same mechanism, which is not doing justice to farmers. And even worse is when they have to wait for 16 months or 15 months or whatever time frame to recover all their money from the first year’s crop. So they do have a very valid point in terms of airing their grievances.” ... New Sugar Industry Tribunal Chairman Semi Leweniqila says he is concerned that some farmers believe there may be dealings in the forecast price calculation that they are not aware of. He says representatives of the Sugarcane Growers Council are fully aware of the process. Leweniqila says the challenge is that the industry measures and pays for sugarcane by weight, but ultimately sells sugar. He says the weight of sugarcane does not directly translate into the amount of sugar produced. Tribunal officials stressed that the final cane price cannot be confirmed until all sugar is sold, with the 15 percent margin acting as a buffer against forecasting errors.

Already nearly 8 lakh tonnes (lt) of raw sugar has been permitted by the government after which it opened the window for another round of applications for the remaining quantity of 10 lt permitted under zero duty (TRQ scheme), sources said adding about 70,000 tonnes have arrived in India which were probably purchased on high sea or diverted from some other destinations. Because about 40 days transit is needed to import raw sugar from Brazil. ... Ex-mill prices have fallen to Rs 43-44 a kg from a peak of Rs 65-67 a kg recorded two weeks ago, he said, adding that the impact on retail prices will take another one to two weeks to become visible. ... headline: Sugar industry needs major reform – FBC News
summary_text: # Sugar industry needs major reform Share Riya Mala Multimedia Journalist riya.mala@fbc.com.fj #### September 8, 2026 5:08 pm [Photo: Supplied] Fiji’s sugar industry needs major reform, with the Government warning that subsidies and short-term interventions cannot solve its long-standing problems. Agriculture Permanent Secretary Dr. Andrew Tukana says the industry must become more productive, commercially sustainable and resilient to climate change. He made the submission while presenting the Ministry of Agriculture, Waterways and Sugar Industry and Ministry of Sugar Industry Annual Report 2021–2022 to the Standing Committee on Economic Affairs. Dr. Tukana says reform is needed across the entire sugar value chain, including production, harvesting, transportation, milling, research, land use, mechanisation and value addition. He says rising input, labour, harvesting and transport costs are putting increasing pressure on smallholder farmers, while climate events are further threatening production. “And the recent merger of the sugar industry portfolio with the agriculture portfolio provides an important area that we can take advantage of, and these are to integrate agricultural extension services with the sugar sector to strengthen research and technology transfer and to have a better coordination mechanism, to align sugar production with water and land management, and to reduce the duplication between government agencies.” Dr. Tukana says not every farmer or piece of land will remain economically viable for sugarcane indefinitely. He says the Government is therefore promoting diversification, including vegetables, legumes, high-value crops, livestock and other commodities. Intercropping, crop rotation and agro-processing are also being explored to provide farmers with alternative income sources. An EU-funded diversification study is assessing where sugar remains commercially viable and where other crops or integrated farming systems could provide better returns. Dr. Tukana says mechanisation is also critical as the industry faces a shortage of labour. “And the other area where as a way forward honorable members is mechanization. We already have a lot of this happening within the agricultural portfolio, we also have a lot of that happening within the sugar portfolio. But at this point in time and we all know that there is a huge shortage of labor so I think the way for us to go forward is to have sustainable mechanization programs.” He says ageing sugar mills, poor infrastructure, transport challenges and climate threats must also be addressed. With more than 90 percent of sugarcane transported by road, Dr. Tukana says Fiji needs a practical mix of road, rail and improved logistics. He says climate resilience must also be prioritised through drought-tolerant varieties, better water management, drainage, soil conservation and early warning systems. Dr. Tukana says the merger of the agriculture and sugar portfolios provides an opportunity for better coordination and stronger support for farmers. ... headline: South Africa set to lift sugar-benchmark price to shield growers. - Fullview | Telling empowering stories, South Africans want to hear
summary_text: South Africa will raise the benchmark price that’s used to calculate duties on sugar imports, a move long-sought by domestic producers like Associated British Foods Plc’s local unit in an industry that’s been battered by cheap foreign competition, according to people familiar with the matter. Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana signed off on the measure earlier this week and the new level is expected to be announced in the official Government Gazette soon, said the people who asked not to be identified because the decision isn’t public yet. The dollar-based reference price for sugar will be increased to $785 a ton, from $680, the people said. The higher amount would strengthen protection for local producers when international prices fall below the benchmark, potentially making it more difficult for cheap imports to displace domestically produced sugar. The Department of Trade, Industry and Competition referred a request for comment to the National Treasury, which said Godongwana can’t comment on the matter until it’s been gazetted. The South African Sugar Association’s Vice Chairman Trix Trikam in a statement on Thursday welcomed the adjustment while cautioning that it may be insufficient to protect local producers against imports from subsidised countries like Brazil. SASA said the industry lost R1.6 billion ($100 million) to cheap imports during the 2025-26 season season. As of June, shipments from abroad had reached 74 652 tons, costing the sector R560 million, it added. The association had sought a substantially larger increase to $905 a ton, arguing that the existing benchmark — unchanged since 2018 — no longer reflects domestic production costs. The country’s International Trade Administration Commission began a review of the reference price in January after receiving competing applications from SASA and the Beverage Association of South Africa. White sugar traded at $514.40 per ton in London on Thursday. The sugar sector has also been under pressure from declining cane returns. Tongaat Hulett, one of the country’s major producers, narrowly avoided liquidation before a rescue agreement involving the state-owned Industrial Development Corp. Beyond the increase in duties, the industry is seeking longer-term measures to improve its competitiveness, including diversification into sugar-derived products and biofuels. South Africa’s sugar master plan identifies trade protection, pricing and local market demand, as well as industry restructuring and diversification, as key priorities for the sector.

headline: The Sweet Protein Changing the Formulation Conversation - NZ Food Technology News
summary_text: As food and beverage manufacturers look for new ways to reduce sugar without compromising taste, thaumatin is attracting renewed attention. Thaumatin is a naturally occurring sweet-tasting protein extracted from the katemfe fruit (Thaumatococcus daniellii), native to West Africa. Around 3,000 times sweeter than sucrose, it is used at extremely low inclusion levels. However, sweetness is only part of what makes thaumatin interesting to formulators. Thaumatin also functions as a flavour modifier, helping enhance the perception of sweetness, mask bitter notes and create a fuller, more rounded taste profile. This can be particularly valuable in formulations containing ingredients such as stevia, plant proteins, minerals, vitamins or botanicals, where bitter, metallic or lingering notes can present a challenge. The key is application. Thaumatin is not a one-for-one replacement for sugar, and its performance depends on the formulation, processing conditions and desired sensory outcome. At such low use levels, accurate dosage, dispersion and consistency become especially important. This is where specialist expertise matters. Hibiscus Solutions has partnered with UK-based Natex, a global leader in thaumatin production and application. Natex brings more than 25 years of specialist experience and builds on over four decades of thaumatin expertise. Using proprietary patented technology, Natex modifies and applies thaumatin to natural sweeteners and other carriers to create high-performance, ready-to-use ingredients. The technology is designed to improve blending and dissolution, deliver balanced sweetness without requiring an additional sweetener, and support product-specific heat and pH resistance — helping formulators achieve more consistent, optimised performance from batch to batch. The Natex Sweetence® ThaumActive® range has been developed to simplify formulation while delivering consistent, optimised sweetness and flavour performance across different applications. As Natex’s exclusive distributor in New Zealand and Australia, Hibiscus Solutions combines access to this specialist technology with local technical, documentation, sampling and formulation support. For manufacturers exploring sugar reduction, flavour balancing or bitterness suppression, thaumatin offers more than intense sweetness — it offers a different approach to building better-tasting products.
