headline: “If a bilateral agreement were negotiated, it would include additional market access for Mauritius special sugars” - BIZWEEK
summary_text: “ ... a bilateral ... were negotiated ... it would include additional market access for Mauritius special sugars” Devesh Dukhira, CEO, Mauritius Sugar Syndicate The demand for special sugars is rising on the American market. However, exporting under the preferential regime of the global Tariff-Rate Quota (TRQ), Mauritius cannot export more than the imposed tons. Thus, for the CEO of the Mauritius Sugar Syndicate, this bilateral agreement that the Ministry of Industry, SMEs and Cooperatives is negotiating with the United States would be beneficial for special sugars while allowing Mauritius to increase its sales and strengthen its presence in this market. ... Maur ... sugars are ... Raw sugar produced in Mauritius is exported to the U.S. market under the preferential regime of the global Tariff-Rate Quota (TRQ). Each year, within the framework of its commitments made at the level of the World Trade Organization (WTO), the United States is in fact obliged to import a minimum of 1.117 million metric tons raw value of raw cane sugar from “historical” suppliers. Mauritius, one of them, benefits from a quota share of 1.2%, which is equivalent to about 12,200 tons of sugar that can be exported to the United States duty-free. ... What about special sugars? Special sugars are unrefined sugars for direct consumption targeted at niche market segments where consumers can appreciate their wholesome flavour and taste, and the nutritional content that they retain. Mauritius has been exporting such sugars to the United States for over forty years, with loyal clients who have been working with us since then. Through one of our customers, it is presently being distributed within the key coffee chains across the US. > “Mauritius can export about 12,200 tons of sugar to the United States duty-free.” Over the past ten years, exports of special sugars to the US market have increased considerably, and the annual TRQs allocated to Mauritius have been filled through supplies of these value-added sugars. Whenever additional TRQs are allocated/reallocated, we have even managed to export larger quantities, having exceeded 17,000 tons sales in 2022/23. ... if special sugars are in high demand on the American market, you are ... able to export more because of the Global Tariff-Rate Quota… ... Indeed, we unfortunately cannot sell more, despite higher demand, because of the limit of this annual TRQ, unless there is a reallocation triggered by the USDA on an ad hoc basis whenever the US market is in short supply. That said, the United States remains a promising market for these sugars, and therefore, there is growth potential. Thus, if there are opportunities, or possibilities to increase this TRQ, it would certainly help the industry to enhance its exports to the United States. It is also in this perspective that the Ministry of Industry, SMEs and Cooperatives is envisaging discussion of a bilateral agreement with the United States, especially if there is a risk that AGOA is not renewed or Mauritius is no longer eligible to benefit from same. The idea proposed is that, if such a bilateral agreement were to be negotiated, it would also include additional market access for Mauritius special sugars. Thus, in addition to the current quota of 12,200 tons, Mauritius could benefit from an additional duty-free TRQ every year for the export of these sugars. This would allow increased sales and strengthen Mauritius’s presence on the US market. ... Does the future of the sugar sector lie in special sugars? The future of the sugar sector rests on value-addition and niche segments in export markets. Special sugars, as differentiated products, bring higher value and allow improvement of the average price, as well as the revenue per ton of sugar for millers and planters. Even in the segment of white sugar, there are high-value products already being exploited, for example, extra-fine white sugar or Bottlers’ Grade sugar intended for bottlers. > “The future of the sugar sector rests on value-addition and niche segments in export markets.” The central idea is therefore to move away from the status of a simple commodity and to position ourselves on markets where additional premiums can be obtained while ensuring customer loyalty. This would generate better remuneration and strengthen the competitiveness of the Mauritian sugar sector. It is important to recall that the sugarcane sector, including bagasse and molasses, presently accounts for about 2% of the national gross domestic product.

headline: - How Mauritius is becoming the world's first fully certified sugarcane origin - Bonsucro
summary_text: ’ ... origin ... ###### 12th August 2026 Editor’s note: Mauritius Sugar Syndicate won a Bonsucro Inspire Award for Best Value Chain Initiative for The Mauritius Bonsucro Project. In Mauritius, sugarcane has shaped the island’s landscape, economy and communities for generations. As global markets increasingly demand transparency and verified sustainability, the Mauritius Sugar Syndicate recognised the need to evolve, and set out to certify every sugar mill on the island to Bonsucro’s sustainability standards. That is why Bonsucro was thrilled to present the Mauritius Sugar Syndicate with an Inspire Award in the Best Value Chain Initiative category, recognising collaborative efforts that create value and drive sustainability across the sugarcane supply chain. ... S ... Sustainability has become essential to the future of the sugar industry, so pursuing Bonsucro certification was a natural step. Mauritius has a long history of producing sugar, and we wanted to make sure that heritage continues in a way that meets the expectations of today’s global markets. One of the main drivers was to strengthen the international reputation of Mauritian sugar. We have always encouraged the adoption of globally recognised quality and food safety certifications, and Bonsucro builds on that by demonstrating our commitment to responsible production across environmental, social and economic issues. Secondly, leadership. We saw an opportunity to show that sustainability can be embraced across an entire national industry. We have worked closely with millers and growers, making sustainability part of the industry’s long-term future. It was also important that the benefits of certification extended to everyone, including smallholders, with accessible, transparent and environmentally responsible practices. ... And finally, we never saw Bonsucro as simply another certification. It was a strategic investment in the future of the Mauritian sugar industry, protecting its heritage and ensuring it remains competitive and resilient. ... Our answer was that it wasn’t about an immediate financial return. It was about making the Mauritian sugar industry more sustainable, more resilient and better prepared for the future. We also shared what we were hearing from customers, who increasingly look for independently verified sustainability credentials. This external perspective meant certification wasn’t simply something MSS or Bonsucro wanted; it was a reflection of where the market is heading. Once people understood that, the focus shifted to implementation. The biggest change was around mindset, particularly in the field. Through training and capacity building, with support from the Bonsucro regional team, producers began to see how better agricultural practices, including the responsible use of agrochemicals, affect not only the environment but also crop quality and the health and safety of those applying them. That shift in understanding was one of the biggest and most rewarding successes. We also found that many producers were already doing the right things, they just weren’t documenting them. Certification requires evidence, so helping people put the right systems and records in place became an important part of the process. This made preparing for the final audit much easier because everyone, from senior management to those working in the fields, had been involved throughout the journey. ... One of the biggest opportunities is to build on the shift in mindset we’ve already seen. Before, the focus was on producing sugar and maximising volumes. Today, there’s a much wider recognition that sustainability is an asset that adds long-term value. That’s becoming even more important as customers look for greater transparency about how their sugar is produced. Looking ahead, I think certification will become more closely linked to climate resilience, biodiversity and carbon emissions. Digital tools will also play a bigger role in helping producers monitor performance and demonstrate progress. For us, the key is to stay ahead of those changes to ensure Mauritius continues to be recognised as a producer that embraces best practice and is prepared for the future. ... Certification has encouraged producers to look more closely at how they use resources, monitor performance and identify ways to improve efficiency. From a marketing perspective, it has been valuable. More customers are looking for independently verified sustainability credentials, particularly in Europe, so Bonsucro certification helps differentiate Mauritian sugar in those markets. However, it remains to be seen whether this differentiation can consistently translate into a premium that fairly rewards producers, who continue to invest substantially in meeting and maintaining these standards.

headline: Kilombero Sugar Unlocks $238 Million Expansion to Secure Tanzania’s Sweetener Market | Streamline
summary_text: A massive $238.5 million investment in Tanzania’s Kilombero Sugar Company aims to double economic output and cement the dominance of the Bwana Sukari brand. ... News ... 6, 20 ... 2:18 ... min ... Deep in the fertile plains of Morogoro, the machinery of Tanzania’s sugar independence is being recalibrated with a massive capital injection that promises to reshape the regional sweetener market. Kilombero Sugar Company, the producer of the ubiquitous Bwana Sukari brand, has secured shareholder approval for a $238.5 million (TZS 571.6 billion) expansion project. This strategic investment, driven by the joint venture between Illovo Sugar Africa and the Tanzanian government, is designed to dramatically increase production capacity, support thousands of outgrowers, and cement Tanzania’s trajectory toward total domestic sugar self-sufficiency. ... ## The $238 Million Bwana Sukari Expansion The approved capital expenditure will fund a comprehensive modernization of the Kilombero facility, located in the Morogoro region. The expansion includes the construction of a new processing factory, the expansion of irrigated cane estates, and the deployment of advanced agricultural technologies to boost yields per hectare. For the consumer, this translates to a more stable supply of the iconic Bwana Sukari brand, which has become synonymous with quality in Tanzanian households. Crucially, the project places a heavy emphasis on the outgrower model. By providing smallholder farmers with improved seed varieties, fertilizer subsidies, and extension services, Kilombero Sugar aims to integrate rural communities directly into the formal agro-industrial value chain. This approach not only secures the raw material supply for the factory but also acts as a powerful engine for rural poverty alleviation and economic diversification. - Capital Injection: $238.5 million (TZS 571.6 billion) approved by shareholders for factory and estate expansion. - Market Dominance: Scaling production of the Bwana Sukari brand to eliminate reliance on imported sweeteners. - Outgrower Support: Integrating thousands of smallholder farmers through subsidized inputs and guaranteed off-take agreements. ... For decades, Tanzania has battled a chronic sugar deficit, forcing the government to periodically authorize duty-free imports to stabilize domestic prices and quell consumer inflation. These import windows, while necessary in the short term, have historically undermined local producers by flooding the market with cheaper, often subsidized, foreign sugar. The Kilombero expansion is the centerpiece of the government’s broader strategy to close this gap permanently. By doubling the company’s economic contribution and significantly increasing national output, the project aims to render sugar imports obsolete. This shift toward import substitution is a critical component of Tanzania’s industrialization agenda, reducing foreign exchange expenditure and insulating the domestic economy from volatile global commodity prices. ... The aggressive expansion of Kilombero Sugar stands in sharp contrast to the protracted crisis gripping Kenya’s state-owned sugar millers. Institutions like Mumias Sugar, Chemelil, and Sony Sugar have been paralyzed by decades of mismanagement, massive debt burdens, and political interference, leaving Kenya heavily dependent on imports from Egypt, Brazil, and neighboring Uganda to meet its annual consumption deficit.

headline: inDepth I The sugar dilemma - Call for new direction as industry faces challenges - The Fiji Times
summary_text: THE sugar industry is draining Fiji’s economy, and the country can no longer afford to continue supporting it in its current form, says People’s Alliance party (PA) president Ratu Josefa Dimuri. Ratu Josefa believes major changes are needed, including considering private management of the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), closing the mills on Viti Levu and making Labasa the main centre for sugar production. “I do not think we can afford to continue depending on this crop for much longer. It is draining the economy rather than contributing to the economy,” he said. Ratu Josefa said sugar used to be one of Fiji’s biggest contributors to the economy but that was no longer the case. “It has now become one of the biggest drains on the economy.” His comments come as Government continues to invest millions of dollars into the industry while facing problems with cane supply, ageing mills, labour shortages and rising costs. Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna has acknowledged that Government was investing significant money into the sector while returns remained a concern. Mr Tunabuna had also confirmed Government was paying about $18million each year to service debts, including money owed to the Exim Bank of India. Ratu Josefa said the situation could not continue. ... “I believe it is time to make that shift. We have to make that shift because we cannot afford to wait any longer.” ... He suggested that the Government consider closing the mills on Viti Levu and concentrating sugar production in Labasa. “I would like to suggest that we close the mills in Viti Levu and only concentrate sugar production at Labasa. We should improve the quality of the crop and increase production there.” But the proposal comes at a difficult time for the Labasa mill. The mill stopped crushing during the first three weeks of the current crushing season because of low or no cane supply. No mill breakdowns were recorded during that period. Mr Tunabuna said the start of the crushing season had been difficult because of the fuel crisis and other disruptions. ... Farmers had signed the Master Award Growers Agreement and decided to continue harvesting. ... “They decided for themselves that they would have to continue, and they did exactly that.” ... The Labasa mill needs between 5500 and 6000 tonnes of cane each day to keep operating. However, it has been receiving only about 3500 to 4000 tonnes. The shortage means the mill cannot operate at its full capacity. ... is ... The future of FSC could also involve private ownership. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has confirmed that selling FSC to a private company is an option. However, he said FSC was a strategic asset and Government needed to consider its importance before making any decision. “Selling is an option, but there are certain things that we call strategic assets, and these are strategic assets,” he said. “They belong to the Government, and what we can do is improve the performance of the industry.” Mr Rabuka said Government was focused on improving the performance of the sugar industry while considering its future. ... A special committee on the sugar industry is consulting farmers and other stakeholders about the problems facing the sector. The committee has already visited sugar-growing areas in the West and is expected to visit the North. ... The problems facing the sugar industry have also led to Fiji importing sugar. Mr Tunabuna said the decision was made to ensure there was enough sugar available for consumers. “The importation was based on the need that we have for sugar,” he said. He said delays in harvesting and low cane supply at the start of the crushing season may have contributed to the need for imports. “Whether it was triggered by the low supply of cane right from the start of the mill, which could have also been part of the problem when we had delayed harvesting.” FSC had prepared for possible supply problems by keeping sugar stocks available. “FSC also knew that was going to come, so we wanted to make sure that we had some available sugar in stock in case some retailers were going to restrict sales of their sugar.,” ... Farmers and harvesting operators are also dealing with changes in mechanical harvesting rates. The Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission reduced the mechanical harvesting rate from $24.63 a tonne to $20.52 a tonne after fuel prices dropped. The new rate is 16.7 per cent lower than the previous interim rate. Some harvesting operators have raised concerns that the lower rate could affect their ability to continue providing services. Mr Tunabuna said the FCCC would have to explain how the new rate was calculated. ... “The FCCC will answer that. But I’m not sure how they formulate their formula charges. They will have to explain,” he said. ... The sugar industry now faces several major challenges at the same time. Farmers are struggling with cane supply and production costs. Mills are old and require regular maintenance. Government is spending millions of dollars to keep the industry operating, while FSC continues to carry debt. At the same time, Fiji is importing sugar to ensure consumers have enough supply. Ratu Josefa believes the country must now consider a different approach. He wants Government to focus sugar production in Labasa, consider private management of FSC and encourage farmers to move into crops that could provide higher and more regular returns. Mr Rabuka said FSC remains a strategic asset and Government is looking at ways to improve its performance.

headline: South Africa’s Gumede to buy ABF’s Illovo Sugar. | Semafor
summary_text: ### ... Scoop ... A South African investor group that recently rescued the debt-laden agricultural producer Tongaat Hulett is planning a takeover of rival Illovo Sugar, according to sources with direct knowledge of the matter. The move would consolidate control of the continent’s sugar, ethanol, and bioenergy markets under a single African-owned giant. The effort has already reached the executive suite of London-based Associated British Foods, the parent company of Illovo. Representatives from Vision Sugar, led by South African billionaire Robert Gumede and Zimbabwean dealmaker Rute Moyo, have initiated contact with ABF CEO George Weston about a deal, one person said. Corporate finance advisory sources estimate that Illovo Sugar holds an enterprise value of between $800 million and $1.1 billion. The transaction, if it comes to pass, spans Illovo’s vast network of sugar estates across South Africa, Zambia, Malawi, Eswatini, Tanzania, and Mozambique, setting up one of the largest agricultural buyouts on the continent in more than a decade. ... A tie-up between Tongaat and Illovo across southern Africa would establish a near-regional monopoly. In South Africa, the combined entity would control more than half of the national sugar milling capacity, leaving Remgro-backed RCL Foods as its only major domestic competitor and likely raising alarm with competition regulators. Beyond South Africa, a merged footprint would grant Vision virtual market exclusivity over primary sugar production across East and South Africa. Vision’s bid for Illovo will also be seen as an energy play. Gumede plans to power and supply regional markets with electricity using both Illovo and Tongaat refineries to produce bio-ethanol and converting leftover sugarcane fiber. For the $20 billion-dollar parent company an outright sale would mark a complete exit from African sugar, freeing up capital to refocus on its core European foods divisions and flagship retail engine, Primark.

headline: Samyang Corporation achieves novel food approval for allulose in Australia and New Zealand
summary_text: Samyang Corporation reported receiving FSANZ approval to sell allulose as a food ingredient in Australia and New Zealand, positioning it as the first allulose producer to enter both markets under this approval. Allulose is described as a rare sugar with about 70% of sucrose’s sweetness and nearly zero calories. The approval creates another option for manufacturers developing reduced-sugar and sugar-free products, and may increase competition among sweetener suppliers. The article does not provide local supply volumes or pricing.

headline: Farmers relieved as global sugar prices rally amid key producer Brazil's presidential election
summary_text: Raw sugar prices rose to a 19-month high of 21.10 US cents per pound on October 13, offering some relief to Australian cane growers after months of low prices and rising farm input costs. The article attributes the rally to weaker-than-expected Brazilian cane crushing and sugar yields, high oil prices that make ethanol production more attractive to Brazilian mills, and uncertainty around Brazil’s election and fuel policy. The outlook is volatile: a shift back toward sugar production could increase global supply and put prices under pressure again.

headline: Australia: Sugar Semi-annual
summary_text: USDA FAS revised Australia’s 2026/27 sugarcane production estimate to 27.9 million tonnes, 1.8% below the prior season, citing very dry conditions across cane-growing regions from April. Despite the smaller cane crop, higher sugar content in harvested cane is expected to lift sugar output 4.4% to 4.0 million tonnes. Raw sugar exports are forecast at 3.5 million tonnes, up 34% year on year, supported by higher production, carry-in stocks and improved world prices. For buyers, the report points to strong export availability overall but identifies weather and harvest progress as factors to monitor.

headline: Cheaper artificial sweetener sucralose ends up in NZ food instead of expensive product thaumatin – MPI probes
summary_text: New Zealand Food Safety is investigating after product sold by ingredient supplier Azelis as thaumatin was found in testing to be more than 99% sucralose. The supplier said the material was sourced from Australia and notified customers after identifying a discrepancy between what it ordered and received. The issue is described by the regulator as a truth-in-labelling matter, not a food-safety risk; the article notes that several New Zealand food brands informed customers. For procurement teams, the report highlights the importance of ingredient identity verification, supplier controls and traceability for sweeteners.

headline: Australia's last grower-owned sugar mill seeks government bailout
summary_text: Isis Central Sugar Mill is seeking a Queensland government loan of up to A$9 million as mechanical failures, including a boiler outage, slowed its 2026 crush and added to financial strain from global market conditions. The mill was 51,000 tonnes behind schedule with a target of just under 1.2 million tonnes of cane. A proposed three-year loan could help fund operations through September 2027; the mill’s CEO is also seeking federal support for a bioenergy precinct that could diversify revenue beyond sugar. The development is significant for growers and suppliers dependent on the mill, which supports around 1,500 supply-chain jobs.
